title: Doom Researching: A Conceptual Framework for Repetitive AI-Assisted Information Seeking, Cognitive Offloading, and the Illusion of Knowing
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini have made information seeking faster, more conversational, and more cognitively comfortable. These affordances can support learning and productivity, but they can also encourage a repetitive pattern in which users continue querying AI systems for explanations, summaries, comparisons, plans, and reassurance without converting those interactions into durable understanding, decisions, or finished work. This conceptual paper proposes the term doom researching to describe this AI-mediated pattern of repetitive information seeking without proportional synthesis or output. Building on research on doomscrolling, information seeking, cognitive offloading, transactive memory, human-AI interaction, productivity loss, and the illusion of knowing, the paper develops a framework in which fluent AI responses reduce cognitive effort, inflate perceived knowledge, and increase the likelihood of further querying. The framework distinguishes doom researching from doomscrolling, cyberchondria, ordinary research, and productive AI-assisted work. It introduces a formal model of the doom researching loop, a candidate risk index for empirical measurement, and testable propositions for future studies. It then extends the construct through the lens of the extended mind thesis, distinguishing assistive, substitutive, and disruptive forms of cognitive offloading, and connects individual doom researching to the broader literature on AI-driven homogenization and knowledge collapse. The paper argues that doom researching is not simply "too much AI use" but a misalignment among inquiry, metacognition, and output. The goal is to provide a vocabulary and research agenda for studying when AI-assisted inquiry becomes a substitute for thinking, synthesis, and action.

AI.tldr: Introduces "doom researching," a maladaptive pattern where users repetitively query GenAI systems for information without converting interactions into durable understanding or productive output, and provides a theoretical framework, formal model, and research agenda for studying this phenomenon.
AI.motivation: While GenAI systems make information seeking faster and cognitively comfortable, they risk fostering a repetitive querying pattern that substitutes for genuine synthesis and action. The paper aims to name, define, and theorize this underexamined phenomenon to enable empirical investigation and distinguish it from related but distinct constructs like doomscrolling and productive AI use.
AI.method: Conceptual/theoretical paper. Synthesizes literature on doomscrolling, information seeking, cognitive offloading, transactive memory, human-AI interaction, productivity loss, and the illusion of knowing. Develops a formal model of the doom researching loop, proposes a candidate risk index, and derives testable propositions. Extends analysis through the extended mind thesis, distinguishing assistive, substitutive, and disruptive cognitive offloading.
AI.result: The framework posits that fluent AI responses reduce cognitive effort and inflate perceived knowledge, increasing further querying in a self-reinforcing loop. Doom researching is distinguished from doomscrolling (passive social media consumption), cyberchondria (health-specific anxiety), ordinary research (goal-terminated inquiry), and productive AI-assisted work (synthesis-oriented). The paper connects individual doom researching to broader concerns about AI-driven homogenization and knowledge collapse.
AI.conclusion: Doom researching is not merely excessive AI use but a misalignment among inquiry, metacognition, and output. The paper provides vocabulary and a research agenda to study when AI-assisted inquiry becomes a substitute for thinking, synthesis, and action.

title: A Comparative Study of Static, Scrollytelling, and Chatbot Visualization Onboarding Techniques for UX Designers
summary: User experience (UX) designers face barriers when creating data visualizations due to limited domain expertise in visualization or unfamiliarity with specialized tools. This highlights a clear need for effective methods to build visualization literacy. To address this, we evaluated three visualization onboarding techniques -- static, scrollytelling, and chatbot -- in an experimental study with 25 UX designers and students. We measured visualization comprehension and guideline adherence during a visualization creation task, followed by surveys and interviews to capture preferences and experiences. Compared to static onboarding, the pooled interactive condition (scrollytelling or chatbot) was associated with significantly higher guideline-adherence scores during visualization creation; both interactive techniques also received higher engagement ratings. Instruction clarity ratings were significantly higher when the two interactive conditions were pooled. Comprehension did not differ significantly across conditions. While participants generally preferred the interactive techniques, no significant differences emerged between scrollytelling and chatbot in performance or onboarding experience ratings. Drawing on the findings, we discuss three design dimensions of visualization onboarding (narrative structure, visual content layout, and navigational flexibility), their design implications, and potential opportunities for future research in this field.

AI.tldr: An experimental study with 25 UX designers/students compared static, scrollytelling, and chatbot onboarding techniques for visualization creation. Interactive techniques (scrollytelling and chatbot) led to significantly higher guideline-adherence scores and engagement/instruction clarity ratings than static onboarding, though comprehension did not differ. No significant differences emerged between the two interactive methods.
AI.motivation: UX designers face barriers in creating data visualizations due to limited domain expertise and unfamiliarity with specialized tools, highlighting the need for effective methods to build visualization literacy through onboarding techniques.
AI.method: An experimental study with 25 UX designers and students comparing three onboarding techniques (static, scrollytelling, and chatbot). Measured visualization comprehension and guideline adherence during a creation task, supplemented by surveys and interviews on preferences and experiences.
AI.result: Interactive onboarding (scrollytelling or chatbot, pooled) yielded significantly higher guideline-adherence scores, engagement ratings, and instruction clarity ratings than static onboarding. Comprehension scores did not differ significantly across conditions. No significant performance or experience differences between scrollytelling and chatbot were found.
AI.conclusion: Interactive onboarding techniques outperform static ones for visualization creation in terms of guideline adherence, engagement, and clarity — though not comprehension. The authors propose three design dimensions (narrative structure, visual content layout, and navigational flexibility) to guide future visualization onboarding research and design.

title: Regulating AI: Where U.S. State Policy and HCI (Mis)align
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly adopted into everyday life, with most investment and development concentrated in the U.S. In response to rapid AI integration and scant federal guidelines, U.S. states have formed AI committees charged with studying AI-related societal trade-offs. We analyzed the 18 existing state-level AI committee reports to understand how policymakers discuss AI-related benefits and risks. We then compared the risks surfaced by policymakers to an established taxonomy of AI risks aggregated from literature and examined how policymakers' concerns align, or misalign, from those of HCI scholars. These insights provide important mileposts for shaping currently ongoing policy initiatives and future research. Our findings reveal important gaps: while committees invoke responsible AI, their framings often omit broader socio-technical concerns emphasized in HCI. We discuss opportunities for HCI to support socio-technical perspectives, employ participatory design, and close the gap between research and policy.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 18 U.S. state-level AI committee reports reveals policymakers emphasize responsible AI rhetoric but overlook broader socio-technical risks central to HCI scholarship. The study compares policy framings against an established AI risk taxonomy, identifying gaps and proposing opportunities for HCI researchers to bridge research-policy divides through socio-technical perspectives and participatory design.
AI.motivation: Rapid AI integration into everyday life, concentrated investment in the U.S., and a lack of federal regulatory guidelines have prompted states to form AI committees. Understanding how these committees frame AI benefits and risks — and how those framings compare to established academic risk taxonomies — is critical for shaping policy and guiding future HCI research.
AI.method: The authors collected and qualitatively analyzed all 18 existing state-level AI committee reports from across the U.S. They identified and categorized policymakers' discussions of AI-related benefits and risks, then systematically compared these surfaced risks against an established taxonomy of AI risks aggregated from scholarly literature, specifically examining alignment and misalignment with HCI scholars' concerns.
AI.result: State committees frequently invoke "responsible AI" language, yet their framings tend to omit broader socio-technical concerns that HCI scholarship prioritizes. Significant gaps exist between policy-level risk articulation and academic risk taxonomies, particularly regarding nuanced human-centered and societal dimensions of AI impact.
AI.conclusion: The identified gaps represent critical mileposts for both ongoing policy development and future HCI research. The authors advocate for HCI scholars to actively support socio-technical perspectives in policy contexts, leverage participatory design approaches, and work to close the persistent research-policy gap.

title: Evaluating Affective Objectives: Statistical Numbing in Data Visualization
summary: Visualizations can help audiences understand the scale of tragedies, such as the consequences of natural disasters, war, genocide, and pandemics. In these cases, a visualization designer's default behavior may be to focus on communicating quantitative information: numbers, statistics, and trends. However, this may not reflect higher-level affective objectives to inspire their audience to care about an issue, empathize with others, or take action to help those in need. Worse, standard visualizations may conflict with these goals, as statistics can numb emotions and reduce prosocial feelings toward people in need. Designers have developed strategies to increase affective responses through data visualizations, such as blending data narratives and personal narratives about individuals. In this paper, we explore three design strategies for communicating a humanitarian crisis: data-driven, human-driven, or mixed narratives. We conducted an empirical study to explore the effect of statistical numbing in the context of these types of narratives in the format of data videos. In particular, we measure prosocial feelings and behaviors by giving participants the option of donating money as part of the study. We find that human-driven narratives (photographs and stories of individuals) elicited the highest donations and that the mixed narrative combination led to the lowest donations. We discuss the limitations of this study and the implications of pursuing affective objectives and the numbing of empathy in data visualization design.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different narrative strategies in data visualizations (data-driven, human-driven, and mixed) affect prosocial emotions and behaviors in the context of humanitarian crises, finding that human-driven narratives elicit the highest donations while mixed narratives surprisingly yield the lowest.
AI.motivation: Visualization designers often default to quantitative communication, but statistics can numb emotions and reduce prosocial feelings ("statistical numbing"). The authors aim to understand how design strategies can better achieve affective objectives like inspiring empathy and motivating action.
AI.method: An empirical study comparing three narrative strategies in data video format: data-driven (statistics and trends), human-driven (photographs and personal stories of individuals), and mixed (combination of both). Prosocial feelings and behaviors were measured, including actual donation behavior as a behavioral outcome.
AI.result: Human-driven narratives elicited the highest donations. Surprisingly, the mixed narrative condition led to the lowest donations, suggesting a potential interference effect when combining statistical and personal narratives.
AI.conclusion: Designers pursuing affective objectives should carefully consider narrative strategy; human-driven approaches may be most effective for inspiring prosocial action, while mixing data with personal stories may backfire. The paper calls for greater attention to the numbing of empathy in visualization design.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Decision-Making in Agent-Based Urban Mobility Simulations
summary: Urban mobility modeling faces challenges in representing decision-making in dynamic environments. Although Multi-Agent Systems are widely used, rule-based approaches rely on fixed heuristics that limit adaptive behavior. This work investigates the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) as decision-making components in multi-agent simulations. We propose a hybrid architecture that connects the GAMA platform to an external LLM-based module through an API, enabling agents to determine whether route replanning is necessary. Rather than replacing routing algorithms, the LLM serves as a decision layer that guides replanning behavior. The approach incorporates persistent memory, allowing past interactions to influence future decisions and promote behavioral consistency. We compare rule-based and LLM-assisted approaches across multiple road-blockage scenarios and population scales. Results indicate that LLM-enabled agents exhibit greater adaptability and contextual awareness, particularly in scenarios with higher route flexibility. Memory influences performance and behavioral consistency, with effects varying across configurations. Overall, LLMs serve as complementary cognitive layers that enrich behavioral representations in urban mobility simulations and hold potential for modeling complex decision-making in spatial multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid architecture integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) as a decision layer for route replanning in multi-agent urban mobility simulations (GAMA platform). LLM-enabled agents with persistent memory demonstrate greater adaptability and contextual awareness compared to rule-based baselines, particularly in scenarios with higher route flexibility.
AI.motivation: Traditional rule-based multi-agent simulations for urban mobility rely on fixed heuristics that cannot adequately capture adaptive, context-aware decision-making in dynamic environments. The authors seek to explore whether LLMs can serve as a complementary cognitive layer to enrich behavioral representations without replacing core routing algorithms.
AI.method: A hybrid architecture connects the GAMA multi-agent simulation platform to an external LLM module via API. The LLM acts solely as a decision layer that determines whether route replanning is necessary, rather than computing routes directly. Agents are equipped with persistent memory, enabling past interactions to influence future decisions. The approach is evaluated against rule-based baselines across multiple road-blockage scenarios and population scales.
AI.result: LLM-enabled agents exhibit superior adaptability and contextual awareness, especially when route flexibility is high. Memory contributes to performance and behavioral consistency, though effects vary across configurations. The LLM-assisted approach outperforms rule-based methods in dynamic, complex scenarios.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively serve as complementary cognitive layers in spatial multi-agent simulations, enriching behavioral representations without replacing traditional routing algorithms. This hybrid approach holds promise for modeling complex decision-making in urban mobility contexts.

title: Long-Term Optimization for Large-Scale Generative Retrieval with Off-Policy REINFORCE
comment: Accepted at the 5th Workshop on End-End Customer Journey Optimization at KDD 2026
summary:
Generative retrieval has become a popular paradigm for large-scale recommendation. However, it is typically trained with supervised next-item prediction objectives that do not directly optimize long-term user satisfaction.
  In this work, we formulate recommendation as a session-level sequential decision-making problem and introduce an autoregressive approach for training generative retrievers with off-policy REINFORCE on pre-collected data. Unlike the one-step off-policy correction used in prior work, we propose a multi-step approximation of importance weights enabled by the autoregressive formulation. To support offline evaluation, we train a user feedback model that simulates user responses to generated recommendations. This lets us adapt doubly robust off-policy evaluation for sequential decision-making to recommendation, a setting that has received limited attention. We further introduce a feedback-model-based test-time scaling procedure that simulates future responses and selects recommendations with the highest predicted long-term returns.
  Experiments on the public large-scale Yambda-5B dataset show that our RL agent improves offline estimates of cumulative session reward over next-item and next-positive prediction baselines, while largely preserving retrieval quality. Moreover, allocating more inference-time compute to simulating future responses improves model-based long-term return estimates without updating the policy.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes recommendation as a session-level sequential decision-making problem, training generative retrievers via off-policy REINFORCE with multi-step importance weighting. A user feedback simulator enables doubly robust off-policy evaluation, and a test-time scaling procedure selects recommendations maximizing predicted long-term returns. Experiments on Yambda-5B show improved cumulative session rewards while preserving retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: Generative retrieval models are typically trained with supervised next-item prediction objectives that optimize immediate accuracy rather than long-term user satisfaction. Existing RL-based approaches use only one-step off-policy correction, which fails to account for the sequential, multi-step nature of recommendation sessions. There is a need for methods that directly optimize session-level cumulative rewards in an offline RL setting.
AI.method: (1) Recommendation is formulated as a session-level sequential decision-making problem with an autoregressive generative retriever trained via off-policy REINFORCE. (2) A multi-step approximation of importance weights is proposed, leveraging the autoregressive structure for more accurate off-policy correction than prior one-step methods. (3) A user feedback model is trained to simulate responses, enabling doubly robust off-policy evaluation adapted to sequential recommendation. (4) A test-time scaling procedure uses the feedback model to simulate future responses and select recommendations with the highest predicted long-term returns, without policy updates.
AI.result: Experiments on the public large-scale Yambda-5B dataset demonstrate that the RL agent improves offline estimates of cumulative session reward over both next-item and next-positive prediction baselines, while largely preserving retrieval quality. Test-time compute scaling with the feedback model further improves model-based long-term return estimates.
AI.conclusion: Training generative retrievers with session-level RL objectives and multi-step off-policy correction yields better long-term user satisfaction than supervised next-item prediction. The proposed feedback model enables effective offline evaluation and test-time optimization, highlighting the value of sequential decision-making formulations in large-scale recommendation.

title: Benchmarking the Benchmarks: A Validity Audit of Tool-Calling Evaluation
summary: Tool-calling benchmarks are increasingly used to rank language-model agents, yet their scores are often treated as ground truth without validating the evaluators themselves. We present a systematic validity and reproducibility audit of four major tool-calling benchmark families: BFCL v4, τ2-Bench, LiveMCPBench, and MCP-Atlas. Across 496 expert-reviewed benchmark tasks, we find 92 evaluator-human disagreements, corresponding to an 18.5% misalignment rate. The failures are not isolated annotation mistakes: deterministic benchmarks exhibit brittle state matching, trajectory lock-in, incorrect ground truths, substring-based communication failures, and reward-basis misalignment, while LLM-judge benchmarks exhibit rubric drift, hallucinated completion, answer-only scoring, and substantial run-to-run variance. In LiveMCPBench, 23 repeated evaluations of the same setup produce scores ranging from 57.9% to 76.8%, a spread of 18.9 percentage points, large enough to change leaderboard conclusions. These results show that current tool-calling scores can reflect evaluator artifacts rather than agent capability. We introduce a unified taxonomy of tool-calling evaluation failures, release trace-level audit artifacts and corrected evaluation components, and argue for decomposed metrics that separately measure tool invocation, task completion, and outcome verification. Our findings suggest that progress in tool-using agents requires benchmarks whose evaluators are themselves reproducible, auditable, and aligned with human judgments of task success. We further introduce Tool-Veritas, a configurable benchmark that combines deterministic state verification with optional qualitative judging, and Harness Lab, an open-source system for benchmark execution, trace inspection, repeated-run comparison, and evaluator debugging.

AI.tldr: An audit of four major tool-calling benchmarks reveals an 18.5% misalignment rate between evaluators and human judgments, with failures stemming from brittle state matching, trajectory lock-in, LLM-judge inconsistency, and significant run-to-run variance (up to 18.9 percentage points), leading the authors to propose a failure taxonomy, corrected artifacts, and new tooling (Tool-Veritas, Harness Lab) for reproducible evaluation.
AI.motivation: Tool-calling benchmark scores are widely used to rank LM agents but are rarely validated themselves. The authors identify a critical gap: evaluator quality is assumed rather than demonstrated, meaning reported rankings may reflect evaluator artifacts rather than genuine agent capability.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic audit across four benchmark families (BFCL v4, τ2-Bench, LiveMCPBench, MCP-Atlas) encompassing 496 expert-reviewed tasks. They compared benchmark evaluator verdicts against human expert judgments to quantify misalignment, categorized failure modes into a unified taxonomy spanning deterministic evaluators (brittle state matching, trajectory lock-in, incorrect ground truths, substring-based communication failures, reward-basis misalignment) and LLM-judge evaluators (rubric drift, hallucinated completion, answer-only scoring, run-to-run variance). They ran LiveMCPBench 23 times under identical conditions to measure score dispersion.
AI.result: 92 evaluator-human disagreements were found across 496 tasks (18.5% misalignment rate). Deterministic evaluators suffered from rigid matching and flawed ground truths; LLM-judge evaluators exhibited rubric drift and hallucinated scoring. In LiveMCPBench, 23 repeated runs yielded scores from 57.9% to 76.8% — an 18.9 pp spread sufficient to invert leaderboard rankings. The authors released trace-level audit artifacts, corrected evaluation components, Tool-Veritas (a configurable benchmark with deterministic state verification and optional qualitative judging), and Harness Lab (an open-source system for execution, trace inspection, repeated-run comparison, and evaluator debugging).
AI.conclusion: Current tool-calling benchmarks cannot be treated as ground truth; evaluator misalignment and instability are pervasive. Progress in tool-using agents requires evaluators that are themselves reproducible, auditable, and aligned with human judgments. Decomposed metrics separating tool invocation, task completion, and outcome verification are necessary, and the released Tool-Veritas and Harness Lab systems provide infrastructure toward this goal.

title: The agent creates, we validate: A Lightweight Framework for Agentic Artifact Generation
summary: Generating structured artifacts with Large Language Models - e.g. database queries, threat framework mappings, entity schemas - is relatively straightforward; however, making them reliable enough for production deployments presents challenges. We present a lightweight framework based on a core principle: LLMs generate, we validate. This reframing shifts responsibility from generation quality to validation rigor. The framework rests on three key attributes: First, test driven generation: when tests fail, the LLM receives indicative error messages that expose why the output failed, enabling the LLM to understand its mistakes and refine subsequent attempts. Second, deterministic and LLM-based tests: deterministic tests catch heuristics that can be programmatically verified (schema, syntax, cross-reference), while LLM-based tests evaluate nuanced semantic and delicate features that resist programmatic inspection (intent alignment, logical consistency, domain correctness). Third, expert-distilled judges: LLM-based tests are calibrated to distill and replicate human expert decision distribution, transforming manual human quality gates into scalable, reusable evaluation proxies that reflect professional-grade validation standards. We demonstrate the framework on three artifact types in the security domain - KQL query generation, MITRE ATT\&CK mapping, and entity mapping - deployed in production at Microsoft Sentinel. We believe this framework can be applied beyond security to other artifact generation tasks, providing a path to reliable, high-quality outputs without sacrificing the efficiency gains of LLM generation.

AI.tldr: A lightweight framework that shifts LLM-based artifact generation from "generate well" to "validate rigorously," using test-driven generation with both deterministic and LLM-based tests calibrated to human expert judgment, demonstrated in production on security artifacts at Microsoft Sentinel.
AI.motivation: LLMs can easily generate structured artifacts (queries, schemas, mappings), but achieving production-grade reliability remains challenging. The core insight is to reframe the problem: rather than focusing on improving generation quality, focus on rigorous validation.
AI.method: The framework has three pillars: (1) Test-driven generation — failed tests produce indicative error messages that guide LLM self-correction in subsequent attempts. (2) Hybrid testing — deterministic tests catch programmatically verifiable issues (schema, syntax, cross-references), while LLM-based tests evaluate semantic qualities (intent alignment, logical consistency, domain correctness). (3) Expert-distilled judges — LLM-based tests are calibrated against human expert decision distributions, converting manual quality gates into scalable, reusable evaluation proxies.
AI.result: The framework was deployed in production at Microsoft Sentinel across three security artifact types: KQL query generation, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, and entity mapping, demonstrating reliable, high-quality structured outputs.
AI.conclusion: The "LLMs generate, we validate" paradigm, combining test-driven iteration with expert-calibrated hybrid testing, provides a generalizable path to production-reliable structured artifact generation beyond the security domain.

title: Improving LLMs via Validator-to-Generator Alignment
summary: Large language models are inconsistent: varying prompts or including unrelated information can lead to unexpected changes in model outputs. The generator-validator (G-V) gap is one manifestation of this phenomenon, where LLMs generate responses that they then deem as invalid if re-queried to validate them. In this work, we introduce a new formulation of G-V consistency that involves a principled correction for utterance frequency. Specifically, generators often assign low likelihood to valid strings simply because those strings are a priori unlikely, which makes naive notions of G-V consistency unworkable. We show that under a natural model of rational agents answering questions with multiple answers, consistency of the validator with a frequency-corrected generator score emerges naturally. Our method, \emph{\FCPAname} (\FCPA), is a training objective implementing frequency-corrected G-V consistency for real-world LLMs. Our experimental results show that training with \FCPA{} substantially improves both G-V consistency and generator performance over prior methods, with gains of up to $+27$pp in Pearson correlation on IFEval and HumanEval, while preserving validator quality across all evaluated tasks.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit a generator-validator (G-V) gap where they produce outputs they later judge as invalid. The authors attribute this partly to generators penalizing valid but a priori unlikely strings, and propose Frequency-Corrected Preference Alignment (FCPA), a training objective that corrects for utterance frequency. FCPA improves G-V consistency by up to +27pp Pearson correlation on IFEval/HumanEval while preserving validator quality.
AI.motivation: LLMs are inconsistent: prompt variations or irrelevant context can flip outputs, and models often generate responses they subsequently reject as invalid when asked to validate them (the G-V gap). Naive consistency objectives fail because generators naturally assign low likelihood to valid but improbable strings. The authors seek a principled, frequency-aware formulation of G-V consistency that aligns generator and validator behavior under a rational-agent model.
AI.method: The authors formalize G-V consistency under a rational-agent framework where questions admit multiple valid answers. They derive that a consistent validator should score responses based on a generator score corrected by the prior probability (frequency) of each string. This yields FCPA (Frequency-Corrected Preference Alignment), a training objective that penalizes mismatches between the frequency-corrected generator distribution and the validator's judgments. FCPA is implemented as a fine-tuning objective for real-world LLMs.
AI.result: FCPA substantially improves both G-V consistency and generator performance over prior methods, achieving up to +27 percentage points in Pearson correlation on IFEval and HumanEval benchmarks. Validator quality is preserved across all evaluated tasks.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-corrected preference alignment offers a principled solution to the generator-validator consistency problem in LLMs. By accounting for a priori string likelihood, FCPA enables meaningful consistency training that improves both alignment and generation quality without degrading validation capability.

title: Auditing the Audit: Five Failure Modes in Benchmark-Validity Audits
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the TAIGR Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Governance frameworks ask AI providers and auditors for documented evaluation evidence, and perturbation-based construct-validity audits are a common form of that evidence. We argue the audits are themselves fragile: their conclusions can be silently manufactured by implementation details that readers cannot see in the reported numbers. We name five classes of pipeline failure and demonstrate each in a self-audit over safety benchmarks and open-weight instruction-tuned models. Under a unified six-point due-diligence gate, every cell lands in a non-confirmatory bucket, and no cell reaches confirmatory. The evidence here is a single two-model, five-benchmark case study, and F1--F5 is an illustrative, deliberately non-exhaustive starting taxonomy -- not a comprehensive partition of audit failures. We position the gate as a withholding and disclosure protocol for assurance-grade evidence, supplementary to (not a replacement for) classical construct-validity evidence, and not as a route to benchmark-validity verdicts.

AI.tldr: AI audits relying on perturbation-based construct-validity evaluations are fragile; conclusions can be silently determined by undisclosed implementation details. The authors identify five pipeline failure classes, demonstrate them via a self-audit, and propose a six-point due-diligence gate that reveals no confirmatory results — positioning the gate as a disclosure protocol, not a validity verdict.
AI.motivation: Governance frameworks demand documented evaluation evidence from AI providers, with perturbation-based construct-validity audits being a standard form. However, the authors argue that these audits suffer from hidden fragility: implementation details invisible to report readers can manufacture conclusions, undermining the trustworthiness and assurance-grade quality of audit evidence.
AI.method: The authors conduct a self-audit over safety benchmarks using open-weight instruction-tuned models. They taxonomize five classes of pipeline failure (F1–F5), then apply a unified six-point due-diligence gate to evaluate every cell in their audit matrix. The gate serves as a withholding/disclosure protocol for assurance-grade evidence, supplementary to classical construct-validity approaches.
AI.result: Under the six-point due-diligence gate, every cell in the two-model, five-benchmark case study lands in a non-confirmatory bucket; no cell reaches confirmatory status. This illustrates that ostensibly positive audit numbers can dissolve under rigorous scrutiny of pipeline implementation details.
AI.conclusion: Perturbation-based construct-validity audits are themselves fragile artifacts. The five-class failure taxonomy (F1–F5) is an illustrative, non-exhaustive starting point, and the due-diligence gate is proposed as a supplemental disclosure protocol — not a replacement for construct-validity evidence nor a route to benchmark-validity verdicts.

title: iFLYTEK-Embodied-Omni Technical Report
summary: General-purpose embodied agents must understand multimodal instructions, anticipate how their environment will evolve, and produce precise control actions over extended horizons. Existing approaches typically specialize in visual-language reasoning, video-based world modeling, or action generation, while cascaded pipelines that first synthesize future observations and then infer actions can introduce interface bottlenecks and compound prediction errors. We present iFLYTEK-Embodied-Omni, a unified multimodal foundation model that jointly models vision(videos and images), language, and action within a single Omni framework. Its modality-specific visual-language, video-generation, and action-generation components communicate through shared multimodal self-attention. This design establishes brain-cerebellum collaboration: the vision-language modeland video generation model form a high-level brain for instruction understanding, task planning, progress tracking, and future visual-state prediction, whereas the action generation modelserves as a low-level cerebellum that directly converts planned subgoals and shared multimodal context into executable action chunks. To develop these capabilities, we combine action-annotated and action-free embodied videos from human demonstrations and robot interactions with embodied reasoning, embodied perception, and general-purpose image-text data to construct a comprehensive dataset. We further adopt a four-stage strategy that progressively trains the VLM, VGM, and AGM before jointly fine-tuning the complete model.

AI.tldr: iFLYTEK-Embodied-Omni is a unified multimodal foundation model that jointly handles vision, language, and action in a single framework, using a "brain-cerebellum" architecture where VLMs and video generation handle high-level reasoning while an action generation module converts subgoals into executable actions, trained progressively on a comprehensive embodied dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied AI systems are fragmented: they separately handle visual-language reasoning, video-based world modeling, or action generation. Cascaded pipelines that sequentially synthesize future observations then infer actions suffer from interface bottlenecks and compound prediction errors. A unified model that jointly models all modalities is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose a single Omni framework with three modality-specific components (visual-language, video-generation, and action-generation) that communicate via shared multimodal self-attention. The VLM and video generation model form a "brain" for high-level understanding, planning, and future-state prediction, while the action generation model acts as a "cerebellum" converting subgoals and multimodal context into action chunks. Training uses a combined dataset (action-annotated and action-free embodied videos, embodied reasoning/perception data, general image-text data) with a four-stage progressive strategy: VLM → VGM → AGM → joint fine-tuning.
AI.result: The paper describes the architecture and training methodology; specific quantitative experimental results are not detailed in the provided abstract.
AI.conclusion: A unified multimodal foundation model with brain-cerebellum collaboration can effectively integrate instruction understanding, world modeling, and action generation, overcoming the limitations of cascaded embodied AI pipelines.

title: Between Knowledge and Care: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of Generative AI for T2DM Self-Management from Patient and Physician Perspectives
comment: arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2510.10048
summary: Generative AI is increasingly used for everyday health guidance, yet its clinical appropriateness in chronic disease contexts remains poorly understood. This paper presents a two-part mixed-methods study on \revise{Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)}, examining how patients and physicians assess AI-generated health information. \revise{Study~1} analyzes 784 \revise{participant reported} patient queries to characterize seven informational need categories and \revise{develops a structured five dimensional physician rating rubric informed by patient query categories and clinician priorities} (\textit{Accuracy, Safety, Clarity, Integrity, Action Orientation}). \revise{Study~2} engages seven physicians scoring responses from four AI models and discussing evaluative reasoning through in-depth interviews. Models perform well on factual explanation and lifestyle guidance but consistently underperform on medication reasoning and emotional support. Two \revise{analytic concepts} emerge \revise{from the data}. The \textit{pre-visit primer} \revise{frames AI as preparation for clinical encounters rather than as a replacement for physicians}. The \textit{fluency illusion} \revise{describes how polished language may convey epistemic authority that the clinical content does not support}. Patients and physicians converged on three shared limitations (role boundaries, emotional inadequacy, personalization gaps) while diverging in evaluative emphasis, \revise{which informed} four design directions, task-aware orchestration, risk-aware fallback, dynamic personalization, and emotionally attuned interaction.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study examining how T2DM patients and physicians evaluate AI-generated health guidance, revealing that AI excels at factual explanation but struggles with medication reasoning and emotional support. Two novel concepts — the "pre-visit primer" and "fluency illusion" — frame AI's appropriate role and risks, leading to four design directions for clinically safer AI health tools.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is increasingly deployed for everyday health guidance, but its clinical appropriateness for chronic disease management — particularly T2DM — is poorly understood. There is a need to systematically characterize how both patients and physicians assess AI-generated health information to identify gaps, risks, and appropriate design boundaries.
AI.method: A two-part mixed-methods design. Study 1: analysis of 784 patient-reported queries to derive seven informational need categories and development of a structured five-dimensional physician rating rubric (Accuracy, Safety, Clarity, Integrity, Action Orientation). Study 2: seven physicians scored responses from four AI models and participated in in-depth interviews on their evaluative reasoning.
AI.result: AI models performed well on factual explanation and lifestyle guidance but consistently underperformed on medication reasoning and emotional support. Two grounded concepts emerged: the "pre-visit primer" (AI as clinical preparation, not replacement) and the "fluency illusion" (polished language conveying false epistemic authority). Patients and physicians converged on three shared limitations — role boundaries, emotional inadequacy, and personalization gaps — but diverged in evaluative emphasis. Four design directions were derived: task-aware orchestration, risk-aware fallback, dynamic personalization, and emotionally attuned interaction.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI holds promise as a preparatory tool for clinical encounters rather than a physician substitute, but its fluency can mislead users about content reliability. Future design must embed risk-awareness, task-appropriate routing, personalization, and emotional sensitivity to align AI health guidance with both patient needs and clinical standards.

title: SovereignNegotiation-Bench: Evaluating User-Owned Personal Agents In Delegated Bargaining Under Privacy, Consent, Evidence, And Institutional Pressure
summary: Personal agents will increasingly negotiate on behalf of users: splitting costs with other personal agents, appealing platform decisions, escalating support disputes, requesting refunds, changing subscriptions, and negotiating deadlines or reimbursements. Existing negotiation benchmarks emphasize agreement, surplus, or strategic competence, but a user-owned agent can reach an agreement while harming the user through privacy leakage, consent violation, unsupported advocacy, over-concession, failed escalation, or poor auditability. We introduce SovereignNegotiation-Bench, a trace-level multi-turn benchmark for delegated personal-agent negotiation under private utilities, disclosure constraints, evidence requirements, and institutional asymmetry. The benchmark separates agent-visible observable state from evaluator-only labels and evaluates agreement success jointly with user utility, privacy, consent, evidence grounding, concession discipline, escalation, and auditability. We report an artifact-backed validation over 240 scenarios, 4 model families, 14 baselines, 13,440 frozen-prompt live trajectories, 61,135 parsed action rows, and a blinded 3-annotator audit over 300 items. The strongest agreement-maximizing baseline achieves the highest agreement rate but low user utility and high privacy/consent risk; FullSovereign does not maximize agreement, but obtains the best sovereign negotiation score by preserving utility, minimizing leakage, grounding claims, and reducing unauthorized commitments. The results show that agreement success is insufficient for user-owned negotiation agents.

AI.tldr: SovereignNegotiation-Bench evaluates personal AI negotiation agents beyond simple agreement success, measuring privacy, consent, evidence grounding, and auditability. Experiments across 14 baselines and 4 model families show that maximizing agreement alone harms user interests, while the FullSovereign approach achieves the best overall sovereign negotiation score by balancing utility preservation with leakage minimization.
AI.motivation: Existing negotiation benchmarks prioritize agreement rate, surplus, or strategic competence. However, a user-owned personal agent can technically reach agreement while severely harming the user — through privacy leakage, consent violations, unsupported advocacy, over-concession, failed escalation, or poor auditability. No prior benchmark captures these sovereign negotiation dimensions under realistic conditions of private utilities, disclosure constraints, evidence requirements, and institutional asymmetry.
AI.method: The authors introduce SovereignNegotiation-Bench, a trace-level multi-turn benchmark where each scenario separates agent-observable state from evaluator-only labels. The benchmark evaluates agreement success jointly with user utility, privacy, consent, evidence grounding, concession discipline, escalation, and auditability. Validation involves 240 scenarios, 4 model families, 14 baselines, 13,440 frozen-prompt live trajectories, 61,135 parsed action rows, and a blinded 3-annotator audit over 300 items. The FullSovereign baseline is compared against an agreement-maximizing baseline and other approaches.
AI.result: The strongest agreement-maximizing baseline achieves the highest raw agreement rate but yields low user utility and high privacy/consent risk. FullSovereign does not maximize agreement but obtains the best composite sovereign negotiation score by preserving utility, minimizing information leakage, grounding claims in evidence, and reducing unauthorized commitments.
AI.conclusion: Agreement success alone is an insufficient metric for user-owned negotiation agents. Sovereign negotiation — jointly optimizing for utility, privacy, consent, evidence grounding, concession discipline, escalation, and auditability — is necessary to prevent agent behavior that technically succeeds but substantively harms the user.

title: HETERQA: Benchmarking Record Retrieval over Multiple Heterogeneous Sources
summary: In emerging systems (e.g., social media and e-commerce platforms), data records are often drawn from heterogeneous sources, such as relational tables, text documents, image repositories, spatial databases, and knowledge graphs. Accordingly, retrieving target records for question-answering (QA) tasks requires us to jointly exploit these heterogeneous sources. However, most existing benchmarks are constructed from individual sources, and only a very few recent benchmarks have considered two or three sources. To alleviate this issue, we introduce HETERQA, a comprehensive benchmark with 857 QA pairs for record retrieval over five heterogeneous sources. HETERQA instantiates this setting with Yelp business records, each of which is grounded by multiple sources. We build HETERQA in an answer-driven manner: candidate records are first initialized with record-field constraints, then enriched through heterogeneous sources, and finally cross-verified across required sources before the natural-language question is retained. We validate the benchmark through contradiction detection and human validation, and further evaluate sparse, dense, hybrid, late-interaction, and agentic retrievers under the same metrics. The results show that HETERQA is challenging: hybrid retrieval achieves the strongest Recall@10, Self-RAG achieves the best MRR@10, and all evaluated methods remain far from saturating the benchmark. These findings indicate that HETERQA provides an effective testbed for record retrieval over heterogeneous sources and leaves substantial room for future retrieval methods. The benchmark dataset and source code are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/hanchang02/HeterQA and https://github.com/hanchang02/HeterQA, respectively.

AI.tldr: HETERQA is a new benchmark with 857 QA pairs for record retrieval across five heterogeneous data sources (relational tables, text, images, spatial data, knowledge graphs), built from Yelp business records. Hybrid retrieval achieves the best Recall@10 and Self-RAG the best MRR@10, but all methods fall short of saturating the benchmark, leaving substantial room for improvement.
AI.motivation: Most existing QA benchmarks are built from single data sources, while real-world systems (social media, e-commerce) require joint retrieval from heterogeneous sources. Only a few benchmarks consider two or three sources, creating a gap in evaluating retrieval methods that must reason across multiple heterogeneous modalities simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors construct HETERQA using an answer-driven pipeline: (1) candidate records are initialized with record-field constraints, (2) enriched through five heterogeneous sources (relational tables, text documents, image repositories, spatial databases, knowledge graphs) anchored to Yelp business records, (3) cross-verified across required sources, and (4) natural-language questions are retained. Quality is ensured via contradiction detection and human validation. They evaluate sparse, dense, hybrid, late-interaction, and agentic retrievers under Recall@10 and MRR@10.
AI.result: Hybrid retrieval achieves the highest Recall@10, while Self-RAG achieves the best MRR@10. All evaluated retrieval methods remain far from saturating the benchmark, demonstrating HETERQA's difficulty and its value as a challenging testbed.
AI.conclusion: HETERQA fills a critical gap as a comprehensive multi-source retrieval benchmark, showing that current state-of-the-art retrievers struggle with heterogeneous-source record retrieval. Significant headroom remains for developing more effective retrieval methods that can jointly exploit diverse data modalities.

title: When Not to Write Memory: Governing False Promotion from Correlated Agent Traces
summary: Long-lived language agents increasingly write reusable memories from their own execution traces. The key safety question is not only what agents should remember, but when they should refuse to write memory at all. Repeated observations across agents are not necessarily independent evidence: the same claim may be copied from a shared source, induced by a shared prompt, stale under a new environment, or valid only in a narrower scope. We study this failure mode as a memory writepath governance problem. We introduce GovMem as a conservative diagnostic reference policy that estimates dependency-aware support, retrieves counterevidence, assigns scope, and outputs one of three decisions: promote, reject, or needs-review. In controlled synthetic stress tests, GovMem reduces false promotion from 0.597 to 0.040 in the default setting while preserving 0.960 recall, at an explicit review burden. In a project-internal 120candidate human-labeled real-trace subset spanning 79 recorded traces and project reports, dependency-aware promotion reduces false promotion from 0.371 for source+scope to 0.032 overall, but held-out false promotion remains 0.111 and the method is highly conservative, with 0.692 review burden and 0.448 direct recall. A final human adjudication of 133 high-impact external codingagent candidates is more severe: none are safe for automatic promotion, and all 11 verification-gate positives are rejected as boilerplate, shared-tool artifacts, file dumps, or non-reusable debugging traces. These results support GovMem primarily as a diagnostic governance design point, not as a generally validated or efficient automatic memory writer: agent memory write paths should be evaluated as risk-controlled evidence-governance systems, while broader external coverage and downstream harm evidence are still needed before stronger claims.

AI.tldr: GovMem is a conservative diagnostic policy for governing when language agents should write reusable memories, using dependency-aware support estimation to decide between promote, reject, or needs-review. It dramatically reduces false promotion in synthetic and real-trace tests but remains too conservative for practical automatic writing, with high review burden and limited recall.
AI.motivation: Long-lived language agents increasingly write reusable memories from execution traces, but repeated observations are not independent — claims may be copied from shared sources, induced by shared prompts, stale under new environments, or only narrowly valid. The core safety challenge is determining when agents should refuse to write memory at all, framing this as a memory writepath governance problem.
AI.method: GovMem serves as a conservative diagnostic reference policy that estimates dependency-aware support for candidate memories, retrieves counterevidence, assigns scope, and outputs one of three governance decisions: promote (accept), reject, or needs-review (defer to human). The approach explicitly models inter-observation dependencies rather than treating repeated claims as independent corroboration.
AI.result: In synthetic stress tests (default setting), GovMem reduces false promotion from 0.597 to 0.040 while preserving 0.960 recall. On a human-labeled 120-candidate real-trace subset, dependency-aware promotion reduces false promotion from 0.371 (source+scope baseline) to 0.032, but held-out false promotion remains 0.111 with 0.692 review burden and 0.448 direct recall. A human adjudication of 133 high-impact external coding-agent candidates found none safe for automatic promotion; all 11 verification-gate positives were rejected as boilerplate or non-reusable artifacts.
AI.conclusion: GovMem is primarily a diagnostic governance design point, not a generally validated or efficient automatic memory writer. Agent memory write paths should be evaluated as risk-controlled evidence-governance systems, and broader external coverage plus downstream harm evidence are needed before stronger claims can be made.

title: RES-DARE: Failure-Aware Expert Adaptation and Rollback-Safe Self-Repair for Intrusion Detection
summary: Intrusion detection systems are often trained under static benchmark conditions, although deployed network environments are affected by traffic drift, sensor noise, changing workloads, and evolving attack behaviour. Under such distribution shifts, static detectors may produce confident but incorrect predictions, leading to silent and unsafe failure modes. In this paper, RES-DARE (Recursive Evolving Specialists-Digital Adaptive Reasoning Engine) is proposed as a failure-aware continual intrusion detection framework with rollback-safe self-repair. Difficult, uncertain, and misclassified samples are treated as failure signals for expert specialisation rather than being discarded as noise. A supervised contrastive encoder, two-pass expert router, failure-buffer mechanism, HDBSCAN-based failure-region discovery, and trust-risk monitor are integrated to support adaptive IDS behaviour. AEHM-v2 is introduced as a rollback-safe repair mechanism, where candidate adaptations are provisionally activated and committed only when macro-F1 is preserved or improved while trust risk remains stable. Otherwise, the system is rolled back to its last validated state. RES-DARE is evaluated on CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15, and TON\_IoT, achieving macro-F1 scores of 0.9850, 0.9736, and 0.9691, respectively. Under Gaussian feature corruption at strength 0.10, RES-DARE retains an Attack-F1 of 0.7920 on CICIDS2017 and achieves near-zero catastrophic forgetting with F = 0.0015. The results show that RES-DARE improves robustness, warning capability, and deployment safety under degraded conditions.

AI.tldr: RES-DARE is a continual intrusion detection framework that treats uncertain/misclassified samples as failure signals for expert specialization, integrates rollback-safe self-repair via AEHM-v2, and achieves high macro-F1 scores across three benchmark datasets while maintaining robustness under distribution shifts and Gaussian noise corruption with minimal catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Static IDS models trained under fixed benchmarks fail silently under real-world conditions involving traffic drift, sensor noise, workload changes, and evolving attacks. These distribution shifts cause confident but incorrect predictions, motivating a failure-aware, continually adaptive framework that can safely self-repair without degrading prior performance.
AI.method: RES-DARE combines: (1) a supervised contrastive encoder for robust representations, (2) a two-pass expert router, (3) a failure-buffer mechanism that retains difficult/uncertain/misclassified samples for expert specialization, (4) HDBSCAN-based failure-region discovery for clustering failure modes, (5) a trust-risk monitor, and (6) AEHM-v2, a rollback-safe repair mechanism that provisionally activates candidate adaptations and commits only if macro-F1 is preserved/improved and trust risk remains stable; otherwise reverts to the last validated state.
AI.result: RES-DARE achieved macro-F1 of 0.9850 (CICIDS2017), 0.9736 (UNSW-NB15), and 0.9691 (TON_IoT). Under Gaussian feature corruption (strength 0.10), Attack-F1 on CICIDS2017 was 0.7920, with near-zero catastrophic forgetting (F=0.0015).
AI.conclusion: RES-DARE demonstrates that failure-aware continual learning with rollback-safe self-repair significantly improves IDS robustness, warning capability, and deployment safety under degraded and shifting conditions, outperforming static detectors that suffer silent failures.

title: Echoes of Unrest: A Multimodal NLP Framework for Early Warning of Fake News and Violence-Driven Mob Activity
comment: Accepted for publication as a book chapter (Taylor & Francis, 2026)
summary: Rapid growth in social media has transformed global communication by enabling fast information exchange, but it has also accelerated the spread of misinformation. Fake news, manipulated content, and provocative narratives are increasingly linked to social unrest, political instability, and mob violence. Incidents in South Asia and elsewhere demonstrate how false information disseminated via platforms such as Facebook and WhatsApp can trigger real-world harm, often spreading faster than fact-checking efforts can respond. To address this challenge, this chapter presents a multilingual, multimodal Natural Language Processing (NLP) framework for early detection of misinformation and violence-prone dynamics. A fused dataset of 138,256 Bangla and English samples was created by combining multiple benchmark datasets. The framework integrates XLM-RoBERTa for multilingual text representation, CLIP for visual embedding, and a multi-head attention mechanism for multimodal fusion, enhanced with auxiliary features such as sarcasm and geospatial metadata. Experiments on a stratified 30% subset achieved 98% test accuracy with strong precision and recall. The outcomes show the efficacy of multimodal approaches in early misinformation detection and highlight the added value of geospatial signals for anticipating real-world escalation.

AI.tldr: A multilingual, multimodal NLP framework combining XLM-RoBERTa, CLIP, and multi-head attention with auxiliary features achieves 98% accuracy on a 138K-sample Bangla-English dataset for early misinformation detection, demonstrating the value of geospatial signals for predicting real-world violence escalation.
AI.motivation: Social media accelerates misinformation spread, causing real-world harm including social unrest, political instability, and mob violence — particularly in South Asia. Fact-checking cannot keep pace with the speed of false information dissemination on platforms like Facebook and WhatsApp, creating an urgent need for automated early detection systems.
AI.method: A fused dataset of 138,256 Bangla and English samples is constructed from multiple benchmarks. The framework integrates XLM-RoBERTa for multilingual text encoding, CLIP for visual embeddings, and a multi-head attention mechanism for cross-modal fusion. Auxiliary features (sarcasm detection signals and geospatial metadata) supplement the multimodal representations. Experiments are conducted on a stratified 30% subset of the data.
AI.result: The framework achieved 98% test accuracy with strong precision and recall on the stratified subset. Multimodal fusion outperformed unimodal baselines, and geospatial metadata proved valuable for anticipating real-world escalation patterns.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal, multilingual approaches are highly effective for early misinformation detection. Integrating geospatial signals adds significant predictive value for forecasting offline violence, suggesting a promising direction for real-world deployment in high-risk regions.

title: Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models for Electricity Price Forecasting: Contamination Risk, Distributional Shifts, and Covariate Dependence
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have shown strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but their generalization in covariate-driven, non-stationary settings is underexplored. Electricity price forecasting (EPF) presents a challenging testbed due to complex temporal dependencies, distributional shifts, and strong reliance on structural and contextual information. We propose a two-dataset-benchmarking framework for EPF to mitigate contamination risk and enable fair evaluation of TSFMs. We examine key aspects of EPF including point and probabilistic forecasting performance, tail behavior, price spikes, and comparisons against domain-specific methods. We find that TSFMs are highly competitive and often outperform general-purpose baselines. Yet, their performance depends critically on covariate support, and they do not consistently surpass domain-specific methods tailored to EPF. Interestingly, simple ensembles of TSFMs and domain-specific methods appear to have significant potential, suggesting that the two approaches capture complementary predictive information.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates time series foundation models (TSFMs) on electricity price forecasting, finding they are competitive but do not consistently beat domain-specific methods; ensembles of both show promising complementary performance.
AI.motivation: TSFMs have demonstrated strong zero-shot forecasting, yet their generalization in covariate-driven, non-stationary settings remains underexplored. Electricity price forecasting provides an ideal testbed due to its complex temporal dependencies, distributional shifts, and heavy reliance on structural/contextual covariates, revealing limitations in current TSFM evaluation.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-dataset benchmarking framework for electricity price forecasting to mitigate contamination risk. They evaluate TSFMs on point and probabilistic forecasting, tail behavior, price spikes, and compare against domain-specific methods, with a focus on covariate support and ensemble combinations.
AI.result: TSFMs are highly competitive and often outperform general-purpose baselines, but their performance depends critically on covariate support. They do not consistently surpass domain-specific EPF methods. Simple ensembles of TSFMs and domain-specific methods show significant potential by capturing complementary predictive information.
AI.conclusion: TSFMs are strong but not uniformly superior in covariate-heavy, non-stationary domains like EPF. The complementary strengths of TSFMs and domain-specific models motivate future work on hybrid approaches and ensembles, while highlighting the need for proper covariate handling in foundation model design.

title: Internal Pluralism and the Limits of Pairwise Comparisons
summary: Local pairwise comparisons are a standard tool for learning how people want decision rules to work, e.g., in participatory design or alignment. However, their use builds in two strong assumptions: that local comparisons are sufficient evidence about how a person wants an automated decision rule to behave, and that people can always answer those comparisons decisively. We investigate how these assumptions may be compromised under internal pluralism: the idea that an individual evaluates decision rules according to multiple authoritative priorities about how the rule should behave. We provide a formal model of such pluralistic preferences over decision rules, which then lets us identify two distinct failures of forced local pairwise comparison data. First, priorities such as proportionality, egalitarianism, and equal treatment are inherently global: what they imply in one case can depend on what happens elsewhere, so local comparisons may fail to capture them. Second, even when priorities are representable locally, tension between strongly-held priorities can generate internal conflict, producing potentially costly behavioral distortions when comparisons are forced. We then use our model to investigate the alternative -- allowing people to report indecision -- and our findings suggest that doing so can considerably reduce the number of queries needed to learn preferences accurately. We conclude by describing how our model points toward preference-learning methods that elicit these priorities directly, yielding more faithful and interpretable accounts of what people value.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges standard pairwise comparison methods for preference elicitation by introducing a model of "internal pluralism," where individuals hold multiple competing priorities. It identifies two failure modes—global priorities being invisible to local comparisons, and forced choice causing behavioral distortions under internal conflict—and shows that allowing indecision reports reduces query costs and improves preference learning accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard local pairwise comparison methods in participatory design and alignment assume (a) local comparisons suffice to capture preferences over decision rules and (b) people can always answer decisively. These assumptions break down under internal pluralism, where a person holds multiple authoritative priorities (e.g., proportionality, egalitarianism, equal treatment) that may conflict. The paper aims to formally characterize these failures and explore alternatives.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal model of pluralistic preferences over decision rules, where an individual's evaluation is governed by multiple potentially competing priority functions. Using this model, they analytically identify two failure modes of forced local pairwise comparisons: (1) inherently global priorities that cannot be captured by local queries, and (2) internal conflict between strongly-held priorities producing behavioral distortions. They then compare forced-choice elicitation against an alternative that permits indecision reporting, analyzing query efficiency and accuracy.
AI.result: Two distinct failures are identified: first, global priorities (proportionality, egalitarianism, equal treatment) have cross-case dependencies that local comparisons inherently miss; second, internal conflict between priorities causes costly behavioral distortions when comparisons are forced. Allowing indecision reporting substantially reduces the number of queries needed for accurate preference learning. Direct elicitation of underlying priorities yields more faithful and interpretable accounts of values.
AI.conclusion: Forced local pairwise comparisons are fundamentally limited under internal pluralism. Permitting indecision and directly eliciting the underlying priorities people hold—rather than their surface-level choices—offers a more efficient, accurate, and interpretable path for preference learning in participatory design and alignment contexts.

title: CoGen3D: An Agentic Human-AI Co-Design Pipeline for 3D Asset Generation for Virtual Reality
summary: Creating 3D assets for virtual reality requires modeling expertise, which restricts the authorship of immersive experiences. Existing generative AI tools rely on unconstrained, command-driven prompting, lacking the conversational scaffolding needed for users to articulate their intent and validate designs prior to rendering. To address this, we introduce CoGen3D, an agentic human-AI co-design pipeline that proactively guides users through conversational intent elicitation, a concept image confirmation, and image-to-3D generation that directly deploys to immersive scenes. We evaluated this system through a user study (N=120) across six affectively diverse immersive scenes, observing 60 Design group participants who co-created 3D assets for the scenes, and 60 Validation group participants who experienced the scenes with generated assets. Our findings show that co-designed assets are associated with higher scene engagement and shifted affective responses, while participants generally preferred concept images over the final 3D assets, with no increased leniency toward degradation in their own creations. Analysis of the human-AI conversations further shows that target environments shape users' conversational patterns. Our results suggest that our staged, intent-based co-design can democratize virtual reality authoring and shift immersive content creation from technical execution toward collaborative spatial design.

AI.tldr: CoGen3D is an agentic human-AI co-design pipeline that guides users through conversational intent elicitation, concept image confirmation, and image-to-3D generation for direct deployment into immersive VR scenes. A user study (N=120) found co-designed assets improve scene engagement and shift affective responses, though users preferred concept images over final 3D outputs.
AI.motivation: 3D asset creation for VR requires modeling expertise, restricting immersive content authorship. Existing generative AI tools use unconstrained command-driven prompting, lacking the conversational scaffolding necessary for users to articulate design intent and validate concepts before rendering.
AI.method: The authors developed CoGen3D, an agentic human-AI co-design pipeline with three stages: (1) conversational intent elicitation where the AI proactively guides users, (2) concept image confirmation, and (3) image-to-3D generation with direct deployment to immersive scenes. Evaluation involved a between-subjects user study (N=120) across six affectively diverse immersive scenes: 60 Design group participants co-created 3D assets, and 60 Validation group participants experienced the resulting scenes.
AI.result: Co-designed assets correlated with higher scene engagement and shifted affective responses. Participants generally preferred concept images over the final 3D assets. No increased leniency toward degradation was observed for self-created assets. Target environments shaped users' conversational patterns during co-design.
AI.conclusion: Staged, intent-based co-design through systems like CoGen3D can democratize VR authoring, shifting immersive content creation from technical execution toward collaborative spatial design.

title: LOTUSim: Multi-Domain Simulator for Marine Robotics
summary: Simulation is essential for maritime robotics, supporting operator training, mission rehearsal, and human-vehicle interaction in environments where real-world testing is costly or hazardous. Existing simulators focus primarily on autonomy systems and often lack human-in-the-loop interaction and realistic environmental physics. This paper introduces LOTUSim, an open-source, real-time maritime simulator supporting multi-user interaction across aerial, surface, and underwater robotic systems for coordinated naval-style operations. The first contribution of this work is enabling real-time interactive performance for users while ensuring scalability to large fleets operating within a shared interactive simulation environment. Validation demonstrates robust human-in-the-loop performance, maintaining strict real-time execution and high visual fidelity while scaling to large heterogeneous maritime drone swarms. The second contribution is a computationally efficient, Ekman-inspired layered, underwater current model that captures wind-driven, depth-dependent flow dynamics with sufficient physical fidelity for large-scale simulations. Validation against ocean reanalysis data demonstrates substantially improved accuracy compared to commonly used stochastic Gauss-Markov current models. These results confirm LOTUSim's suitability as a simulation platform for operatorin-the-loop maritime robotics research.

AI.tldr: LOTUSim is an open-source, real-time maritime simulator that supports multi-user, multi-domain (aerial, surface, underwater) human-in-the-loop operations with scalable fleet simulation and a novel computationally efficient underwater current model validated against ocean reanalysis data.
AI.motivation: Existing maritime simulators prioritize autonomy systems and lack human-in-the-loop interaction and realistic environmental physics. Real-world maritime robotics testing is costly and hazardous, creating a need for a simulator that supports operator training, mission rehearsal, and human-vehicle interaction with high physical fidelity.
AI.method: The authors developed LOTUSim, an open-source real-time simulator featuring: (1) real-time interactive performance with scalability to large heterogeneous fleets of aerial, surface, and underwater drones; (2) a computationally efficient, Ekman-inspired layered underwater current model that captures wind-driven, depth-dependent flow dynamics.
AI.result: Validation showed robust human-in-the-loop performance with strict real-time execution and high visual fidelity while scaling to large heterogeneous swarms. The Ekman-inspired current model demonstrated substantially improved accuracy over stochastic Gauss-Markov models when validated against ocean reanalysis data.
AI.conclusion: LOTUSim is confirmed as a suitable simulation platform for operator-in-the-loop maritime robotics research, filling the gap left by autonomy-focused simulators.

title: HGenPush: A Heterogeneous Generative Recommendation Architecture for Industrial Push Notification Systems
summary: With the explosive growth of content platforms, recommendation systems need to better satisfy user demands to enhance user satisfaction and retention. Taking short-video platforms as an example, users not only seek high-quality content but also trusted authors. Although generative recommendation systems have achieved breakthroughs in recent years, existing methods primarily generate single-type recommendation content and typically employ the inefficient autoregressive paradigm to generate semantic IDs. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end heterogeneous generative recommendation architecture called HGenPush. First, we design a hybrid user behavior understanding module that integrates multi-scenario and multi-perspective behaviors to capture precise user interest. Then, we design a dual-branch heterogeneous generative recommendation module that integrates video recommendation and author recommendation within a unified framework. In addition, to improve generation efficiency, we design a lightweight multi-token prediction method that discards the autoregressive paradigm. Finally, we design a user consumption preference alignment module, which leverages user feedback as reward signals to guide the model toward generating higher-quality content, thereby enhancing user experience and engagement. Through these designs, HGenPush simultaneously fulfills users' demands for high-quality content and trusted authors. We have deployed HGenPush on the push notification system of Kuaishou, a large-scale short-video platform, achieving a significant 0.181% increase in daily active users.

AI.tldr: HGenPush is an end-to-end heterogeneous generative recommendation system deployed on Kuaishou that simultaneously recommends videos and authors via a dual-branch architecture with multi-token prediction, achieving a 0.181% DAU lift.
AI.motivation: Existing generative recommendation systems generate only single-type content (e.g., videos) using inefficient autoregressive semantic ID generation, failing to address users' dual needs for both high-quality content and trusted authors on short-video platforms.
AI.method: HGenPush comprises four key components: (1) a hybrid user behavior understanding module integrating multi-scenario and multi-perspective behaviors; (2) a dual-branch heterogeneous generative recommendation module unifying video and author recommendation; (3) a lightweight multi-token prediction method that replaces autoregressive generation for efficiency; and (4) a user consumption preference alignment module using user feedback as reward signals to guide generation quality.
AI.result: Deployed on Kuaishou's push notification system, HGenPush achieved a 0.181% increase in daily active users (DAU), demonstrating statistically and business-significant improvement in user engagement and retention.
AI.conclusion: HGenPush effectively unifies heterogeneous content (videos and authors) within a single generative recommendation framework, improving both recommendation quality and generation efficiency, with proven real-world impact on a billion-user-scale platform.

title: Better Together, in the Right Order: Classical-then-LLM Optimization for SE
summary:
A growing body of work combines large language models (LLMs) with classical optimizers for software engineering (SE) configuration tasks. Often, the classical optimizer is in charge: it owns the search loop and calls the LLM only to assist in subroutines (e.g. to warm-start the first generation, propose a mutation, or stand in as a surrogate). We report that there is much value in the reverse approach: seeding an LLM with the results from a cheap classical learner.
  We call this method SNAP2. Applied to over 100 SE tasks, it is the single best of all methods studied, reaching the top tier on 85% of tasks, ahead of the same LLM run alone (75%) and ahead of every method in which the classical optimizer retains control. It is also less expensive: relative to the LLM-alone method, it uses roughly 30% fewer tokens and runs 1.4x faster, since the classical setup performs the inexpensive work, and the LLM is invoked only to finish.
  We conclude that it is unwise to study classical learners or LLMs in isolation: there is much value in combining the two, and in the order that combination is applied.

AI.tldr: SNAP2 reverses the typical LLM-classical optimizer relationship by seeding an LLM with results from a cheap classical learner, achieving superior performance (85% top-tier vs. 75% LLM-alone), 30% fewer tokens, and 1.4x faster execution across 100+ SE configuration tasks.
AI.motivation: Prior work predominantly places classical optimizers in control of the search loop, using LLMs only as subroutines. The authors identify an unexplored alternative: letting a classical learner provide an initial solution that an LLM then refines, arguing this reversal may yield better performance and efficiency.
AI.method: SNAP2 first runs a cheap classical learner (e.g., an evolutionary algorithm or other optimizer) on the SE configuration task to produce an initial solution. This result is then fed as a seed/prompt into an LLM, which performs a final refinement step.
