The LLM is invoked only once at the end, inverting the standard control flow where the optimizer owns the search loop.
AI.result: Evaluated on over 100 SE configuration tasks, SNAP2 achieved top-tier results on 85% of tasks, surpassing the LLM-alone method (75%) and all classical-optimizer-controlled methods. It used ~30% fewer tokens and ran 1.4x faster than the LLM-alone baseline.
AI.conclusion: Studying classical learners and LLMs in isolation is suboptimal; combining them yields significant gains, and the ordering of that combination critically matters. Seeding an LLM with classical optimizer output (SNAP2) is more effective and efficient than the reverse, common approach.

title: Not All Refusals Are Equal: How Safety Alignment Fails Cybersecurity at Scale
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures. Under review at NeurIPS 2026
summary: There is no doubt that safety alignment is an essential step in LLM training. However, conceptually it does not distinguish between various domains and the level of potential harm of a query, which creates significant complications in the fields like cyber security, where a model should not be constrained by its safety circuits to accomplish the goals of legitimate, authorized operations. In this work, we share our findings from a large scale abliteration experiment on 24 open-source LLMs and show that domain-specific abliteration is achievable with standard methodology on the example of a 1T-parameter Kimi K2. Building on recent work showing that refusal in LLMs occupies a multi-dimensional subspace within layers, we find that it is also distributed widely across layers, especially in trillion-parameter MoE architectures, and so we aim to capture the part of it that represents harmful concepts in the cybersecurity domain exclusively. We also investigate the correlation between models' features and the effect of domain-specific abliteration, identifying that the type of safety training and architecture are the most reliable predictors. Finally, we classify the models into 3 \emph{abliteration susceptibility} tiers and put forward a set of conjectures as to why a particular effect from this intervention might be observed in a given model.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a large-scale study on domain-specific abliteration — selectively removing safety refusal mechanisms in LLMs for specific domains like cybersecurity — conducted across 24 open-source models, including the 1T-parameter Kimi K2. The authors find that refusal representations are distributed across many layers (especially in MoE architectures), demonstrate successful domain-specific abliteration, and classify models into three susceptibility tiers based on safety training type and architecture.
AI.motivation: Standard safety alignment in LLMs applies blanket restrictions without distinguishing between harmful and legitimate use-cases within specific domains (e.g., cybersecurity). This creates complications where models are overly constrained by safety circuits, preventing them from performing authorized, legitimate operations. The authors seek to understand whether safety refusal can be ablated in a domain-specific manner rather than globally.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale abliteration experiment on 24 open-source LLMs, including the 1T-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Kimi K2. They build on prior work showing refusal occupies a multi-dimensional subspace within layers and investigate its distribution across layers. They apply standard abliteration methodology targeting only the cybersecurity domain's harmful concepts, analyze which model features (safety training type, architecture) correlate with abliteration effectiveness, and classify models into susceptibility tiers.
AI.result: Domain-specific abliteration is achievable using standard methodology, as demonstrated on Kimi K2. Refusal representations are distributed widely across layers, particularly in trillion-parameter MoE architectures. The type of safety training and model architecture are the most reliable predictors of abliteration susceptibility. Models can be classified into three distinct susceptibility tiers.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific abliteration is feasible and can selectively remove safety constraints in targeted domains like cybersecurity while preserving alignment elsewhere. The distribution of refusal across layers — especially in large MoE models — and the importance of safety training type and architecture as predictors offer insights into why different models respond differently to abliteration interventions.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Data-Efficient Code-Switched ASR
summary: Audio-language models can be prompted for code-switched speech, but their decoding is not optimized for code-switching and often fails at language boundaries. We propose a practical reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards recipe for data-efficient adaptation of audio-language models to code-switched ASR using group relative policy optimization, combining an error rate reward with a script fidelity reward that penalizes wrong writing systems and a two-pass draft-and-refinement procedure. Using Qwen2-Audio as a reproducible testbed across 10 language pairs, training on only TTS code-switched speech, we show that RLVR with 10% of the data matches LoRA supervised fine-tuning trained on the full dataset, with the largest gains on typologically distant pairs. The error rate reward eliminates translation errors while the script fidelity reward separately reduces script contamination without degradation. These gains transfer zero-shot to a human-recorded code-switching corpus.

AI.tldr: RLVR with a two-pass draft-and-refinement approach and dual rewards (error rate + script fidelity) on TTS data enables data-efficient code-switched ASR adaptation, matching full-data SFT with only 10% of data and zero-shot transferring to human speech.
AI.motivation: Audio-language models struggle with code-switched speech, frequently failing at language boundaries because their decoding is not optimized for code-switching. The authors aim to address this with a data-efficient adaptation method.
AI.method: Using Qwen2-Audio as the backbone, the authors apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), an RLVR method, with two verifiable rewards: (1) an error rate reward (WER/CER) to reduce translation errors, and (2) a script fidelity reward to penalize incorrect writing system usage. A two-pass draft-and-refinement procedure is employed. Training uses only TTS code-switched speech across 10 language pairs, with varying amounts of data (down to 10%).
AI.result: RLVR with 10% of TTS data matches LoRA SFT trained on the full dataset. The largest gains occur on typologically distant language pairs. The error rate reward eliminates translation errors, while script fidelity reward reduces script contamination without degrading performance. Gains transfer zero-shot to a human-recorded code-switching corpus.
AI.conclusion: RLVR with verifiable rewards is a highly data-efficient and effective strategy for adapting audio-language models to code-switched ASR, outperforming supervised fine-tuning at low data regimes and generalizing to real human speech.

title: QuantFlow: A Federated Mamba-Based Post-Transformer Foundation Model for Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Time-series forecasting supports decisions in finance, en-ergy, transportation, public health, and industrial monitoring. Recent foundation models improve transfer across forecast-ing tasks, but many depend on centralized data and Trans-former attention, which restricts their use for long, high-di-mensional, and privacy-sensitive signals. This paper presents QuantFlow, a probabilistic forecasting framework that com-bines inverted sequence embedding, bidirectional Mamba state-space decoders, quantile regression, and federated learning. Each variable is embedded over the complete ob-servation window, processed in forward and reverse direc-tions, and projected to five conditional quantiles. TSMixup expands temporal diversity through Dirichlet-weighted inter-polation while preserving sequence structure. Experiments cover cryptocurrency, traffic, electricity, Electricity Trans-former Temperature, influenza, and weather data. QuantFlow obtains mean squared errors of 0.2834 on ETTm1 and 0.2218 on Weather, and a 20-client non-IID deployment retains use-ful accuracy after three communication rounds without cen-tralizing raw records. The results indicate that selective state-space modelling is a promising basis for scalable, uncer-tainty-aware, and privacy-conscious time-series prediction, while also revealing limitations on irregular epidemiological signals and long-horizon generalization.

AI.tldr: QuantFlow is a probabilistic time-series forecasting framework that integrates inverted sequence embedding, bidirectional Mamba state-space models, quantile regression, and federated learning to achieve scalable, uncertainty-aware predictions without centralizing raw data. It achieves strong MSE on standard benchmarks and retains accuracy under non-IID federated settings with minimal communication rounds.
AI.motivation: Existing time-series foundation models rely on centralized data and Transformer attention mechanisms, which are computationally expensive for long sequences, struggle with high-dimensional data, and are unsuitable for privacy-sensitive domains (e.g., healthcare, finance). There is a need for a scalable, uncertainty-aware, and privacy-preserving forecasting alternative.
AI.method: QuantFlow employs: (1) inverted sequence embedding, where each variable is embedded across the full observation window rather than per-timestep; (2) bidirectional Mamba state-space decoders that process sequences in both forward and reverse directions; (3) quantile regression to project outputs to five conditional quantiles for probabilistic forecasting; (4) TSMixup, a Dirichlet-weighted interpolation strategy that augments temporal diversity while preserving sequence structure; and (5) federated learning for decentralized, privacy-preserving training across clients.
AI.result: QuantFlow achieves MSE of 0.2834 on ETTm1 and 0.2218 on Weather benchmarks. In a 20-client non-IID federated deployment, useful accuracy is retained after only three communication rounds without centralizing raw records. Limitations are observed on irregular epidemiological signals and long-horizon generalization.
AI.conclusion: Selective state-space modeling (Mamba) combined with quantile regression and federated learning provides a promising foundation for scalable, uncertainty-aware, and privacy-conscious time-series forecasting, though challenges remain with irregular signals and long-horizon extrapolation.

title: ASK in the Dark: Uncertainty-Gated LLM Assistance under Partial Observability
comment: Accepted at the IJCAI-ECAI Joint Workshop on Planning for Complex Real-World Applications and Bridging the Gap Between AI Planning and (Reinforcement) Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning agents operating under partial observability must act on incomplete information, making them natural candidates for guidance from small language models (SLMs) that carry broad reasoning priors. Yet integrating SLM guidance into this setting has proven difficult: across all test environments, vanilla uncertainty-gated approaches achieve an overwrite rate at or near zero, meaning the SLM almost never contributes an independent action. We trace this failure to the bare egocentric prompt, which provides insufficient context for genuine reasoning, and identify it as a context problem rather than a capacity problem. We propose ASK+, which supplies the SLM with trajectory-aware context (a partially revealed map, visited positions, and action history) and structured chain-of-thought reasoning, converting it from a passive redundancy check into a more informative consultant that occasionally corrects the policy. We further establish that the predictive entropy signal used for selective querying measures action uncertainty rather than state uncertainty and remains informative in POMDPs, making uncertainty-gated assistance viable beyond fully observable settings. The stateful prompt drives substantial gains: on DoorKey, where vanilla ASK matches PPO (both 89%), ASK+ reaches 93% success; on FourRooms, success climbs from 53% to 70%; on HigherLower, accuracy reaches 73.7%, matching the SLM-only upper bound. Across all environments, Qwen3.5-2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-4B, confirming that prompt design and selective gating dominate the impact of model scale, enabling guidance without large models.

AI.tldr: SLMs can guide RL agents under partial observability, but standard ego-centric prompts fail because they lack context. The proposed ASK+ provides trajectory-aware context and chain-of-thought reasoning, transforming the SLM from a passive validator into an informative consultant. This yields significant performance gains across multiple POMDP environments, and a 2B model matches or exceeds a 4B model, showing that prompt design matters more than scale.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning agents under partial observability (POMDPs) could benefit from SLM guidance, but naive uncertainty-gated approaches fail because the SLM almost never contributes actions. The authors identify this as a context problem—bare egocentric prompts provide insufficient information for meaningful reasoning—not a capacity problem.
AI.method: ASK+ augments the SLM with trajectory-aware context (partially revealed map, visited positions, action history) and structured chain-of-thought reasoning. The SLM is queried selectively based on predictive entropy, which the authors show measures action uncertainty (not state uncertainty) and remains informative in POMDPs. This converts the SLM into a more informative consultant that occasionally overrides the policy.
AI.result: ASK+ achieves substantial gains: DoorKey success rises from 89% (vanilla ASK/PPO) to 93%; FourRooms from 53% to 70%; HigherLower accuracy reaches 73.7%, matching the SLM-only upper bound. Qwen3.5-2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-4B across all environments, confirming that prompt design and selective gating dominate model scale.
AI.conclusion: Effective SLM guidance in POMDPs hinges on providing rich, trajectory-aware context rather than larger models. Predictive entropy remains a viable uncertainty signal in partially observable settings. The ASK+ framework enables small models to serve as effective consultants, with prompt engineering and selective gating outweighing model capacity.

title: Enactive Drift Regulation and the Emergence Machine: A Framework for Coherent Adaptation Through Regulated Interaction
summary: Adaptive systems increasingly operate in environments characterized by persistent non-stationarity, where patterns reorganize rather than merely vary. While existing approaches such as online learning, continual learning, and adaptive filtering address performance degradation under changing data distributions, they typically treat drift as noise, error, or distribution shift to be corrected. This paper argues that such framings miss a more fundamental challenge: the loss of organizational coherence over time. We introduce Enactive Drift Regulation (EDR) as a general adaptive principle that treats drift as a regulatory signal indicating breakdowns in coherence between a system's internal organization and its environment. Rather than treating prediction optimization or retraining as sufficient, EDR reframes adaptation as the regulation of structure-maintaining, reorganizing, or transitioning internal dynamics to sustain viable operation under change. We present the Emergence Machine as an architectural instantiation of EDR, organized around regimes, attractors, coherence measures, reorganization dynamics, and memory across regimes. By shifting the focus from error minimization to coherence regulation, this work provides a principled framework for long-duration adaptation under non-stationarity and offers a bridge between adaptive control and enactive accounts of cognition.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Enactive Drift Regulation (EDR), a framework that reimagines adaptation to non-stationary environments not as error correction but as maintaining organizational coherence. It presents the Emergence Machine architecture to operationalize EDR through attractors, coherence measures, and reorganization dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches (online learning, continual learning, adaptive filtering) treat distribution drift as noise or error to be corrected, but this misses a deeper problem: systems lose organizational coherence under persistent non-stationarity where patterns reorganize, not merely vary. The authors argue a principled framework is needed for long-duration adaptation that addresses this fundamental breakdown.
AI.method: The authors develop EDR conceptually as a regulatory principle where drift signals breakdowns in system-environment coherence. They then propose the Emergence Machine architecture, which instantiates EDR through five key components: regimes, attractors, coherence measures, reorganization dynamics, and memory across regimes, shifting adaptation from error minimization to coherence regulation.
AI.result: The paper presents EDR as a general adaptive principle and the Emergence Machine as its architectural realization. It claims this reframing provides a principled framework for long-duration adaptation under non-stationarity and bridges adaptive control with enactive cognitive science.
AI.conclusion: By reframing adaptation as coherence regulation rather than error minimization, EDR offers a more adequate response to persistent non-stationarity. The Emergence Machine architecture operationalizes this principle, enabling systems to sustain viable operation by maintaining, reorganizing, or transitioning internal dynamics, thereby connecting adaptive control theory with enactive cognition.

title: Second MOASEI Competition at AAMAS'2026: A Technical Report
comment: Report from the MOASEI'2026 Competition held at AAMAS'2026
summary: We describe the 2026 Methods for Open Agent Systems Evaluation Initiative (MOASEI) Competition, a benchmark event for evaluating multi-agent decision-making under open-system conditions. Building on the inaugural 2025 competition, the 2026 edition retained wildfire fighting, cybersecurity, and ride-sharing domains while adding a bonus wildfire track with frame openness, in which agent equipment states such as suppressant capacities and firefighting range vary over time. The competition also expanded its reporting metrics to emphasize total task completions, mean task-completion time, and mean value of completed tasks. Participation in 2026 was limited: eight teams registered, but only one team submitted a final entry, and that entry targeted the ride-sharing track. The submitted DLC approach used planning and replanning to solve routing problems across agents as passengers appeared. This report summarizes the 2026 competition design, highlights differences from the previous year, and reports ride-sharing evaluation results against baseline policies. DLC is recognized as the 2026 ride-sharing track winner among submitted teams.

AI.tldr: Summary of the 2026 MOASEI Competition, a benchmark for multi-agent decision-making in open systems. One team (DLC) submitted to the ride-sharing track and won; the report details competition design, metric changes, and evaluation results.
AI.motivation: To advance evaluation of multi-agent decision-making under open-system conditions, where environments are dynamic, unpredictable, and agent capabilities may change over time (e.g., frame openness), building on the prior 2025 competition.
AI.method: The competition offered four domains: wildfire fighting, cybersecurity, ride-sharing, and a bonus wildfire track featuring frame openness (time-varying agent equipment states like suppressant capacities and range). Metrics emphasized total task completions, mean task-completion time, and mean value of completed tasks. The sole submitted entry (DLC) used planning and replanning to solve routing problems across agents as passengers appeared dynamically in the ride-sharing domain. Evaluation compared DLC against baseline policies.
AI.result: Eight teams registered but only one (DLC) submitted a final entry, targeting the ride-sharing track. DLC was recognized as the 2026 ride-sharing track winner among submitted teams.
AI.conclusion: The 2026 MOASEI Competition introduced expanded metrics and a novel bonus track with frame openness, but suffered from very limited participation. The sole submission, DLC, demonstrated effective planning-and-replanning for dynamic ride-sharing routing, highlighting both the competition's benchmark value and the need to attract broader engagement in future iterations.

title: AI Overviews in Academic Search: Evaluating AI-generated Summaries of Search Results in a Domain-specific Search Engine
summary: Evaluating search engine results pages (SERPs) to assess result relevance is a demanding step in academic search. In a formative mixed-methods design study, we examine AI-generated SERP-level summaries as a support feature in an academic search engine for social science information. First, we manually evaluated summaries of the top five results for 10 queries using two general-purpose models, one commercial and one open, deriving an exploratory six-category error taxonomy and five safeguards for scholarly deployment. We then conducted a within-subjects user study (n = 30) comparing interfaces with and without AI summaries. Confirmatory analyses showed consistent but non-significant trends favoring AI summaries for subjective workload, perceived usefulness, satisfaction, and decision-making confidence. Exploratory analyses suggested lower mental demand, with frustration also tending to be lower. Behaviorally, participants rarely expanded the summaries and descriptively made slightly fewer result clicks and query reformulations when summaries were available. Drawing on Information Foraging Theory and participant feedback, we suggest that AI summaries may concentrate SERP-level information scent to support early triage. Overall, the findings indicate that SERP-level AI summaries are a context- and user-dependent aid rather than a universal improvement, while contributing an error taxonomy, safeguard-aware deployment guidance, and concrete design implications for scholarly search.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates AI-generated SERP-level summaries as a support feature in academic search. Through manual evaluation (deriving an error taxonomy and safeguards) and a within-subjects user study (n=30), results show non-significant but consistent trends favoring AI summaries for workload, usefulness, satisfaction, and confidence. The authors frame findings using Information Foraging Theory, suggesting AI summaries concentrate information scent to aid early triage, while concluding the feature is a context- and user-dependent aid rather than a universal improvement.
AI.motivation: Evaluating SERPs for result relevance is a demanding, high-effort step in academic search. The authors aim to explore whether AI-generated SERP-level summaries can alleviate this burden for social science researchers, addressing a gap in understanding how such summaries affect user behavior, cognition, and experience in scholarly contexts.
AI.method: A formative mixed-methods design study with two phases: (1) Manual evaluation of AI summaries (from one commercial and one open model) for the top five results across 10 queries, yielding an exploratory six-category error taxonomy and five deployment safeguards. (2) A within-subjects user study (n=30) comparing interfaces with vs. without AI summaries, measuring subjective workload (NASA-TLX), perceived usefulness, satisfaction, decision-making confidence, and behavioral metrics (clicks, query reformulations, summary expansion). Analysis included both confirmatory and exploratory statistical testing, supplemented by qualitative participant feedback and interpretation through Information Foraging Theory.
AI.result: Confirmatory analyses showed consistent but non-significant trends favoring AI summaries across all subjective measures. Exploratory analyses indicated lower mental demand and a trend toward lower frustration with summaries. Behaviorally, participants rarely expanded summaries and descriptively made slightly fewer result clicks and query reformulations when summaries were present. The manual evaluation produced a six-category error taxonomy and five safeguards for scholarly deployment.
AI.conclusion: AI-generated SERP-level summaries function as a context- and user-dependent aid rather than a universal improvement for academic search. They may concentrate SERP-level information scent to support early triage, but their benefits are nuanced. The paper contributes an error taxonomy, safeguard-aware deployment guidance, and concrete design implications for integrating AI summaries into scholarly search interfaces.

title: The Moving Target: A Longitudinal Audit of Trustworthiness Drift Across Twelve Checkpoints of Open-Source Chat LLMs
comment: 22 pages, 2 figures; accepted as a poster at the ICML 2026 TAIGA Workshop
summary: Model cards quote trust-benchmark scores without recording when they were measured, and the same number is routinely carried across successive checkpoints of one release line as if the model behind it had not shifted. We test whether it has shifted by auditing four open-source release lines, Yi, Qwen, Mistral, and Gemma, at three successive generations each, on a fixed basket of trust benchmarks under multiple prompt templates. Mean absolute adjacent-generation drift lands well above an independence-based no-drift reference null, and the gap persists when we drop a benchmark, drop a release line, or switch to strict scoring. We therefore conclude that a trust score attached to a release line should not be carried forward to the next checkpoint without remeasurement; it should instead be reported as a checkpoint-bound, dated artefact, which we package as a longitudinal model card. Closed APIs, larger models, canonical benchmark protocols, and fixed month-cadence rules lie outside the audited scope and require their own evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper audits four open-source LLM release lines (Yi, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma) across three generations each, showing that trust benchmark scores drift significantly between adjacent checkpoints. It argues against carrying forward static trust scores and proposes longitudinal model cards with checkpoint-bound, dated measurements.
AI.motivation: Current practice treats trust-benchmark scores as static properties of a release line, carrying the same number across successive checkpoints without remeasurement. This implicitly assumes no model drift, which the authors test and challenge.
AI.method: The authors audit four open-source release lines at three successive generations each, evaluating on a fixed basket of trust benchmarks using multiple prompt templates. They compute mean absolute adjacent-generation drift and compare it against an independence-based no-drift reference null. Robustness is checked by dropping benchmarks, dropping release lines, and switching to strict scoring.
AI.result: Mean absolute adjacent-generation drift significantly exceeds the no-drift null across all conditions, and the gap remains robust to dropping a benchmark, dropping a release line, or using strict scoring. This indicates that model trust properties shift meaningfully between checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Trust scores should not be carried forward without remeasurement. Instead, they should be reported as checkpoint-bound, dated artefacts, packaged in a longitudinal model card. Closed APIs, larger models, canonical benchmark protocols, and fixed monthly cadences require separate evaluation.

title: Vision Token Manipulation Attacks on Cloud-Edge Inference of Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Cloud-edge Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) inference enables efficient deployment by splitting computation between edge devices and cloud servers. In this process, intermediate vision tokens are transmitted from the edge to the cloud over a communication link, thereby exposing a new attack surface. We study vision token manipulation attack (VTM-Attack) under a black-box man-in-the-middle setting, where an adversary intercepts and manipulates a subset of transmitted vision tokens under a budget constraint. We propose four naïve attack strategies and an optimization-based token selection method. Experiments on 6 state-of-the-art LVLMs (3B-72B) across 4 benchmarks show that manipulating only 10\% of vision tokens can reduce accuracy by up to 88.31\%. These results reveal a critical vulnerability in cloud-edge LVLM inference.

AI.tldr: A new attack called VTM-Attack targets cloud-edge LVLM inference by intercepting and manipulating a small subset of vision tokens transmitted from edge to cloud. Manipulating only 10% of vision tokens reduces accuracy by up to 88.31%, exposing a critical vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Cloud-edge LVLM inference splits computation between edge devices and cloud servers, but transmitting intermediate vision tokens over a communication link introduces a new attack surface. The authors aim to investigate whether an adversary performing a man-in-the-middle attack can manipulate these tokens to degrade model performance, revealing a previously unexamined security weakness.
AI.method: The authors propose the Vision Token Manipulation Attack (VTM-Attack) under a black-box man-in-the-middle threat model. An adversary intercepts and manipulates a subset of vision tokens within a budget constraint. They introduce four naïve attack strategies plus an optimization-based token selection method. Attacks are evaluated on 6 state-of-the-art LVLMs (ranging from 3B to 72B parameters) across 4 benchmarks.
AI.result: Manipulating only 10% of vision tokens achieves up to 88.31% accuracy reduction on the evaluated LVLMs. The attack is effective across all 6 models tested, from 3B to 72B parameters, demonstrating the vulnerability is pervasive and severe.
AI.conclusion: Cloud-edge LVLM inference is critically vulnerable to vision token manipulation attacks. Even a budget-constrained adversary manipulating a small fraction of tokens can nearly destroy model accuracy, highlighting an urgent need for defenses in cloud-edge deployment pipelines.

title: LuxSQA: Ask Me in Luxembourgish with TTS-Augmented Spoken Question Answering
summary: Spoken Question Answering (SQA) remains largely focused on high-resource languages and carefully recorded speech, limiting the reach of speech-LLM methods in low-resource settings. This paper investigates whether text-to-speech (TTS) can provide task-specific training data for Luxembourgish SQA without requiring a large human-recorded QA corpus. Starting from existing text-based QA resources, we translate questions into Luxembourgish, synthesize spoken questions with multiple TTS systems, and pair them with textual answers. We train a parameter-efficient SLAM-style architecture that connects a frozen Whisper encoder to frozen multilingual LLM backends through a learned projector and LoRA adapters. We compare MMS-TTS, Qwen3-TTS, and OmniVoice variants, including single-source corpora of about 48k questions and a 4TTS multi-source mix of approximately 230k questions. Evaluation on LLAMA-LB-Test with two real Luxembourgish speaker conditions shows that multi-source and voice-design-based synthetic training configurations yield the strongest SQA performance. The results also show that no-reference TTS quality scores do not monotonically predict downstream QA performance, indicating that synthetic speech must be evaluated as task-specific training data rather than only as natural-sounding audio.

AI.tldr: TTS-generated Luxembourgish speech paired with text QA data enables spoken QA in a low-resource language. Multi-source TTS training data outperforms single-source, and standard TTS quality metrics do not predict downstream QA accuracy.
AI.motivation: Spoken Question Answering is underexplored in low-resource languages due to the scarcity of human-recorded speech QA corpora. The authors aim to determine whether TTS can substitute for real recordings in training SQA systems for Luxembourgish.
AI.method: Existing text QA resources are translated into Luxembourgish, then synthesized using multiple TTS systems (MMS-TTS, Qwen3-TTS, OmniVoice). A parameter-efficient SLAM architecture couples a frozen Whisper encoder to frozen multilingual LLMs via a learned projector and LoRA adapters. Single-source (~48k questions) and multi-source 4TTS mixes (~230k questions) are compared on the LLAMA-LB-Test benchmark with two real speaker conditions.
AI.result: Multi-source TTS training configurations and voice-design-based synthetic data yield the strongest SQA performance. No-reference TTS quality scores do not monotonically predict downstream QA performance, indicating synthetic speech must be evaluated as task-specific training data, not merely for naturalness.
AI.conclusion: TTS-generated data is a viable substitute for human-recorded speech in low-resource SQA. Practitioners should prioritize multi-source synthetic data and task-specific evaluation over generic TTS quality metrics when building speech-language models for underrepresented languages.

title: GRAFT: Grafted Reference Audio for Fine-grained Pronunciation in Zero-shot Text-to-Speech
summary: We present GRAFT, a per-word pronunciation conditioning mechanism for text-to-speech neural codec language modeling. Existing systems reach high intelligibility and naturalness but inherit the ambiguity of text and mispronounce rare proper nouns, loanwords and technical terms. Even phoneme-conditioned models offer no direct acoustic handle for per-word pronunciation. GRAFT controls the pronunciation of a chosen word from a short spoken sample of it, encoded with the model's own speech tokenizer and bound to the word's position in the prompt. Voice conversion during training-data construction disentangles the hint speaker from the target speaker, so the hint may come from any voice while the output stays in the target voice. In a blind English listening study, human raters rank GRAFT first by a clear margin, judging its rendering of the difficult word closest to a reference recording of that word. On a five-language objective benchmark, GRAFT reduces target-word phoneme error rate by 22-39% over the identical text-only backbone and outperforms competitive open-source zero-shot systems, both phoneme- and text-conditioned, on target-word pronunciation, while preserving speaker similarity and naturalness.

AI.tldr: GRAFT is a per-word pronunciation conditioning mechanism for TTS neural codec language models that uses short spoken samples to control the pronunciation of individual words, reducing phoneme error rates by 22-39% while preserving speaker similarity and naturalness.
AI.motivation: Existing TTS systems mispronounce rare proper nouns, loanwords, and technical terms due to text ambiguity. Even phoneme-conditioned models lack a direct acoustic handle for per-word pronunciation control. GRAFT addresses this gap by enabling explicit pronunciation control via spoken exemplars.
AI.method: GRAFT conditions per-word pronunciation using a short spoken sample of the target word, encoded with the model's own speech tokenizer. The hint is bound to the word's position in the prompt. Voice conversion during training-data construction disentangles the hint speaker from the target speaker, allowing the hint to come from any voice while preserving the target voice in the output.
AI.result: In a blind English listening study, human raters ranked GRAFT first by a clear margin for rendering difficult words closest to a reference recording. On a five-language objective benchmark, GRAFT reduces target-word phoneme error rate by 22-39% over the identical text-only backbone and outperforms competitive open-source zero-shot systems on pronunciation while preserving speaker similarity and naturalness.
AI.conclusion: GRAFT effectively combines the flexibility of neural codec language modeling with precise per-word pronunciation control, offering significant improvements in handling challenging lexical items across multiple languages without sacrificing voice quality or naturalness.

title: Automated Data Readiness for Scientific AI
summary: Leadership computing facilities steward large-scale scientific datasets that routinely require substantial transformation before serving as AI training data. However, no existing framework fully unifies automated transformation, readiness assessment, provenance tracking, and agent-native deployment. We present REDI, an open-source framework that addresses this gap through a unified five-stage pipeline (ingest, preprocess, transform, structure, and output) with per-stage instrumentation for reproducibility and deployment as an agent-callable skill; companion tool SetGo automates FAIR compliance and catalog publication. Evaluated across climate, proteomics, materials science, and nuclear fusion, REDI transforms all datasets from raw to AI-ready, with outputs validated against domain-expert references, and preliminary results show near-ideal parallel scaling to 100 nodes on Frontier for the climate case. Provenance-instrumented profiling reveals file I/O as the dominant pipeline cost, with format selection a first-order optimization lever. These results establish REDI as a cross-domain platform providing automated data readiness for scientific AI, transforming data preparation bottlenecks into reproducible, reusable community assets.

AI.tldr: REDI is an open-source, agent-native framework that automates the transformation of large-scale scientific datasets into AI-ready formats through a five-stage pipeline with provenance tracking, demonstrating near-ideal scaling on HPC systems and validated across four scientific domains.
AI.motivation: Leadership computing facilities manage massive scientific datasets that require significant transformation before they can be used as AI training data. Existing frameworks fail to unify automated transformation, readiness assessment, provenance tracking, and agent-native deployment into a single system, creating a bottleneck in scientific AI workflows.
AI.method: REDI implements a unified five-stage pipeline: (1) ingest, (2) preprocess, (3) transform, (4) structure, and (5) output. Each stage is instrumented for reproducibility and provenance tracking. The framework deploys as an agent-callable skill. A companion tool, SetGo, automates FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) compliance and catalog publication. Evaluation covers four domains: climate, proteomics, materials science, and nuclear fusion. Parallel scaling was tested on the Frontier supercomputer up to 100 nodes.
AI.result: REDI successfully transformed all datasets from raw to AI-ready state across all four domains, with outputs validated against domain-expert references. Near-ideal parallel scaling was demonstrated on Frontier up to 100 nodes for the climate use case. Provenance-instrumented profiling identified file I/O as the dominant pipeline cost and revealed format selection as a first-order optimization lever.
AI.conclusion: REDI establishes itself as a cross-domain platform for automated data readiness in scientific AI, converting data preparation bottlenecks into reproducible, reusable community assets. The framework's provenance instrumentation, agent-native design, and FAIR compliance automation distinguish it from prior approaches.

title: Post-Lecture Interactive Environments for Conceptual Learning: A Randomized Comparison of Mixed Reality and Tangible Instruction in Undergraduate STEM Education
summary: Developing conceptual understanding in engineering requires learners to connect spatial reasoning with abstract representations, yet lecture-based instruction often provides limited support for this process. Interactive learning environments, including mixed reality (MR) and tangible tools, may help students revisit difficult concepts through action, feedback, and visible system response. This pilot randomized study compared two post-lecture interventions, an immersive MR application and a tangible Engineering Toolkit, with lecture-only instruction in undergraduate solid mechanics. Twenty-four participants completed a baseline assessment, a common lecture, and a post-instruction knowledge test; participants in the interactive conditions also completed usability and learner-experience measures. Learning outcomes were analyzed using ANCOVA with baseline knowledge as a covariate and were supported by normalized learning gains. Instructional modality had a significant effect on post-test performance, $F(2, 20) = 3.60$, $p = .048$, partial $η^2 = .263$. Both interactive conditions outperformed lecture-only instruction in planned contrasts. MR showed the highest normalized learning gain ($g = .57$), whereas the tangible toolkit showed higher usability and learner confidence. In the MR condition, virtual reality sickness symptoms measured via the Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire remained low before and after the intervention, suggesting that the MR application was well-tolerated by participants. These results suggest that post-lecture interactive environments may support immediate conceptual learning while offering different modality-specific strengths that require larger, time-matched follow-up studies.

AI.tldr: A pilot RCT compared mixed reality (MR), a tangible toolkit, and lecture-only instruction for teaching solid mechanics. Both interactive conditions outperformed lecture-only; MR showed the highest learning gains, while the tangible toolkit rated higher on usability and confidence. MR also produced low VR sickness, suggesting good tolerability.
AI.motivation: Lecture-based engineering instruction provides limited support for connecting spatial reasoning with abstract representations. Interactive environments like MR and tangible tools may better support conceptual understanding through action, feedback, and visible system response.
AI.method: Pilot randomized controlled trial with 24 undergraduate participants. All received a baseline assessment and common lecture, then were assigned to one of three conditions: immersive MR application, tangible Engineering Toolkit, or lecture-only. A post-instruction knowledge test was administered. ANCOVA (covarying baseline knowledge) and normalized learning gains were used to analyze outcomes. Usability, learner experience, and VR sickness (VRSQ) were also measured.
AI.result: ANCOVA showed a significant effect of modality on post-test performance: F(2,20)=3.60, p=.048, partial η²=.263. Both interactive conditions outperformed lecture-only in planned contrasts. MR had the highest normalized learning gain (g=.57). The tangible toolkit showed higher usability and learner confidence. VRSQ scores remained low pre- to post-intervention in the MR condition.
AI.conclusion: Post-lecture interactive environments support immediate conceptual learning, with MR and tangible tools offering distinct modality-specific strengths. Larger, time-matched follow-up studies are warranted.

title: MUTE: Return-Preserving Communication Unlearning for Efficient Multi-Agent Coordination
summary: Inter-agent communication is critical for coordinating Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) agents under partial observability to perform effectively in cooperative games; however, real-world bandwidth constraints demand sparse interactions. Prior approaches primarily address this trade-off by optimizing information-theoretic surrogates. We argue that these statistical proxies are fundamentally misaligned with the true objective: a message can be highly informative yet irrelevant to the joint return of the task. In this work, we propose Message Unlearning for Targeted Efficiency (MUTE), a framework that views communication reduction as a value-guided machine unlearning problem. MUTE rigorously quantifies the Counterfactual Message Value using an attention-based estimator, and systematically unlearns the transmission of low-value messages from a policy trained without any communication constraints. This is achieved through a dual-objective mechanism that enforces communication sparsity while preserving the return of the original joint policy. We derive a theoretical upper bound on the performance gap induced by this sparsification, guaranteeing controlled return degradation. We also empirically evaluate MUTE on various complex multi-agent environments, achieving 80% to 90% bandwidth reduction while maintaining performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: MUTE frames communication reduction in MARL as a value-guided machine unlearning problem, using Counterfactual Message Value to identify and prune low-value messages, achieving 80-90% bandwidth reduction with minimal performance loss.
AI.motivation: Existing sparse communication methods for MARL optimize information-theoretic proxies (e.g., mutual information), which are misaligned with the true objective of maximizing joint return. A message can be statistically informative but task-irrelevant, leading to suboptimal communication pruning.
AI.method: MUTE introduces: (1) an attention-based Counterfactual Message Value estimator to quantify each message's contribution to joint return; (2) a value-guided unlearning framework that trains a sparsifier to suppress low-value messages via a dual-objective mechanism balancing sparsity and return preservation; (3) a theoretical upper bound on performance degradation from sparsification.
AI.result: MUTE achieves 80-90% bandwidth reduction across various complex multi-agent environments while maintaining performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Framing communication reduction as value-guided unlearning rather than information-theoretic optimization provides a more principled approach to sparse MARL communication, enabling substantial bandwidth savings with formal performance guarantees.

title: Improving Access to Historical Archives with Real-time RAG-based Systems
summary: Digitized historical archives are large, heterogeneous cultural heritage repositories, but access methods for such archives face challenges such as noisy optical character recognition (OCR) output and rigid keyword-based retrieval, which limit retrieval quality. In this work, we present an end-to-end archival processing and retrieval framework that integrates large language models (LLMs) into the archival pipeline. Our system introduces two core components: (i) an LLM-based OCR refinement module that improves text quality, and (ii) a semantic retrieval and cross-encoder reranking pipeline supporting natural-language question answering via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Our evaluations are done on a historical archival dataset of 500,000 Swiss newspaper segments spanning over three centuries (1762 to 2001). Experiments are conducted across 384 natural-language test queries. Our results highlight that LLM refinements reduce OCR errors by up to 44.52% (CER) and 60.95% (WER). More importantly, this is accompanied by downstream information retrieval improvements. Compared to traditional keyword baselines, our reranking pipeline increases NDCG@10 by 31.9% (from 65.99% to 87.05%) and achieves statistically significant gains in both answer correctness and context relevance. These results demonstrate that integrating LLMs with established document processing and retrieval pipelines can elevate digital libraries from static repositories to interactive, semantically searchable archival systems.

AI.tldr: A framework integrating LLMs into archival pipelines: OCR refinement reduces errors by up to 60.95% WER, and semantic retrieval with cross-encoder reranking improves NDCG@10 by 31.9% on a 500,000-document Swiss newspaper dataset spanning 1762–2001.
AI.motivation: Digitized historical archives suffer from noisy OCR output and rigid keyword-based retrieval, limiting access quality. The authors aim to modernize archival search by leveraging LLMs for both text cleanup and semantic, natural-language querying.
AI.method: An end-to-end framework with two core components: (1) an LLM-based OCR refinement module that post-corrects noisy historical text, and (2) a semantic retrieval pipeline combining dense retrieval with cross-encoder reranking, topped by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for natural-language QA. Evaluated on 500,000 Swiss newspaper segments (1762–2001) with 384 test queries.
AI.result: OCR refinement reduced CER by up to 44.52% and WER by up to 60.95%. The reranking pipeline improved NDCG@10 from 65.99% (keyword baseline) to 87.05%, a 31.9% relative gain. Statistically significant improvements were also observed in answer correctness and context relevance metrics.
AI.conclusion: LLM integration into archival document processing and retrieval pipelines transforms digital libraries from static repositories into interactive, semantically searchable systems, with both OCR quality and downstream IR performance substantially improved.

title: OmniPresent: Generating Coherent Presentation Suites from Scientific Papers
summary: Transforming static research papers into dynamic media such as posters, slides, and videos is essential for effective dissemination but remains a labor-intensive challenge. Existing automated approaches often treat these formats in isolation and consequently fail to maintain semantic consistency across the entire presentation suite. We address this fragmentation by formalizing the task of unified presentation suite generation and proposing $\textbf{OmniPresent}$ to orchestrate the creation of coherent deliverables. Our framework adopts a renderable HTML representation to enable centralized content planning and a self-correcting verify-and-repair loop that actively resolves conflicts across modalities. We further facilitate scalable research in this domain by releasing $\textbf{OmniPreBench}$, a comprehensive dataset comprising over one thousand papers with paired artifacts, and establishing a rigorous VLM-based evaluation protocol. Empirical results confirm that our method generates high-quality and faithful presentation suites that significantly surpass strong baselines in both accuracy and visual appeal.

AI.tldr: OmniPresent introduces a unified framework for transforming static research papers into semantically consistent presentation suites (posters, slides, videos) using renderable HTML with a self-correcting verify-and-repair loop. The authors also release OmniPreBench, a 1,000+ paper dataset with paired artifacts, and a VLM-based evaluation protocol, demonstrating superior accuracy and visual quality over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing automated tools for converting research papers into dynamic media formats (posters, slides, videos) treat each format in isolation, leading to semantic inconsistency across the presentation suite. There is a need for a unified approach that ensures coherence across all deliverables.
AI.method: The proposed framework, OmniPresent, uses a renderable HTML representation for centralized content planning across modalities. It employs a self-correcting verify-and-repair loop to actively detect and resolve cross-modal conflicts. The authors also introduce OmniPreBench (1,000+ papers with paired artifacts) and a VLM-based (Vision-Language Model) evaluation protocol for rigorous assessment.
AI.result: Empirical results show that OmniPresent significantly outperforms strong baselines in both accuracy and visual appeal, generating high-quality, faithful presentation suites.
AI.conclusion: OmniPresent effectively unifies paper-to-multimedia generation, resolving cross-format inconsistency through centralized HTML planning and iterative self-correction. The accompanying benchmark and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for scalable future research in this domain.

title: Git Hash Chain Malleability
summary: Git commit signing is widely entrusted to serve as evidence that a commit hash uniquely and immutably identifies a specific piece of signed content. We show this invariant does not hold. Given any signed commit, an attacker without access to the signing key, and without breaking SHA2 can produce a second, distinct commit with an identical tree, identical metadata, a valid signature, and a ``Verified'' badge from a Git Forge such as Github, differing only in its commit hash. The modified commit cascades to modify the values of all the subsequent, dependent commit hashes, hence we introduce the terminology ``hash chain malleability'' to describe this phenomenon. The malleability in signed Git hashes is feasible due to the inherent malleability present in many of the data representations that make up a commit. In this paper we show three such malleation routes: (i) algebraic inversion s -> n-s for ECDSA; (ii) structural insertion of an unhashed OpenPGP subpacket (RFC4880 5.2.3) for RSA and EdDSA; and (iii) non-canonical DER length re-encoding (X.690 10.1) inside the CMS envelope for S/MIME. Algebraic inversion for ECDSA signatures and subpacket insertion were found to pass local verification (git verify-commit), and all three methods yield a persistent, independent ``Verified'' record on Github. We discuss the consequences of Git hash chain malleation for hash-based commit blocking, dependency pinning (Nixpkgs, Go modules, Github Actions), and reproducible-build systems that treat the commit hash as a content-addressable primary key, and we provide proof-of-concept tooling that automates all three routes.

AI.tldr: Git's signed commits are not immutable: attackers can create distinct, validly-signed commits with different hashes but identical content, breaking the assumption that a commit hash uniquely identifies signed content. Three malleation techniques are demonstrated, all producing "Verified" badges on GitHub.
AI.motivation: To expose a critical security flaw in the widely-held assumption that signed Git commit hashes are immutable and uniquely identify specific content. This assumption underpins commit blocking, dependency pinning, and reproducible builds, making the vulnerability practically significant.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate three distinct malleation routes: (1) ECDSA algebraic inversion (s → n-s), exploiting signature symmetry; (2) OpenPGP unhashed subpacket insertion (RFC4880 §5.2.3) for RSA and EdDSA, injecting data outside the signed digest; (3) non-canonical DER length re-encoding (X.690 §10.1) within the CMS envelope for S/MIME. All were tested against `git verify-commit` locally and GitHub's verification infrastructure.
AI.result: All three methods produce a second, distinct commit with identical tree, identical metadata, a valid signature, and a "Verified" badge on GitHub, differing only in commit hash. This cascades to alter all subsequent dependent commit hashes—termed "hash chain malleability." ECDSA inversion and subpacket insertion pass local verification; all three yield persistent independent Verified records on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Git hash chain malleability undermines security schemes relying on commit hash immutability, including hash-based commit blocking, dependency pinning (Nixpkgs, Go modules, GitHub Actions), and reproducible-build systems. The authors provide proof-of-concept tooling for all three attack routes.

title: Gemma 4 Technical Report
summary: We introduce Gemma 4, a new generation of open-weight, natively multimodal language models in the Gemma model family. Designed to advance compute efficiency and reasoning, the Gemma 4 model suite features dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, ranging from 2.3B to 31B parameters. Alongside improved vision and audio encoders for all model sizes, we propose a unified, encoder-free architecture for our 12B model, which ingests raw audio and image patches. Furthermore, we integrate a thinking mode, enabling Gemma models to generate reasoning traces prior to responding. We improve inference speed, memory, and compute efficiency, as well as long-context abilities through critical design choices. Gemma 4 establishes a leap in performance across STEM, multimodal, and long-context benchmarks, and rivals larger, frontier open models in human-rated tasks.

AI.tldr: Gemma 4 introduces a new generation of open-weight, natively multimodal language models (2.3B–31B) with dense and MoE architectures, featuring a unified encoder-free design for the 12B model, a thinking mode for reasoning traces, and significant improvements in efficiency, long-context capabilities, and benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: To advance compute efficiency and reasoning capabilities in open-weight multimodal language models, enabling competitive performance with larger frontier models while maintaining practical deployability across diverse scales.
AI.method: The Gemma 4 suite employs dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures (2.3B–31B parameters), improved vision/audio encoders across all sizes, and a novel unified encoder-free architecture for the 12B model that directly ingests raw audio and image patches. A thinking mode is integrated to generate reasoning traces before responding. Critical design choices optimize inference speed, memory usage, compute efficiency, and long-context handling.
AI.result: Gemma 4 achieves a significant leap in performance on STEM, multimodal, and long-context benchmarks, and rivals larger frontier open models in human-rated evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The Gemma 4 model family demonstrates that open-weight, natively multimodal models with thoughtful architectural innovations (encoder-free design, thinking mode, MoE scaling) can achieve frontier-competitive performance while maintaining efficiency across a range of model sizes.

title: Federated Learning for Object Detection: Enabling Collaborative Drone Learning Without Centralizing Data
summary:
Object detection is a fundamental capability for AI-driven perception in safety-critical drone and edge-vision systems, including disaster response, operational security environments, infrastructure monitoring and defense applications. Robust model performance in such environments depends on large, continuously updated datasets. However, training high-performing detectors typically requires centralizing aerial imagery, which raises privacy, regulatory, storage, and bandwidth challenges. This is especially problematic in distributed drone deployments, where visual data is generated onboard and is often impractical or undesirable to transfer to a centralized infrastructure.
  In this work, we apply Federated Learning (FL) for object detection, enabling drones to improve a shared model while keeping image data local and private. We implement a federated object detection pipeline using the Sherpa.ai FL platform on the KIIT-MiTA dataset, and compare it with Single-drone and Centralized baselines using mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU thresholds of 0.50 and 0.50-0.95. In our experiments, the proposed FL approach remains close to Centralized training while dramatically improving over Single-drone training, with the best lightweight model (YOLO26 nano), suitable for deployment even on very limited edge infrastructure, achieving relative gains of 52.89% and 67.80% in mAP@0.50 and mAP@0.50:0.95, respectively. These results show that FL enables scalable, high-performing, and privacy-preserving object detection across distributed drone fleets without data centralization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Federated Learning (FL) framework for drone-based object detection, enabling collaborative model training without centralizing sensitive aerial imagery. Using the Sherpa.ai FL platform on the KIIT-MiTA dataset, the FL approach achieves performance close to centralized training and significantly outperforms single-drone training, with the lightweight YOLOv8 nano model yielding relative gains of 52.89% (mAP@0.50) and 67.80% (mAP@0.50:0.95) over the single-drone baseline.
AI.motivation: Training high-performance object detectors for drone and edge-vision systems typically requires centralizing aerial imagery, which introduces privacy, regulatory, storage, and bandwidth challenges — particularly acute in distributed drone deployments where onboard visual data is impractical or undesirable to transfer. The authors aim to address the tension between model performance and data privacy/communication constraints.
AI.method: The authors implement a federated object detection pipeline using the Sherpa.ai FL framework. They evaluate on the KIIT-MiTA aerial imagery dataset and compare three training paradigms: (1) Federated Learning (FL) across multiple drones, (2) Centralized training with all data aggregated, and (3) Single-drone training in isolation. Performance is measured via mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU thresholds of 0.50 and 0.50–0.95. The lightweight YOLOv8 nano architecture is assessed for edge-deployability.
AI.result: The FL approach achieves performance close to the Centralized baseline while dramatically outperforming the Single-drone baseline. Specifically, the YOLOv8 nano model under FL achieves relative improvements of 52.89% in mAP@0.50 and 67.80% in mAP@0.50:0.95 compared to single-drone training. This demonstrates that FL enables scalable, privacy-preserving object detection without significant performance degradation.
AI.conclusion: Federated Learning is a viable and effective paradigm for privacy-preserving object detection across distributed drone fleets. It delivers near-centralized performance while eliminating the need for data centralization, making it suitable for safety-critical applications in disaster response, infrastructure monitoring, and defense where data sensitivity and bandwidth constraints are paramount.

title: SwarmResearch: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Open-Ended Discovery
summary: Long-running coding agents such as autoresearch can persistently discover optimizations for open-ended problems. However, they tend to converge onto a single high-level approach, then proceed with low-level edits while missing other superior approaches to the problem. We hypothesize two harness-level design choices contribute to this behavior: accumulating context in a single long-running agent and only exposing a single program state to edit. We introduce SwarmResearch, an orchestrator-subagent harness in which a Shepherd Agent uses global context to steer a population of Search Agents, each operating with local context in their respective git branch. On open-ended optimization tasks, SwarmResearch discovers better or comparable solutions to state-of-the-art LLM-guided evolution and multi-agent techniques on 13/15 tasks, driven by higher-level exploration. Compared with fixed scaling of serial and parallel agents, SwarmResearch's orchestrator-guided scaling discovers better-performing solutions by adapting parallelism at different search depths.

AI.tldr: SwarmResearch proposes an orchestrator-subagent architecture where a Shepherd Agent guides multiple Search Agents with isolated git branches, overcoming the convergence limitations of single-agent approaches. It achieves superior or comparable results on 13/15 open-ended optimization tasks by enabling higher-level exploration through adaptive parallelism.
AI.motivation: Long-running coding agents for open-ended optimization tend to prematurely converge on a single high-level approach and then only perform low-level edits, missing superior alternative solutions. The authors identify two harness-level design flaws: accumulating context in a single long-running agent and exposing only a single program state to edit.
AI.method: SwarmResearch uses an orchestrator-subagent harness: a Shepherd Agent maintains global context and steers a population of Search Agents. Each Search Agent operates with local context in its own isolated git branch. The orchestrator adaptively scales parallelism at different search depths, enabling higher-level exploration across diverse approaches rather than converging on one.
AI.result: SwarmResearch discovers better or comparable solutions to state-of-the-art LLM-guided evolution and multi-agent techniques on 13 out of 15 open-ended optimization tasks. Compared to fixed scaling of serial and parallel agents, the orchestrator-guided approach finds better-performing solutions by dynamically adapting parallelism at varying search depths.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling global orchestration from local search via a Shepherd Agent and isolated Search Agents effectively mitigates premature convergence in long-running coding agents, enabling higher-level exploration and superior optimization outcomes through adaptive parallelism.

title: Scalable Semantic Steering of Embedding Projections
comment: Accepted as a short paper at IEEE VIS 2026. 5 pages, 2 figures
summary: Low-dimensional projections support interactive visual analysis of high-dimensional data embeddings, but their structure often does not align with analyst-defined semantic relationships. Recent LLM-augmented semantic steering methods address this gap by externalizing analyst intent from user-defined groups of seed examples, but they propagate intent through per-item LLM reasoning, causing LLM calls and cost to grow linearly with collection size. We propose a scalable semantic steering method that shifts semantic computation from individual items to user-defined groups. A single LLM call generates structured profiles for all groups, which are embedded and combined with seed centroids to form hybrid semantic prototypes. The method then propagates intent without retraining, using embedding-space soft assignment, abstention, and alignment-scaled updates before reprojection. On a 5K-document LitCovid corpus, our method achieves global alignment comparable to per-item LLM steering while reducing LLM calls by over three orders of magnitude. An image case study shows that the same prototype-based mechanism extends to multimodal embeddings. These results suggest that group-level representations can make semantic steering more practical for larger embedding collections.

AI.tldr: A scalable semantic steering method for high-dimensional embeddings that shifts LLM computation from per-item reasoning to group-level prototypes, reducing LLM calls by over 1000x while maintaining comparable alignment quality.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-augmented semantic steering methods for interactive visual analysis require per-item LLM reasoning, causing computational cost to scale linearly with dataset size. This makes them impractical for large embedding collections. The authors aim to break this linear dependency by shifting semantic reasoning to the group level.
AI.method: The method uses a single LLM call to generate structured textual profiles for all user-defined groups simultaneously. These profiles are embedded and combined with seed centroid embeddings to form hybrid semantic prototypes. Intent is propagated to all data points via embedding-space soft assignment, abstention (for ambiguous points), and alignment-scaled updates, all without retraining, before reprojection.
AI.result: On a 5K-document LitCovid corpus, the method achieves global alignment quality comparable to per-item LLM steering while reducing LLM calls by over three orders of magnitude. An image case study further demonstrates that the prototype-based mechanism extends to multimodal embeddings.
AI.conclusion: Group-level semantic representations can make LLM-augmented semantic steering significantly more practical and scalable for large embedding collections, without sacrificing alignment quality.

title: Dynamic Airspace Management for UAVs in Evolving Urban Environments: Collaborative Coordination and Human Safety
summary: The low-altitude economy is an emerging industry with significant development potential, in which the safety of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations is a critical challenge. Particularly within complex urban topographies and human-populated environments, UAV airspace management must prioritize collision avoidance and human safety. We propose Pharos, a collaborative multi-UAV airspace management system. Pharos lies between the distributed local perception paradigm and the centralized fine-grained control paradigm. Pharos coordinates the safe parallel execution of UAVs in shared airspace while innovatively accounting for the impact of human fear. Pharos is implemented using the MAPPO algorithm due to its faster convergence and higher rewards than other typical MARL algorithms (HAPPO and HATRPO). To evaluate Pharos, we developed a 3D simulation system using real urban data. Visualization results demonstrate its effective airspace coordination capability. Regarding performance verification, Pharos reduced human fear by 52.72% compared to the benchmark Ipopt. Moreover, we designed spatial entropy as a system evaluation metric to quantify space utilization, which improved performance by 70.82% and 2.03% compared to the benchmarks Ipopt and A-star, respectively. The source code is available at an anonymized repository: https://github.com/pharos-anonymized/source-code.git.

AI.tldr: Pharos is a collaborative multi-UAV airspace management system that uses the MAPPO reinforcement learning algorithm to coordinate UAV operations while accounting for human fear. It achieves 52.72% reduction in human fear compared to Ipopt and improves spatial utilization by 70.82% over Ipopt and 2.03% over A-star.
AI.motivation: The low-altitude economy faces critical safety challenges for UAV operations in complex urban environments. Existing approaches fall into two extremes — distributed local perception (lacking global coordination) and centralized fine-grained control (lacking scalability). A middle-ground solution is needed that can coordinate multiple UAVs in shared airspace while explicitly considering human psychological factors (fear) in urban settings.
AI.method: The authors propose Pharos, a collaborative multi-UAV airspace management system positioned between distributed and centralized paradigms. It uses the Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) algorithm — chosen over HAPPO and HATRPO for its faster convergence and higher rewards. A novel contribution is the explicit modeling of human fear as a factor in airspace coordination. Evaluation is conducted via a custom 3D simulation system built on real urban data. The authors also introduce spatial entropy as a novel metric to quantify space utilization efficiency.
AI.result: Pharos achieved a 52.72% reduction in human fear compared to the Ipopt benchmark. For space utilization measured by spatial entropy, Pharos outperformed Ipopt by 70.82% and A-star by 2.03%. Visualization results qualitatively demonstrate effective airspace coordination capability in 3D urban simulations.
AI.conclusion: Pharos demonstrates that a MARL-based collaborative approach can effectively balance UAV operational safety with human psychological comfort in urban airspace management, outperforming traditional optimization (Ipopt) and path-planning (A-star) baselines on both fear reduction and spatial utilization.

title: TRIAGE: Trustworthy Retrieval Instrumentation And Graph Evaluation
summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) that underpin Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Graph-RAG) are increasingly built automatically by LLM-driven extraction rather than curated by experts. Proper evaluation would require instrumenting all pertinent stages: extraction, graph construction, and inference, coherently enough to localize failures, so that a failure at one stage is not discovered as a wrong answer at the end. We introduce TRIAGE, a stage-aware instrumentation framework for automated, document-grounded graph-RAG that asks not only whether the underlying graph can be trusted but at what cost it can be queried. TRIAGE attaches stage-specific, independently interpretable metrics to three stages: the KG Implementation (triple confidence, source coverage, and schema and canonicalization checks), the KG Validation by expert (graph-level structural quality, with correctness and completeness computed only as offline calibration when a reference is available), and the KG Usage (retrieval coverage, faithfulness, and retrieval cost); the deployed metrics need no gold annotations, the gold-requiring ones serving only as offline calibration. At usage time these metrics form a diagnostic chain of necessary conditions whose first broken link localizes the failure, and the diagnosis maps to the stage levers that can remedy it: extraction, graph and schema, or retrieval. TRIAGE is a theoretical framework with a proof of concept and a reproducible evaluation protocol.

AI.tldr: TRIAGE is a stage-aware instrumentation framework for Graph-RAG systems that attaches independently interpretable metrics to three stages—KG Implementation, KG Validation, and KG Usage—forming a diagnostic chain of necessary conditions that localizes failures to specific stages (extraction, graph/schema, or retrieval), enabling targeted remediation without requiring gold annotations at deployment time.
AI.motivation: As KGs underpinning Graph-RAG are increasingly built automatically via LLM-driven extraction rather than expert curation, failures can occur at any stage (extraction, graph construction, inference) but are typically discovered only at the end as wrong answers. There is a need for stage-aware evaluation that can localize failures coherently across all pertinent stages.
AI.method: TRIAGE defines a three-stage instrumentation framework: (1) KG Implementation metrics—triple confidence, source coverage, schema/canonicalization checks; (2) KG Validation metrics—graph-level structural quality, with correctness and completeness computed offline when references are available; (3) KG Usage metrics—retrieval coverage, faithfulness, and retrieval cost. These metrics form a diagnostic chain of necessary conditions; the first broken link localizes the failure and maps to actionable stage levers (extraction, graph/schema, or retrieval). Deployment metrics require no gold annotations; gold-requiring metrics serve only as offline calibration.
AI.result: The paper presents TRIAGE as a theoretical framework with a proof of concept and a reproducible evaluation protocol, demonstrating that stage-specific instrumentation can coherently localize failures in automated document-grounded Graph-RAG pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Stage-aware instrumentation like TRIAGE enables trustworthy, cost-aware evaluation of automatically constructed KGs for Graph-RAG by localizing failures to specific stages, mapping diagnoses to actionable remedies, and decoupling deployment metrics from gold-annotation dependence.

title: Attributing Structured-Output Gains in Function Calling: Interface Alignment versus Procedural Transfer
summary: Structured-output benchmarks reward both task decisions and interface compliance, so prompt-induced function-calling gains require attribution before they can be interpreted as transferable skill. We introduce a four-layer gain-attribution protocol for prompt-prepended skill injection, combining canonicalized rescoring, format-only controls, repaired/balanced induction, and portability checks. Applied to the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) and scoped with API-Bank, MATH-500, and MultiHop-RAG, the protocol shows that several apparent gains are better attributed to interface alignment than to procedural transfer: format-only prompts match or exceed full skills in key BFCL cells, repaired/balanced induction removes the largest sub-frontier gains, and API-Bank target-native gains are matched within 0.5 percentage points (pp) by length-matched generic procedural prompts. These findings treat format compliance as a useful engineering capability while clarifying what a structured-output score certifies. We release BFCL-CANONICAL and recommend canonicalized metrics, balanced induction, and format-only baselines for function-calling skill-gain attribution. Code and data are available at https://github.com/couragec/skill-injection-attribution.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a four-layer gain-attribution protocol to determine whether prompt-induced improvements on structured-output benchmarks reflect genuine transferable skill or merely better interface compliance. Applied to the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL), the protocol reveals that many reported gains stem from format alignment rather than procedural transfer, with format-only prompts matching or exceeding full-skill prompts and generic procedural prompts matching target-native gains within 0.5 pp. The authors release BFCL-CANONICAL and recommend canonicalized metrics, balanced induction, and format-only baselines for proper function-calling skill evaluation.
AI.motivation: Structured-output benchmarks conflate task decision quality with interface compliance, making it unclear whether prompt-induced function-calling gains represent transferable procedural skill or merely improved format adherence. Without proper attribution, benchmark scores overstate genuine capability improvements.
AI.method: The authors propose a four-layer gain-attribution protocol: (1) canonicalized rescoring to normalize evaluation, (2) format-only control prompts to isolate interface compliance effects, (3) repaired/balanced induction to correct for skewed or incomplete training signals, and (4) portability checks across diverse benchmarks (API-Bank, MATH-500, MultiHop-RAG) to test whether gains transfer beyond the original task setting.
AI.result: Format-only prompts match or exceed full-skill prompts in key BFCL cells. Repaired/balanced induction removes the largest sub-frontier gains. On API-Bank, length-matched generic procedural prompts match target-native gains within 0.5 percentage points. These findings indicate that apparent skill gains are largely attributable to interface alignment rather than procedural transfer.
AI.conclusion: Format compliance should be treated as a distinct engineering capability, not conflated with procedural skill. The authors recommend adopting canonicalized metrics, balanced induction, and format-only baselines as standard practice for function-calling skill-gain attribution, and release BFCL-CANONICAL to support this evaluation methodology.

title: JavaVulBench: A Java Vulnerability Benchmark with Realistic Splits, a Unified Multi-Backend Harness, and a Leakage-Aware Evaluation Mode
summary: We release \textsc{JavaVulBench}, a benchmark dataset and evaluation harness for Java vulnerability detection. The dataset contains $\sim$30{,}600 Java methods spanning 1{,}740 CVEs and 700+ projects, labelled at both method and line granularity, with per-CVE publication dates and five realistic split strategies: random, project-disjoint, temporal, deduplicated, and unseen CWE-family. The harness provides a single \texttt{LlmPrediction} schema across three backend families (encoder classifiers, local generative models served by Ollama, and API-served LLMs routed through OpenRouter) so that twelve reference detectors CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, and eight API/open-weight LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Sonnet~4, DeepSeek-v3, DeepSeek-Coder-v2, Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B/7B, CodeLlama-13B) are evaluated under identical conditions from a single command.
