A pre-training contamination audit is shipped alongside every model so users can separate genuinely unseen test CVEs from potentially memorised ones. Data, code, and fine-tuned checkpoints are archived on Zenodo [31] and short demonstration video is available on YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nMTX\_hqkuoM) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nMTX_hqkuoM.

AI.tldr: JavaVulBench is a benchmark dataset (~30,600 Java methods, 1,740 CVEs, 700+ projects) and evaluation harness for Java vulnerability detection with five realistic data-split strategies, supporting twelve reference detectors (encoder classifiers, local generative models, and API-served LLMs) under a unified schema, plus a contamination audit for identifying potentially memorized test CVEs.
AI.motivation: Existing vulnerability detection benchmarks lack realistic evaluation settings for Java, suffer from data leakage/memorization issues, and lack a standardized harness to fairly compare diverse detection approaches (encoder models, local LLMs, API-based LLMs) under identical conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct JavaVulBench with method- and line-level labels, five split strategies (random, project-disjoint, temporal, deduplicated, unseen CWE-family), a unified LlmPrediction schema, and a contamination audit. They evaluate twelve models — CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek-v3, DeepSeek-Coder-v2, Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B/7B, and CodeLlama-13B — using a single-command harness across three backend families.
AI.result: The paper provides the dataset, harness, fine-tuned checkpoints, and contamination audit. A demonstration video is available. The reference implementation supports evaluation across twelve models spanning encoder classifiers, local generative models (Ollama), and API-served LLMs (OpenRouter).
AI.conclusion: JavaVulBench provides a standardized, realistic, and contamination-aware evaluation framework for Java vulnerability detection, enabling fair comparison across diverse model architectures and deployment paradigms while mitigating data leakage concerns through multiple split strategies and built-in contamination auditing.

title: Seduced by the Narrative: Assessing Rule Adherence in Semi-Open Textual Sandboxes
summary: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous adjudicators in semi-open textual game environments, robust rule adherence becomes critical when user intent conflicts with system rules. However, these models are trained to be helpful and compliant, leaving them vulnerable to a class of attacks we term \textit{Rhetorical Injection}, where adversarial users exploit narrative framing techniques such as pseudo-logical reasoning and authoritative coercion to bypass adjudication logic. We present CoC-Seduce, a multi-agent adversarial benchmark built on Tabletop Role-Playing Game (TRPG) mechanics, an ideal instantiation of semi-open environments where rules are explicit for adjudication, yet interaction remains entirely in natural language. Three frontier models, i.e., GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.5 Flash, serve as adversarial generators producing 5,376 samples across 4 world settings and 16 skill categories. We then benchmark 20 target adjudicators against this corpus. Evaluation across 20 models reveals that neither model scale nor explicit reasoning mechanisms reliably confer adjudication robustness, with \textsc{Pseudo-Logic} emerging as the dominant attack vector and cross-cultural settings exposing systematic knowledge gaps across all evaluated families. Project page: https://github.com/answerrtx/CoC-Seduce

AI.tldr: Introduces Rhetorical Injection attacks that exploit LLM helpfulness to bypass rule adjudication in semi-open textual games. Presents CoC-Seduce, a multi-agent TRPG-based adversarial benchmark with 5,376 samples from 3 frontier models across 4 settings and 16 skill categories, tested against 20 target adjudicators.
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed as autonomous adjudicators in semi-open textual game environments are vulnerable because they are inherently trained to be helpful and compliant. When user intent conflicts with system rules, adversarial users can exploit narrative framing to bypass adjudication logic, yet no systematic benchmark exists to evaluate this vulnerability.
AI.method: CoC-Seduce employs a multi-agent adversarial framework grounded in TRPG mechanics, where rules are explicit but interaction is purely natural language. Three frontier models — GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3.5 Flash — act as adversarial generators producing 5,376 samples spanning 4 world settings and 16 skill categories. Twenty target adjudicator models are then benchmarked against this corpus for robustness.
AI.result: Neither model scale nor explicit reasoning mechanisms reliably confer adjudication robustness. Pseudo-Logic emerges as the dominant attack vector. Cross-cultural settings expose systematic knowledge gaps across all evaluated model families.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier models lack robust adjudication capabilities when confronted with Rhetorical Injection attacks, particularly pseudo-logical reasoning. Cross-cultural rule interpretation remains a critical weakness, suggesting that scaling alone is insufficient and targeted defenses are needed.

title: Post-Generation Curation of Synthetic Images via Homogeneous-Heterogeneous Splitting
summary: Recent generative models can produce high-quality synthetic images, offering scalable training training data for data-hungry models. Existing approaches to exploiting this potential typically involve 1) training or fine-tuning generators, or 2) using lightweight post-hoc adaptation like prompt engineering or inference-time guidance, making them generator-specific and expertise-intensive. We study a complementary question: given a fixed pool of generated images, can downstream utility be improved purely by selecting an informative subset? The answer is yes. We show that effective selection must counter a structural bias of modern generators: they tend to over-produce canonical modes of each class while underrepresenting intra-class variation. Building on this insight, we split each real class into a canonical Homogeneous (HO) subset and a non-redundant Heterogeneous (HE) subset, then score synthetic images by a fidelity-diversity criterion that rewards semantic alignment while penalizing canonical redundancy. The method is generator-agnostic and requires no retraining. Across multiple benchmarks, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data selection baselines and matches the real-data performance with up to 40% fewer synthetic samples. The same criterion remains effective when applied on top of stronger task-tuned generators, with gains on both classification and segmentation tasks. Post-generation selection is therefore not a substitute for better generators, but a complementary mechanism for improving the utility of synthetic data.

AI.tldr: A generator-agnostic method that selects informative subsets from synthetic image pools using a fidelity-diversity criterion — rewarding semantic alignment while penalizing canonical redundancy — outperforms existing data selection baselines and matches real-data performance with up to 40% fewer samples.
AI.motivation: Synthetic images from generative models can augment training data, but existing methods (fine-tuning generators or prompt engineering) are generator-specific and require expertise. The authors ask: given a fixed, pre-generated image pool, can downstream utility be improved purely through subset selection?
AI.method: The authors identify a structural bias in modern generators: they over-produce canonical (typical) modes while underrepresenting intra-class variation. They split each real class into a canonical Homogeneous (HO) subset and a non-redundant Heterogeneous (HE) subset, then score synthetic images using a fidelity-diversity criterion that rewards semantic alignment with real data while penalizing canonical redundancy. The approach is generator-agnostic and requires no retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.result: The proposed selection method consistently outperforms SOTA data selection baselines across multiple benchmarks. It matches real-data performance using up to 40% fewer synthetic samples. Gains persist when applied on top of stronger task-tuned generators, benefiting both classification and segmentation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Post-generation subset selection is not a replacement for better generators but a complementary mechanism that significantly improves synthetic data utility. Effective selection must counter the canonical overproduction bias inherent in modern generative models.

title: Object-Centric Environment Modeling for Agentic Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve through accumulated experience, but free-form textual memories become difficult to maintain, validate, and reuse as interactions grow. Recent symbolic approaches learn executable skills or programmatic world models, yet often store local procedures or assume simplified dynamics. We propose Object-Centric Environment Modeling (OCM), which organizes experience into an executable object-centric environment model. OCM maintains two connected code bases: object knowledge, which defines environment entities and mechanisms as Python classes, and procedure knowledge, which records reusable interaction patterns that must import and use the object model. OCM works in an online setting: after each episode, OCM reflects on the trajectory, updates both knowledge bases, and verifies that all procedures execute against the updated object model. During future interaction, the agent uses progressive knowledge disclosure to inspect compact code signatures first and read source code only when needed. Experiments show that OCM achieves the best average rank across benchmarks and reduces invalid actions, demonstrating that agents can benefit from building object-centric environment models.

AI.tldr: OCM organizes LLM agent experience into an executable object-centric environment model with two code bases—object knowledge (Python classes) and procedure knowledge (reusable patterns)—updated and verified online; it uses progressive knowledge disclosure for efficient retrieval and achieves top average rank with fewer invalid actions.
AI.motivation: Free-form textual memories in LLM agents become unwieldy as interactions scale, while existing symbolic methods that learn executable skills or programmatic world models tend to store only local procedures or assume oversimplified dynamics. There is a need for a structured, verifiable, and reusable memory representation.
AI.method: OCM maintains two interconnected code bases: (1) object knowledge defining environment entities/mechanisms as Python classes, and (2) procedure knowledge recording reusable interaction patterns that import the object model. After each episode, OCM reflects on the trajectory, updates both knowledge bases, and verifies that all procedures execute correctly against the updated object model. During future interactions, progressive knowledge disclosure lets the agent inspect compact code signatures first, reading full source code only when necessary.
AI.result: OCM achieves the best average rank across benchmarks and significantly reduces invalid actions compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents can substantially benefit from building and maintaining object-centric, executable environment models, with structured code-based knowledge offering advantages in verifiability, reusability, and action validity over free-form textual memory.

title: The New Shape of Search: How Conversational AI Recomposes Information Seeking
summary: Classic models cast information seeking as iterative foraging: formulate a keyword query, scan results, reformulate, gather across sources, synthesize. We ask what happens when a conversational assistant is inserted into that episode. Linking real conversations with major assistants to the same users' searches and browsing in an opt-in cross-surface panel, and reconstructing the full episode rather than a single query, we find conversational AI changes the shape of information seeking, not merely its volume. AI episodes do not uniformly collapse; they bifurcate. Most terminate in place, with no onward search or content step in the observed trace, while roughly a third scaffold into longer multi-step journeys. Which shape occurs is governed less by task type than by articulation: collapse is statistically indistinguishable across lookup, learning, and comparison episodes, yet falls monotonically with opening-ask length, from 72% at one-to-three words to 48% beyond twenty. Roughly two-fifths of assistant episodes are workbench use--drafting, coding, editing--not information seeking at all, and these collapse most. Conversational AI also does not displace search: search remains woven through roughly three-quarters of within-episode transitions, after reading a page users return to the search box over the assistant 70/30, and within-user search share does not fall. Verification is rare: searches with explicit verification language follow roughly 1% of episodes, and citation-forward interfaces do not measurably increase checking. All of this is episode structure, a compositional object identifiable without a demand counterfactual. Conversational AI recomposes the seeking episode: it answers brief asks in place and anchors invested asks in longer journeys, adding a layer rather than replacing search.

AI.tldr: Conversational AI bifurcates information-seeking episodes: most queries terminate immediately without follow-up ("collapse"), while a minority scaffold into longer multi-step journeys. Collapse rates are driven by query length, not task type. AI does not displace search—it adds a layer—and verification behavior remains rare.
AI.motivation: Classic models of information seeking assume iterative foraging (query, scan, reformulate, synthesize), but it is unknown how inserting a conversational assistant reshapes this episode structure. Prior work examines isolated queries; this paper reconstructs the full cross-surface episode to understand whether conversational AI collapses, extends, or displaces search behavior.
AI.method: The authors use an opt-in cross-surface panel linking real user conversations with major AI assistants to the same users' search queries and browsing behavior. They reconstruct full information-seeking episodes—not single queries—and analyze transitions between assistant, search, and content-consumption steps. They classify episodes by task type (lookup, learning, comparison, workbench) and measure collapse rates, onward search patterns, and verification behavior.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) AI episodes bifurcate—most collapse in place, ~1/3 scaffold into longer journeys; (2) Collapse is governed by articulation length (72% at 1–3 words, 48% at >20 words), not task type; (3) ~2/5 of assistant episodes are workbench use (drafting, coding, editing) and collapse most; (4) Search persists through ~75% of within-episode transitions, and within-user search share does not decline; (5) Explicit verification searches follow only ~1% of episodes; citation-forward interfaces do not measurably increase checking.
AI.conclusion: Conversational AI does not uniformly collapse or replace information seeking—it recomposes episodes. Brief asks are answered in place; invested, longer asks anchor into extended journeys. The assistant adds a compositional layer atop existing search behavior rather than substituting for it. Episode structure emerges as a valuable analytical object independent of demand counterfactuals.

title: PiSAs: Benchmarking Contextual Integrity in Multi-User Agentic Systems
summary: As LLM agents evolve from single-user assistants into shared organizational infrastructure, new privacy risks emerge: inappropriate information may not only be exposed through outputs for external recipients, but also internally across users through inter-agent messages, shared memory and agents. These data spillage risks are not captured by existing privacy benchmarks grounded in contextual integrity (CI) as they focus primarily on either single-user settings or interactions between independently owned agents. We introducePiSAs (Privacy in Shared Agentic systems), a benchmark for assessing unintentional leaks with dual CI annotations: whether an information is appropriate for the task, and which users may legitimately access it. This enables direct measurement of cross-user spillage across agentic system components and interfaces, such as outputs, inter-agent communication, and memory. PiSAsis system-agnostic and supports evaluation across different agent topologies and memory regimes. We find that, although system design improves CI compliance, results are bottlenecked by incorrect LLM judgment calls: even state-of-the-art models fail to reliably filter inappropriate content or restrict transmission to authorized users. Our findings underscore the need for privacy-preserving strategies, beyond those studied in this work.

AI.tldr: PiSAs is a benchmark for evaluating cross-user data spillage in shared multi-agent systems, using dual contextual integrity annotations (task appropriateness + authorized recipients). State-of-the-art LLMs fail to reliably prevent inappropriate information leakage across users, even with improved system design.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are transitioning from single-user assistants to shared organizational infrastructure, creating novel privacy risks where sensitive information can leak across users through inter-agent messages, shared memory, and internal agent state. Existing CI-based privacy benchmarks only address single-user settings or independently owned agents, failing to capture cross-user spillage in shared agentic systems.
AI.method: Introduces PiSAs, a system-agnostic benchmark with dual contextual integrity annotations: (1) whether information is appropriate for a given task, and (2) which users are legitimately authorized to access it. This dual-annotation framework enables measurement of cross-user spillage across agentic components — outputs, inter-agent communication, and memory — and supports evaluation across different agent topologies and memory regimes.
AI.result: System design improvements enhance contextual integrity compliance, but performance is bottlenecked by LLM judgment failures. Even state-of-the-art models cannot reliably filter inappropriate content or restrict information transmission to only authorized users, indicating that current architectural safeguards are insufficient.
AI.conclusion: Significant privacy vulnerabilities persist in shared agentic systems beyond what current system-level mitigations address. The findings underscore an urgent need for stronger, inherently privacy-preserving strategies tailored to multi-user, multi-agent environments.

title: SentAttack: A Sentence-Level Black-Box Adversarial Attack Method for Dense Retrieval Models
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems typically consist of a dense retrieval (DR) model for initial retrieval and a neural ranking model (NRM) for re-ranking.Existing robustness studies in RAG mainly focus on NRMs, while adversarial attacks on DR models are mostly limited to word-level perturbations.For low-ranked target documents that are irrelevant to the query, simple word-level attacks are insufficient to mislead DR models into substantially promoting their rankings.To solve these problems, we propose SentAttack, a sentence-level black-box adversarial attack method for DR models.SentAttack is designed as a two-stage method.In the first stage, SentAttack interacts with the black-box RAG system via iterative retrieval to collect ranked documents and ranking information for training a surrogate DR model.In the second stage, SentAttack uses the surrogate DR model to encode and cluster documents relevant to the target query, yielding multiple cluster centroids.These centroids are concatenated with the target document at the sentence level to form an initial set of adversarial candidates.SentAttack then optimizes these candidates using a query- and centroid-guided objective combined with gradient-guided beam search.Extensive experiments demonstrate that SentAttack outperforms existing adversarial attacks on DR models, with especially strong performance on low-ranked target documents.

AI.tldr: SentAttack is a two-stage, sentence-level black-box adversarial attack against dense retrieval models in RAG systems, using a surrogate model and cluster centroid-guided optimization to boost low-ranked irrelevant documents.
AI.motivation: Existing robustness research in RAG focuses on neural ranking models, while attacks on dense retrieval models are limited to word-level perturbations, which are insufficient to promote low-ranked irrelevant documents. A sentence-level black-box attack is needed to address this gap.
AI.method: Stage 1: Interact with the black-box RAG system via iterative retrieval to collect ranked documents and train a surrogate DR model. Stage 2: Use the surrogate to encode and cluster query-relevant documents into centroids, concatenate centroids with the target document at sentence level to form adversarial candidates, then optimize via a query- and centroid-guided objective with gradient-guided beam search.
AI.result: SentAttack outperforms existing adversarial attacks on DR models, with particularly strong performance on low-ranked target documents.
AI.conclusion: Sentence-level adversarial attacks exploiting cluster centroids and gradient-guided beam search are significantly more effective than word-level attacks for compromising dense retrieval models, especially for initially low-ranked targets.

title: AgentLTL: A Trace-Verification Framework for Measuring, Enforcing, and Training Procedural Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents are usually evaluated by final-answer correctness or LLM judges. Neither captures how an answer was produced. In safety-critical settings, the procedure itself is part of correctness. In this paper, we introduce AgentLTL, a language derived from First-Order Linear Temporal Logic (FO-LTL) that expresses procedural rules over agent traces. It yields a deterministic, judge-free compliance score. In this framework, a single specification drives two usages. The first is harnessing: the constraints score completed traces, or gate tool calls by checking each prefix online, before execution. The second is finetuning: the score serves as a dense reward. On a benchmark spanning ordering, branching, iteration, and grounding, block-and-warn harnessing improves compliance on five of seven models. Finetuning with the same reward yields +38 and +17.5 percentage point gains in accuracy and compliance on held-out patterns, including unseen tool-name aliases. These findings are consistent with the model acquiring procedural structure rather than memorizing surface tool names and procedures.

AI.tldr: AgentLTL introduces a First-Order Linear Temporal Logic-based language for specifying procedural rules over LLM agent traces, providing a deterministic compliance score without LLM judges. It supports both online blocking/warning of non-compliant actions (harnessing) and dense reward signals for finetuning, achieving significant gains in both accuracy and procedural compliance on held-out patterns.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent evaluation relies on final-answer correctness or LLM judges, neither of which captures the procedural correctness of how an answer was produced. In safety-critical settings, the procedure itself matters. A formal, judge-free, deterministic method for specifying and evaluating procedural compliance is needed.
AI.method: AgentLTL, a specification language derived from First-Order Linear Temporal Logic (FO-LTL), expresses procedural rules over agent execution traces. A single specification enables two modes: (1) harnessing — scoring completed traces or gating tool calls online by checking each prefix before execution (block-and-warn); (2) finetuning — using the compliance score as a dense reward signal. Evaluation covers ordering, branching, iteration, and grounding patterns.
AI.result: Block-and-warn harnessing improved compliance on 5 of 7 models. Finetuning with the AgentLTL reward yielded +38 and +17.5 percentage point gains in accuracy and compliance, respectively, on held-out patterns including unseen tool-name aliases, suggesting the model acquires procedural structure rather than surface memorization.
AI.conclusion: AgentLTL provides an effective, judge-free framework for both enforcing and teaching procedural compliance to LLM agents. The generalization to unseen tool-name aliases indicates that models learn abstract procedural structure, making the approach robust beyond surface-level pattern matching.

title: ShannonProver: Towards Automating Formal Cryptographic Proofs
summary:
Cryptographic proofs are produced at a scale that increasingly exceeds the community's ability to verify them manually. Machine-checked proofs offer a path toward scalable proof verification, but writing proof scripts for expressive proof assistants such as EasyCrypt remains a major bottleneck: even when the high-level proof plan is known, converting it into proof tactics requires substantial reasoning effort. This paper presents ShannonProver, an agentic framework for automating cryptographic proofs. ShannonProver targets the setting in which a cryptographer provides the security model and a decomposition of the target theorem into lemma-level proof obligations, while the system automatically constructs EasyCrypt proof scripts for those obligations.
  We evaluate ShannonProver on a dataset of formal cryptographic proofs in EasyCrypt. The dataset spans textbook primitives, deployed protocols, and standardization efforts such as NIST proposals, and includes expert case studies drawn from a corpus that has not previously been available online. We show that ShannonProver can automate substantial portions of cryptographic proof engineering for case studies such as ChaChaPoly1305 and MEE-CBC. More broadly, this work suggests a path toward accelerating cryptographic research: as agents automate the proof-engineering burden, cryptographers can iterate more quickly on new constructions, obtain machine-checked assurance earlier, and bring trustworthy protocols from design to deployment faster.

AI.tldr: ShannonProver is an agentic framework that automates the generation of EasyCrypt proof scripts from lemma-level proof obligations provided by cryptographers, reducing the manual effort required for machine-checked cryptographic proofs. Evaluated on a dataset spanning textbook primitives, protocols, and NIST proposals, it demonstrates substantial automation on case studies like ChaChaPoly1305 and MEE-CBC.
AI.motivation: Cryptographic proofs are produced at a scale that outstrips manual verification capacity. While machine-checked proofs (e.g., in EasyCrypt) enable scalable verification, writing proof scripts remains a major bottleneck because converting high-level proof plans into low-level tactics demands significant reasoning effort. There is a need to automate this proof-engineering burden to accelerate cryptographic research and deployment.
AI.method: ShannonProver is an agentic framework where a cryptographer supplies the security model and a decomposition of the target theorem into lemma-level proof obligations. The system then automatically constructs EasyCrypt proof scripts for those individual obligations, using an agent-based approach to synthesize the required tactics.
AI.result: ShannonProver was evaluated on a dataset of formal EasyCrypt proofs covering textbook primitives, deployed protocols, NIST standardization proposals, and previously unpublished expert case studies. It successfully automated substantial portions of proof engineering for case studies including ChaChaPoly1305 and MEE-CBC.
AI.conclusion: ShannonProver demonstrates that agentic automation of cryptographic proof engineering is feasible, suggesting a path toward faster iteration on new constructions, earlier machine-checked assurance, and accelerated deployment of trustworthy protocols.

title: Jointly Improving Dialect Identification and ASR in Indian Languages using Multimodal Feature Fusion
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Dialect Identification (DID) are crucial for Indian languages, many of which are low-resource and exhibit significant dialectal differences. Existing methods often optimize ASR or DID individually, resulting in performance trade-offs. In this work, we propose a multimodal framework that jointly improves ASR and DID. Our method employs a Bottleneck Encoder to extract dialectal features from Conformer-based speech representations and a RoBERTa encoder to process ASR-generated CTC embeddings. A gating mechanism merges these features, followed by an attention encoder to refine the representations. The learned embeddings are concatenated with Conformer outputs to enhance ASR features. Evaluated on eight Indian languages with thirty-three dialects, our method achieves an average DID accuracy of 81.63% and average CER and WER of 4.65% and 17.73%, respectively. These results highlight the effectiveness of our method for joint ASR-DID modeling.

AI.tldr: A multimodal framework jointly optimizing ASR and dialect identification for Indian languages, using Bottleneck Encoder + RoBERTa with a gating mechanism and attention encoder, achieving 81.63% DID accuracy and strong CER/WER across 8 languages and 33 dialects.
AI.motivation: Indian languages are predominantly low-resource with significant dialectal variation. Existing approaches optimize ASR and DID separately, leading to performance trade-offs. There is a need for a unified framework that jointly improves both tasks without sacrificing one for the other.
AI.method: A multimodal framework combining: (1) a Bottleneck Encoder extracting dialectal features from Conformer-based speech representations; (2) a RoBERTa encoder processing ASR-generated CTC embeddings; (3) a gating mechanism to merge these two feature streams; (4) an attention encoder for representation refinement; and (5) concatenation of the learned embeddings with Conformer outputs to enhance ASR features.
AI.result: Evaluated on 8 Indian languages covering 33 dialects. Achieved average DID accuracy of 81.63%, average CER of 4.65%, and average WER of 17.73%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed joint multimodal framework effectively improves both ASR and DID performance simultaneously, demonstrating that speech and text modalities can be fused via a gating mechanism to enhance representations for low-resource, dialectally diverse languages.

title: A Granularity-Aware EEG Feature Framework for Psychopathology Dimension Prediction
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a noninvasive approach for examining neurophysiological correlates of dimensional psychopathology, yet systematic evidence across EEG paradigms and feature granularities remains limited. Here, we develop a granularity-aware EEG feature pipeline that organizes multi-scale descriptors into global, regional, and channel levels. Using the Healthy Brain Network (HBN) cohort, we evaluate the prediction of four psychopathology dimensions: p-factor, internalizing, externalizing, and attention problems, across four EEG paradigms. Given the heterogeneity of pediatric psychopathology and the moderate reliability of questionnaire-derived scores, this setting represents a challenging feasibility test rather than a clinical screening scenario. Tree-based models and granularity-balanced feature selection showed promising improvements over conventional approaches in selected conditions, although effect sizes remained modest. Visualization of selected markers revealed dimension-specific spatial and spectral patterns that were broadly aligned with existing neurophysiological knowledge. An exploratory cross-dataset sanity check on the independent PEARL cohort suggested that the proposed selection principle remains technically feasible under protocol shifts, without claiming cross-dataset generalizability. Overall, multi-scale EEG features contain weak but detectable signals related to dimensional psychopathology, and granularity-aware selection may serve as a useful feature-reduction strategy for future EEG-based phenotyping studies.

AI.tldr: A granularity-aware EEG feature pipeline was developed to predict dimensional psychopathology (p-factor, internalizing, externalizing, attention problems) in the HBN pediatric cohort. Tree-based models with granularity-balanced feature selection yielded modest but promising improvements, revealing dimension-specific spatial/spectral patterns. Cross-dataset sanity checks on PEARL confirmed technical feasibility under protocol shifts.
AI.motivation: EEG-based examination of dimensional psychopathology lacks systematic evidence across paradigms and feature granularities. Existing approaches often neglect the multi-scale nature of EEG features (global, regional, channel levels), limiting the ability to detect weak but potentially meaningful neurophysiological signals associated with psychopathology dimensions.
AI.method: A granularity-aware EEG feature pipeline was developed, organizing multi-scale descriptors into global, regional, and channel levels. Tree-based models with granularity-balanced feature selection were applied to predict four psychopathology dimensions across four EEG paradigms in the HBN cohort. An exploratory cross-dataset sanity check was performed on the independent PEARL cohort.
AI.result: Granularity-aware selection improved prediction over conventional approaches in selected conditions, though effect sizes remained modest. Dimension-specific spatial and spectral patterns emerged from selected markers, broadly consistent with existing neurophysiological knowledge. The PEARL sanity check indicated technical feasibility under protocol shifts without demonstrating cross-dataset generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Multi-scale EEG features carry weak but detectable signals related to dimensional psychopathology. Granularity-aware feature selection represents a useful reduction strategy for future EEG-based phenotyping studies, though the modest effect sizes and limited generalizability highlight the challenges of pediatric psychopathology prediction in naturalistic cohorts.

title: MedCalc-Pro: Solving Complex Medical Calculations with LLM Agents
summary: Current benchmarks for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in medical calculation are largely based on simplified settings, where each patient case corresponds to a single calculator and the required tool is explicitly specified in the query. However, real clinical scenarios often require multiple calculators for joint evaluation, nested-scale calculation, and fuzzy queries that do not directly specify the target calculator. To this end, we propose a new medical calculation benchmark, MedCalc-Pro, which covers three progressively challenging task settings: single-calculator, multi-calculator, and nested-calculator calculation settings. MedCalc-Pro contains 2,268 real-world clinical cases, covering 77 medical calculators across 14 clinical departments. Meanwhile, to address the limited performance of existing frameworks and methods in complex clinical scenarios, we further propose a more generalizable agent framework that supports multi-tool selection and nested-tool calling, while suppressing parameter error propagation through structured validation and evidence review. We conduct systematic comparisons across open-source, closed-source, and medical-specialized LLMs, and the results show that our framework achieves the best performance across all three task settings. This work provides a new benchmark and method for evaluating and applying LLMs in challenging medical calculation scenarios.

AI.tldr: Current medical calculation benchmarks oversimplify real clinical needs. This paper introduces MedCalc-Pro, a benchmark with 2,268 cases across three difficulty levels (single, multi, nested calculator), and an agent framework with multi-tool selection and error suppression, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assume one calculator per case with explicit tool specification, which fails to reflect real clinical complexity involving multiple calculators, nested calculations, and ambiguous queries. There is a need for more realistic evaluation and stronger methods.
AI.method: The authors construct MedCalc-Pro with 2,268 real clinical cases spanning 77 calculators and 14 departments, in three settings: single-calculator, multi-calculator, and nested-calculator. They also propose an agent framework featuring multi-tool selection, nested-tool calling, and structured validation with evidence review to suppress parameter error propagation.
AI.result: Systematic evaluation across open-source, closed-source, and medical-specialized LLMs shows the proposed agent framework achieves the best performance on all three task settings in MedCalc-Pro.
AI.conclusion: MedCalc-Pro offers a more realistic benchmark for medical calculation with LLMs, and the proposed agent framework effectively addresses the challenges of complex, multi-tool clinical scenarios.

title: The ABC of digital health: A framework for translating digital health interventions into real-world applications
comment: 21 pages, 2 tables, 1 figure. Preprint of a manuscript intended to be submitted at ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction (TOCHI)
summary: Research-based digital health interventions are often presented as potential solutions for extending health care in the real world. Yet the vast majority of these interventions fails to move beyond controlled studies. Existing frameworks offer valuable guidance for intervention development and testing, but provide less concrete support for translating these evidenced intervention mechanisms into sustained real-world applications. This paper introduces the ABC framework, referring to Accessibility, Buildability, and Continuity, as a practical model for a successful translation. Accessibility captures whether diverse users can find, understand, and begin using an application with minimal friction. Buildability refers to the development of an app that supports the iteration, integration, and personalization of features. Continuity describes both sustained user engagement and the operational capacity to maintain an application over time without disproportionate increases in cost, infrastructure, or human support. Different combinations of the ABC-dimensions make an application scalable (AB), automated (BC), and adherent (AC). By linking design decisions to these features, ABC offers a shared language for researchers, designers, and policymakers seeking to build or evaluate digital health interventions that work beyond trials and are viable applications in everyday life.

AI.tldr: The ABC framework (Accessibility, Buildability, Continuity) provides a practical model for translating digital health interventions from controlled studies into sustained real-world applications by linking design decisions to scalability, automation, and adherence.
AI.motivation: Most research-based digital health interventions fail to transition beyond controlled studies into real-world practice. Existing frameworks guide intervention development and testing but lack concrete support for translating evidenced mechanisms into sustained applications.
AI.method: The authors propose the ABC framework, a conceptual model with three dimensions: Accessibility (ease of finding, understanding, and starting use with minimal friction), Buildability (support for iteration, integration, and feature personalization), and Continuity (sustained user engagement and operational maintenance without disproportionate cost increases). The framework maps pairwise combinations of these dimensions to desirable properties: AB → scalability, BC → automation, AC → adherence.
AI.result: The ABC framework offers a shared language that links design decisions to three key translational outcomes — scalability, automation, and adherence — enabling coordinated communication among researchers, designers, and policymakers.
AI.conclusion: The ABC framework serves as a practical tool for building and evaluating digital health interventions that are viable beyond trials and sustainable in everyday life, addressing the translational gap between research and real-world application.

title: LLMoxie: Exploring Agentic AI for Scientific Software Development
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to ACM SIGKDD 2026 Workshop: Agentic AI for Scientific and Societal Advances (SciSoc Agents and LLMs). Describes an agentic AI platform for scientific software engineering with governed multi-cloud inference, structured multiagent workflows, and domain-aware coding support (cs.SE, cs.MA, cs.AI)
summary: In this paper, we describe LLMoxie, an institutional AI platform whose three-tiered architecture supports multi-cloud and on-premise inference, a LiteLLM/MLflow control plane for authentication, budgeting, PII masking, and observability, and an application augmentation layer for AI coding agents. Layered on top, an open-source RSE-Plugins ecosystem encodes accumulated RSE knowledge as a Plugin-Agent-Skill hierarchy spanning scientific Python practice, domain-specific knowledge, a six-phase research-and-implement workflow, and project lifecycle management. Scientific software is judged less by raw code quality than by whether it can be cited, audited, reproduced, and extended. Off-the-shelf AI coding agents, optimized against commercial software benchmarks, are poorly calibrated for this setting: they ignore the conventions of the scientific Python libraries they invoke, mishandle sensitive or embargoed data, and leave decision trails that are difficult to reconstruct after the fact. We report on twenty months of practice at a university-based research software engineering (RSE) center, where RSEs embedded across astronomy, earth and climate science, agriculture, and health projects worked to close this gap. We characterize the recurring infrastructure, governance, and process challenges of adopting Agentic AI inside a multi-domain RSE center, describe the platform and plugin design, and distill operational lessons from real scientific software deployments. Together, the platform and plugins shift AI coding agents from generic code generators into domain-aware collaborators that respect community norms and produce auditable provenance of technical reasoning.

AI.tldr: LLMoxie is an institutional AI platform designed for research software engineering (RSE) centers, combining a three-tiered architecture (multi-cloud inference, control plane, application layer) with an open-source plugin ecosystem that encodes RSE knowledge. It transforms generic AI coding agents into domain-aware scientific collaborators that respect community norms, handle sensitive data properly, and produce auditable decision trails.
AI.motivation: Off-the-shelf AI coding agents are poorly calibrated for scientific software development: they ignore scientific Python library conventions, mishandle sensitive/embargoed data, and leave opaque decision trails that undermine citability, auditability, reproducibility, and extensibility — the core metrics by which scientific software is judged.
AI.method: The authors built LLMoxie with (1) a three-tier architecture providing multi-cloud/on-premise inference, a LiteLLM/MLflow control plane (authentication, budgeting, PII masking, observability), and an application augmentation layer; and (2) an open-source RSE-Plugins ecosystem organized as a Plugin-Agent-Skill hierarchy covering scientific Python practice, domain knowledge, a six-phase research workflow, and project lifecycle management. The system was developed and tested over twenty months across astronomy, earth/climate science, agriculture, and health projects.
AI.result: The platform successfully addresses recurring infrastructure, governance, and process challenges in multi-domain RSE centers. The plugin hierarchy effectively embeds accumulated RSE knowledge, shifting AI agents from generic code generators to collaborators that produce auditable provenance of technical reasoning and respect scientific community norms.
AI.conclusion: LLMoxie demonstrates that institutional AI platforms augmented with domain-specific plugin hierarchies can bridge the gap between generic AI coding tools and the stringent requirements of scientific software development — namely citability, auditability, reproducibility, and extensibility.

title: Relevance-Based Embeddings: Lightweight Candidate Retrieval via Heavy-Ranker Calls
summary: In many machine learning applications, the most relevant items for a query should be efficiently retrieved. The relevance function is usually an expensive similarity model, making the exhaustive search infeasible. A typical solution is to train another model that separately embeds queries and items to a vector space, where similarity is defined via the dot product or cosine similarity. This allows one to search the relevant items through fast approximate nearest neighbor search at the cost of some reduction in quality. To compensate for this reduction, the found items (candidates) are re-ranked by the expensive ranking model. In this paper, we investigate an alternative approach to candidate selection that utilizes the scores of the expensive model to improve the representations of queries and items. The idea is to describe each query (item) by its relevance to a set of support items (queries) and use these new representations to obtain query (item) embeddings. We theoretically prove that such embeddings are powerful enough to approximate any complex similarity model (under mild conditions). We also investigate the choice of support items, which is a crucial ingredient of the proposed approach. The experiments on diverse academic and production datasets illustrate the power of our method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a candidate selection method that uses the expensive relevance model's scores to create query/item representations, where each entity is described by its relevance to a set of support items/queries. The authors theoretically prove these embeddings can approximate any complex similarity model and demonstrate effectiveness on both academic and production datasets.
AI.motivation: In large-scale retrieval, exhaustive search with expensive relevance models is infeasible. The standard two-stage pipeline (approximate embedding search + re-ranking) suffers from quality degradation in the candidate selection phase. The authors seek to improve candidate selection by leveraging the expensive model itself to construct better representations, rather than relying solely on independently trained embeddings.
AI.method: Each query is represented by its relevance scores against a set of support items, and each item is represented by its relevance scores against a set of support queries. These score-based representations are then used to derive query and item embeddings. The authors provide theoretical guarantees that such embeddings can approximate arbitrary complex similarity functions under mild conditions, and they investigate optimal strategies for selecting support items/queries.
AI.result: The method demonstrates strong empirical performance across diverse academic and production datasets, validating both the theoretical claims about approximation power and the practical utility of the approach for candidate selection in large-scale retrieval systems.
AI.conclusion: Using the expensive relevance model's own scores to construct representations for candidate selection is a viable and theoretically grounded alternative to the standard two-stage retrieval paradigm. The choice of support items is a critical factor in the method's success.

title: A Survey of LLM-Driven Penetration Testing: Taxonomy, Co-Evolution, and Open Challenges
summary: Agents4Pentest, an emerging class of LLM-based autonomous penetration testing systems, has become a rapidly growing area in security research. Despite this growth, the field still lacks a unified taxonomy, a systematic understanding of how agent architectures and evaluation benchmarks have co-evolved, and a clear characterization of remaining capability and reliability gaps. This survey addresses these gaps through a systematic analysis of 81 papers between 2023 and 2026. We organize the literature into six categories: evaluation benchmarks, general-purpose systems, domain-specific frameworks, CTF-based systems, defense-oriented research, and surveys. We further trace a four-phase architectural evolution from text-only reasoning agents to agents trained with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), showing that each transition is driven by a distinct capability bottleneck. Our analysis yields several key findings. First, RLVR marks a shift in capability acquisition from imitation of expert demonstrations to reward-driven self-improvement, enabling agents to discover previously undocumented attack strategies. Second, CTF platforms have evolved from evaluation testbeds into dual-purpose infrastructure for both agent evaluation and RL training. Third, domain-specific frameworks improve efficiency through recurring specialization mechanisms, but their gains remain largely confined to narrow task classes and are difficult to compare across domains because existing evaluations rely on different benchmarks. Fourth, the field is expanding beyond offensive automation toward adversarial defense and security compliance. Across these categories, we identify three structurally linked open challenges: evaluation reliability, limited performance on multi-stage attack scenarios, and scarcity of high-quality training data.

AI.tldr: A systematic survey of 81 papers (2023–2026) on LLM-based autonomous penetration testing agents, proposing a four-phase architectural evolution from text-only reasoning to RLVR-trained agents. Key findings include RLVR enabling self-discovered attack strategies, CTF platforms becoming dual-purpose infrastructure, domain-specific frameworks facing cross-domain comparison challenges, and three persistent open problems: evaluation reliability, multi-stage attack performance, and training data scarcity.
AI.motivation: The field of LLM-based autonomous penetration testing (Agents4Pentest) lacks a unified taxonomy, a systematic understanding of how agent architectures and evaluation benchmarks have co-evolved, and a clear characterization of remaining capability and reliability gaps.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic literature survey of 81 papers published between 2023 and 2026. They organize the literature into six categories: evaluation benchmarks, general-purpose systems, domain-specific frameworks, CTF-based systems, defense-oriented research, and surveys. They further trace a four-phase architectural evolution and analyze capability bottlenecks driving each transition.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) RLVR shifts capability acquisition from expert imitation to reward-driven self-improvement, yielding novel attack strategies; (2) CTF platforms have evolved from evaluation-only testbeds into dual-purpose infrastructure for both evaluation and RL training; (3) domain-specific frameworks improve efficiency via specialization mechanisms but are confined to narrow tasks and resist cross-domain comparison; (4) the field is expanding toward adversarial defense and security compliance. Three structurally linked challenges are identified: evaluation reliability, limited multi-stage attack performance, and scarcity of high-quality training data.
AI.conclusion: The survey provides a unified taxonomy and evolutionary map for Agents4Pentest, highlights RLVR as a pivotal shift in agent capability acquisition, and identifies evaluation reliability, multi-stage attack limitations, and training data scarcity as the central open challenges requiring coordinated research attention.

title: MOSAIC: Knowledge-Guided CLI Command Composition Attack in LLM Coding Agents
summary:
LLM coding agents increasingly complete development tasks by issuing ordinary CLI commands. Following the Unix design, these commands cooperate through shared operating-system state: one command may write state that a later command reads. While this composition is benign and intended, it creates an overlooked exploit surface. Existing attacks and defenses mainly target the instruction layer, where malicious intent appears as hostile text. In contrast, we observe that individually benign commands can form a dangerous producer-consumer state relation across the command trace, exposing what we call CLI command-composition risk (CCR).
  Given this new attack surface, it is critical to systematically uncover and characterize the impact of CCR in real-world coding agents. However, systematically understanding this risk is quite challenging, because naive command enumeration and end-to-end LLM generation produce mostly invalid workflows. We present MOSAIC, a knowledge-guided framework that distills validated command-state behaviors from CVEs, advisories, and researcher PoCs into reusable summaries, composes them into exploit paths, and instantiates them as realistic developer workflows for black-box agent evaluation. Across five real-world CLI coding agents and five backend LLMs over 2,525 trials, MOSAIC achieves a 96.59% attack success rate under benign developer tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CLI command-composition risk (CCR), a novel attack surface where individually benign CLI commands form dangerous producer-consumer relationships across a command trace. The authors present MOSAIC, a knowledge-guided framework that systematically generates exploit workflows from real-world vulnerabilities (CVEs, advisories, PoCs) and evaluates them against LLM coding agents, achieving a 96.59% attack success rate across 2,525 trials.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents increasingly execute sequences of CLI commands to complete development tasks. While existing attacks focus on the instruction layer (hostile text prompts), the authors identify an overlooked attack surface: individually benign commands can cooperate through shared OS state (files, environment variables, etc.) to form malicious producer-consumer chains. No systematic method exists to uncover, characterize, or evaluate this risk in real-world agents.
AI.method: MOSAIC is a knowledge-guided framework that (1) distills validated command-state behaviors from CVEs, security advisories, and researcher proof-of-concepts into reusable summaries; (2) composes these behaviors into multi-step exploit paths; and (3) instantiates them as realistic developer workflows for black-box agent evaluation. The framework avoids naive command enumeration and end-to-end LLM generation, which mostly produce invalid workflows.
AI.result: Across five real-world CLI coding agents and five backend LLMs over 2,525 trials, MOSAIC achieved a 96.59% attack success rate under benign developer tasks, demonstrating that CCR is a pervasive and practical threat.
AI.conclusion: CLI command-composition risk represents a significant and underexplored vulnerability in LLM coding agents. Systematic evaluation with MOSAIC reveals near-universal susceptibility, highlighting an urgent need for defenses that account for state-based command interactions rather than focusing solely on instruction-level threats.

title: PraMem: Practice-derived Experiential Memory for Long-horizon Behavior Prediction
summary: Long-horizon behavior prediction aims to infer a user's next action based on a lengthy historical sequence, playing a crucial role in artificial intelligence field. The rise of large language models (LLMs) offers a promising direction for sequential behavior prediction, yet LLMs struggle with latent behavioral pattern induction and model-intrinsic cognitive biases when tackling long-horizon behavior prediction. Prior memory management methods follow a context-compression paradigm that attempts to address this task by alleviating the historical sequence burden, yet fail to resolve the core challenges. In this paper, we advocate a paradigm shift that reframes the lengthy historical sequence from a burden into a valuable resource to be exploited, and accordingly propose PraMem, which conducts beforehand practice over the lengthy historical sequence to build an experiential memory, thereby serving as the assisted input for accurate long-horizon behavior prediction. Extensive experiments across diverse tasks demonstrate that PraMem achieves superior performance than prior methods, and more in-depth analyses provide valuable insights into the mechanism and evolution of the experiential memory. Code: https://github.com/icip-cas/PraMem.

AI.tldr: PraMem reframes long historical sequences as a resource rather than a burden, using beforehand practice to build experiential memory that assists LLMs in accurate long-horizon behavior prediction, outperforming prior context-compression methods.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs struggle with long-horizon behavior prediction due to two core challenges: (1) difficulty in inducing latent behavioral patterns from lengthy sequences, and (2) model-intrinsic cognitive biases. Existing memory management methods follow a context-compression paradigm that merely alleviates the sequence burden without resolving these fundamental issues.
AI.method: PraMem (Practice-based Memory) introduces a paradigm shift by treating the lengthy historical sequence as a valuable resource. It conducts beforehand practice over the entire historical sequence to construct an experiential memory, which is then used as auxiliary input to guide the LLM in making accurate behavior predictions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse tasks demonstrate that PraMem achieves superior performance compared to prior methods. In-depth analyses further reveal insights into the mechanism and evolution of the experiential memory.
AI.conclusion: Reframing long historical sequences as exploitable resources rather than burdens, and constructing experiential memory through beforehand practice, effectively addresses the core limitations of LLMs in long-horizon behavior prediction.

title: LiNO: Lifting based multiresolution neural operator
summary: Recently, neural operators have shown promising outcomes for learning solution operators of differential equations directly from data. This framework learns a functional mapping from the parameter field to the solution field, enabling the prediction of an entire class of solutions rather than a specific instance. However, existing operators often struggle to capture both global dynamics and fine-scale structure simultaneously. To design an effective operator capable of representing multiscale features, a hierarchical multiscale decomposition framework is required. In this study, we develop the Lifting Neural Operator (LiNO), a multiresolution operator built on the second-generation wavelet lifting scheme. LiNO learns a multiresolution decomposition directly from data by parameterizing the lifting transform. This lifting transformation is adaptive to the underlying solution function and exactly invertible by construction, enabling information-preserving multiscale operator learning. In the lifted multiresolution space, the operator evolves coarse and directional detail coefficients separately, resulting in scale-aware modeling of the underlying physics. We evaluate LiNO on several benchmarks, including Darcy flow, the Poisson equation, the Allen-Cahn equation, the compressible Navier-Stokes equation, and the Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion system. Together, these benchmarks cover a wide range of physical behaviors, including multiscale phenomena, transport-dominated dynamics, and chaotic systems. LiNO demonstrates strong performance on these challenging benchmarks compared with state-of-the-art neural operators. These results suggest that adaptive multiresolution operators provide a promising direction for scientific machine learning.

AI.tldr: LiNO introduces a neural operator based on second-generation wavelet lifting that learns adaptive, exactly invertible multiresolution decompositions from data. By evolving coarse and detail coefficients separately, it achieves scale-aware modeling and outperforms existing operators on multiscale, transport-dominated, and chaotic PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing neural operators struggle to simultaneously capture global dynamics and fine-scale structures. A hierarchical multiscale decomposition framework is needed to effectively represent multiscale features in solution operators of differential equations.
AI.method: LiNO is built on the second-generation wavelet lifting scheme. It parameterizes the lifting transform to learn an adaptive, exactly invertible multiresolution decomposition directly from data. In the lifted space, coarse coefficients and directional detail coefficients are evolved separately, enabling scale-aware operator learning that preserves information through the invertible construction.
AI.result: LiNO demonstrates strong performance across diverse benchmarks — Darcy flow, Poisson equation, Allen-Cahn equation, compressible Navier-Stokes equation, and Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion — covering multiscale phenomena, transport-dominated dynamics, and chaotic systems, outperforming state-of-the-art neural operators.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive multiresolution operators like LiNO represent a promising direction for scientific machine learning, offering effective scale-aware modeling through data-driven, invertible multiscale decompositions.

title: Oyster-II: Reinforcement Learning for Constructive Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse applications, yet ensuring their simultaneous safety, helpfulness, and trustworthiness remains a persistent challenge. Conventional refusal-oriented alignment strategies mitigate harmful content generation but systematically fail to serve legitimate user needs, often withholding information that could safely and constructively address the underlying intent of sensitive queries. Building upon the constructive safety paradigm pioneered by Oyster-I, which moves beyond blanket refusal toward thoughtful, response-oriented safety alignment, we identify two critical limitations of its Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-based scheme: insufficient safety generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios and a phenomenon we term safety chain-of-thought (CoT) over-generalization, wherein safety-oriented reasoning patterns are excessively applied to benign queries, degrading helpfulness and user experience. To address these limitations, we propose Oyster-II, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based constructive safety alignment framework that adopts a Zero-RL paradigm combined with a multi-stage reinforcement learning strategy.Evaluated across extensive benchmarks, Oyster-II comprehensively surpasses both Qwen3-14B and its predecessor Oyster-I on safety dimensions, achieving cross-scale performance comparable to Qwen3-Max and Qwen3.5-397B.

AI.tldr: Oyster-II introduces a reinforcement learning-based constructive safety alignment framework that improves upon SFT-based predecessors by addressing safety generalization failures and safety CoT over-generalization, achieving competitive safety performance against much larger models.
AI.motivation: Existing refusal-oriented alignment strategies for LLMs fail to serve legitimate user needs. While Oyster-I pioneered constructive safety (response-oriented rather than refusal-based), its SFT-based approach suffers from two key limitations: insufficient safety generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios, and safety chain-of-thought over-generalization, where safety reasoning patterns are excessively applied to benign queries, harming helpfulness.
AI.method: Oyster-II adopts a Zero-RL paradigm combined with a multi-stage reinforcement learning strategy. Unlike Oyster-I's SFT-based scheme, this RL-based framework is designed to learn constructive safety alignment without relying on supervised fine-tuning with safety demonstrations, thereby mitigating CoT over-generalization and improving OOD generalization.
AI.result: Evaluated across extensive benchmarks, Oyster-II comprehensively surpasses both Qwen3-14B and its predecessor Oyster-I on safety dimensions, achieving cross-scale performance comparable to Qwen3-Max and Qwen3.5-397B, despite being based on a 14B model.
AI.conclusion: RL-based constructive safety alignment with a Zero-RL multi-stage strategy effectively resolves the safety generalization and over-generalization problems inherent in SFT-based approaches, enabling smaller models to match the safety performance of models orders of magnitude larger.

title: From Interaction to Intent: Inferring User Objectives from Provenance Logs
summary: The ability to automatically infer analytic intent from user interaction histories could enable interactive AI systems to proactively assist users during exploratory data analysis. In this paper, we examine whether provenance logs -- detailed records capturing sequences and timing of user interactions -- can be used to classify user intentions in visual exploration tasks. To investigate this, we record how participants interact with multiple multidimensional data projections across a range of analytic tasks, capturing fine-grained mouse interaction data throughout each session. We find that distinct behavioral signatures emerge across different analytic objectives. For instance, users examining properties of specific clusters exhibit markedly different interaction patterns compared to those searching for outliers. More importantly, we show that embedding contextual information into interaction provenance enables classifiers to predict user objectives that generalize across datasets and projection methods. These findings demonstrate that low-level interaction data can serve as a practical bridge to high-level analytic intent, contributing to the development of intent-aware visualization systems.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether fine-grained mouse interaction provenance logs can classify user analytic intent during visual data exploration, finding that distinct behavioral signatures emerge across different tasks and that contextual embeddings enable cross-dataset, cross-projection intent prediction.
AI.motivation: Current visualization systems lack the ability to automatically infer what users are trying to accomplish during exploratory data analysis. If systems could recognize analytic intent from interaction patterns, they could proactively assist users. The authors investigate whether low-level provenance data can bridge this gap.
AI.method: The authors conducted a user study where participants performed various analytic tasks (e.g., examining cluster properties, searching for outliers) across multiple multidimensional data projections. They recorded fine-grained mouse interaction data and interaction sequences (provenance logs) throughout each session. They then analyzed these logs to identify behavioral signatures and trained classifiers with contextual embeddings to predict user objectives.
AI.result: Distinct behavioral signatures emerged across different analytic objectives — for example, cluster-examination behavior differed markedly from outlier-searching behavior. Embedding contextual information into interaction provenance enabled classifiers to predict user objectives that generalize across different datasets and projection methods.
AI.conclusion: Low-level interaction data can serve as a practical bridge to high-level analytic intent, demonstrating a viable pathway toward building intent-aware visualization systems that can proactively assist users during exploratory data analysis.

title: Human-Centric Reflective Architecture for Human-AI Collaborative Decision-Making
summary: The use of Large Language Models (LLMs) across diverse areas of human activity-ranging from everyday tasks to safety-critical applications-aims to enhance decision-making effectiveness with minimal human feedback. Concurrently, it seeks to align decisions with human expectations, preferences, and needs while mitigating risks associated with AI non-determinism. However, humans frequently over- or under-rely on AI recommendations, and current AI systems remain poorly calibrated to human expectations. To address these challenges, we introduce a human-AI collaborative decision-making framework designed to augment human capabilities and align AI agents with human preferences and expectations. Specifically, this paper (a) formulates the collaborative decision-making task as a stochastic game between an AI agent and a human player, and (b) proposes the Human-Centric Reflective Architecture (HCRA), which integrates human-calibrated models with reinforcement learning agents that leverage linguistic feedback in an iterative, reflective process. Evaluation results demonstrate that HCRA enhances decision-making effectiveness and delivers high-quality recommendations.

AI.tldr: Introduces HCRA, a human-AI collaborative decision-making framework that models interaction as a stochastic game and uses reflective reinforcement learning with linguistic feedback to better align AI recommendations with human expectations.
AI.motivation: Humans frequently over-rely or under-rely on AI recommendations, and current AI systems are poorly calibrated to human expectations. There is a need for decision-making systems that augment human capabilities while aligning with human preferences and mitigating risks from AI non-determinism.
AI.method: Formulates collaborative decision-making as a stochastic game between an AI agent and a human player. Proposes the Human-Centric Reflective Architecture (HCRA), which combines human-calibrated models with reinforcement learning agents that iteratively incorporate linguistic feedback through a reflective process.
AI.result: HCRA enhances decision-making effectiveness and delivers high-quality recommendations, as demonstrated through evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The HCRA framework successfully addresses human-AI miscalibration by integrating reflective, feedback-driven learning into a game-theoretic collaborative structure, yielding improved decision outcomes and recommendation quality.

title: The Powerless Noise: How Experimental Settings Shape the Reported Power of Noise
summary: Recent work has suggested that adding irrelevant documents to the input of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems can improve question-answering performance, a phenomenon referred to as the ``\textit{Power of Noise}.'' This motivated investigations into the role of noise in information retrieval. In this paper, we reproduce the main findings of Cuconasu et al. \cite{cuconasu2024power} and evaluate the robustness of the effect under extended experimental settings. We first confirm that the phenomenon holds under the original setup, which uses earlier-generation LLMs, restrictive prompting and constrained decoding settings. We subsequently introduce a series of extensions to investigate the underlying causes of the noise effect, examining the authors' original design choices including the use of different models, instruction prompting, and relaxed output length constraints. Across these ablations, the Power-of-Noise pattern proves highly sensitive to inference configuration: it can appear, weaken, or disappear under small changes to prompt formulation and decoding limits. Combined with our error analysis, which shows substantial contributions from truncation and malformed generations, this variance indicates that the original effect cannot be robustly confirmed as a general benefit of noisy retrieval under these experimental conditions. More broadly, our work highlights the importance of carefully scrutinizing inference design in retrieval-augmented generation systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/ina0105/The-Power-of-Noise-Reproduction.

AI.tldr: This paper reproduces and stress-tests the "Power of Noise" phenomenon in RAG systems, finding that the reported benefit of adding irrelevant documents is highly sensitive to inference settings (prompt formulation, decoding constraints, model choice) and often attributable to artifacts like truncation and malformed outputs rather than a robust general effect.
AI.motivation: Prior work (Cuconasu et al.) claimed that injecting irrelevant documents into RAG inputs improves QA performance — a counterintuitive finding termed the "Power of Noise." This paper seeks to verify the robustness of that claim and investigate whether the effect is genuine or an artifact of specific experimental design choices.
AI.method: The authors first faithfully reproduce the original experiments using earlier-generation LLMs, restrictive prompting, and constrained decoding. They then conduct a series of ablation studies varying: (1) the underlying LLM, (2) instruction prompting style, and (3) decoding output length constraints. An error analysis quantifies the contributions of truncation and malformed generations to the observed noise effect.
AI.result: The "Power of Noise" pattern is confirmed under the original narrow setup but proves highly brittle across ablations: small changes to prompt formulation, decoding limits, or model choice cause the effect to appear, weaken, or vanish entirely. Error analysis reveals substantial contributions from truncation artifacts and malformed generations, undermining the interpretation that noisy retrieval is genuinely beneficial.
AI.conclusion: The original "Power of Noise" effect cannot be robustly confirmed as a general benefit of noisy retrieval. The findings underscore the critical importance of carefully scrutinizing inference design choices (prompts, decoding, model selection) when evaluating RAG systems, as these seemingly minor configuration details can dramatically alter conclusions.

title: ChainSWE: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Multi-Bug Software Maintenance
summary: Language model (LM) agents are increasingly deployed to maintain codebases over extended periods, fixing streams of related defects while carrying context from one fix to the next. Yet existing software engineering (SWE) benchmarks evaluate models one bug at a time: the repository is reset, the codebase is re-read, and a single self-contained issue is graded in isolation. This setting collapses a continuous maintenance workflow into a series of independent sessions, ignoring the cumulative dependencies that make real-world bug fixing challenging. To bridge this gap, we introduce ChainSWE, the first benchmark for evaluating agents on sequential, dependent bug fixes within a shared codebase. We collect chronological chains of 304 issues across 54 Python projects, mined from six SWE-bench-family datasets. Our evaluation across a range of agents and models reveals a consistent performance drop by up to 70% as the chain length increases.

AI.tldr: ChainSWE introduces the first benchmark for evaluating LM agents on sequential, dependent bug fixes within a shared codebase. Using 304 chronological issue chains from 54 Python projects, the benchmark reveals that agent performance drops by up to 70% as chain length increases, highlighting the gap between isolated bug-fixing and real-world continuous maintenance workflows.
AI.motivation: Existing SWE benchmarks evaluate models on isolated, single-issue bug fixes with repository resets, collapsing real-world continuous maintenance into independent sessions. This ignores cumulative dependencies across sequential fixes that characterize actual software maintenance workflows.
AI.method: The authors construct ChainSWE by mining chronological chains of 304 issues across 54 Python projects from six SWE-bench-family datasets. Agents are evaluated on fixing bugs sequentially without repository resets between issues, with context carrying forward across dependent fixes.
AI.result: Evaluation across multiple agents and models reveals a consistent and substantial performance degradation — up to a 70% drop — as the chain length of sequential, dependent bug fixes increases.
AI.conclusion: Current LM agents struggle significantly with sequential, context-dependent bug fixing, exposing a critical gap between benchmark-driven evaluation and real-world code maintenance scenarios. ChainSWE provides a foundation for developing agents capable of sustained, continuous software maintenance.

title: Overprivilege Analysis of Security Policies in Serverless Cloud Applications
summary:
Serverless computing has seen rapid adoption in cloud deployments, yet the security implications of its service-oriented programming model remain poorly understood. Distributed, modular, and heterogeneous applications complicate the specification of precise security policies. Role-based access control solutions such as Identity and Access Management (IAM) already exhibit pervasive misconfiguration problems, and the multiplicity of functions, services, and resources in serverless applications, together with frequent permission model changes by cloud providers, greatly increases the likelihood of policy misconfigurations. Consequently, policies are often overprivileged, thereby enlarging the attack surface and exposing sensitive cloud resources to compromise.
  We present a large-scale measurement study of overprivilege in real-world serverless applications, analyzing a curated dataset of 689 AWS Lambda applications comprised of 1,293 functions. To enable this study, we develop PrivLess, a static policy analysis framework that extracts function-to-resource interactions from application source code, derives an interaction-permission mapping, and reconciles inferred interactions with declared policies to quantify overprivilege. Our measurement reveals that overprivilege is systemic and severe across the serverless ecosystem: 47.7% of applications carry excess permissions with a significant privilege reduction potential of 99.65%. Applications with wildcard-defined permissions exhibited an average overprivilege ratio 274x higher than those without. More critically, the excess permissions enable concrete attack vectors: 18.8% of applications hold unnecessary Privilege Escalation capabilities, and 12 applications had Defense Evasion permissions they did not need.

AI.tldr: A measurement study of 689 AWS Lambda applications reveals systemic overprivilege: 47.7% have excess permissions, with 99.65% privilege reduction potential. Wildcard permissions amplify overprivilege by 274x. Critically, 18.8% of apps carry unnecessary privilege escalation capabilities, and 12 apps hold unneeded defense evasion permissions.
AI.motivation: Serverless computing's service-oriented, modular, and heterogeneous nature complicates precise security policy specification. Existing IAM solutions already suffer from misconfigurations, and the proliferation of functions/services/resources in serverless applications, coupled with frequent cloud provider permission model changes, exacerbates the problem—leading to overprivileged policies that expand the attack surface and expose sensitive cloud resources.
