AI.method: The authors develop PrivLess, a static policy analysis framework that (1) extracts function-to-resource interactions from application source code, (2) derives an interaction-permission mapping, and (3) reconciles inferred interactions with declared IAM policies to quantify overprivilege. The framework is applied to a curated dataset of 689 AWS Lambda applications comprising 1,293 functions.
AI.result: 47.7% of applications carry excess permissions with a privilege reduction potential of 99.65%. Applications using wildcard-defined permissions exhibit an average overprivilege ratio 274× higher than those without. 18.8% of applications hold unnecessary Privilege Escalation capabilities, and 12 applications possess unneeded Defense Evasion permissions.
AI.conclusion: Overprivilege in serverless applications is systemic and severe, creating concrete attack vectors including privilege escalation and defense evasion. The findings underscore the urgent need for automated, code-aware policy analysis tools to enforce least-privilege in serverless deployments.

title: Where do LLMs Fall Short in CBT-Guided Affective Reasoning?
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII), 2026
summary: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) provides a structured framework for understanding a user's mental state by examining the interaction between cognitive and behavioral factors. However, out-of-the-box LLMs respond fluently and empathetically, yet collapse into validation & reflection, regardless of what the user actually needs. They know theoretical CBT (scoring up to 96% accuracy on licensing exam questions) but fail to apply it effectively. We explore this gap with a knowledge-guided framework that treats CBT dialogue as controlled affective reasoning: user narratives are decomposed into Beck's Cognitive Conceptualization structure, grounded in clinical SNOMED CT concepts validated via Natural Language Inference, and a Multiple Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) strategy selection between Validation & Reflection, Socratic Questioning, or Alternative Perspectives. To measure whether such guidance actually changes behavior, we introduce the Protocol Leverage Force (F), a behavior-level metric that captures how far an intervention shifts a model away from its default response. Across three open-weight LLMs and 14 RealCBT-derived case studies, evaluated with human experts, valence-arousal trajectories, and linguistic entrainment, F shows that simply introducing protocol definitions via single chain-of-thought prompting fails to change LLM behavior, while MCoT on these definitions guides strategy selection better. Still, the effect stays within 1% (approx. 1.2-1.3%), and all models remain biased toward Validation & Reflection. These results show CBT knowledge alone does not ensure effective application, giving the affective-computing community instrumentation to measure where LLMs fall short.

AI.tldr: LLMs know CBT theory but fail to apply it effectively, defaulting to validation responses. A knowledge-guided MCoT framework using Beck's Cognitive Conceptualization and SNOMED CT concepts improves strategy selection marginally (~1.2-1.3%), but models remain biased toward Validation & Reflection, demonstrating that knowledge alone is insufficient for effective clinical application.
AI.motivation: LLMs score high on CBT licensing exams (up to 96%) but collapse into generic validation and reflection responses in practice, regardless of what the user actually needs. This gap between theoretical knowledge and applied skill in affective computing contexts requires both explanation and measurement.
AI.method: A knowledge-guided framework treating CBT dialogue as controlled affective reasoning, comprising: (1) decomposition of user narratives into Beck's Cognitive Conceptualization structure; (2) grounding in clinical SNOMED CT concepts validated via Natural Language Inference; (3) Multiple Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) strategy selection among Validation & Reflection, Socratic Questioning, and Alternative Perspectives. Evaluation introduces Protocol Leverage Force (F), a behavior-level metric measuring how far an intervention shifts a model from its default response. Three open-weight LLMs tested on 14 RealCBT-derived case studies, assessed via human experts, valence-arousal trajectories, and linguistic entrainment.
AI.result: Single chain-of-thought prompting with protocol definitions fails to change LLM behavior. MCoT on these definitions yields better strategy selection, but the effect size remains small (~1.2-1.3%). All models remain biased toward Validation & Reflection regardless of intervention.
AI.conclusion: CBT knowledge alone does not ensure effective application in LLMs. The Protocol Leverage Force (F) metric provides the affective computing community with instrumentation to quantify where and how LLMs fall short in clinical dialogue contexts.

title: Weighted Conformal Prediction for Lab-to-Track Thermal Transfer in EV Motorsport Powertrains
comment: 8 pages, 3 tables, github like for the codes and dataset:https://github.com/nearpot/Weighted-Conformal-Thermal-Transfer
summary: Predicting thermal volatility in high-performance EV powertrains is difficult as internal temperatures are rarely observable outside the lab, and models calibrated on lab drive cycles fail when deployed against real-world loads. We study this lab-to-track transfer problem using conformal prediction, offering distribution-free uncertainty bounds. We implement Ensemble Batch Prediction Intervals (EnbPI; Xu & Xie, 2021), a leave-one-out bootstrap-ensemble conformal method for autocorrelated time series, and calibrate it on real CALCE lithium-ion cycler data (A123 SP20 cells, FUDS profile). We evaluate it under a genuine, measured covariate shift: a second real CALCE test condition (US06 Highway Driving Schedule at 45°C). The unweighted EnbPI bound, achieving its nominal 95% coverage in-distribution (measured: 95.00%), degrades to 70.13% empirical coverage under this real shift. We introduce a weighted EnbPI procedure combining EnbPI's ensemble residuals with density-ratio weighting (Tibshirani et al., 2019), estimating the density ratio via a probabilistic domain classifier. This recovers coverage to 72.42%, a modest, honestly-reported improvement, not a complete fix. We additionally apply the calibrated model to real 2023 Formula 1 telemetry (Monza and Silverstone, driver VER) as an unsupervised out-of-distribution diagnostic. Because no internal thermal channel exists in public trackside telemetry, we report only unsupervised flag rates (65.6% at Monza, 58.0% at Silverstone, well above the 5% in-distribution base rate) and note inconsistent associations between flags and braking/DRS zones. We conclude that conformal domain adaptation is a promising but only partially solved tool for this problem, detailing exactly where it falls short.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses predicting EV powertrain thermal volatility under real-world load shifts using conformal prediction. Standard EnbPI achieves 95% coverage in-distribution but drops to 70.13% under covariate shift. A proposed density-ratio-weighted EnbPI modestly recovers coverage to 72.42%. The method is also applied diagnostically to F1 telemetry, yielding high unsupervised flag rates, revealing conformal domain adaptation as promising but incomplete.
AI.motivation: Predicting internal thermal behavior in high-performance EV powertrains is challenging because temperatures are unobservable outside controlled lab settings, and models calibrated on lab drive cycles fail under real-world loads. This lab-to-track transfer problem motivates the need for distribution-free uncertainty quantification to ensure safety and reliability during deployment.
AI.method: The authors implement Ensemble Batch Prediction Intervals (EnbPI), a leave-one-out bootstrap ensemble conformal method designed for autocorrelated time series. They calibrate on CALCE lithium-ion cycler data (A123 SP20 cells, FUDS profile) and evaluate under a real covariate shift (US06 Highway Driving Schedule at 45°C). They introduce a weighted EnbPI variant that combines EnbPI's ensemble residuals with density-ratio weighting (Tibshirani et al., 2019), estimating the density ratio via a probabilistic domain classifier. The calibrated model is also applied to 2023 F1 telemetry (Monza, Silverstone, driver VER) as an unsupervised OOD diagnostic, reporting only flag rates due to absent internal thermal channels.
AI.result: Unweighted EnbPI achieved 95.00% empirical coverage in-distribution but degraded to 70.13% under the real US06 covariate shift. Weighted EnbPI recovered coverage to 72.42%, a modest improvement. On F1 telemetry, unsupervised flag rates were 65.6% (Monza) and 58.0% (Silverstone), substantially exceeding the 5% in-distribution base rate, with inconsistent associations between flags and braking/DRS zones.
AI.conclusion: Conformal domain adaptation is a promising direction for battery thermal uncertainty quantification under distribution shift but remains only partially solved. The density-ratio weighting provides marginal gains rather than a complete fix, and F1 diagnostics reveal high flag rates without ground truth, highlighting the gap between current methods and practical deployability.

title: VERITAS: Towards a General-Purpose Replication Tool for Scientific Research
summary: AI tools are accelerating scientific publication while the systems that review it struggle to keep up, and independent verification of published research has become both harder and more important. As manual replication is slow and expensive, a growing line of work uses coding agents to automate parts of the process. Existing efforts are largely packaged as benchmarks with companion agents that only run inside the benchmark's own pipeline, and no general-purpose replication tool exists. We present VERITAS, a domain-agnostic replication framework built around CLI coding agents. Given a paper, a code repository, or both, VERITAS extracts the paper's claims, runs the methodology while resolving issues as they arise, and judges each claim against the evidence from experiment runs. The pipeline returns an importance-weighted Replication Score, a severity-rated log of every fix applied, and the patched codebase. We evaluate VERITAS on CORE-Bench and ReplicationBench, 65 papers spanning computer science, social science, medicine, and astrophysics. Against two strong Claude Code baselines on the same model and host environment, VERITAS achieves state-of-the-art performance and leads on every metric on both benchmarks.

AI.tldr: VERITAS is a domain-agnostic automated replication framework that uses CLI coding agents to extract claims from papers, execute methodologies with runtime issue resolution, and judge claims against experimental evidence — achieving state-of-the-art on CORE-Bench and ReplicationBench across 65 papers in multiple disciplines.
AI.motivation: AI tools are accelerating publication output, but peer review and independent verification cannot keep pace. Manual replication is slow and expensive. While coding agents have been applied to automate replication, existing efforts are locked into benchmark-specific pipelines with no general-purpose tool available. There is a clear need for a reusable, domain-agnostic replication framework.
AI.method: VERITAS takes a paper, code repository, or both as input. It proceeds in three stages: (1) claim extraction from the paper, (2) methodology execution using CLI coding agents that resolve runtime issues (e.g., missing dependencies, environment errors) as they emerge, and (3) claim adjudication, where each extracted claim is judged against evidence from the completed experiment runs. The final output includes an importance-weighted Replication Score, a severity-rated log of all fixes applied, and the patched codebase.
AI.result: Evaluated on CORE-Bench and ReplicationBench — 65 papers spanning computer science, social science, medicine, and astrophysics — VERITAS outperformed two strong Claude Code baselines using the same model and host environment, achieving state-of-the-art results and leading on every reported metric across both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: VERITAS demonstrates that a general-purpose, domain-agnostic replication framework is feasible and can outperform bespoke benchmark agents. It provides a practical tool for independent verification of published research, with transparent outputs (Replication Score, fix logs, patched code) that support reproducibility auditing.

title: The User-In-Context Framework: Understanding Variation in How Users Respond to AI Chatbots
summary: People respond to artificial intelligence chatbots (AICs) in highly variable ways. In this paper, we adapt Bronfenbrenner's theory into a heuristic framework for understanding this variation. The framework places the human user at the center while also placing the AI there and reconceptualizing the proximal processes as the repeated, reciprocal, and coadaptive interactions between the user and a personalized AIC. The surrounding systems identify the contextual factors that shape how the user experiences, interprets, responds to, and is changed by these interactions. Because stateful AICs learn from accumulated exchanges with their users and have memory, users are responding not only to an AIC but also to a version of the AIC that their own prior interactions have helped create. This extension preserves Bronfenbrenner's emphasis on proximal processes while accounting for the unique dynamics of personalized AICs. The resulting framework provides a structured map of where and how variation in human and AIC relationships arises, as well as having implications for researchers, practitioners, and AIC designers.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory into a heuristic framework to explain variability in human-AI chatbot (AIC) interactions. The framework centers the user, places the AI alongside them, and reconceptualizes proximal processes as repeated, reciprocal, coadaptive interactions with a personalized AIC that learns and remembers prior exchanges.
AI.motivation: People exhibit highly variable responses to AI chatbots, and existing theoretical frameworks do not adequately account for this variation. The authors seek to provide a structured, theoretically grounded map of where and how this variation arises.
AI.method: The authors adapt Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory, placing both the human user and the AI at the center. They reconceptualize proximal processes as the repeated, reciprocal, coadaptive interactions between user and personalized AIC. Surrounding systems (micro-, meso-, exo-, macro-, chrono-) identify contextual factors shaping user experience. The framework accounts for stateful AICs that learn from accumulated exchanges and possess memory, meaning users respond to a version of the AIC partially shaped by their own prior interactions.
AI.result: The resulting heuristic framework provides a structured map of where and how variation in human-AIC relationships emerges. It preserves Bronfenbrenner's emphasis on proximal processes while accommodating the unique dynamics of personalized, stateful AICs.
AI.conclusion: The framework has implications for researchers studying human-AI interaction, practitioners deploying AICs, and designers building personalized chatbot systems, offering a systematic lens for understanding and investigating variability in these relationships.

title: Silicon Sampling via Cross-Survey Transfer
summary: Silicon sampling-using large language models (LLMs) to simulate human survey respondents-has emerged as a promising approach for augmenting traditional survey research. However, most evaluations rely on distributional comparisons rather than individual-level prediction, which risks conflating pattern matching with coherent respondent-level prediction. We propose cross-survey transfer, a more rigorous evaluation framework in which an LLM is given a respondent's answers to one set of questions and must predict their answers to entirely different questions from the same survey. Using data from the Taiwan Election and Democratization Study (TEDS) 2024, three open-weight LLMs (27B-120B parameters), and supervised machine learning baselines, we find that: (1) zero-shot LLMs achieve 52% accuracy on genuinely unseen items, closing to within 6 percentage points (pp) of a supervised random forest trained on same-population data; (2) a stable construct predictability hierarchy emerges, from 67% for partisan attitudes to 23% for sovereignty; and (3) variance collapse and safety alignment effects-two commonly cited LLM limitations-turn out to be more nuanced than previously reported, with variance collapse affecting supervised models as well and alignment effects varying dramatically across model families. These findings clarify both the promise and boundaries of silicon sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces cross-survey transfer, a rigorous framework evaluating LLMs as "silicon samples" by predicting individual respondents' answers to unseen survey questions. Testing on Taiwanese political survey data, zero-shot LLMs achieve 52% accuracy (within 6pp of supervised baselines), reveal a stable construct predictability hierarchy (partisan attitudes easiest, sovereignty hardest), and show that variance collapse and safety alignment effects are more nuanced than previously assumed.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of silicon sampling rely on distributional comparisons (aggregate-level pattern matching) rather than individual-level prediction, risking conflation of superficial pattern matching with genuine coherent respondent simulation. The authors aim to establish a stricter, individual-level benchmark that tests whether LLMs can maintain coherent respondent "personas" across disjoint question sets.
AI.method: The authors propose cross-survey transfer: given a respondent's answers to one subset of survey items (training block), the LLM must predict the same respondent's answers to a completely different subset (test block). They apply this to TEDS 2024 data using three open-weight LLMs (27B–120B parameters) and compare against supervised ML baselines (random forest), measuring accuracy, construct-level predictability hierarchies, variance collapse, and safety alignment effects.
AI.result: (1) Zero-shot LLMs reach 52% accuracy on unseen items, within 6pp of a supervised random forest trained on same-population data. (2) A stable predictability hierarchy emerges: partisan attitudes (67%) > other constructs > sovereignty (23%). (3) Variance collapse also affects supervised models, not just LLMs. (4) Safety alignment effects vary substantially across model families, contradicting prior monolithic characterizations.
AI.conclusion: Silicon sampling shows genuine promise for individual-level respondent simulation, but with clear boundaries. The cross-survey transfer framework provides a more stringent evaluation standard. The nuanced findings on variance collapse and alignment effects call for model-specific rather than universal characterizations of LLM limitations in social science applications.

title: Next-Gen Sponsored Search: Crafting the Perfect Query with Inventory-Aware RAG (InvAwr-RAG) Based GenAI
summary: Sponsored search plays a crucial role in e-commerce revenue generation, where advertisers strategically bid on keywords to capture the attention of users through relevant search queries. However, the process of identifying pertinent keywords for a given query presents significant challenges because of a vast and evolving keyword landscape, ambiguous intentions, and topic diversity. This paper highlights an opportunity for to earn a considerable amount of Ads revenue and user engagement where a significant proportion of queries fail to retrieve any sponsored ads. To utilize this opportunity, we introduce the Inventory-Aware RAG-based Generative AI model (InvAwr-RAG), which integrates advanced semantic retrieval and real-time inventory data. This model combines dynamically generated and historically successful queries to align with available inventory and ad campaigns while diversifying rewritten queries to enhance relevance and user engagement. Preliminary results show a significant 68% increase in fill rate and balanced relevance metrics, indicating a strong potential for increased ad revenue. The InvAwr-RAG model sets a new standard in dynamic query optimization, significantly improving ad relevancy, advertiser ROI, and user experience on Walmart's digital platform.

AI.tldr: Walmart introduces InvAwr-RAG, an inventory-aware RAG-based model that rewrites queries failing to retrieve sponsored ads, achieving a 68% increase in ad fill rate while maintaining relevance metrics.
AI.motivation: A significant proportion of search queries on Walmart's platform fail to retrieve any sponsored ads, representing a substantial missed revenue opportunity. The challenge stems from a vast, evolving keyword landscape, ambiguous user intent, and topic diversity that make it difficult to identify pertinent keywords for a given query.
AI.method: The proposed InvAwr-RAG model integrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with advanced semantic retrieval and real-time inventory data. It combines dynamically generated queries with historically successful queries, aligning rewritten queries to both available ad inventory and active ad campaigns while diversifying outputs to enhance relevance and user engagement.
AI.result: Preliminary results demonstrate a 68% increase in fill rate alongside balanced relevance metrics, indicating strong potential for increased ad revenue without compromising retrieval quality.
AI.conclusion: The InvAwr-RAG model sets a new standard for dynamic query optimization in sponsored search, significantly improving ad relevancy, advertiser ROI, and user experience on Walmart's digital platform.

title: Knowledge-Centric Information Systems
summary: For decades, data engineering has developed mature architectural principles for integrating, governing, validating, cataloging, and serving organizational data. The rise of large language models does not eliminate these concerns; it exposes a broader version of them. Organizational knowledge is becoming executable infrastructure: systems increasingly retrieve it, assemble it, reason over it, and act on it. This paper argues that enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) systems suggest a transition toward an architectural discipline for representing, maintaining, governing, and operationally delivering organizational knowledge. We refer to this discipline as \emph{knowledge architecture}. We offer a conceptual model and taxonomy showing how classical data-engineering guarantees must be redefined when the managed unit shifts from records to knowledge artifacts: extract, transform, and load (ETL) becomes knowledge ingestion, change-data capture (CDC) becomes knowledge change detection, lineage becomes provenance, catalogs become knowledge catalogs, materialized views become knowledge views, and medallion architectures become raw--curated--operational knowledge layers. Emerging formats such as large language model (LLM) Wiki and the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) are treated as early evidence of this transition, not as its endpoint. The central claim is that knowledge architecture becomes useful when organizational knowledge ceases to be a passive information resource and becomes an operational asset used by humans, agents, workflows, and models to execute work.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "knowledge architecture" as a new enterprise discipline that extends classical data engineering principles to manage organizational knowledge as executable, operational infrastructure for AI systems—redefining ETL, CDC, lineage, catalogs, views, and medallion architectures for knowledge artifacts rather than data records.
AI.motivation: Data engineering has mature principles for data integration and governance, but the rise of LLMs and enterprise AI exposes a broader challenge: organizational knowledge is no longer a passive resource but is increasingly retrieved, assembled, reasoned over, and acted upon by systems. Existing data-engineering guarantees must be redefined when the managed unit shifts from records to knowledge artifacts.
AI.method: The paper develops a conceptual model and taxonomy that maps classical data-engineering constructs (ETL, CDC, lineage, catalogs, materialized views, medallion architectures) onto their knowledge-architecture counterparts (knowledge ingestion, knowledge change detection, provenance, knowledge catalogs, knowledge views, raw–curated–operational layers). It also surveys emerging formats like LLM Wiki and OKF as early evidence.
AI.result: The authors identify a systematic mapping from data-engineering guarantees to knowledge-architecture concerns and present early-format evidence (LLM Wiki, OKF) that organizations are already moving toward treating knowledge as operational infrastructure rather than static information.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge architecture becomes a necessary discipline when organizational knowledge transitions from a passive information resource to an operational asset executed by humans, agents, workflows, and models. The paper frames this as an architectural transition, not merely a tooling shift.

title: PPE-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating MLLM Unlearning under Private-Public Entanglement
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong capabilities, but they may memorize private information from web data, raising privacy concerns. Machine unlearning offers a way to remove such private knowledge without retraining from scratch. However, existing MLLM unlearning benchmarks have two major limitations. First, they rely on simplified images that contain only the single target individual, failing to reflect the visual complexity of real-world photos. Second, they typically assume that the forget set and retain set are fully separated, ignoring the fact that private information is often visually entangled with benign public information. For example, a private individual may appear with a public figure or in front of a well-known landmark, where unlearning the private target should not damage the public context. To address these limitations, we propose PPE-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating MLLM unlearning under private-public entanglement. Each image contains a target individual to be forgotten and public information to be preserved, including public figure and landmark. We further introduce two simple but effective methods to better preserve public information during unlearning. Through experiments, we find that existing unlearning methods can reduce private information leakage, but often substantially harm adjacent public information.

AI.tldr: PPE-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating MLLM unlearning that addresses the problem of private-public visual entanglement, where private individuals appear alongside public figures or landmarks. Existing unlearning methods reduce privacy leakage but often damage adjacent public information.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM unlearning benchmarks use simplified images with only a single target individual and assume clean separation between forget and retain sets. In reality, private information is visually entangled with benign public content (e.g., a private person photographed with a public figure or at a landmark), and unlearning must preserve the public context.
AI.method: The authors introduce PPE-Bench, a benchmark where each image contains both a target individual to be forgotten and public information (public figure or landmark) to be preserved. They also propose two simple methods designed to better protect public information during the unlearning process.
AI.result: Existing unlearning methods can effectively reduce private information leakage, but they often cause substantial collateral damage to adjacent public information, compromising the utility of the retained knowledge.
AI.conclusion: MLLM unlearning under private-public entanglement remains a challenging open problem. PPE-Bench provides a more realistic evaluation setting, and the proposed methods offer initial steps toward unlearning that respects visual context boundaries.

title: Distill Where the Student Goes: Teacher-Regularized RL for English-Evidence Cross-Lingual RAG
summary: Cross-lingual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is often deployed in an English-evidence regime, where users query in diverse languages but retrieved passages remain English. In this setting, generation can fail despite strong base models: English evidence induces language drift (English or code-switching outputs) and models use evidence unreliably when producing non-English answers. We attribute these failures to two post-training challenges: (i) errors are prefix-dependent, so fixed-trajectory supervision suffers from prefix mismatch; and (ii) sequence-level (partly discrete / judge-based) rewards yield noisy credit assignment and high-variance updates. We propose TR-RAG, a teacher-regularized RL recipe that couples reward optimization with on-policy distillation on student-visited prefixes. A compact student samples on-policy answers, while a stronger frozen teacher is queried only on those prefixes and provides a prefix-wise student-to-teacher reverse-KL anchor. We further introduce a reward decomposition for English-evidence multilingual generation, combining language consistency, character 3-gram recall, and an LLM-judge score for evidence-grounded correctness. Across three benchmarks -- BioASQ-ENKB5, Hotpot-ENKB5, and naturally multilingual MKQA -- and two backbones, TR-RAG improves the composite of language adherence and evidence-grounded correctness over strong baselines. Crucially, the teacher anchor acts as a safety net: on in-domain languages it prevents the large language-consistency collapses (up to ~27 percentage points) that reward-only RL can suffer by drifting below even the base model, while on distant out-of-distribution languages -- where reward-only RL stalls at the base model's ceiling -- it still improves evidence grounding; and on character 3-gram recall the compact student sometimes surpasses its 70B teacher.

AI.tldr: TR-RAG addresses failures in cross-lingual RAG (English evidence, non-English queries) by combining RL optimization with teacher-regularized on-policy distillation. A compact student model samples answers, while a frozen teacher provides prefix-wise reverse-KL regularization, coupled with decomposed rewards (language consistency, character n-gram recall, LLM-judge grounding). This prevents language drift and improves evidence grounding across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Cross-lingual RAG systems where users query in diverse languages but retrieved evidence remains English suffer from two key failure modes: (1) language drift — models produce English or code-switched outputs instead of the target language; (2) unreliable evidence usage when generating non-English answers. These stem from two post-training challenges: prefix-dependent errors causing prefix mismatch in fixed-trajectory supervision, and noisy credit assignment with high-variance updates from sequence-level discrete/judge-based rewards.
AI.method: TR-RAG (Teacher-Regularized RL) couples reward optimization with on-policy distillation on student-visited prefixes. A compact student samples answers on-policy; a frozen, stronger teacher is queried only on those prefixes, providing a prefix-wise reverse-KL anchor (student-to-teacher). The reward function is decomposed into three components: language consistency, character 3-gram recall, and an LLM-judge score for evidence-grounded correctness. The teacher anchor serves as a regularizer to stabilize RL training.
AI.result: Across BioASQ-ENKB5, Hotpot-ENKB5, and MKQA with two backbones, TR-RAG improves the composite of language adherence and evidence-grounded correctness over strong baselines. On in-domain languages, the teacher anchor prevents large language-consistency collapses (up to ~27 pp) that reward-only RL suffers. On distant out-of-distribution languages where reward-only RL stalls at the base model's ceiling, TR-RAG still improves evidence grounding. On character 3-gram recall, the compact student sometimes surpasses its 70B teacher.
AI.conclusion: Teacher regularization via on-policy prefix-wise distillation is an effective safety net for RL-based cross-lingual RAG training, preventing language drift while enabling evidence-grounding improvements even in challenging OOD language settings. The decomposed reward design and prefix-anchored distillation together yield robust multilingual generation from English-only evidence.

title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Risk Aversion in Language Models
comment: ICML 2026 Agents in the Wild workshop
summary: Training AIs to be risk-averse in resources could offer a failsafe in the event that AIs turn out misaligned. Misaligned but risk-averse AIs would tend to prefer low-risk, low-reward strategies like cooperation over high-risk, high-reward strategies like rebellion, limiting the downsides of any misalignment. But we can only feasibly train AIs to be risk-averse on low-stakes gambles, and we will only be safe if their risk aversion generalizes to astronomically-high-stakes gambles. Will it? To shed light on this question, we introduce RiskAverseOOD: a benchmark for measuring how well risk aversion generalizes out of distribution. We then offer some initial results. Using a variety of methods to make Qwen3-8B choose risk-aversely when the stakes are low, we find that we can induce substantial risk aversion when the stakes are astronomically high. Our models' learned risk aversion generalizes at least partially across 98 orders of magnitude. From a baseline 2% rate of choosing a safe `Cooperate' option, we see rates around 70% (SFT and tie training), 52% (DPO), and 39% (activation steering). In another experiment, our fine-tuned reward model reliably scores risk-averse reasoning above risk-neutral or excessively risk-averse alternatives (99.6% pairwise accuracy). We replicate these effects at different scales (Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-14B) and across model families (Gemma-3-12B-IT and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). Overall, we find that risk aversion learned at low stakes can generalize OOD to astronomically high stakes, though not yet consistently enough to serve as a reliable failsafe. Achieving that level of consistency is an open problem.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether risk aversion trained on low-stakes scenarios generalizes to astronomically high-stakes situations, as a potential failsafe against misaligned AI. Using the RiskAverseOOD benchmark, the authors show that risk aversion can partially generalize across 98 orders of magnitude in Qwen3 models, with cooperation rates rising from 2% to 39–70% depending on the training method, though consistency remains insufficient for reliable deployment.
AI.motivation: If AI systems become misaligned, risk-averse AIs would prefer safe, cooperative strategies over dangerous, high-risk ones like rebellion. Training risk aversion is only feasible on low-stakes gambles, so the critical question is whether this aversion generalizes to astronomically-high-stakes scenarios where misalignment would be catastrophic.
AI.method: The authors introduce RiskAverseOOD, a benchmark for measuring out-of-distribution generalization of risk aversion. They apply multiple methods — SFT, DPO, tie training, and activation steering — to Qwen3-8B to induce risk-averse behavior at low stakes, then test generalization to astronomically high stakes. They also train a reward model to score risk-averse reasoning and replicate across model scales (Qwen3-1.7B, 14B) and families (Gemma-3-12B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct).
AI.result: Risk aversion generalizes partially across 98 orders of magnitude. Cooperation rates improved from a 2% baseline to ~70% (SFT/tie training), 52% (DPO), and 39% (activation steering). The fine-tuned reward model achieved 99.6% pairwise accuracy in scoring risk-averse reasoning. Results replicated across scales and model families, though generalization is not yet consistent enough for a reliable failsafe.
AI.conclusion: Learned risk aversion can generalize out-of-distribution to astronomically high stakes, which is encouraging for the failsafe approach. However, the inconsistency of this generalization means it cannot yet serve as a dependable safety mechanism; achieving robust consistency remains an open problem.

title: A Sliding-Window-Based Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Assembly Flow Shop Scheduling with Multi-Product Delivery
summary: Multi-product kitting delivery imposes significant challenges for real-time scheduling in hybrid manufacturing systems that integrate processing and assembly, as dynamic order arrivals simultaneously alter supply dependencies and the set of feasible job-machine assignments. This paper proposes a sliding-window-based reinforcement learning (SWRL) framework for end-to-end online scheduling in the flexible assembly flow shop scheduling problem with complex kitting constraints. The problem is formulated as a heterogeneous graph-based Markov decision process that captures the dual-layer kitting structure and the tail-product bottleneck dynamics that produce a sparse reward landscape. To address the resulting challenges, SWRL integrates a sliding-window filtering mechanism that filters inactive nodes and prioritizes kitting-critical operations, a spatiotemporal graph encoding network that tracks bottleneck shifts across consecutive decision states, and a dynamic action mapping module with a constrained waiting strategy that adapts to the changing action space under variable topologies. Experiments on real-world instances from a home appliance manufacturer demonstrate that SWRL achieves consistent tardiness reductions over classical dispatching rules and existing deep reinforcement learning methods, and exhibits robust performance across varying resource configurations, order loads, and arrival concentrations.

AI.tldr: A sliding-window reinforcement learning framework with graph-based state representation and dynamic action mapping for online scheduling of multi-product kitting in hybrid manufacturing systems, demonstrating superior tardiness reduction on real-world appliance manufacturing data.
AI.motivation: Multi-product kitting delivery in hybrid manufacturing (processing + assembly) creates a challenging online scheduling problem where dynamic order arrivals simultaneously alter supply dependencies and feasible job-machine assignments. Existing methods struggle with the dual-layer kitting structure and the sparse reward landscape caused by tail-product bottleneck dynamics.
AI.method: SWRL formulates the problem as a heterogeneous graph-based Markov decision process (MDP). It employs three key components: (1) a sliding-window filtering mechanism that removes inactive nodes and prioritizes kitting-critical operations; (2) a spatiotemporal graph encoding network that tracks bottleneck shifts across consecutive decision states; and (3) a dynamic action mapping module with constrained waiting strategy to handle variable topology and changing action spaces.
AI.result: On real-world instances from a home appliance manufacturer, SWRL achieves consistent tardiness reductions over both classical dispatching rules and existing deep reinforcement learning methods, with robust performance across varying resource configurations, order loads, and arrival concentrations.
AI.conclusion: The SWRL framework effectively addresses the end-to-end online scheduling problem in flexible assembly flow shops with complex kitting constraints, offering a scalable and robust solution validated on industrial data.

title: Identifying Deceptive Patterns Across Three Age Groups: A Heuristic-Based Cognitive Walkthrough Study of Mobile Apps
summary: Deceptive patterns are tactics used to manipulate users into performing unintended actions. Today, many of these deceptive patterns are implemented in mobile apps targeting diverse age groups. In this paper, we employ a heuristic-based cognitive walkthrough to explore how deceptive patterns are tailored to three age groups, specifically teens (12-17), adults (18-49), and older adults (50+), across different app categories. By analyzing 30 apps spanning 6 categories, we found that 93% of these apps use the nagging pattern. Furthermore, our findings reveal that entertainment apps contain significantly more deceptive patterns than other app categories, such as music/books. Our data also shows that entertainment apps for older adults use sneaking patterns more frequently than entertainment apps for teens or adults. These findings call for the development of more ethical, age-specific design guidelines to protect users from targeted digital manipulation attempts.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 30 mobile apps across 6 categories reveals that 93% employ nagging deceptive patterns, entertainment apps contain the most deceptive patterns overall, and entertainment apps targeting older adults use sneaking patterns more frequently than those for teens or adults.
AI.motivation: Deceptive patterns in mobile apps manipulate users across age groups, but little is known about how these patterns are differentially tailored to specific age demographics. This study aims to uncover age-specific targeting of deceptive design.
AI.method: Heuristic-based cognitive walkthrough of 30 mobile apps spanning 6 categories, stratified across three age groups: teens (12–17), adults (18–49), and older adults (50+).
AI.result: 93% of apps use nagging patterns. Entertainment apps contain significantly more deceptive patterns than other categories (e.g., music/books). Entertainment apps for older adults employ sneaking patterns more frequently than those targeting teens or adults.
AI.conclusion: The findings underscore the need for ethical, age-specific design guidelines to safeguard users from targeted digital manipulation, particularly given the prevalence of nagging and the differential deployment of sneaking in older-adult-targeted entertainment apps.

title: Organizational Memory for Agentic Business Process Execution
summary: LLM-based agents offer new opportunities for automating business process execution beyond the limits of rule-based systems. However, general-purpose LLMs lack the organization-specific knowledge required for reliable execution, which is typically fragmented across human-oriented artifacts such as policies, process models, and standard operating procedures. While such knowledge can technically be encoded in individual prompts or agent-specific retrieval setups, this approach does not scale in enterprises, as it gives rise to knowledge silos and rule duplicates, and makes consistent updates and learning across agents difficult. We argue that this calls for an organizational memory for agentic business process execution: a shared, governed, and agent-consumable reference layer of evolving organization-specific procedural knowledge about how work should be executed. We derive requirements for such a memory, propose an architecture for its curation and consumption, and demonstrate its effectiveness in a proof-of-concept based on a procurement scenario.

AI.tldr: Proposes an organizational memory system — a shared, governed, agent-consumable knowledge layer — to supply LLM-based agents with organization-specific procedural knowledge for business process execution, addressing scalability issues of ad-hoc prompt engineering.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents hold promise for automating business processes but lack organization-specific procedural knowledge. Encoding this knowledge via individual prompts or per-agent retrieval creates knowledge silos, duplicates rules, and impedes consistent updates and cross-agent learning at enterprise scale.
AI.method: The authors derive formal requirements for an organizational memory tailored to agentic process execution, propose a reference architecture covering both curation (governed authoring and evolution of procedural knowledge) and consumption (how agents access and apply this memory), and validate the approach via a proof-of-concept implementation in a procurement scenario.
AI.result: The proof-of-concept demonstrates that the proposed organizational memory architecture effectively enables LLM-based agents to reliably execute business processes by consuming shared, governed procedural knowledge, thereby overcoming the scalability and consistency limitations of siloed prompt-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: An organizational memory acting as a governed, evolving reference layer for procedural knowledge is essential for scaling LLM-based agents in enterprise business process automation. The proposed architecture provides a viable foundation, with the procurement scenario validating its practical effectiveness.

title: Enhancement of E-commerce Sponsored Search Relevancy with LLM
comment: eCom 24: ACM SIGIR Workshop on eCommerce, July 18, 2024, Washington, DC, USA
summary: Sponsored search plays a crucial role as a revenue stream for search engines, wherein advertisers competitively bid on keywords that align with the users' search queries. The task of matching relevant keywords to these queries is complicated by the vast and ever-evolving space of keywords, the ambiguity of user and advertiser intentions, and the wide range of topics and languages involved. Consequently, ensuring that ads are pertinent to user queries presents significant challenges. In the fast-paced world of e-commerce, the accuracy of sponsored search results is vital for boosting user satisfaction and optimizing business operations. This paper presents the development of an advanced Ad Relevance Model within a sponsored search framework, utilizing the power of a pretrained large language model. We detail a pioneering adaptation of the LLAMA2 7B model through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which markedly enhances search precision and operational efficiency, thus opening new avenues for improving user interactions in extensive online marketplaces such as Walmart.com. We introduce a novel query and ad title classifier, which discerns the relevance of search interactions across three categories: Relevant, Partially Relevant, and Irrelevant. Our approach involved adapting the pretrained model specifically for the e-commerce sponsored search context, training it on a large dataset. The fine-tuned model demonstrated a marked improvement in ad relevance accuracy, achieving 89.43% accuracy on a comprehensive test dataset -- outperforming both the baseline model and other advanced language models like GPT-4. The integration of LoRA with the based model represents a significant stride in customizing language models for e-commerce applications, resulting in enhanced search accuracy, cost efficiency, and operational privacy -- a triad essential for the modern digital marketplace.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an ad relevance model for sponsored search at Walmart.com, fine-tuning LLAMA2 7B via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to classify query-ad pairs into Relevant, Partially Relevant, or Irrelevant categories. The model achieves 89.43% accuracy, outperforming baselines and GPT-4, while offering cost efficiency and operational privacy.
AI.motivation: Sponsored search keyword-query matching is challenging due to the vast, dynamic keyword space, ambiguous user/advertiser intent, and diverse topics/languages. Inaccurate ad relevance harms user satisfaction and business operations in fast-paced e-commerce environments like Walmart.com.
AI.method: The authors adapt the pretrained LLAMA2 7B model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for the e-commerce sponsored search domain. A query-ad title classifier is introduced that categorizes relevance into three classes: Relevant, Partially Relevant, and Irrelevant. The model is fine-tuned on a large dataset of search interactions.
AI.result: The LoRA fine-tuned LLAMA2 7B model achieved 89.43% accuracy on a comprehensive test dataset, outperforming both the baseline model and other advanced language models including GPT-4.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LoRA with LLAMA2 represents a significant advance in customizing LLMs for e-commerce sponsored search, delivering improved search accuracy, cost efficiency, and operational privacy — a triad of benefits essential for modern digital marketplaces.

title: Dependencies that Bundle Code and Execution
summary: Applications are built from many dependencies. Each dependency is distributed by package registries but it only contains compiled code and does not ship execution state, so runtimes rebuild that state from scratch on every startup. Execution caching records this preparation result so subsequent starts can skip it, but no existing system publishes execution state to a registry for downstream consumers to reuse. We introduce LIBCACHE, the first system to distribute per-dependency execution caches through a package registry as first-class artifacts alongside compiled code. Each library maintainer produces an execution cache from the library's own test suite and publishes it to Maven Central alongside the JAR. At application build time, LIBCACHE merges all per-dependency caches into a single unified cache that covers the classes exercised across every dependency's test suite. We evaluate LIBCACHE on three real-world Java projects across twelve workloads. LIBCACHE speeds up application startup by up to 1.91x and outperforms a cache built from a single workload in 10 of 12 workloads, with the largest average gain for batik (1.60x vs. 1.27x). Cache production adds 10-47% to build time for applications, and execution caches average 18x the size of the corresponding JAR. Our main contribution is LIBCACHE, which establishes that execution caches are distributable supply chain artifacts and that merging per-dependency caches delivers broader startup coverage than any single observation run.

AI.tldr: LIBCACHE is a system that distributes per-dependency execution caches as first-class artifacts through package registries (Maven Central). Library maintainers publish caches generated from test suites alongside JARs. At build time, these caches are merged into a unified cache, yielding up to 1.91x startup speedup and outperforming single-workload caches in 10 of 12 workloads.
AI.motivation: Applications consist of many dependencies distributed as compiled code without execution state. Runtimes (e.g., JVM) must rebuild this state on every startup, incurring repeated overhead. While execution caching exists locally, no system publishes execution state to registries for downstream reuse, leaving a gap in the software supply chain for distributable cached execution artifacts.
AI.method: LIBCACHE introduces per-dependency execution caches as first-class Maven Central artifacts. Each library maintainer runs the library's test suite to generate an execution cache (capturing class loading, initialization, and compilation state) and publishes it alongside the JAR. At application build time, LIBCACHE merges all dependency caches into a single unified cache covering all exercised classes. This merged cache is then used at application startup to skip redundant runtime preparation.
AI.result: Evaluated on three real-world Java projects across twelve workloads, LIBCACHE achieves up to 1.91x startup speedup. It outperforms a cache built from a single workload in 10 of 12 workloads. For batik, the average gain is 1.60x vs. 1.27x for single-workload caching. Cache production adds 10–47% to application build time. Execution caches average 18× the size of the corresponding JAR.
AI.conclusion: LIBCACHE demonstrates that execution caches are viable distributable supply chain artifacts. Merging per-dependency caches provides broader startup coverage than any single observation run, establishing a new paradigm for reducing startup latency through the package registry ecosystem.

title: TIER: Trajectory-Invariant Explanation Regularization for Membership Privacy
summary: Explainability is central to building trustworthy AI, yet explanation interfaces can inadvertently provide adversaries with an expanded privacy-related attack surfaces. Recent studies show that advanced membership-inference attacks succeed by exploiting confidence-drop trajectories, induced through attribution-guided perturbations, as discriminative features, rather than directly using confidence scores or explanation vectors. Existing defenses against membership inference fail to directly mitigate such explanation-driven attacks. In this work, we investigate whether, during training, a model's own gradients can be leveraged as defense signals against such attacks, thereby aligning explanation profiles between members and non-members. To this end, we propose a Trajectory-Invariant Explanation Regularization (TIER) defense that penalizes erratic fluctuations in confidence drops simulated through gradient-guided perturbations and simultaneously minimizes the distributional shifts via KL-divergence. Unlike conventional adversarial training, which emphasizes label robustness, our approach targets explanation robustness by enforcing self-consistency through KL-divergence and reducing the variance of confidence drops between members and non-members. Extensive experiments confirm that our method effectively mitigates these attacks, delivering privacy protection while maintaining model utility and explanation fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TIER, a defense against explanation-driven membership inference attacks that uses a model's own gradients during training to align confidence-drop trajectories between members and non-members, preserving privacy without sacrificing utility or explanation fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses against membership inference attacks fail to counter explanation-driven attacks that exploit confidence-drop trajectories induced by attribution-guided perturbations. This creates a need for defenses specifically targeting explanation-level leakage.
AI.method: The authors propose Trajectory-Invariant Explanation Regularization (TIER), which penalizes erratic fluctuations in confidence drops simulated via gradient-guided perturbations and minimizes distributional shifts between member and non-member explanation profiles using KL-divergence. Unlike adversarial training focused on label robustness, TIER enforces explanation self-consistency and reduces variance in confidence-drop trajectories.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that TIER effectively mitigates explanation-driven membership inference attacks while maintaining model utility and explanation fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging a model's own gradients as defense signals during training can successfully align explanation profiles between members and non-members, providing an effective countermeasure against explanation-driven privacy attacks without degrading model performance.

title: Hierarchical Sparse Attention Done Right: Toward Infinite Context Modeling
summary: Scaling modern large language models (LLMs) to long contexts is limited by the quadratic computation cost, and poor length extrapolation of dense attention. Chunk-wise sparse attention offers a promising alternative, but all existing methods fall short of full attention because of their inaccurate chunk selection. We propose Hierarchical Landmark Sparse (HiLS) Attention, a chunk-wise sparse attention mechanism that learns chunk selection end-to-end under the language-modeling (LM) loss. HiLS factorizes attention hierarchically: each query performs attention independently with each retrieved chunk to extract chunk-specific information, and the resulting outputs are fused according to chunk retrieval scores. By incorporating retrieval scores into the forward attention computation, HiLS optimizes them directly with the LM loss, enabling end-to-end retrieval learning and native sparse training. Experimental results show that HiLS-Attention achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases better than, full attention at in-domain context lengths. Meanwhile, HiLS-Attention extrapolates more than $64\times$ the training context length with 90% retrieval accuracy, far beyond full attention. Moreover, existing full-attention models can be converted to HiLS-Attention with lightweight continued pretraining, preserving in-domain performance while acquiring ultra-long-context extrapolation. Together with its sparse KV access and computation, HiLS-Attention breaks the usual efficiency-performance trade-off, enabling long-context LLMs that are both more efficient and more effective on general long-context tasks than their full-attention counterparts.

AI.tldr: HiLS Attention is a chunk-wise sparse attention mechanism that learns chunk selection end-to-end via the LM loss. It achieves performance comparable to or better than full attention at in-domain lengths, extrapolates 64× beyond training context length with 90% retrieval accuracy, and allows existing full-attention models to be converted with lightweight continued pretraining.
AI.motivation: Scaling LLMs to long contexts is hindered by the quadratic computation cost and poor length extrapolation of dense attention. Existing chunk-wise sparse attention methods underperform full attention due to inaccurate chunk selection, and retrieval modules are typically trained with auxiliary losses rather than optimized directly under the language modeling objective.
AI.method: HiLS factorizes attention hierarchically: each query performs independent attention with each retrieved chunk to extract chunk-specific information, then fuses outputs according to chunk retrieval scores. Crucially, retrieval scores are incorporated into the forward attention computation, allowing them to be optimized directly by the LM loss — enabling end-to-end retrieval learning and native sparse training without auxiliary objectives.
AI.result: HiLS-Attention matches or exceeds full attention performance at in-domain context lengths, extrapolates over 64× the training context length with 90% retrieval accuracy, and full-attention models can be converted to HiLS with lightweight continued pretraining — retaining in-domain performance while gaining ultra-long-context extrapolation capability.
AI.conclusion: By combining sparse KV access and computation with end-to-end learned retrieval, HiLS-Attention breaks the efficiency-performance trade-off, yielding long-context LLMs that are both more efficient and more effective than full-attention counterparts on general long-context tasks.

title: Safe Inference-Time Alignment via Lagrangian Reward Augmentation
summary: Inference-time alignment steers a frozen language model during decoding using auxiliary reward signals, avoiding the cost of repeated weight updates. However, existing inference-time alignment methods typically optimize a single scalar score, so explicit safety constraints must either be ignored or encoded through manually tuned penalties. We propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a general inference-time alignment framework under safety constraints. Starting from a KL-regularized constrained objective with a reward model and a cost model, LARA dualizes the constraint and reduces the optimization problem to a one-dimensional convex problem over a nonnegative dual variable. Estimated on a small calibration set, this dual variable defines an augmented reward that can be used as a drop-in scoring signal within existing inference-time alignment methods. For sequence-level sampling methods, such as Best-of-N reranking, the calibrated dual variable corresponds to the solution of the expected-cost constrained problem. For token-level reward-guided decoding methods, the same construction yields a principled dual-calibrated heuristic rather than an exact constrained-policy guarantee. We evaluate LARA on both sequence-level and token-level inference-time alignment methods, and find that LARA improves the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, with Best-of-N achieving the best performance among inference-time methods, approaching finetuning-based direct alignment baselines.

AI.tldr: LARA introduces a Lagrangian dual framework for inference-time alignment that incorporates explicit safety constraints by converting a constrained optimization problem (reward maximization subject to cost constraints) into an unconstrained problem with an augmented reward signal, calibrated via a small dataset, improving the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff across both sequence-level and token-level decoding methods.
AI.motivation: Existing inference-time alignment methods optimize a single scalar reward, forcing safety constraints to be handled implicitly through manually tuned penalties. This lacks principled constraint handling. The authors aim to provide a rigorous framework for incorporating explicit safety constraints into inference-time alignment without retraining.
AI.method: LARA formulates a KL-regularized constrained objective with separate reward and cost models, then applies Lagrangian duality to convert it into a one-dimensional convex problem over a nonnegative dual variable. This dual variable is estimated on a small calibration set and defines an augmented reward (reward minus scaled cost). The augmented reward drops directly into existing inference-time methods: for Best-of-N reranking it yields the exact solution to the expected-cost constrained problem; for token-level guided decoding (e.g., FUDGE, RAD) it provides a principled dual-calibrated heuristic.
AI.result: LARA consistently improves the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff across both sequence-level (Best-of-N) and token-level inference-time alignment methods. Best-of-N with LARA achieves the best performance among inference-time methods, approaching the performance of finetuning-based direct alignment baselines.
AI.conclusion: LARA provides a simple, principled, and plug-and-play approach to incorporate safety constraints into inference-time alignment. By reducing constrained decoding to a one-dimensional calibration problem, it enables existing methods to achieve better safety-helpfulness tradeoffs without weight updates, with Best-of-N+LARA rivaling fine-tuned alignment methods.

title: Evaluating Generative Agents with Actions Grounded in Socially Distributed Task Environments using Incognita
summary: Effective agency in social environments depends on when an agent seeks knowledge, when it acts, and whether its actions are justified by acquired information. Existing grounded benchmarks provide executable actions, persistent state, and verifiable outcomes, while social simulation environments provide rich interaction among language agents. We study an evaluation setting that combines these requirements. We define socially distributed task environments as interactive environments where task-relevant knowledge is partitioned across role-isolated participants and consequential actions are accessible only through them. Communication serves as exploration over role-partitioned knowledge, while grounded action serves as exploitation over environment state. We introduce Incognita, a Concordia-based framework that separates social interaction from grounded execution. The evaluated agent routes messages to a user or specialist entities; specialists mediate admissible operations; a deterministic sub-environment executes accepted operations over a canonical state; and an offline evaluator scores outcomes with inherited rewards. Incognita-Retail transforms tau-bench retail into a multi-entity environment while preserving final-state reward semantics. We evaluate three generative agent models on 18 tasks stratified by social breadth, with 540 trials. Progress appears in reward and behavior: success rises from 0 percent to 8.9 percent and 17.2 percent, while premature finalization falls from 100 percent to 87 percent and 58 percent. Stronger models elicit more hidden knowledge, contact more entities, and attempt more grounded writes, yet reliability remains low. These findings show that socially distributed task environments expose behavior before reliable success, including knowledge elicitation, source selection, grounded action attempts, and premature completion belief.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Incognita, a framework for evaluating language agents in socially distributed task environments where knowledge is partitioned across role-isolated entities and actions require grounded execution. Evaluations on 18 tasks show modest success rates (0%→17.2%) with stronger models improving knowledge elicitation but reliability remaining low.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks either provide grounded execution (actions, state, verifiable outcomes) OR rich social simulation, but not both. Real-world agency requires both: knowing when to seek knowledge from others, when to act, and whether actions are justified. The authors argue that combining these requirements creates a distinct evaluation regime exposing behaviors invisible in either paradigm alone.
AI.method: The authors define socially distributed task environments and implement Incognita on top of Concordia. The framework separates: (1) social interaction routing (agent ↔ user/specialists), (2) specialist-mediated grounded operations, (3) a deterministic sub-environment for canonical state execution, and (4) offline reward scoring. Incognita-Retail adapts tau-bench retail tasks into multi-entity environments preserving final-state reward semantics. Three generative agent models are evaluated across 18 tasks varying in social breadth, with 540 total trials.
AI.result: Success rates: 0% (weakest model), 8.9%, and 17.2% (strongest). Premature finalization drops from 100% to 87% to 58%. Stronger models elicit more hidden knowledge, contact more entities, and attempt more grounded writes, but overall reliability remains low. Key behavioral gaps identified include knowledge elicitation, source selection, grounded action attempts, and premature completion belief.
AI.conclusion: Socially distributed task environments expose critical behavioral gaps in language agents before reliable success is achieved. The dissociation between improved behaviors (elicitation, entity contact, write attempts) and persistently low success rates indicates that current models lack robust integration of social exploration with grounded exploitation, making this a valuable evaluation paradigm for future agent development.

title: Who Responds When the Driver Is Gone? A Framework for Human Intent Understanding
summary: As autonomous vehicles progress toward fully driverless mobility, a critical question emerges: who understands and responds to passengers when the human driver is absent? Existing autonomous driving systems primarily optimize predefined navigation and control objectives from external scene observations, but they remain limited in perceiving and reasoning about in-cabin human intent. In this paper, we propose Intent2Drive, a unified framework for holistic human intent understanding and human-aligned planning. Instead of treating passenger intent as explicit commands alone, Intent2Drive models intent as a latent cognitive state shaped by language, personal attributes, emotional and physical conditions, behavioral signals, and situational context. To support this formulation, we construct a Holistic Intent Dataset (HID) that provides structured supervision over both explicit and implicit intent cues. Built upon HID, our Theory-of-Mind-inspired Human Intent Reasoner (HIR) infers a Latent Human State (LHS) and further translates it into a planner-compatible Human Intent Objective (HIO). We then introduce a Hierarchical Intent-Conditioned Planner (HICP) that incorporates HIO into route-level and trajectory-level planning, enabling driving behaviors to remain aligned with passenger needs across different planning horizons. Extensive experiments show that Intent2Drive improves structured human intent inference and HIO construction while preserving competitive closed-loop planning performance. These results demonstrate a promising step toward passenger-responsive autonomous driving systems that can reason about, interpret, and act upon human intent in driverless mobility.

AI.tldr: Intent2Drive proposes a unified framework for understanding in-cabin passenger intent and generating human-aligned driving plans in autonomous vehicles, using a Theory-of-Mind-inspired reasoner to infer latent human states and a hierarchical intent-conditioned planner to produce responsive driving behaviors.
AI.motivation: As autonomous vehicles become fully driverless, existing systems lack the ability to perceive and reason about in-cabin human passenger intent. Current approaches optimize for external navigation and control objectives but fail to account for the absence of a human driver who normally interprets and responds to passenger needs.
AI.method: The framework consists of three core components: (1) A Holistic Intent Dataset (HID) providing structured supervision over explicit and implicit intent cues; (2) A Theory-of-Mind-inspired Human Intent Reasoner (HIR) that infers a Latent Human State (LHS) from language, personal attributes, emotional/physical conditions, behavioral signals, and situational context, then translates it into a Human Intent Objective (HIO); and (3) A Hierarchical Intent-Conditioned Planner (HICP) that incorporates HIO into both route-level and trajectory-level planning horizons.
AI.result: Intent2Drive improves structured human intent inference and HIO construction while maintaining competitive closed-loop planning performance, demonstrating effective passenger-responsive driving behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The work represents a promising step toward passenger-responsive autonomous driving systems capable of reasoning about, interpreting, and acting upon human intent in driverless mobility contexts.

title: Swarm-Driven Multi-Agent Reasoning for Smart City Security
summary: Modern smart cities are interconnected cyber-physical ecosystems where heterogeneous devices exchange data and control commands. Coordinated attacks may appear as weak and distributed indicators, including low-rate scanning, abnormal credential use, protocol misuse, or delayed lateral movement, with each signal remaining below local alert thresholds. Therefore, smart-city security is not only an anomaly detection task but also a reasoning task under uncertainty, partial observability, and adversarial manipulation. This work presents TPSC-Sec, an LLM-based multi-agent approach for stable security reasoning in smart cities. TPSC-Sec decomposes analysis across specialized agents that inspect traffic behavior, protocol interactions, identity usage, and temporal attack progression. Their independent threat hypotheses are aggregated by the proposed Threat-Pheromone Swarm Consensus mechanism, which reinforces supported hypotheses, suppresses contradictions, and preserves temporal consistency, thereby driving competing interpretations toward a stable collective decision. We further introduce Adaptive Verified TPSC, which adds verification-aware calibration, context-sensitive weighting, and disagreement-adaptive control to reduce unsupported LLM outputs and reasoning inconsistency. Experiments over 500 runs show that TPSC-Sec achieves a high consensus acceptance rate of 0.97 plus or minus 0.02, hypothesis-support concentration above 0.99, a consensus margin of 2.08 plus or minus 0.21, low aggregate risk of 0.23 plus or minus 0.04, high inter-agent agreement of 0.82 plus or minus 0.06, and strong support-quality correlation of r equals 0.93. Adaptive agent selection reduces the number of active agents by 50 percent while improving system fitness by 11.6 percent. These results demonstrate robust, interpretable, and efficient security reasoning for adversary-resilient smart-city environments.

AI.tldr: TPSC-Sec is an LLM-based multi-agent framework that uses a Threat-Pheromone Swarm Consensus mechanism to aggregate independent threat hypotheses from specialized security agents, achieving stable, interpretable, and adversary-resilient security reasoning in smart-city cyber-physical ecosystems.
AI.motivation: Smart cities are complex cyber-physical ecosystems vulnerable to coordinated, distributed attacks whose individual signals fall below detection thresholds. Security in this context requires reasoning under uncertainty, partial observability, and adversarial manipulation, which goes beyond simple anomaly detection.
AI.method: TPSC-Sec deploys specialized LLM-based agents that independently analyze traffic behavior, protocol interactions, identity usage, and temporal attack progression. Their threat hypotheses are aggregated via a Threat-Pheromone Swarm Consensus mechanism that reinforces supported hypotheses, suppresses contradictions, and maintains temporal consistency. An Adaptive Verified TPSC extension adds verification-aware calibration, context-sensitive weighting, and disagreement-adaptive control to reduce hallucination and reasoning inconsistency, along with adaptive agent selection.
AI.result: Over 500 runs: consensus acceptance rate of 0.97±0.02, hypothesis-support concentration above 0.99, consensus margin of 2.08±0.21, aggregate risk of 0.23±0.04, inter-agent agreement of 0.82±0.06, support-quality correlation r=0.93. Adaptive agent selection reduces active agents by 50% while improving system fitness by 11.6%.
AI.conclusion: TPSC-Sec delivers robust, interpretable, and efficient security reasoning for adversary-resilient smart-city environments, demonstrating that swarm-inspired consensus among specialized LLM agents can effectively handle distributed threat detection with high reliability.

title: Beyond Item Order: Temporal Gap Tokenization for Generative Recommendation with Semantic IDs
summary: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation has recently emerged as a scalable paradigm for sequential recommendation, where each item is represented by a compact sequence of discrete codes and next-item prediction is formulated as code generation. Existing methods, however, typically construct user histories as sequences of static item identifiers, leaving the elapsed time between consecutive interactions outside the generative input. This temporal blindness is problematic because inter-interaction gaps provide useful cues about interest continuity and preference drift. In this paper, we propose ChronoSID, a lightweight temporal augmentation framework for semantic-ID-based generative recommendation. ChronoSID injects temporal signals into the standard three-stage semantic-ID pipeline from two complementary perspectives. First, we introduce Time-Aware Field-Aware Masked Auto-Encoding (TA-FAMAE), which regularizes item representation learning with an auxiliary time-gap prediction objective. Second, we discretize historical interaction intervals into fixed log-scale gap tokens and interleave them with semantic ID tuples as the encoder input of the sequence-to sequence generator. This design preserves the compact SID generation paradigm while enabling the model to capture time-aware transition patterns. Experiments on Amazon review benchmarks show that ChronoSID consistently improves over ReSID and other competitive generative recommendation baselines. Ablation studies further verify the contribution of both temporal components, and diagnostic analyses show clearer gains under long-gap scenarios where user interests are more likely to drift.

AI.tldr: ChronoSID is a lightweight framework that injects temporal signals into semantic-ID-based generative sequential recommendation by (1) regularizing item representations with a time-gap prediction objective and (2) interleaving discretized time-gap tokens with semantic ID tuples, consistently improving performance especially under long-gap scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic-ID-based generative recommenders represent user histories as sequences of static item identifiers, ignoring elapsed time between interactions. This temporal blindness overlooks crucial signals about interest continuity and preference drift encoded in inter-interaction gaps.
AI.method: ChronoSID augments the standard three-stage semantic-ID pipeline with two components: (1) Time-Aware Field-Aware Masked Auto-Encoding (TA-FAMAE), which adds an auxiliary time-gap prediction objective to regularize item representation learning; and (2) discretization of historical interaction intervals into fixed log-scale gap tokens, interleaved with semantic ID tuples as encoder input to the seq2seq generator, preserving compact SID generation while capturing time-aware transition patterns.
AI.result: ChronoSID consistently improves over ReSID and other competitive generative baselines on Amazon review benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm both temporal components contribute, and diagnostic analyses reveal clearer gains under long-gap scenarios where user interest drift is more likely.
AI.conclusion: Temporal augmentation via ChronoSID effectively addresses the temporal blindness of semantic-ID-based generative recommenders, demonstrating that lightweight time-aware modeling can yield consistent and interpretable gains, particularly in long-interval settings prone to preference drift.

title: Schedulable Job-Level Dependencies for Cause-Effect Chains via Graph Neural Networks
summary: Modern automotive software architectures comprise large sets of mixed-criticality functions executing on shared multi-core platforms with strict real-time and end-to-end timing requirements. Sensor-to-actuator data propagation in such systems is typically expressed via cause-effect chains with worst-case data-age budgets. Job-level dependencies (JLDs) have been introduced to provide a schedule-agnostic mechanism for bounding the data age independently of the underlying scheduler. The state-of-the-art methods for synthesizing JLDs, however, do not check whether the produced JLDs are enforceable under a concrete scheduling policy or jointly schedulable at the system level. In this paper we propose the first machine-learning-based JLD synthesis method, built around a two-level Graph Neural Network with temperature-controlled sampling that learns the structural patterns connecting cause-effect chain configurations to their JLD solutions. Since learned outputs may not be correct by construction, we embed the GNN in a novel Generate-and-Verify architecture in which a safe DP data-age checker, together with a per-chain EDF feasibility checker and a system-level demand-bound test, accept or reject each candidate. We show that the ML-based generator substantially outperforms the original greedy heuristic while achieving orders-of-magnitude lower synthesis time, demonstrating that learned structural priors can effectively replace exponential propagation-tree enumeration on this class of real-time scheduling problems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the first machine-learning-based method for synthesizing job-level dependencies (JLDs) in mixed-criticality automotive systems, using a two-level Graph Neural Network with temperature-controlled sampling embedded in a Generate-and-Verify architecture. The approach significantly outperforms prior greedy heuristics in solution quality while achieving orders-of-magnitude faster synthesis times.
