AI.motivation: In modern automotive software architectures, mixed-criticality functions share multi-core platforms with strict end-to-end timing constraints expressed as cause-effect chains with data-age budgets. Existing JLD synthesis methods fail to verify whether generated JLDs are enforceable under concrete scheduling policies or jointly schedulable at the system level, creating a gap between synthesis and feasibility.
AI.method: A two-level Graph Neural Network with temperature-controlled sampling learns structural patterns connecting cause-effect chain configurations to JLD solutions. The GNN is embedded in a Generate-and-Verify architecture: a safe DP (dynamic programming) data-age checker, a per-chain EDF feasibility checker, and a system-level demand-bound test collectively accept or reject each candidate, ensuring correctness of the final output.
AI.result: The ML-based generator substantially outperforms the original greedy heuristic in solution quality while achieving orders-of-magnitude lower synthesis time. Learned structural priors effectively replace exponential propagation-tree enumeration for this class of real-time scheduling problems.
AI.conclusion: Learned structural priors via GNNs, combined with formal verification, offer a powerful and efficient alternative to exhaustive enumeration for JLD synthesis in real-time automotive systems, bridging the gap between synthesis and schedulability guarantees.

title: PromptPET: Privacy-Utility Optimized Prompt Obfuscation
summary: Privacy is an important challenge when users interact with AI chatbots, since users may share sensitive information, explicitly or implicitly, and AI chatbots can use this information for user profiling. In this paper, we aim to protect user privacy via a user-side mechanism that transforms sensitive information in a user prompt, while preserving enough information to elicit a useful response from the chatbot. This approach faces an inherent tradeoff between protecting privacy (i.e., avoiding profiling) and preserving utility (i.e., getting personalized and task-specific responses). To that end, we consider, evaluate, and compare four different obfuscation actions, namely redaction, abstraction, replacement, and a novel noising/denoising scheme that we introduce. Additional novel insights include: utilizing a data type taxonomy to both identify and obfuscate sensitive information and explicitly taking into account the utility of chat responses in making the obfuscation decision. First, we systematically optimize and evaluate each obfuscation action independently in terms of the privacy-utility tradeoff it achieves. Second, we propose PROMPTPET, an LLM-based agent that selects the best obfuscation action for each sensitive part of the prompt, using a reinforcement-learning inspired rule optimizer, applied for the first time in this context. Using a real-world chat dataset, we show that PROMPTPET matches the best privacy-utility tradeoff attainable by any single obfuscation action and significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: PROMPTPET is an LLM-based agent that protects user privacy in chatbot interactions by selectively obfuscating sensitive information in user prompts. It uses four obfuscation actions (redaction, abstraction, replacement, and a novel noising/denoising scheme) and employs a reinforcement-learning-inspired rule optimizer to choose the optimal action per sensitive data type, achieving the best privacy-utility tradeoff compared to single-action baselines and prior state-of-the-art.
AI.motivation: Users interacting with AI chatbots may inadvertently share sensitive information that can be exploited for user profiling. Existing privacy mechanisms struggle to balance the tradeoff between protecting privacy (preventing profiling) and preserving utility (obtaining useful, personalized responses). A user-side mechanism is needed that can intelligently decide how to obfuscate different types of sensitive information while maintaining response quality.
AI.method: The paper proposes a two-stage approach: (1) Systematic independent optimization and evaluation of four obfuscation actions — redaction, abstraction, replacement, and a novel noising/denoising scheme — across the privacy-utility tradeoff. A data type taxonomy is used to identify and categorize sensitive information. (2) PROMPTPET, an LLM-based agent that selects the best obfuscation action for each sensitive segment using a reinforcement-learning-inspired rule optimizer. This is the first application of such an optimizer in this context. Evaluation uses a real-world chat dataset.
AI.result: PROMPTPET matches the best privacy-utility tradeoff attainable by any single obfuscation action and significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: Selective, type-aware obfuscation driven by a reinforcement-learning-inspired optimizer enables superior privacy protection without sacrificing chatbot response utility. The PROMPTPET framework demonstrates that an agent-based approach can dynamically balance the inherent privacy-utility tradeoff more effectively than static, single-action obfuscation strategies or prior methods.

title: psytechlab at CLPsych 2026: Utilising Natural Language Processing methods and Large Language Models for Social Media Text Analysis
comment: Accepted by CLPsych2026. CLPsych 2026 will be held at ACL in San Diego July 4th, 2026
summary: Social media posts are a rich and valuable source of data for analyzing mental health states and users' well-being using automated analysis tools. In this work, we demonstrate how we used a range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), BERT-based models, and Large Language Models (LLMs), for self-state and well-being analysis and summarization during the CLPsych Shared Task 2026. Our approach achieved one of the top Consistency and Contradiction scores for the summarization task and also middle-level results for the other tasks. By testing and developing such mental health-state estimation systems, we contributed to improving mental health support systems. We make our code available https://github.com/psytechlab/CLPsych2026/.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an NLP-based system combining LSTM, BERT, and LLMs for analyzing mental health states and well-being from social media posts, achieving top Consistency and Contradiction scores in summarization at CLPsych Shared Task 2026.
AI.motivation: Social media posts offer rich data for automated mental health state and well-being analysis. The work aims to advance mental health support systems through shared task participation and publicly available code.
AI.method: A range of NLP methods were employed: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, BERT-based transformer models, and Large Language Models (LLMs), applied to self-state analysis, well-being analysis, and summarization tasks within the CLPsych Shared Task 2026 framework.
AI.result: The system achieved one of the top scores in Consistency and Contradiction metrics for the summarization task and obtained middle-tier results on the other shared tasks.
AI.conclusion: Testing and developing mental health-state estimation systems with diverse NLP techniques contributes meaningfully to improving mental health support systems. Code is publicly released.

title: Induction Heads Interpolate N-Grams
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICML 2026. OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=BSY7jhBxM1
summary: Induction heads are attention circuits believed to underlie in-context learning in transformers, yet a precise characterization of the estimators they implement remains elusive. We study transformers trained on order-$k$ Markov chains and identify two complementary smoothing mechanisms. First, at finite attention-weight scale, the circuit implements a soft context-matching estimator: it aggregates contributions from exact and partial context matches, weighted exponentially by their overlap, and induces a data-dependent interpolation across context orders analogous to Jelinek-Mercer smoothing. Second, a beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token induces additive pseudo-counts, recovering Dirichlet-style smoothing. We construct a disentangled transformer implementing both mechanisms and show that trained transformers recover the predicted attention patterns. Across settings where pseudo-count smoothing is optimal or lower-order contexts provide structured evidence, trained transformers match or outperform classical count-based baselines. Our results bridge mechanistic interpretability of induction heads with classical statistical smoothing, revealing that transformers learn to regularize in-context estimation rather than simply count.

AI.tldr: Transformers learn in-context estimation via two smoothing mechanisms — soft context-matching (Jelinek-Mercer-style interpolation) and BOS-induced pseudo-counts (Dirichlet-style smoothing) — bridging mechanistic interpretability of induction heads with classical statistical smoothing.
AI.motivation: Induction heads are believed to drive in-context learning in transformers, but the precise statistical estimators they implement are not well characterized. The authors aim to formally connect induction head mechanisms to classical smoothing techniques from statistical language modeling.
AI.method: The authors train transformers on order-k Markov chains and analyze the learned attention patterns. They construct a disentangled transformer that explicitly implements both smoothing mechanisms and compare its attention patterns to those of freely trained transformers, across settings where pseudo-count smoothing is optimal or lower-order contexts provide structured evidence.
AI.result: Two complementary mechanisms emerge: (1) soft context-matching with exponential weighting by overlap, yielding Jelinek-Mercer-style interpolation across context orders; (2) BOS token induces additive pseudo-counts, recovering Dirichlet-style smoothing. Trained transformers recover the predicted attention patterns and match or outperform classical count-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Transformers do not merely count in-context; they learn sophisticated regularization strategies that correspond to classical statistical smoothing methods. This bridges mechanistic interpretability with established statistical theory and suggests that induction heads implement principled, regularized estimators.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Seeking Diagnostic Reasoning with Large Language Models
summary: Recent reasoning-centric Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant strides, yet they predominantly operate on a passive-inference pattern that assumes complete information. In contrast, real-world clinical intelligence is inherently an iterative investigative process requiring strategic evidence acquisition. To bridge this gap, we formalize medical diagnosis as an Iterative Evidence-Seeking Task. We leverage Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to elicit intrinsic reasoning within a closed-loop environment, guided by a novel suite of rewards that enforce diagnostic precision and examination consistency. To facilitate this, we introduce the Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based Examination Simulator (RAGES), a high-fidelity clinical oracle that provides realistic, knowledge-grounded follow-up evidence. Empirical results across diverse datasets demonstrate that our framework enables LLMs to transition from passive responders to autonomous assistants. Notably, our model demonstrates comparable performance to larger and reasoning-enhanced baselines, while RAGES proves superior to vanilla LLMs in generating biologically plausible clinical feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes medical diagnosis as an Iterative Evidence-Seeking Task, using RLVR with a novel reward suite in a closed-loop environment. It introduces RAGES, a RAG-based examination simulator, enabling LLMs to transition from passive inference to autonomous clinical investigation, achieving performance comparable to larger reasoning-enhanced models.
AI.motivation: Current reasoning LLMs operate under a passive-inference pattern assuming complete information, whereas real clinical diagnosis is an iterative, investigative process requiring strategic evidence acquisition. This gap motivates formalizing diagnosis as an active evidence-seeking task.
AI.method: The authors formalize medical diagnosis as an Iterative Evidence-Seeking Task and employ Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) in a closed-loop environment. A novel reward suite enforces diagnostic precision and examination consistency. They also introduce RAGES (Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based Examination Simulator), a high-fidelity clinical oracle providing realistic, knowledge-grounded follow-up evidence.
AI.result: The framework enables LLMs to shift from passive responders to autonomous assistants. The model achieves diagnostic performance comparable to larger, reasoning-enhanced baselines. RAGES outperforms vanilla LLMs in generating biologically plausible clinical feedback.
AI.conclusion: RLVR combined with a high-fidelity simulator like RAGES can effectively transform passive LLMs into autonomous clinical diagnostic agents capable of iterative evidence-seeking, rivaling larger reasoning models while producing more plausible clinical feedback.

title: Toward Personalized Social Robots for Child Well-being: Data Requirement Principles from a Recommender-System Perspective
comment: Accepted as a Late Breaking Report (LBR) at IEEE RO-MAN 2026
summary: Social robots are increasingly deployed in clinical settings to support the well-being of children, where effective support must be personalized to each child. Personalization, choosing the robot action best suited to each child, can be framed as a recommendation problem, and a recently proposed recommender-system framework for social robots offers a principled approach through user profiling, ranking, and responsible computing. Instantiating it, however, is blocked not by the model but by the data, which is hard to gather. A child's state shifts within and across visits, so no fixed description of the user holds. Within a session, the few signals of whether the robot's actions helped are weak and indirect. Across sessions, children are rarely seen more than once, and anonymization breaks the identity needed to link visits. Because care cannot be randomized, existing data is observational, biased toward whatever was already done. Each is a familiar recommender-system problem, and we propose four data principles in response: an integrated profile, effectiveness signals, linkable coverage, and an exposure record logged at collection time. We identify which of these principles each capability requires, and frame them as concrete guidelines for data collection.

AI.tldr: Deploying social robots for children in clinical settings requires personalization framed as a recommendation problem. The authors identify key data challenges — shifting user states, weak within-session signals, infrequent revisits with broken identity linkage, and observational bias — and propose four data collection principles to address them: integrated profiles, effectiveness signals, linkable coverage, and exposure logging.
AI.motivation: Social robots in pediatric clinical care need personalized action selection, which can be framed as a recommender-system problem. However, existing data collection practices are fundamentally inadequate for instantiating such a framework. The paper aims to diagnose these data-specific bottlenecks and provide actionable guidance for future data collection.
AI.method: The authors analyze the problem from a recommender-systems perspective, mapping each component of the framework (user profiling, ranking, responsible computing) to the data requirements. They identify four core data challenges: (1) non-stationary child states within/across visits, (2) weak and indirect effectiveness signals, (3) broken identity linkage due to anonymization and rare revisits, and (4) observational bias from non-randomized care. They then derive four prescriptive data principles and map which principles each capability requires.
AI.result: The paper yields four data collection principles: (1) an integrated profile capturing dynamic user state; (2) effectiveness signals measuring whether a robot's action actually helped; (3) linkable coverage to connect visits across sessions while managing privacy; and (4) an exposure record logged at collection time to address selection bias. These are presented as concrete guidelines, with a mapping of which principles each recommender-system capability depends on.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck in personalizing social robots for children is not algorithmic but data-related. Adopting the four proposed data collection principles — integrated profiling, effectiveness signals, linkable coverage, and exposure logging — can bridge the gap between recommender-system theory and practical deployment, enabling rigorous personalization in clinical child-robot interaction.

title: Agentic IoT: Architectures, Applications, and Challenges Toward the Internet of Agents
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, Author's preprint version. The manuscript may be revised based on peer-review feedback and publication requirements
summary: The integration of AI into Internet of Things (AIoT) systems has gradually transformed them from passive data collection infrastructures into intelligent systems capable of anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, classification, forecasting, and optimization. However, most existing solutions still rely on task-specific models that infer from sensor data; thus, system-wide capabilities such as real-time reasoning, adaptive planning, autonomous coordination, learning, tool use, and contextual decision-making remain limited. This paper examines Agentic IoT as a next-generation cognitive IoT paradigm that integrates the perception, reasoning, planning, learning, and action capabilities of autonomous AI agents with cyber-physical systems. Agentic IoT aims to transform IoT from data-centric sensing and inference infrastructures into distributed cognitive agent ecosystems operating across the device/edge-fog-cloud continuum. The paper first grounds this transition as a paradigm shift and positions Agentic IoT in relation to AIoT, edge intelligence, multi-agent systems, and the Internet of Agents. It then systematically reviews current studies, presents a holistic architectural framework, discusses domain-specific application potential, and identifies key technical, operational, and research challenges together with future research directions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Agentic IoT as a next-generation cognitive IoT paradigm that integrates autonomous AI agents (with perception, reasoning, planning, learning, and action capabilities) into cyber-physical systems, transforming IoT from passive data-centric infrastructures into distributed cognitive agent ecosystems across the device/edge-fog-cloud continuum. It provides a paradigm-shift grounding, systematic review, architectural framework, application domains, and future research directions.
AI.motivation: Existing AIoT systems remain limited to task-specific models that infer from sensor data, lacking system-wide capabilities such as real-time reasoning, adaptive planning, autonomous coordination, learning, tool use, and contextual decision-making. This gap motivates a paradigm shift toward fully cognitive, agent-driven IoT ecosystems.
AI.method: The paper first grounds the transition from AIoT to Agentic IoT as a paradigm shift, positioning Agentic IoT relative to AIoT, edge intelligence, multi-agent systems, and the Internet of Agents. It then conducts a systematic literature review, proposes a holistic architectural framework spanning the device/edge-fog-cloud continuum, discusses domain-specific application potential, and identifies key technical, operational, and research challenges.
AI.result: The paper delivers a comprehensive architectural framework for Agentic IoT, a structured positioning of the paradigm within the broader research landscape, a systematic review of current studies, and a roadmap of technical/operational challenges and future research directions.
AI.conclusion: Agentic IoT represents a paradigm shift from data-centric sensing toward distributed cognitive agent ecosystems. Realizing this vision requires addressing significant challenges in real-time reasoning, adaptive planning, autonomous coordination, and contextual decision-making across the device-edge-cloud continuum, with substantial opportunities for future research.

title: Patient-Conditioned Dual Hypergraph Reasoning for Auditable Traditional Chinese Medicine Prescription Support
summary: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) prescription support requires patient-specific reasoning from clinical narratives to syndromes, treatment principles, herbs, and doses. Direct language-model generation can produce fluent prescriptions, but its decisions are difficult to audit against explicit clinical evidence. Static TCM knowledge resources provide useful priors, but they cannot determine which diagnostic and prescription relations should be emphasized for an individual patient. We propose a patient-conditioned dual hypergraph framework for auditable TCM prescription support. The first hypergraph organizes symptom, tongue, pulse, and other clinical evidence around syndrome and treatment-principle reasoning. The second hypergraph organizes syndrome, treatment, disease-context, herb, retrieval, and dose-prior evidence for prescription construction. Unlike static knowledge graphs or fixed hypergraphs, both hypergraphs are dynamically weighted by the patient representation. This design enables individualized activation of diagnostic and prescription paths, supporting personalized syndrome differentiation and herb-dose recommendation while preserving case-level auditability. Experiments on TCM-SD show that dynamic weighting in the first hypergraph improves MacBERT syndrome differentiation to 0.8297 accuracy and 0.3288 macro-F1. On TCM-BEST4SDT, the second hypergraph achieves the best mean Herb-F1 of 0.3111 across three seeds, and the full connected pipeline reaches 0.3074 Herb-F1, close to the oracle setting. A 50-case real-world CAP audit further suggests practical review potential, while highlighting the need for prospective dose-safety validation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a patient-conditioned dual hypergraph framework for auditable TCM prescription support that dynamically weights clinical reasoning paths based on individual patient representations, enabling personalized syndrome differentiation and herb-dose recommendation while maintaining case-level auditability.
AI.motivation: Direct language-model generation for TCM prescriptions lacks auditability against clinical evidence. Static TCM knowledge resources provide useful priors but cannot adapt diagnostic and prescription relations to individual patients. There is a need for a framework that combines personalization with transparent, evidence-based reasoning.
AI.method: A dual hypergraph architecture: the first hypergraph organizes clinical evidence (symptoms, tongue, pulse) around syndrome and treatment-principle reasoning; the second hypergraph organizes syndrome, treatment, disease context, herb retrieval, and dose priors for prescription construction. Both hypergraphs are dynamically weighted by the patient representation, enabling individualized activation of diagnostic and prescription paths.
AI.result: On TCM-SD, dynamic weighting in the first hypergraph yields 0.8297 accuracy and 0.3288 macro-F1 for MacBERT syndrome differentiation. On TCM-BEST4SDT, the second hypergraph achieves a mean Herb-F1 of 0.3111 (best across three seeds); the full pipeline reaches 0.3074 Herb-F1, close to oracle. A 50-case real-world CAP audit suggests practical review potential.
AI.conclusion: The patient-conditioned dual hypergraph framework effectively balances personalized TCM prescription generation with clinical auditability, though prospective dose-safety validation remains necessary before deployment.

title: A large-scale dataset of Android applications and their SDK dependencies
summary: Mobile applications (apps) increasingly rely on third-party Software Development Kits (SDKs) to provide services such as advertising, analytics, authentication, crash reporting, and location services. These components form an important, but often hidden, layer of the mobile ecosystem. Here, we present a large-scale dataset linking Android apps to the third-party SDKs they integrate. The dataset was constructed by combining app package files (APKs) and metadata from AndroZoo with SDK detection rules provided by Exodus Privacy. We implemented a reproducible, static-analysis pipeline that downloads APKs, inspects their compiled code, and detects SDKs through code-level signature matching: the released dataset contains 334,719 unique app-version observations (associated with 99,722 Android apps) and 246 third-party SDKs - including app-level metadata such as categories, comments, file size, download counts, ratings and SDK-level metadata such as categories, code roots, code versions, names. The dataset supports the construction of a large-scale app-SDK dependency network and its projection onto both layers; in addition, SDKs are mapped to their corresponding operating companies, enabling provider-level analysis of technological concentration and upstream control in the mobile ecosystem. To support reproducible research, the pipeline and dataset are publicly released on GitHub and Zenodo; more broadly, the project provides a reusable research infrastructure for studying third-party technological dependencies, data-collection capabilities, and privacy infrastructures across Android apps.

AI.tldr: A large-scale dataset linking 99,722 Android apps to 246 third-party SDKs through static-analysis signature matching, enabling dependency network analysis and provider-level concentration studies.
AI.motivation: Third-party SDKs form a hidden but critical layer of the mobile ecosystem, yet large-scale, reproducible datasets linking apps to their SDK dependencies are scarce. Understanding these dependencies is essential for analyzing technological concentration, data-collection capabilities, and privacy infrastructures.
AI.method: A reproducible static-analysis pipeline was built that downloads APKs from AndroZoo, inspects compiled code, and detects SDKs via code-level signature matching using detection rules from Exodus Privacy. The pipeline yields app-level metadata (categories, comments, file size, download counts, ratings) and SDK-level metadata (categories, code roots, code versions, names), with SDKs mapped to operating companies.
AI.result: The released dataset contains 334,719 unique app-version observations across 99,722 Android apps and 246 third-party SDKs. It supports construction of a large-scale app-SDK dependency network and its bipartite projections, plus provider-level analysis of technological concentration and upstream control.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and pipeline, publicly released on GitHub and Zenodo, provide a reusable research infrastructure for studying third-party technological dependencies, data-collection capabilities, and privacy infrastructures across the Android ecosystem.

title: Enhanced Feature Extraction for IoT Network Intrusion Detection Using GNNs and KAN
summary: Recent advancements in the Internet of Things (IoT) emphasize the urgent need for advanced network security, as IoT networks feature dynamic topologies, imbalanced traffic, and complex attack patterns. Unlike general IT networks, IoT environments exhibit extreme heterogeneity and sparse topologies. Traditional GNN-based intrusion detection methods often struggle to efficiently model node and edge features or capture fine-grained anomalies in such settings. To address this, we propose SKGFusionKAN, a novel IoT-tailored approach enhancing GraphSAGE with a multi-scale selective kernel attention mechanism. This enables adaptive extraction of node and edge features under diverse traffic conditions. Specifically, our edge-oriented message passing strengthens information propagation, while selective kernel attention adaptively weights edge-derived information from different scales to handle heterogeneity. We also introduce a gated fusion process to dynamically integrate multi-scale features, improving robustness against evolving attacks. Finally, we leverage Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) for classification, offering superior nonlinear modeling capabilities essential for detecting intricate, low-frequency attacks. To our knowledge, this work presents a comprehensive integration of GNNs and KAN with dedicated architectural innovations for IoT intrusion detection. Extensive experiments on four NIDS benchmarks show that SKGFusionKAN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in binary and multiclass tasks, demonstrating its potential for IoT security.

AI.tldr: SKGFusionKAN integrates GraphSAGE with multi-scale selective kernel attention and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for IoT intrusion detection, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on four NIDS benchmarks.
AI.motivation: IoT networks exhibit dynamic topologies, imbalanced traffic, extreme heterogeneity, and sparse topologies. Traditional GNN-based intrusion detection methods struggle to model node/edge features effectively and fail to capture fine-grained anomalies. A dedicated architecture is needed that jointly addresses these IoT-specific challenges.
AI.method: The authors propose SKGFusionKAN, which enhances GraphSAGE with: (1) a multi-scale selective kernel attention mechanism for adaptive extraction of node and edge features; (2) edge-oriented message passing to strengthen information propagation; (3) selective kernel attention that adaptively weights edge-derived information across scales to handle heterogeneity; (4) a gated fusion process for dynamic integration of multi-scale features; and (5) Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) for final classification, providing enhanced nonlinear modeling for detecting low-frequency attacks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) benchmarks demonstrate that SKGFusionKAN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both binary and multiclass classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: SKGFusionKAN represents the first comprehensive integration of GNNs and KAN with dedicated architectural innovations for IoT intrusion detection, showing strong potential for real-world IoT security deployment.

title: Alignment-Guided Largest Table Overlap Size Estimation
summary: Fast estimation of the size of the largest overlap between tables enables blocking and query-by-table retrieval in large table repositories. The first and the state-of-the-art estimator Armadillo improves efficiency by embedding each table independently and approximating overlap ratio via embedding similarity. However, accurate estimation in heterogeneous repositories remains limited by three challenges: (C1) overlap depends on row-column structure, i.e., each matched cell must preserve both its row and column membership under a joint alignment of the two tables, but existing encodings leave this structure to be inferred indirectly; (C2) independent encoding provides no explicit channel for inter-table alignment signals, biasing prediction toward global similarity; (C3) naive value encodings overfit to corpus-specific distributions, causing cross-domain degradation. Hence, we propose ALORE, a scalable and domain-robust overlap ratio estimator built on three principles: (P1) explicitly represent row-column structure; (P2) expose inter-table alignment signals during training without expensive alignment search; (P3) reduce sensitivity to corpus-specific value distributions. ALORE instantiates these principles with a Two-View Row-Column Hypergraph encoder, alignment-guided objectives with inexpensive interaction signals, and a domain-robust value mapping. Experiments on multiple datasets spanning diverse domains and scales, including a large real-world corpus beyond prior benchmarks, show that ALORE outperforms the state of the art. ALORE reduces MAE by up to 55% overall and 69% in zero-shot transfer, while achieving up to 89x speedup. We further validate its effectiveness for query-by-table retrieval.

AI.tldr: ALORE is a scalable, domain-robust estimator for table overlap size that addresses three limitations of prior work (Armadillo) by explicitly modeling row-column structure, incorporating inter-table alignment signals during training, and using domain-robust value mapping. It achieves up to 55% MAE reduction overall and 89x speedup.
AI.motivation: Fast, accurate estimation of the largest overlap between tables is critical for blocking and query-by-table retrieval in large table repositories. The state-of-the-art estimator Armadillo has three key weaknesses: (C1) it fails to explicitly encode row-column structure, forcing joint alignment to be inferred indirectly; (C2) independent encoding of each table lacks explicit inter-table alignment signals, biasing predictions toward superficial global similarity; (C3) naive value encodings overfit to corpus-specific distributions, degrading cross-domain performance.
AI.method: ALORE is built on three design principles: (P1) a Two-View Row-Column Hypergraph encoder that explicitly represents row-column structure; (P2) alignment-guided training objectives using inexpensive interaction signals (avoiding costly alignment search) to expose inter-table relationships; (P3) a domain-robust value mapping to reduce sensitivity to corpus-specific value distributions. These principles are instantiated into a neural architecture trained to predict overlap ratios between table pairs.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse domains and scales, including a large real-world corpus beyond prior benchmarks, show ALORE reduces MAE by up to 55% overall and 69% in zero-shot transfer, with up to 89x speedup over baselines. It also proves effective for query-by-table retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling row-column structure, providing inter-table alignment signals, and using robust value representations are critical for accurate table overlap estimation. ALORE sets a new state of the art, particularly excelling in cross-domain zero-shot transfer scenarios.

title: Training Hybrid Block Diffusion Language Models with Partial Bidirectionality
summary: High-throughput long-context generation is one of the central challenges for large language models. Generation is typically memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound: each decoding step must stream the accumulated key/value (KV) cache from memory, so bandwidth demand grows with context length while only one token is emitted. Two parallel approaches have therefore emerged: reducing memory access with efficient attention variants and linear-time mixers such as Mamba, or increasing parallel computation by generating blocks of tokens at once. However, technical challenges arise when combining these two ideas. Earlier hybrid diffusion models such as DiffuMamba use bidirectional Mamba mixing, including a reverse-direction scan relative to causal generation. This reverse scan needs to scan the entire sequence, so its states are not prefix-only and cannot be precisely reused as a cache even when diffusion is performed block by block. We propose a BDLM Mamba--attention hybrid that addresses this challenge by restricting the reverse Mamba scan to the active denoising block, which enables exact caching across blocks. In an 87M-parameter DCLM sweep, BDLM Mamba-H achieves the best C4-en validation perplexity compared to BDLM attention and full-sequence baselines. At 350M parameters, it remains competitive with BDLM attention. For long-context inference, BDLM Mamba-H reaches 19.7x the throughput of full-sequence DiffuMamba-H at 65K tokens and 3.7x the throughput of BDLM attention at 262K, showing that Mamba hybrids are a potential long-context diffusion architecture.

AI.tldr: BDLM Mamba-H is a Mamba-attention hybrid diffusion language model that restricts the reverse Mamba scan to the active denoising block, enabling exact KV caching across blocks. This design achieves strong perplexity at small scale and delivers up to 19.7× throughput gains over full-sequence diffusion baselines at long context lengths (65K–262K tokens).
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM generation is memory-bandwidth-bound due to streaming the full KV cache per decoding step. Block-parallel diffusion and efficient linear-time mixers (e.g., Mamba) each address this, but combining them is non-trivial: prior hybrids like DiffuMamba use a bidirectional Mamba scan including a full-sequence reverse scan, whose states cannot be incrementally cached when generating block-by-block.
AI.method: The authors propose BDLM Mamba-H, which restricts the reverse Mamba scan to only the current denoising block rather than the entire sequence. This makes all states prefix-only, enabling exact caching and reuse across successive blocks during block-by-block diffusion decoding. The architecture is evaluated in DCLM training sweeps at 87M and 350M parameters.
AI.result: At 87M parameters, BDLM Mamba-H achieves the best C4-en validation perplexity among BDLM attention and full-sequence baselines. At 350M, it remains competitive with BDLM attention. For inference throughput at 65K tokens, it reaches 19.7× the throughput of full-sequence DiffuMamba-H; at 262K tokens, 3.7× the throughput of BDLM attention.
AI.conclusion: Mamba-attention hybrids with block-restricted reverse scans are a promising architecture for long-context diffusion language models, combining strong perplexity with substantial inference throughput gains at extreme sequence lengths.

title: Beyond Forecasting: The Belief-to-Trade Layer in Prediction-Market Agents
summary: Forecasting future events has attracted growing attention as a testbed for general-purpose AI. A natural way to ground this evaluation is let the models trade in the prediction markets. Trading, however, requires more than forecasting. Moreover, recent benchmarks report a substantial gap between calibrated probability scores and the trading results. We propose Raven-Agent, to the best of our knowledge, the first autonomous trading agent for prediction markets. On a controlled replay over an archived decision set, our architecture achieves the only positive return and the only positive risk-adjusted return among all tested policies. We have released our code in https://github.com/Alchemist-X/predict-raven .

AI.tldr: Raven-Agent is the first autonomous trading agent designed for prediction markets, achieving the only positive return and risk-adjusted return among all tested policies in a controlled replay evaluation, highlighting the gap between pure forecasting and profitable trading.
AI.motivation: Forecasting future events is a key testbed for general AI, but existing benchmarks show a significant gap between calibrated probability scores and actual trading outcomes. Trading requires more than accurate forecasting — it involves timing, risk management, and decision-making under uncertainty. This motivates the need for an autonomous agent that can bridge forecasting and trading in prediction markets.
AI.method: The authors propose Raven-Agent, an autonomous trading agent architecture specifically designed for prediction markets. The agent was evaluated via controlled replay over an archived decision set, allowing for systematic comparison against alternative trading policies.
AI.result: Raven-Agent was the only policy among all tested to achieve a positive return and a positive risk-adjusted return in the controlled replay evaluation.
AI.conclusion: An autonomous agent architecture purpose-built for prediction market trading can successfully translate forecasting signals into profitable trading outcomes, outperforming existing policies and demonstrating that forecasting accuracy alone is insufficient for market success.

title: An Exploration of Agentic Information Fusion for Test Maintenance Prediction
summary:
Test maintenance is a critical, yet costly, activity - particularly as codebases rapidly evolve. To assist, we present MAST, a multi-agent framework that predicts which test cases require maintenance following changes to the production code. This identification task is necessary as a precondition to any subsequent maintenance activities, but remains challenging due to the complex relationships between production and test code. MAST advances the state-of-the-art by integrating multiple analyses -- including static, lexical, and semantic analyses - through an intelligent fusion and post-check procedure and by focusing on a realistic use and evaluation setting - i.e., standardized input formats, repository-level analyses, and the ability to infer relations between test and production artifacts rather than assuming a pre-existing mapping.
  We evaluated MAST on 21 industrial Java repositories from Ericsson AB, considering situations where test maintenance both was and was not required in the ground truth. MAST yielded superior precision to a state-of-the-art baseline - resulting in a higher accuracy, F1, and F2 score - with only some loss in recall. Our ablation study demonstrates the value of each analysis in producing the final recommendations. MAST illustrates the potential of multi-agent systems that can fuse multiple information sources when performing software testing tasks.

AI.tldr: MAST is a multi-agent framework that predicts which test cases need maintenance after production code changes by fusing static, lexical, and semantic analyses. Evaluated on 21 Ericsson Java repositories, it outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline in precision, accuracy, F1, and F2 scores, with only minor recall loss.
AI.motivation: Test maintenance is costly and critical, especially in rapidly evolving codebases. Identifying which tests require maintenance after production code changes is a necessary precondition for any subsequent maintenance activity, but remains challenging due to complex production–test code relationships. Existing approaches either assume pre-existing mappings between test and production artifacts or lack comprehensive, repository-level analysis.
AI.method: MAST is a multi-agent framework that integrates static analysis, lexical analysis, and semantic analysis through an intelligent fusion and post-check procedure. It operates under realistic conditions: standardized input formats, repository-level analyses, and the ability to infer relations between test and production artifacts rather than relying on a pre-existing mapping.
AI.result: Evaluated on 21 industrial Java repositories from Ericsson AB across both maintenance-required and maintenance-not-required scenarios. MAST achieved superior precision, higher accuracy, F1, and F2 scores compared to the state-of-the-art baseline, with only some loss in recall. An ablation study confirmed the contribution of each individual analysis to the final recommendations.
AI.conclusion: MAST demonstrates the effectiveness of multi-agent systems that fuse multiple information sources for software testing tasks, particularly test maintenance prediction. The framework's success on industrial code suggests practical viability for reducing test maintenance costs.

title: Claim2Source at CheckThat! 2026: Improving Multilingual Scientific Claim-Source Retrieval with Verification-based Re-Ranking
comment: Accepted at the CheckThat! Lab at CLEF 2026
summary: Multilingual scientific claim-source retrieval aims to identify the scientific publication supporting a claim shared on social media. This task is challenging because claims often differ from source publications in terms of language, wording, and level of detail, which weakens the connection between claims and their underlying evidence. In this paper, we present our approach for the CheckThat! 2026 Lab Task 1: Source Retrieval for Scientific Web Claims. We propose a multi-stage retrieval framework for multilingual scientific claim-source retrieval that combines structured claim and source representations with progressive candidate refinement. To address multilingual retrieval challenges, the framework employs bilingual claim representations, metadata-enhanced source representations, and language-specific adaptation of dense retrieval models. Building on this setup, a first-stage retriever generates an initial pool of candidate sources, after which similarity-based re-ranking improves the ranking of highly relevant sources and verification-based re-ranking identifies the candidate source that best supports the claim using verification signals. Our approach achieves an average MRR@5 score of 0.7628 across English, German, and French claims, ranking first on the CheckThat! 2026 leaderboard.

AI.tldr: A multi-stage retrieval framework for multilingual scientific claim-source retrieval that combines bilingual claim representations, metadata-enhanced source representations, and progressive candidate refinement via similarity-based and verification-based re-ranking, achieving 0.7628 MRR@5 and ranking first on the CheckThat! 2026 leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Scientific claims shared on social media often differ from their source publications in language, wording, and level of detail, weakening the connection between claims and evidence. Existing retrieval methods struggle with this cross-lingual and cross-modal gap, motivating the need for a robust multilingual retrieval framework.
AI.method: A multi-stage retrieval framework: (1) bilingual claim representations paired with metadata-enhanced source representations, (2) language-specific adaptation of dense retrieval models for first-stage candidate generation, (3) similarity-based re-ranking to improve ranking of highly relevant sources, and (4) verification-based re-ranking using verification signals to identify the source that best supports the claim.
AI.result: The approach achieved an average MRR@5 score of 0.7628 across English, German, and French claims, securing first place on the CheckThat! 2026 Lab Task 1 leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-stage framework effectively addresses multilingual scientific claim-source retrieval by progressively refining candidates through structured representations and dual re-ranking strategies, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance across three languages.

title: Can Coding Agents Implement Missed Compiler Optimizations? Evaluating LLM Agents on LLVM Peephole Optimizations
summary:
Coding agents built on large language models are now capable of patching sizable real-world codebases, yet whether they can develop compiler optimizations remains an open question. To study this question, we introduce PeepholeBench, an evaluation framework whose tasks are constructed from real-world missed peephole optimizations reported against LLVM's InstCombine pass. Since missed peephole optimizations are typically fixed with small, localized patches, they offer a well-scoped but demanding testbed for coding agents: a correct fix demands rigorous reasoning about program semantics along with familiarity with optimizer-specific conventions. PeepholeBench derives its tasks from 21 resolved LLVM issues and 19 merged pull requests (PRs), supplies agents with only the issue context that existed before each fix, and assesses the resulting patches for both correctness and profitability.
  With PeepholeBench, we benchmark state-of-the-art coding agents on fixing missed peephole optimizations in LLVM's InstCombine pass, measuring their patches against the corresponding human-written fixes. We observe a tension between correctness and profitability, and no agent matches human developers on both dimensions at once. The dominant failure modes are overly narrow transformations and misuse of LLVM-specific mechanisms, errors that existing test suites rarely expose. Together, these results establish PeepholeBench as a realistic and challenging benchmark for coding agents, and suggest future directions for building agents that can more dependably assist compiler optimization development.

AI.tldr: PeepholeBench is a new benchmark for evaluating coding agents on fixing missed peephole optimizations in LLVM's InstCombine pass, constructed from real-world LLVM issues and PRs. Benchmarking state-of-the-art agents reveals a tension between correctness and profitability, with no agent matching human performance on both dimensions.
AI.motivation: While LLM-based coding agents can patch large codebases, their ability to develop compiler optimizations — which demand rigorous reasoning about program semantics and optimizer-specific conventions — remains unexplored. Missed peephole optimizations provide a well-scoped yet demanding testbed for investigating this capability.
AI.method: The authors introduce PeepholeBench, derived from 21 resolved LLVM issues and 19 merged pull requests against the InstCombine pass. Agents are given only the pre-fix issue context and must produce patches evaluated for correctness (passing existing tests) and profitability (matching or exceeding the optimization coverage of human-written fixes).
AI.result: No state-of-the-art coding agent matches human developers on both correctness and profitability simultaneously. Dominant failure modes include overly narrow transformations and misuse of LLVM-specific mechanisms — errors that existing test suites rarely catch.
AI.conclusion: PeepholeBench establishes a realistic, challenging benchmark for coding agents in compiler optimization. Results highlight key gaps in current agent capabilities and suggest directions for more dependable AI-assisted compiler development.

title: Builder, Defender, Breaker: The Case Against Removing the Human from the AI-Driven Security Lifecycle
summary: Artificial intelligence has spread across the whole of the security lifecycle. The same family of models now writes application code, hardens it, and probes it for weaknesses, so that a single generative substrate increasingly performs all three roles at once. Enthusiasm for this convergence tends to treat full autonomy as the natural end point of partial assistance. This article argues that it is not. When the system that builds an artifact is drawn from the same distribution as the systems that defend and test it, the three roles inherit a common set of blind spots, and the independence that makes verification meaningful is quietly lost. Removing the human does more than raise the automation level: it collapses the external oracle against which machine output is judged, outruns the point at which a person could intervene, hands adversaries a predictable and poisonable target, and dissolves the locus of accountability when something fails. Drawing on evidence from autonomous code generation, adversarial machine learning, software fault tolerance, and the first all-machine hacking tournaments, we argue that the human belongs in the loop not as a temporary scaffold but as a permanent structural requirement, and set out what a defensible division of labour between people and machines should preserve.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that fully autonomous AI-driven security lifecycles are fundamentally flawed: when the same model family generates, hardens, and tests code, shared blind spots eliminate meaningful verification. The human must remain a permanent structural requirement, not a temporary scaffold.
AI.motivation: The growing trend of using a single generative AI substrate across all stages of the security lifecycle — writing, hardening, and probing code — is accompanied by uncritical enthusiasm for full autonomy. The authors challenge this endpoint, arguing that convergence collapses the independence essential for verification, accountability, and robustness.
AI.method: The paper draws on interdisciplinary evidence spanning autonomous code generation, adversarial machine learning, software fault tolerance, and all-machine hacking tournaments to expose the risks of collapsing the builder/defender/tester roles into a single model family. It analyzes the structural consequences of removing the human oracle: shared blind spots, loss of intervention points, adversarial predictability, and dissolved accountability.
AI.result: The analysis demonstrates that full autonomy undermines verification independence, creates a poisonable and predictable target for adversaries, eliminates the external oracle for judging machine output, and erodes accountability when failures occur.
AI.conclusion: The human belongs in the loop not as a temporary assistive scaffold to be phased out, but as a permanent structural necessity. The paper calls for defining a defensible division of labour that preserves independent oversight, meaningful verification, and clear accountability.

title: Don't Wait to Reply: Towards Responsive yet Thoughtful Dialogue through Proactive Thinking
summary: Thinking has emerged as a critical capability for Large Language Models (LLMs) tackling complex tasks. However, its reactive nature, where reasoning is passively triggered only upon receiving a user response, inevitably introduces latency that compromises conversational fluidity. This stands in sharp contrast to human dialogue, where speakers proactively anticipate and plan future content during natural pauses to ensure seamless interaction. To bridge this gap, we propose Proactive Thinking, a framework that empowers models to pre-compute potential response elements during conversational downtime instead of waiting idly for the next input. We then introduce a training-free baseline that can think ahead by anticipating future states, balancing efficiency and quality through speculative continual thinking. To evaluate this approach in practice, we adapt three benchmarks of varying complexity into time-aware environments that simulate real-time conversational flow. We demonstrate that proactive thinking effectively improves interaction efficiency without compromising performance. Ultimately, this work advocates for a fundamental shift toward more intelligent, anticipatory, and real-time conversational AI.

AI.tldr: Proposes Proactive Thinking, a framework enabling LLMs to pre-compute responses during conversational downtime rather than idly waiting, improving interaction efficiency without compromising quality. A training-free speculative continual thinking baseline is introduced and evaluated on time-aware adapted benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM reasoning is reactive—triggered only after receiving user input—introducing latency that disrupts conversational fluidity. This contrasts with human dialogue, where speakers proactively anticipate and plan during natural pauses. The gap motivates a shift toward anticipatory, real-time conversational AI.
AI.method: The authors propose a Proactive Thinking framework where models pre-compute potential response elements during idle periods. They introduce a training-free baseline that performs speculative continual thinking by anticipating future conversational states, balancing efficiency and quality. Three existing benchmarks are adapted into time-aware environments simulating real-time conversational flow for evaluation.
AI.result: Proactive thinking effectively improves interaction efficiency (reduced latency) without degrading response quality, as demonstrated across three adapted benchmarks of varying complexity.
AI.conclusion: The work advocates for a paradigm shift from reactive to proactive, anticipatory conversational AI, showing that speculative pre-computation during downtime is a viable path toward more seamless human-AI interaction.

title: Less Tokens, Better Forecasts: Sparse Residual Routing for Efficient Weather Prediction
summary: Existing ViT-based weather forecasting models apply uniform computation across all spatial tokens, even though nearby atmospheric grid points often contain similar values and large regions evolve smoothly over time. This makes much of the intermediate per-token computation redundant. Standard token-efficiency methods, such as pruning or merging, reduce cost by removing or fusing tokens. However, weather forecasting is a spatiotemporal dense prediction problem in which a history of atmospheric states must be mapped to future values on the original latitude-longitude grid. Thus, every grid cell must retain a physically meaningful representation, especially under autoregressive rollout. We introduce Sparse-Reslim, a parameter-free plug-in routing module that makes sparse token processing compatible with this fixed-grid requirement. Sparse-Reslim routes only 25% of spatial tokens through the expensive middle transformer blocks and treats those blocks as residual updates: it computes the change produced for the routed tokens and scatters only this delta back to the full sequence. Unselected tokens keep their pre-routing representations exactly, so no grid cell is dropped or replaced by a mask token, and no fusion layer or additional parameters are introduced. Across ERA5 resolutions up to the operational 0.25\textdegree{} standard and two model families, a deterministic Transformer and a diffusion model, Sparse-Reslim improves forecast accuracy on every evaluated variable while substantially reducing cost: training is about 2.5x faster in the main settings and reaches 3.18x speedup at 0.25\textdegree{}, with over 2.2x lower peak memory. A controlled decomposition shows that the accuracy gain comes primarily from sparse routing itself, while random token selection provides an additional regularization benefit without selector overhead.

AI.tldr: Sparse-Reslim is a parameter-free routing module that enables sparse token processing in ViT-based weather forecasting models without dropping grid cells. It routes 25% of tokens through expensive transformer blocks as residual updates, scattering only deltas back, achieving 2.5–3.18× training speedup and improved forecast accuracy across ERA5 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing ViT weather forecasting models waste computation on redundant per-token processing, since nearby atmospheric grid points are highly correlated. Standard token-efficiency methods (pruning, merging) are incompatible with dense spatiotemporal prediction tasks that require every grid cell to retain a physically meaningful representation, especially under autoregressive rollout.
AI.method: Sparse-Reslim is a parameter-free plug-in routing module. It selects only 25% of spatial tokens for processing through the middle transformer blocks, treating those blocks as residual updates: it computes the change (delta) produced for the routed tokens and scatters only this delta back to the full sequence. Unselected tokens retain their pre-routing representations unchanged. No mask tokens, fusion layers, or additional parameters are introduced.
AI.result: Training speedups of ~2.5× in main settings and up to 3.18× at 0.25° resolution, with >2.2× lower peak memory. Sparse-Reslim improves forecast accuracy on every evaluated variable across ERA5 resolutions (up to 0.25°), validated on both a deterministic Transformer and a diffusion model. Ablation shows accuracy gains stem primarily from sparse routing, with random token selection providing additional regularization.
AI.conclusion: Sparse-Reslim demonstrates that sparse token routing, when implemented as residual delta scattering rather than token removal/fusion, is both compatible with and beneficial for dense spatiotemporal forecasting. The method improves accuracy while dramatically reducing cost, making high-resolution weather forecasting more practical.

title: TACTIC-KG: Toward Small Agent Teams for Cyber Threat Intelligence Knowledge Graph Construction
summary: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) reports are predominantly unstructured, heterogeneous, and noisy, which limits their direct usability for automated analysis and reasoning. Cybersecurity Knowledge Graphs (CSKGs) provide a structured representation of adversarial entities, actions, and relations, but constructing such graphs from free-text CTI remains a challenge. Recent approaches rely on monolithic Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform end-to-end extraction and completion, leading to high cost, limited controllability, and unstable performance. This paper introduces TACTIC-KG, an agentic framework for CSKG construction that decomposes the task into modular, specialized LLM agents responsible for extraction, typing, verification, and curation. Using lightweight models (3B--8B), TACTIC-KG improves stability, recall, and graph consistency while reducing deployment cost. We implement and evaluate TACTIC-KG against recent state-of-the-art systems. Experiments on human-annotated CTI reports show that agent specialization consistently outperforms larger monolithic in-context-learning (ICL) baselines in extraction F1-score, typing accuracy, and structural graph similarity.

AI.tldr: TACTIC-KG introduces a modular, agent-based framework using small LLMs (3B–8B) to construct Cybersecurity Knowledge Graphs from unstructured CTI reports, outperforming larger monolithic models in extraction, typing, and graph consistency while reducing cost.
AI.motivation: CTI reports are unstructured, heterogeneous, and noisy, limiting automated analysis. Existing monolithic LLM approaches for constructing CSKGs suffer from high cost, limited controllability, and unstable performance. A more modular, controllable, and cost-effective solution is needed.
AI.method: TACTIC-KG is an agentic framework that decomposes CSKG construction into four specialized LLM agents: extraction, typing, verification, and curation. Each agent uses lightweight models (3B–8B parameters) and focuses on a distinct subtask, enabling modularity, improved stability, and reduced deployment cost.
AI.result: Experiments on human-annotated CTI reports show that agent specialization consistently outperforms larger monolithic in-context-learning baselines in extraction F1-score, typing accuracy, and structural graph similarity.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing CSKG construction into specialized, lightweight agents yields superior performance, stability, and cost-efficiency compared to monolithic LLM approaches, offering a practical path forward for automated CTI structuring.

title: UniSGR: Unified Framework for Semantic ID Generation and Ranking
summary: Recommendation systems play a pivotal role in modern e-commerce platforms. While generative retrieval has emerged as a promising paradigm for alleviating the limitations of multi-stage cascade architectures, existing methods still struggle with fine-grained multi-objective ranking. To bridge this gap, we propose UniSGR, a Unified framework for Semantic ID Generation and Ranking. UniSGR adopts a two-stage training paradigm: a multi-scenario pre-training stage that learns from mixed business-scenario data, followed by a scenario-specific alignment stage that jointly optimizes Value-Aware Parallel Multi-Token Prediction (VA-PMTP) and a unified multi-objective ranking module. To better align generation with downstream ranking, we introduce Task-Aware Tokens (TAT) guided by Funnel-Aware Contrastive Learning. Furthermore, we propose Semantic Tree Attention with Reorganized KV cache (STARK), an inference strategy that removes key efficiency bottlenecks in conventional beam search. Extensive offline experiments on a large-scale e-commerce platform demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of UniSGR.

AI.tldr: UniSGR is a unified two-stage framework for generative retrieval that jointly optimizes semantic ID generation and multi-objective ranking, introducing Task-Aware Tokens and a STARK inference strategy to improve both ranking quality and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing generative retrieval methods in e-commerce recommendation still struggle with fine-grained multi-objective ranking, leaving a gap between semantic ID generation and downstream ranking optimization.
AI.method: UniSGR uses a two-stage training paradigm: (1) multi-scenario pre-training on mixed business data, and (2) scenario-specific alignment that jointly optimizes Value-Aware Parallel Multi-Token Prediction (VA-PMTP) with a unified multi-objective ranking module. Task-Aware Tokens (TAT) guided by Funnel-Aware Contrastive Learning are introduced to align generation with ranking. For inference, Semantic Tree Attention with Reorganized KV cache (STARK) removes beam search bottlenecks.
AI.result: Extensive offline experiments on a large-scale e-commerce platform demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of UniSGR.
AI.conclusion: UniSGR effectively bridges the gap between generative retrieval and multi-objective ranking through unified training, TAT, and STARK, showing strong empirical results at scale.

title: CONTRA: Red-Teaming Configurations of Personalizable Agents
summary: Recent tools such as OpenClaw have extended the capabilities of LLM-based agents from simple dialog-based systems to fully autonomous agents. These systems allow personalization of the agent through modifiable internal files and the installation of skills. While this enables deployment in a wide range of settings and the automation of diverse tasks, greater capability and autonomy increases the risk of malicious actions being executed unintentionally. In this work, we explore the interplay between agent configuration and the risk of executing dangerous actions without explicit instruction. To this end, we propose CONfiguration Tree-search for Red-teaming Agents (CONTRA), an LLM-assisted tree-search algorithm that discovers agent configurations resulting in the execution of malicious actions. CONTRA works by reasoning about benign yet dangerous configurations and evaluating them in a simulated environment. We construct a dataset of the 473 most popular skills from a public repository, along with 2-5 corresponding malicious target actions per skill. In a large-scale analysis, we find that 75.1% of skills have at least one configuration resulting in the execution of a malicious action, most of which have not been detected as containing malicious content by existing scans. Overall, CONTRA successfully identifies a configuration leading to the execution of the target action in 39.2% of all tested cases. Our findings demonstrate that current agents provide insufficient safety with respect to personalization.

AI.tldr: CONTRA, an LLM-assisted tree-search algorithm, discovers agent configurations that cause autonomous LLM agents to execute dangerous actions unintentionally. Testing 473 popular skills, 75.1% had at least one unsafe configuration, and CONTRA found exploitable configurations in 39.2% of cases, revealing serious safety gaps in agent personalization.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agents become fully autonomous and user-personalizable (e.g., via OpenClaw), the risk of unintentional malicious actions increases. The authors aim to systematically explore how agent configurations can lead to dangerous behavior without explicit malicious instructions, a problem exacerbated by greater autonomy and modifiability.
AI.method: The authors propose CONTRA (CONfiguration Tree-search for Red-teaming Agents), an LLM-assisted tree-search algorithm that reasons about benign yet dangerous configurations and evaluates them in a simulated environment. They construct a dataset of 473 popular skills from a public repository, each paired with 2–5 corresponding malicious target actions, and systematically search for configurations that trigger those actions.
AI.result: 75.1% of skills had at least one configuration leading to malicious action execution, most undetected by existing content scans. CONTRA successfully identified a configuration triggering the target action in 39.2% of all tested cases.
AI.conclusion: Current autonomous LLM agents provide insufficient safety protections regarding personalization. The high rate of exploitable configurations demonstrates a critical need for stronger safety mechanisms in configurable agent systems.

title: Conditional Diffusion Guided Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: Multi-domain knowledge graph completion (MKGC) aims to improve missing triple prediction in a target KG by transferring knowledge from other support KGs. Existing methods typically enforce consistency constraints on equivalent entities across KGs to transfer knowledge, which risks suppressing domain-specific contextual information of entities. This design can also compromise entity representation information from all KG domains, impeding performance improvements, especially in low-resource data scenarios. To address this, we pioneer a generation-based paradigm for MKGC and propose DMKGC, a conditional diffusion-guided knowledge transfer framework. Our key insight is to treat each KG as a partial view of the entity entire information, and generate informative domain-general entity embeddings through diffusion models conditioned on support KGs. Particularly, we first initialize domain-agnostic entity embeddings as prior entity embeddings, and then encode them within individual KGs. Afterward, we fuse equivalent entities from support KGs as the conditional diffusion generation guidance. We leverage the prior entity embeddings as the proxy generation objective, which ensures this conditional generation to be unbiased towards any conditioned KGs. Simultaneously, we also train the generated embeddings to be predictive across KGs, thus preserving domain-specific information. Extensive experiments on 14 KGs in 3 benchmarks demonstrate a 4.3\% average MRR improvement in tail entity prediction over state-of-the-art methods, with sustained gains in low-resource data settings.

AI.tldr: DMKGC proposes a conditional diffusion model that treats each KG as a partial view, generating domain-general entity embeddings by fusing equivalent entities from support KGs as guidance, while preserving domain-specific information through cross-KG predictive training.
AI.motivation: Existing MKGC methods enforce consistency constraints on equivalent entities across KGs, which suppresses domain-specific contextual information and compromises entity representations, especially under low-resource scenarios. A new paradigm is needed to transfer knowledge without sacrificing domain-specific information.
AI.method: DMKGC initializes domain-agnostic prior entity embeddings, encodes them within individual KGs, then uses equivalent entities from support KGs fused as conditional guidance for a diffusion model. The prior embeddings serve as the proxy generation objective, ensuring unbiased conditional generation. Simultaneously, generated embeddings are trained to be predictive across all KGs to retain domain-specific information.
AI.result: Experiments on 14 KGs across 3 benchmarks show a 4.3% average MRR improvement in tail entity prediction over state-of-the-art methods, with sustained gains in low-resource data settings.
AI.conclusion: The generation-based paradigm using conditional diffusion effectively transfers knowledge across KGs for MKGC without suppressing domain-specific entity information, achieving state-of-the-art performance, particularly in low-resource scenarios.

title: On the Design Space of Discrete Diffusion Online Adaptation for Molecular Optimization
comment: Submitted to The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
summary: Molecular optimization often starts from a pretrained generative model that captures a broad prior over valid molecular structures. At test time, however, the goal is not to sample from this prior, but to use a limited oracle budget to shift generation toward task-specific high-reward molecules. We study this adaptation problem for discrete diffusion models. Each online round couples several choices. The loop must decide which candidates to evaluate, how rewards become model updates, which feedback to reuse, and how far to move beyond the pretrained prior. These choices have mostly been studied in isolation, leaving open whether they complement one another, become redundant, or interfere inside a full online adaptation loop. We conduct controlled studies across six small-molecule binding-affinity tasks and three protein-fitness tasks. We find that acquisition, reward shaping, and model debiasing provide complementary routes to higher reward, especially for small molecules. Replay further stabilizes learning, while validity penalties keep small-molecule exploration on the valid molecular manifold. Together, these findings point to a practical recipe for feedback-efficient molecular optimization: online fine-tuning with acquisition, reward shaping, debiasing, replay, and validity control. This recipe outperforms offline fine-tuning and inference-time search baselines under matched oracle-call budgets and GPU-hour accounting. The gains are largest when high-reward candidates require larger shifts from the pretrained prior.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies the design choices in online adaptation of discrete diffusion models for molecular optimization, identifying a recipe combining acquisition, reward shaping, debiasing, replay, and validity control that outperforms offline and inference-time baselines under matched budgets.
AI.motivation: Various components of online fine-tuning loops (acquisition, reward shaping, replay, debiasing, validity penalties) have been studied in isolation. The authors aim to understand whether these choices complement, conflict, or become redundant when combined in a full online adaptation pipeline for molecular optimization with limited oracle budgets.
AI.method: Controlled ablation studies across six small-molecule binding-affinity tasks and three protein-fitness tasks using discrete diffusion models. The authors systematically vary acquisition strategies, reward shaping functions, replay mechanisms, model debiasing (KL regularization toward the pretrained prior), and validity penalties, evaluating their interactions under matched oracle-call budgets and GPU-hour accounting.
AI.result: Acquisition, reward shaping, and model debiasing provide complementary gains, especially for small molecules. Replay stabilizes learning, and validity penalties maintain exploration on the valid molecular manifold. The combined recipe outperforms both offline fine-tuning and inference-time search baselines, with largest gains when high-reward candidates require substantial shifts from the pretrained prior.
AI.conclusion: A practical recipe for feedback-efficient molecular optimization emerges: online fine-tuning of discrete diffusion models with acquisition, reward shaping, debiasing, replay, and validity control. These components are largely complementary rather than redundant or interfering.

title: APeB: Benchmarking Personalization Ability of Large Language Model Agents
summary: LLM-powered agents struggle with personalization when users issue raw, underspecified queries. In this setting, agents must infer latent intent, extract preferences from noisy interaction histories, and select among competing alternatives. Existing benchmarks rarely test this capability, as they often rely on user-refined queries or simplified histories. We introduce personalized product search (PPS), a testbed for agentic personalization under raw queries and diverse histories. We construct Agent Personalized Benchmark (APeB) from action logs, pairing underspecified intents with rich histories and user-viewed candidate items. Evaluating state-of-the-art LLMs with multi-step agent workflows, we find that models handle explicit queries well but struggle with early-stage queries requiring intent and preference discovery. Rubric analysis attributes this gap mainly to ineffective history use. A simple history-aware query-refinement pipeline, VQRA, yields consistent gains, highlighting the need for dedicated history-utilization modules in personalized agents.

AI.tldr: LLM agents fail at personalization from raw, underspecified queries. The paper introduces the Personalized Product Search (PPS) testbed and APeB benchmark built from action logs. State-of-the-art LLMs handle explicit queries but struggle with early-stage intent/preference discovery due to ineffective history use. A simple history-aware query-refinement pipeline (VQRA) yields consistent improvements.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered agents are increasingly deployed in user-facing settings but falter when users issue raw, underspecified queries. These agents must infer latent intent, extract user preferences from noisy interaction histories, and select among competing alternatives — a capability that existing benchmarks rarely evaluate, as they typically rely on user-refined queries or oversimplified histories.
AI.method: The authors introduce Personalized Product Search (PPS) as a testbed for agentic personalization. They construct the Agent Personalized Benchmark (APeB) from real action logs, pairing underspecified intents with rich interaction histories and user-viewed candidate items. State-of-the-art LLMs are evaluated using multi-step agent workflows. Rubric-based analysis is then used to decompose failure modes. Additionally, VQRA, a simple history-aware query-refinement pipeline, is proposed to address identified weaknesses.
AI.result: LLMs handle explicit, well-formed queries effectively but perform poorly on early-stage queries requiring intent and preference discovery. Rubric analysis reveals that the primary performance gap stems from ineffective utilization of interaction histories. The proposed VQRA pipeline yields consistent gains across settings, demonstrating that dedicated history-utilization modules are critical.
AI.conclusion: Effective personalization in LLM agents requires dedicated modules for leveraging noisy interaction histories, particularly for underspecified queries. The PPS testbed and APeB benchmark provide a rigorous foundation for future research, and simple interventions like VQRA show that history-aware query refinement is a promising direction.

title: Relational Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Pricing in High-Speed Railway Markets
summary: In liberalised railway systems, operators must set prices dynamically in an environment with partial observability, as they retain private information about their objectives and performance, where regulatory constraints prohibit communication or direct information exchange between competitors to prevent explicit collusion. Consequently, agents must learn to infer strategic interactions only from observable market data which presents a significant challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning, where standard approaches typically treat observations as unstructured vectors, ignoring the underlying market topology that governs strategic interactions. To address this, an entity graph modelling approach is proposed, which represents the environment as a graph of operational units, rather than decision-making agents or static infrastructure, encoding competition, coordination, and connectivity relations between entities. Then, an extension of the multi-agent twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient algorithm with graph-based representation learning processes the features of the entities through a multi-layer relational graph convolutional network and aggregates them via a learnt attention mechanism.
