Experimental results in a rail pricing reinforcement learning environment show that this novel framework achieves higher revenue and stability in two different settings of increasing market complexity compared to a representative selection of relational and non-relational baselines. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Kinrre/RelationalRailPricing-RL

AI.tldr: Proposes an entity-graph representation for multi-agent RL in liberalized railway pricing, where agents cannot directly communicate due to competition law. The method models the market as a graph of operational entities (not agents) and uses relational GCNs with learned attention within a MATD3 framework, outperforming baselines in revenue and stability on a rail pricing simulator.
AI.motivation: In liberalized railway markets, competing operators face a partially observable environment where they cannot exchange private information due to regulatory constraints against collusion. Existing MARL approaches treat observations as flat vectors and ignore the underlying market topology (competition, coordination, connectivity relations), limiting agents' ability to infer strategic interactions from observable data alone.
AI.method: 1) Entity graph modeling: the environment is represented as a graph of operational units (e.g., train services, stations) with edges encoding competition, coordination, and connectivity, rather than agents or static infrastructure. 2) Algorithm: extends MATD3 (Multi-Agent Twin Delayed DDPG) with a multi-layer Relational Graph Convolutional Network (R-GCN) that processes entity features, followed by a learned attention mechanism to aggregate entity representations into agent-level policies. The framework is evaluated on a custom rail pricing RL environment under two settings of increasing market complexity.
AI.result: The proposed framework achieves higher revenue and greater stability compared to a representative set of relational and non-relational baselines across both market complexity settings in the rail pricing environment.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the market as an entity graph with relational structure and attention-based aggregation enables agents to learn strategic interactions indirectly from market observables, yielding superior pricing policies under regulatory constraints that prohibit direct information sharing.

title: Submitted and Diagnostic Analysis of Full-Text Temporal Retrieval for LongEval-Sci
summary: LongEval-Sci evaluates scientific retrieval under collection change, where a system should be effective on the current corpus and remain usable as documents accumulate over time. This paper reports both official Task 1 results and development diagnostics for LongEval-Sci 2026. We compare the official PyTerrier BM25 and Qwen3 dense baselines with full-text BM25, additive and router variants, temporal full-text retrieval, temporal+citation retrieval, RM3 query expansion, cross-encoder reranking, and reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). In the official DCTR evaluation, the temporalized full-text runs are our strongest submissions: FT BM25+temporal and FT BM25+temporal+citation obtain the best ARP on all three snapshots (0.285, 0.267, and 0.180 nDCG@10) and reduce snapshot-3 relative change from 0.481 for the BM25 pivot to 0.368. Citation features match the temporal-only variant but do not provide a measurable additional gain in the official summary. Our internal snapshot-1 diagnostics show a complementary pattern: full-text BM25 is the strongest single development retriever (DCTR nDCG@10 = 0.3302, MAP = 0.2853), RRF gives the best deep recall (Recall@1000 = 0.9667), and some uncalibrated overlays can sharply degrade top-rank quality. We therefore conclude that full-text retrieval is the strongest foundation, temporal integration can improve official longitudinal effectiveness when applied to that foundation, and citation evidence still requires cleaner ablation and calibration. Beyond ranking, we also report a qualitative weekly IR-system update-monitoring analysis based on ingestion velocity and stale-coverage drift.

AI.tldr: LongEval-Sci 2026 evaluates scientific retrieval systems under corpus growth over time. The paper compares BM25 and dense baselines with various retrieval enhancements, finding that temporalized full-text BM25 achieves the best longitudinal ranking performance, while full-text BM25 alone is strongest in static settings and reciprocal rank fusion yields the best deep recall. A qualitative monitoring analysis of system drift over weekly updates is also presented.
AI.motivation: Scientific document collections grow continuously, but most retrieval evaluations are static. There is a need to assess how retrieval systems maintain effectiveness as corpora expand over time (collection change), ensuring systems are usable not only on current snapshots but remain robust longitudinally.
AI.method: The study compares multiple retrieval approaches on LongEval-Sci 2026 Task 1: (1) official PyTerrier BM25 and Qwen3 dense baselines, (2) full-text BM25 with additive and router variants, (3) temporal full-text retrieval, (4) temporal+citation retrieval, (5) RM3 query expansion, (6) cross-encoder reranking, and (7) reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). Evaluation uses the DCTR (Document Collection Temporal Retrieval) metric — nDCG@10 and ARP across three temporal snapshots — plus internal diagnostics (MAP, Recall@1000). A qualitative weekly monitoring analysis based on ingestion velocity and stale-coverage drift is also conducted.
AI.result: Full-text BM25+temporal achieved the best official ARP across all three snapshots (0.285, 0.267, 0.180 nDCG@10) and reduced snapshot-3 relative degradation from 0.481 (BM25 pivot) to 0.368. Citation features matched but did not surpass the temporal-only variant. In internal snapshot-1 diagnostics, full-text BM25 was the strongest single retriever (nDCG@10=0.3302, MAP=0.2853), RRF achieved best deep recall (Recall@1000=0.9667), and uncalibrated overlays degraded top-rank quality.
AI.conclusion: Full-text retrieval is the strongest foundation for scientific retrieval under collection change. Temporal integration improves longitudinal effectiveness when applied to full-text retrieval. Citation evidence requires further ablation and calibration to yield measurable gains. Complementary monitoring via ingestion velocity and stale-coverage drift provides practical insights for IR system maintenance.

title: SMOCS: A Streaming Framework for Simplified Deployment, Monitoring, and Optimization of ML Systems in Production
summary: Machine learning has demonstrated significant potential for real-time monitoring, optimization, and control of scientific facilities. However, deploying and maintaining ML models in operational environments remains a substantial engineering challenge. Each facility presents unique data protocols, non-standard formats, and infrastructure constraints, forcing teams to rebuild integration pipelines for every new application. We present SMOCS (Streaming Monitoring Optimization and Control System), a Kafka-based containerized framework that addresses this challenge through three contributions: 1) a layered abstraction over Apache Kafka that separates infrastructure from application logic, 2) a three-thread agent architecture that temporally decouples data ingestion, model training, and real-time inference enabling continuous online learning from live data streams, and 3) a configuration-driven deployment model that enables domain experts to operate ML pipelines without software engineering expertise. SMOCS is facility platform-agnostic, fault-isolated by design, and horizontally scalable through Docker containerization. The framework is publicly available as open-source software on the Jefferson Lab Github.

AI.tldr: SMOCS is a Kafka-based containerized framework that simplifies deploying and maintaining ML models in scientific facilities through layered abstraction, a decoupled three-thread agent architecture for continuous online learning, and configuration-driven deployment accessible to non-engineers.
AI.motivation: Deploying ML models in operational scientific facilities is a persistent engineering challenge due to unique data protocols, non-standard formats, and infrastructure constraints at each site, forcing teams to repeatedly rebuild integration pipelines for every new application.
AI.method: SMOCS offers three key contributions: (1) a layered abstraction over Apache Kafka that decouples infrastructure from application logic; (2) a three-thread agent architecture that temporally separates data ingestion, model training, and real-time inference for continuous online learning; and (3) a configuration-driven deployment model enabling domain experts to operate ML pipelines without software engineering skills. The system is containerized via Docker for horizontal scalability and fault isolation.
AI.result: SMOCS is facility/platform-agnostic, fault-isolated by design, horizontally scalable, and has been released as open-source software on the Jefferson Lab GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: SMOCS provides a reusable, scalable, and accessible framework that lowers the barrier for deploying ML-driven monitoring, optimization, and control systems across diverse scientific facilities.

title: Agentic and Generative AI for Open-Source Intelligence and Cyber Investigations: Taxonomy, Evaluation, Challenges, and Future Directions
summary: The rapid growth of publicly available digital information has rendered manual open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis insufficient for modern intelligence, cybersecurity, and cyber investigation. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI systems, capable of tool use, multi-step reasoning, and iterative intelligence generation, have emerged as promising solutions, yet evaluation frameworks have not kept pace with reported capabilities. This survey systematically reviews 74 studies and makes four contributions. First, it establishes agentic AI as a distinct analytical category rather than an extension of LLM prompting, organising the literature through an 11-category taxonomy covering LLM foundations, agentic architectures, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), knowledge graphs, prompt engineering, domain adaptation, evaluation benchmarks, and risk. Second, it identifies the hallucination-validation gap as a corpus-level finding: although hallucination is recognised as a major reliability concern in over twenty studies, end-to-end hallucination is empirically measured in only one OSINT-specific RAG-based system, non-reproducible conditions, while related reasoning and factual-correction studies evaluate general-domain question answering rather than OSINT. Third, it maps existing research to the OSINT lifecycle, showing strong support for collection and analysis but limited coverage of verification, reporting, dissemination, and decision support. Fourth, it derives a ten-point research agenda addressing evaluation, benchmarking, hallucination measurement, adversarial robustness, dark-web coverage, multimodal intelligence, and governance. It concludes that a human-AI co-pilot model, where LLMs assist collection and triage while analysts retain responsibility for verification and decision-making, represents the most defensible near-term deployment architecture.

AI.tldr: A systematic survey of 74 studies on agentic AI for OSINT, establishing an 11-category taxonomy, identifying a critical hallucination-validation gap, mapping research onto the OSINT lifecycle, and proposing a ten-point research agenda advocating for a human-AI co-pilot deployment model.
AI.motivation: The explosive growth of publicly available digital information has made manual OSINT analysis inadequate for modern intelligence and cybersecurity needs. While LLMs and agentic AI systems show promise for automating multi-step intelligence tasks, evaluation frameworks lag behind reported capabilities, creating an urgent need to systematically assess the state of the field and identify critical gaps.
AI.method: A systematic literature review of 74 studies, organized through an 11-category taxonomy encompassing LLM foundations, agentic architectures, RAG, knowledge graphs, prompt engineering, domain adaptation, evaluation benchmarks, and risk. The authors map findings onto the OSINT lifecycle stages (collection, analysis, verification, reporting, dissemination, decision support) and derive a structured research agenda from identified gaps.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Agentic AI constitutes a distinct analytical category beyond mere LLM prompting; (2) A hallucination-validation gap exists — over 20 studies acknowledge hallucination as a major reliability concern, yet only one OSINT-specific RAG system empirically measures end-to-end hallucination, under non-reproducible conditions, while related work focuses on general-domain QA; (3) Research strongly supports collection and analysis phases but neglects verification, reporting, dissemination, and decision support.
AI.conclusion: The human-AI co-pilot model — where LLMs assist with collection and triage while human analysts retain responsibility for verification and decision-making — represents the most defensible near-term deployment architecture. The paper provides a ten-point research agenda addressing evaluation, benchmarking, hallucination measurement, adversarial robustness, dark-web coverage, multimodal intelligence, and governance.

title: The Role of Prompt Language and Translation-Theory-Driven Prompts in Large Language Models: A Case Study on Spanish-Chinese Journalistic Translation
comment: Published in the Proceedings of the 27th Annual Conference of the European Association for Machine Translation (EAMT 2026), pp. 927-945. ACL Anthology entry forthcoming
summary: This study examines how prompt language and translation theory-driven prompt design influence the quality of Spanish-Chinese journalistic translations generated by GPT-5.2. A parallel corpus of four editorials from El Pais was translated under 48 experimental conditions (4 prompt types, 3 prompt languages, and 4 articles). Translation quality was assessed using BLEU and BERTScore-F1 for automated evaluation, alongside human evaluation based on the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) framework. Automated metrics identified the baseline prompt (BASE) as the best-performing condition, whereas human evaluation ranked the brief-oriented prompt (BRIEF) highest (MQM: 8.66 vs. 7.84), a reversal likely attributable to the single-reference constraint inherent in automated measures. Sub-error type analysis revealed that translation theory-driven prompts selectively reduced Awkward style errors, while Unidiomatic style errors persisted across conditions. Prompt language had a negligible impact under both evaluation paradigms. These results indicate that translation theory-driven prompts can yield measurable quality gains under expert evaluation of journalistic translations, although their pedagogical implications for language learners remain suggestive and require validation through user-based studies.

AI.tldr: Automated and human evaluations of GPT-5.2 Spanish-Chinese journalistic translations diverge: BLEU/BERTScore favor baseline prompts, while MQM human evaluation favors brief-oriented prompts. Translation theory-driven prompts selectively reduce Awkward style errors but not Unidiomatic style errors, and prompt language has negligible impact.
AI.motivation: To investigate how prompt language and translation theory-driven prompt design affect the quality of LLM-generated Spanish-Chinese journalistic translations, and to compare automated metrics (BLEU, BERTScore) with human evaluation (MQM) in assessing these effects.
AI.method: A parallel corpus of four editorials from El País was translated using GPT-5.2 under 48 experimental conditions (4 prompt types × 3 prompt languages × 4 articles). Translation quality was evaluated via automated metrics (BLEU, BERTScore-F1) and human evaluation using the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) framework, including sub-error type analysis.
AI.result: Automated metrics ranked the baseline prompt (BASE) highest, while human MQM evaluation ranked the brief-oriented prompt (BRIEF) highest (8.66 vs. 7.84). This reversal is attributed to the single-reference constraint of automated measures. Translation theory-driven prompts selectively reduced Awkward style errors, but Unidiomatic style errors persisted. Prompt language showed negligible impact under both evaluation paradigms.
AI.conclusion: Translation theory-driven prompts produce measurable quality gains under expert human evaluation for journalistic translations. However, pedagogical implications for language learners remain suggestive and require validation through user-based studies.

title: Labeled-Data-Free Meta-Learning: Efficient Task Generation Using Pre-trained Models and Unlabeled Data
summary: Meta-learning without labeled data is crucial for real-world applications, where obtaining labeled datasets can be expensive or restricted due to privacy concerns. Data-Free Meta-Learning (DFML) addresses this challenge by leveraging pre-trained models without access to training data. However, existing DFML methods rely on model inversion to generate training data, a process that is generally difficult and computationally expensive due to the need to generate high-dimensional data matching the original distribution. To address this limitation, we propose a novel meta-learning setting that avoids model inversion by jointly leveraging pre-trained models and unlabeled data. Our method generates meta-training tasks by assigning soft labels from pre-trained models to unlabeled data. Since the quality of these tasks can vary, we introduce a task-weighting mechanism based on task confidence and class distribution balance to ensure effective meta-learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach substantially reduces computational cost and improves generalization, achieving up to 104-fold speedup and 8.4 percent to 36.4 percent improvements in few-shot classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art DFML methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new meta-learning setting that uses pre-trained models and unlabeled data to generate meta-training tasks via soft labels, avoiding computationally expensive model inversion. A task-weighting mechanism based on confidence and class balance further improves learning, achieving up to 104x speedup and 8.4–36.4% accuracy gains over existing Data-Free Meta-Learning methods.
AI.motivation: Existing Data-Free Meta-Learning (DFML) methods avoid using real training data by employing model inversion to generate synthetic data from pre-trained models. However, model inversion is difficult and computationally expensive, especially for high-dimensional data, limiting practical applicability. The authors aim to overcome this bottleneck by eliminating the need for model inversion entirely.
AI.method: The proposed method jointly leverages pre-trained models and unlabeled data. Meta-training tasks are generated by assigning soft labels (predicted class probabilities) from pre-trained models to unlabeled examples. Since task quality varies, the authors introduce a task-weighting mechanism that scores tasks based on two criteria: (1) task confidence (reliability of the soft labels) and (2) class distribution balance, ensuring that low-quality or imbalanced tasks do not degrade meta-learning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the approach dramatically reduces computational cost (up to 104-fold speedup) while improving few-shot classification accuracy by 8.4% to 36.4% compared to state-of-the-art DFML methods.
AI.conclusion: Avoiding model inversion by using pre-trained models with unlabeled data and soft-label-based task construction, combined with confidence-aware task weighting, provides a far more efficient and effective solution for meta-learning in data-restricted settings.

title: OptiAgent: End-to-End Optimization Modeling via Multi-Agent Iterative Refinement
summary: We propose OptiAgent, a multi-agent framework that, given a natural language description of an Operations Research problem, is able to output a solver-ready mathematical formulation as well as executable code. Our architecture prioritizes the mathematical modeling step, where dedicated agents extract structures, such as decision variables and constraints, enabling iterative self-correction. We introduce a novel multi-loop validation architecture with four specialized feedback mechanisms, each targeting a distinct failure mode such as misinterpretation, structural defects, mathematical inconsistencies, validation failures, and code errors. Alongside accuracy, our modular design improves the process of solving optimization problems by improving transparency, as each agent exposes its reasoning and feedback, making the full modeling process auditable. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on 3 out of 4 benchmarks across LP, MILP, and Nonlinear Programming tasks, while remaining highly competitive on the remaining dataset.

AI.tldr: OptiAgent is a multi-agent framework that converts natural language descriptions of OR problems into solver-ready mathematical formulations and executable code, using a multi-loop validation architecture with four specialized feedback mechanisms for iterative self-correction. It achieves SOTA on 3 of 4 benchmarks across LP, MILP, and NLP tasks.
AI.motivation: Automating the conversion of natural language Operations Research problem descriptions into correct mathematical formulations and executable solver code is challenging due to multiple failure modes: misinterpretation of problem semantics, structural defects in formulation, mathematical inconsistencies, and code errors. Existing approaches lack transparency and robust self-correction across these failure modes.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework centered on mathematical modeling. Dedicated agents extract structural components (decision variables, constraints, objectives) from natural language descriptions. The key novelty is a multi-loop validation architecture employing four specialized feedback mechanisms, each targeting a distinct failure mode: (1) misinterpretation, (2) structural defects, (3) mathematical inconsistencies/validation failures, and (4) code errors. This enables iterative self-correction with full auditability, as each agent exposes its reasoning and feedback.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on 3 out of 4 benchmarks spanning Linear Programming (LP), Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), and Nonlinear Programming (NLP) tasks, with competitive performance on the remaining dataset.
AI.conclusion: The modular multi-agent design with specialized feedback loops effectively addresses diverse failure modes in automated OR problem formulation, achieving strong empirical results while improving transparency and auditability of the modeling process.

title: LBR: Towards Mitigating Length Bias in Large Language Models for Recommendation
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful backbones for recommender systems by reformulating recommendation as a token-level generation task. Despite their promise, we identify a pervasive yet underexplored issue: $\textit{Length Bias}$. Because items are represented by textual descriptions of varying lengths, LLM-based recommenders can be systematically biased in two ways. On the input side, longer item descriptions occupy more tokens in the context and thus receive disproportionately large aggregate attention mass during user preference modeling. On the output side, decoding based on summed autoregressive log-likelihood score inherently disfavors long items. Worse still, conventional length normalization can introduce an additional bias and even degrade recommendation performance.
  To address this problem, we propose $\textbf{LBR}$ ($\textbf{L}$ength $\textbf{B}$ias $\textbf{R}$eduction), a lightweight and model-agnostic framework for mitigating length bias in LLM-based recommendation. LBR mitigates input-side bias via Length-Aware Attention Calibration, which incorporates a length-dependent offset into attention logits to neutralize attention skew. For the output side, LBR introduces Effective Information Length Normalization, replacing naive token count with an information-theoretic length surrogate derived from the branching structure of the prefix tree. Extensive experiments on three real-world Amazon datasets and two representative LLM-based recommenders demonstrate that LBR substantially alleviates length bias while consistently improving recommendation accuracy and fairness, with negligible additional training and inference overhead (with an average NDCG@5 gain of 16.82%). The code is available at https://github.com/Void-JackLee/LBR.

AI.tldr: LLM-based recommenders suffer from length bias — longer item descriptions receive disproportionate attention on the input side, and decoding favors shorter items on the output side. The authors propose LBR, a lightweight framework that corrects both biases via Length-Aware Attention Calibration and Effective Information Length Normalization, achieving 16.82% average NDCG@5 gains with negligible overhead.
AI.motivation: LLM-based recommenders represent items as textual descriptions of varying lengths, which introduces a systematic Length Bias. On the input side, longer descriptions consume more tokens and thus capture disproportionate aggregate attention mass. On the output side, summed autoregressive log-likelihood scoring inherently penalizes long items. Conventional length normalization can introduce additional bias and even harm performance. This problem is pervasive yet underexplored.
AI.method: LBR (Length Bias Reduction) is a lightweight, model-agnostic framework with two components: (1) Length-Aware Attention Calibration, which adds a length-dependent offset to attention logits to neutralize attention skew toward longer input sequences; (2) Effective Information Length Normalization, which replaces naive token-count normalization with an information-theoretic length surrogate derived from the branching structure of the prefix tree, correcting output-side scoring bias.
AI.result: Experiments on three real-world Amazon datasets using two representative LLM-based recommenders show that LBR substantially alleviates length bias while consistently improving both recommendation accuracy and fairness. The method achieves an average NDCG@5 gain of 16.82% with negligible additional training and inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Length bias is a significant and underexplored problem in LLM-based recommendation that manifests on both the input and output sides. LBR provides an effective, efficient, and model-agnostic solution, demonstrating that explicitly addressing length bias yields substantial accuracy and fairness improvements without meaningful computational cost.

title: Benefits of Applying Software Design Patterns to Backend Rust Applications
summary: Software design patterns' effects on code quality have mostly been studied in the context of object-oriented languages. In the programming language Rust, which comes with novel language concepts, compile-time safety guarantees and a distinct type system, there has been little research on design patterns. This work investigates how patterns affect software quality and compile-time enforcement of invariants through a case study on three representative components of production backend applications. An evaluation framework based on criteria derived from the SQuaRE quality model, incorporating benchmarking, static code analysis and expert interviews, is developed to assess the refactored code. The patterns typestate and newtype are applied to address existing code smells in the selected use cases. While the typestate pattern improves faultlessness and testability significantly, it comes at the cost of more structural code that can degrade readability. Code with extensive branching logic and a high number of invariants is likely to benefit most from the pattern. The newtype pattern combined with the "Parse, don't validate" principle offers high returns in software quality at a low cost and prevents invalid states during runtime. Overall, this work provides an initial empirical assessment of design patterns in Rust and establishes a foundation for further studies involving additional use cases and patterns.

AI.tldr: A case study evaluating the typestate and newtype design patterns in Rust, using a custom framework based on the SQuaRE quality model. Typestate improves faultlessness and testability but can harm readability; newtype combined with "Parse, don't validate" offers high quality gains at low cost.
AI.motivation: Design patterns' effects on code quality are well-studied in object-oriented languages, but Rust—with its unique ownership system, compile-time safety guarantees, and distinct type system—lacks empirical research on how patterns affect software quality and invariant enforcement.
AI.method: A case study on three production backend components, applying typestate and newtype patterns to refactor code smells. Evaluation uses a custom framework derived from the SQuaRE quality model, combining benchmarking, static code analysis, and expert interviews.
AI.result: Typestate significantly improves faultlessness and testability but degrades readability due to increased structural code; it benefits components with extensive branching and many invariants most. The newtype plus "Parse, don't validate" pattern yields high software quality returns at low cost and prevents invalid runtime states.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first empirical assessment of design patterns in Rust, establishing a foundation for future studies with additional use cases and patterns.

title: Security Analysis for SCONE Logic Locking
summary: SCONE [DAC'25] expands a logic locking interface with additional encoded inputs derived from the original primary inputs, and admits two realizations: a \textit{with-ES} variant, where the critical encoding stage is implemented in hardware, and a \textit{without-ES} variant, where the locked design directly exposes an encoded interface of width $n+m$. We show that both realizations are vulnerable, but for different reasons. For the without-ES variant, we prove that, when the added encoded inputs are deterministic linear functions of the original inputs, the valid encoded-input space remains $n$-dimensional despite the nominal expansion to $n+m$ inputs. Hence, the widened interface does not yield $m$ additional or independent brute-force dimensions. For the with-ES variant, we present a polynomial-time white-box attack that exactly recovers the added-input count and the implemented linear encoding relation from the locked netlist, achieving 100\% recovery over all evaluated instances. We also develop a black-box procedure that certifies the same dimensionality collapse from valid encoded-input samples without reconstructing the hidden encoder. Experiments on ISCAS-85 and ITC-99 benchmarks validate both results, and we further demonstrate exact white-box recovery on an ARM Cortex-M0 RTL benchmark. Finally, we propose a lightweight non-linear mitigation and show that it does not exhibit the vulnerabilities identified in this paper under all representative attack sets considered in SCONE.

AI.tldr: SCONE's logic locking scheme is broken: the without-ES variant suffers from dimensionality collapse (the encoded-input space remains n-dimensional despite nominal expansion), and the with-ES variant is vulnerable to a polynomial-time white-box attack that perfectly recovers the linear encoding. A black-box certification method confirms the collapse, and a lightweight non-linear mitigation is proposed.
AI.motivation: SCONE [DAC'25] claims to enhance logic locking security by expanding the primary input interface with additional encoded inputs. This paper aims to rigorously evaluate both realizations of SCONE (with-ES and without-ES) to determine whether the approach genuinely increases the brute-force search space and resists state-of-the-art attacks.
AI.method: For the without-ES variant, the authors provide a formal proof that when encoded inputs are deterministic linear functions of original inputs, the valid input space dimension remains n (no additional brute-force dimensions). For the with-ES variant, they develop a polynomial-time white-box attack that exactly recovers the number of added inputs and the linear encoding relation from the locked netlist. They also devise a black-box certification procedure that detects dimensionality collapse using only valid encoded-input samples. Experiments are conducted on ISCAS-85 and ITC-99 benchmarks, with additional white-box validation on an ARM Cortex-M0 RTL benchmark. A lightweight non-linear mitigation is proposed and evaluated against the attack sets from the original SCONE paper.
AI.result: The white-box attack achieved 100% recovery of the added-input count and linear encoding across all evaluated instances, including the ARM Cortex-M0 RTL benchmark. The black-box procedure successfully certified dimensionality collapse from valid encoded-input samples. The proposed non-linear mitigation did not exhibit the identified vulnerabilities under any representative attack sets considered in the original SCONE work.
AI.conclusion: Both realizations of SCONE are fundamentally vulnerable: the without-ES variant offers no additional brute-force resistance due to dimensionality collapse, and the with-ES variant's linear encoding is fully recoverable in polynomial time. SCONE does not achieve its claimed security objectives. A non-linear encoding scheme can mitigate these specific vulnerabilities, but further security analysis is warranted.

title: KARMA: Knowledge graph-based Automated Reasoning Materialization and Alignment
summary: Template-based contrastive synthesis is scalable, but its candidates often differ only in a few entity-slots while sequence-level optimization spreads supervision over mostly shared templates. We formalize this as the Resolution Mismatch Problem and propose KARMA, which enumerates schema-constrained paths over domain knowledge graphs and verbalizes them into slot-aligned contrastive candidates. Slot-Parallel Alignment (SPA) then applies a decoupled slot-level objective to route preference supervision to discriminative entity-slots, with slot-aware masked attention serving as an optional packed-evaluation implementation. Across biomedical, computer-science, and chemistry benchmarks, KARMA outperforms base LLM and same-data SFT baselines, and compares favorably with sequence and token-level preference methods.

AI.tldr: KARMA addresses the Resolution Mismatch Problem in template-based contrastive synthesis by generating slot-aligned contrastive candidates from knowledge graphs and applying Slot-Parallel Alignment (SPA) to route supervision to discriminative entity-slots, outperforming SFT and other preference optimization baselines.
AI.motivation: Template-based contrastive data synthesis for LLM alignment suffers from a Resolution Mismatch Problem: candidates differ only in few entity-slots, but sequence-level optimization dilutes supervision across largely shared template tokens. This mismatch prevents preference optimization from focusing on the semantically discriminative spans.
AI.method: KARMA operates in two stages: (1) it enumerates schema-constrained paths over domain knowledge graphs and verbalizes them into slot-aligned contrastive candidate pairs where differences are localized to specific entity-slots; (2) Slot-Parallel Alignment (SPA) applies a decoupled slot-level preference objective that routes supervision to individual discriminative slots rather than the full sequence, with an optional slot-aware masked attention mechanism for efficient packed evaluation.
AI.result: Across biomedical, computer-science, and chemistry benchmarks, KARMA outperforms both the base LLM and same-data SFT baselines, and compares favorably against sequence-level and token-level preference optimization methods.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly aligning contrastive supervision with the granularity at which candidates actually differ — via knowledge-graph-grounded slot-aligned synthesis and slot-level preference objectives — yields more effective LLM alignment than standard sequence-level approaches.

title: Trading Confidence: Comprehensive Uncertainty Estimation in Algorithmic Trading
comment: Accepted at the Pacific Asia Conference on Information Systems (PACIS 2025). 17 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful approach in financial trading, enabling agents to learn optimal strategies through direct market interaction. However, financial markets are highly uncertain, with price fluctuations driven by stochastic volatility, model limitations, and regime shifts. Traditional RL models struggle in dynamic environments, often failing to adapt to sudden market disruptions, leading to suboptimal trading decisions. To address this challenge, we propose an uncertainty-aware RL framework that integrates distributional, epistemic, and aleatoric uncertainty estimations. Our approach enhances uncertainty estimation using SHAP-weighted reconstruction uncertainty, MC Dropout, and an LSTM-based technical indicator consensus mechanism. Experimental results on five major U.S. stock indices demonstrate that RL agents equipped with uncertainty estimation significantly outperform traditional models in return and risk management. This study advances uncertainty estimation in RL-based financial trading, with future research extending its application to other asset classes and alternative RL architectures for greater adaptability.

AI.tldr: Proposes an uncertainty-aware RL framework for financial trading that combines distributional, epistemic, and aleatoric uncertainty estimation (SHAP-weighted reconstruction, MC Dropout, LSTM consensus) to improve return and risk management across five US stock indices.
AI.motivation: Traditional RL models fail in dynamic financial markets due to stochastic volatility, model limitations, and regime shifts, resulting in poor adaptation to sudden market disruptions and suboptimal trading decisions.
AI.method: An uncertainty-aware RL framework integrating three uncertainty types: (1) distributional uncertainty via SHAP-weighted reconstruction uncertainty, (2) epistemic uncertainty via MC Dropout, and (3) aleatoric uncertainty via an LSTM-based technical indicator consensus mechanism. Evaluated on five major US stock indices.
AI.result: RL agents equipped with the proposed uncertainty estimation framework significantly outperform traditional models in both return generation and risk management across all five tested US stock indices.
AI.conclusion: Integrating multi-faceted uncertainty estimation enhances RL-based trading performance. Future work will extend the framework to other asset classes and explore alternative RL architectures for improved adaptability.

title: Personalized Causal Recourse: A Human-In-The-Loop Approach
comment: Accepted at the 4th World Conference on eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI 2026)
summary: Algorithmic recourse addresses the challenge of providing tailored recommendations to users affected by unfavorable machine learning decisions, in potentially high-stakes scenarios. Traditional approaches to recourse often rely on the closest counterfactual explanations or assume a priori knowledge of a user's causal structure, resulting in interventions that overlook individual contexts and specific feature interactions. To overcome these limitations, we study a human-in-the-loop framework that iteratively approximates the user's structural causal model through interactive queries via Bayesian inference before producing recourse recommendations. This framework exploits humans' feedback to improve the identification of causal effects, allowing personalized recourse that is plausible, cost-effective, and aligned with the actual causal dependencies of each user. As a proof of concept, we evaluate this framework through simulated human responses. Our simulations across linear and non-linear causal models show promising results, though challenges remain in capturing complex, non-linear structures, emphasizing the importance of accurate approximations and robust noise distribution modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a human-in-the-loop framework for algorithmic recourse that uses Bayesian inference and interactive queries to iteratively approximate each user's structural causal model, enabling personalized, plausible, and cost-effective interventions, with simulations across linear and non-linear models validating the approach while highlighting challenges in modeling complex non-linear structures.
AI.motivation: Traditional algorithmic recourse methods either rely on closest counterfactual explanations (which ignore causal dependencies) or assume a priori knowledge of the user's causal structure (which is unrealistic and overlooks individual context). Both approaches fail to provide interventions that respect each user's actual causal mechanisms and specific feature interactions.
AI.method: A human-in-the-loop framework is developed that iteratively approximates a user's structural causal model (SCM) through interactive queries. Bayesian inference is employed to update beliefs about the causal structure based on human feedback, and this learned causal model is then used to generate recourse recommendations. Simulated human responses are used as a proof-of-concept evaluation.
AI.result: Simulations across both linear and non-linear causal models demonstrate promising results for the proposed framework. However, challenges persist in accurately capturing complex non-linear structures, underscoring the need for robust noise distribution modeling and precise causal approximation.
AI.conclusion: The human-in-the-loop framework offers a promising direction for personalized algorithmic recourse by leveraging interactive human feedback to infer causal dependencies. Accurate causal approximation and robust noise modeling remain critical open challenges, especially for complex non-linear settings.

title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: A General-Purpose Verification Framework
summary: Scaling pre-training, post-training, and test-time compute have become the central paradigms for improving the capabilities of LLMs. In this work, we identify verification, the ability to determine the correctness of a solution, as a new scaling axis. To unlock this and demonstrate its effectiveness, we introduce LLM-as-a-Verifier, a general-purpose verification framework that provides fine-grained feedback for agentic tasks without requiring additional training. Unlike standard LM judges that prompt LLMs to produce discrete scores for candidate solutions, LLM-as-a-Verifier computes the expectation over the distribution of scoring token logits to generate continuous scores. This probabilistic formulation enables verification to scale along multiple dimensions: (1) score granularity, (2) repeated evaluation, and (3) criteria decomposition. In particular, we show that scaling the scoring granularity leads to better separation between positive and negative solutions, resulting in more calibrated comparisons. Moreover, scaling repeated evaluation and criteria decomposition consistently lead to additional gains in verification accuracy through variance and complexity reduction. We further introduce a cost-efficient ranking algorithm for selecting the best solution among candidates using the verifier's continuous scores. LLM-as-a-Verifier achieves state-of-the-art performance on Terminal-Bench V2 (86.5%), SWE-Bench Verified (78.2%), RoboRewardBench (87.4%), and MedAgentBench (73.3%). Beyond verification, the fine-grained signals from LLM-as-a-Verifier can also serve as a proxy for estimating task progress. We build an extension for Claude Code, enabling developers to monitor and improve their own agentic systems. Finally, we show that LLM-as-a-Verifier can provide dense feedback for RL, improving the sample efficiency of SAC and GRPO on robotics and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Introduces LLM-as-a-Verifier, a training-free framework that scales verification by computing continuous scores from LLM token logits, achieving SOTA on multiple agentic benchmarks and enabling applications in progress estimation and RL reward shaping.
AI.motivation: Existing LM judges produce discrete scores, limiting granularity and calibration. The authors identify verification as a novel scaling axis alongside pre-training, post-training, and test-time compute, and aim to unlock finer-grained, more calibrated verification signals without additional training.
AI.method: LLM-as-a-Verifier computes the expectation over scoring token logit distributions to produce continuous scores. This probabilistic formulation enables scaling along three dimensions: (1) score granularity via more scoring tokens, (2) repeated evaluation for variance reduction, and (3) criteria decomposition for complexity reduction. A cost-efficient ranking algorithm selects the best candidate using continuous scores.
AI.result: Achieves SOTA on Terminal-Bench V2 (86.5%), SWE-Bench Verified (78.2%), RoboRewardBench (87.4%), and MedAgentBench (73.3%). Scaling granularity improves positive/negative separation; repeated evaluation and criteria decomposition consistently improve verification accuracy. The framework also enables task progress estimation and improves sample efficiency of SAC and GRPO in RL settings.
AI.conclusion: Verification is a distinct and effective scaling axis for LLMs. Probabilistic, continuous scoring via logit expectations outperforms discrete judging, generalizes across diverse agentic domains, and can be leveraged for progress monitoring and dense RL rewards.

title: Autonomous Information Seeking: A Roadmap for Agentic Recommender Systems
summary: The rapid integration of large language model-based agents into recommender systems has driven a shift from static, ranking-based pipelines toward autonomous and interactive systems that can reason, plan, and act. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of this emerging landscape by introducing a unified taxonomy grounded in the level of autonomy and three core paradigms of agentic recommender systems: agent-assisted recommendation, agent-as-recommender, and agent-as-user-simulator. The autonomy framework organizes existing methods along increasing capabilities in proactivity, context awareness, interaction flexibility, and adaptivity. Building on this framework, the survey analyzes how each paradigm adopts different agentic architectures and how agents enhance key components such as profiles, memory, tool use, workflows, and optimization mechanisms. We further examine evaluation methodologies for agentic recommendation, covering automated metrics, LLM-based judging, and simulation-based assessment, and discuss their limitations in capturing reasoning quality, user experience, and system behavior. Beyond existing evaluation protocols, we further discuss unresolved issues in evaluating agentic recommender systems, including trajectory-level assessment, agent contribution analysis, and calibration of user simulation. Lastly, the survey outlines open challenges in lifelong user modeling, contextual abstraction, multimodal alignment, controllability, trustworthiness, privacy, scalability, and efficiency. Together, these analyses establish a unified foundation for understanding the current progress of agentic recommender systems and highlight promising opportunities for developing more autonomous, reliable, and human-aligned recommendation agents.

AI.tldr: This survey taxonomizes agentic recommender systems into three paradigms—agent-assisted recommendation, agent-as-recommender, and agent-as-user-simulator—organized by increasing autonomy levels, and systematically examines architectures, evaluation methodologies, and open challenges.
AI.motivation: The shift from static, ranking-based recommender pipelines to autonomous, interactive LLM-based agent systems lacks a unified organizational framework. Existing work is fragmented across diverse paradigms without a coherent taxonomy connecting autonomy levels, architectural choices, and evaluation practices.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified taxonomy grounded in four dimensions of autonomy (proactivity, context awareness, interaction flexibility, adaptivity) and three core paradigms: (1) agent-assisted recommendation, where agents augment traditional pipelines; (2) agent-as-recommender, where agents autonomously drive the full recommendation process; and (3) agent-as-user-simulator, where agents emulate user behavior for training and evaluation. The survey systematically analyzes agentic architectures across components—profiles, memory, tool use, workflows, and optimization mechanisms—and evaluates assessment methodologies including automated metrics, LLM judging, and simulation-based evaluation.
AI.result: The survey identifies that current evaluation protocols inadequately capture reasoning quality, user experience, and system behavior. Key gaps include trajectory-level assessment, agent contribution analysis, and user simulation calibration. Open challenges span lifelong user modeling, contextual abstraction, multimodal alignment, controllability, trustworthiness, privacy, scalability, and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Agentic recommender systems represent a paradigm shift toward autonomous, interactive recommendation. The proposed taxonomy and analyses establish a unified foundation for the field, while highlighting that significant research is needed in evaluation rigor, long-term user modeling, and responsible deployment to realize reliable, human-aligned recommendation agents.

title: From Codebases to LLMs: Non-Inclusive Naming in Linux Foundation Repositories
summary: Since 2020, the Linux Foundation and the multi-organization Inclusive Naming Initiative (INI) have encouraged open-source projects to replace non-inclusive terms such as master/slave and whitelist/blacklist. Although these recommendations have been widely adopted, there is limited empirical evidence on their long-term adoption across Linux Foundation (LF) projects or their implications for AI-assisted software development. In this paper, we present NISCAN, a multilingual static-analysis framework that detects non-inclusive terminology across source code and related software artifacts using the INI vocabulary. Using NISCAN, we conduct the first ecosystem-scale study of inclusive naming across 461 Linux Foundation repositories. Our analysis shows that non-inclusive terminology has declined by approximately 47% since 2020, yet adoption remains incomplete: 62.7% of repositories still contain at least one Tier-1 non-inclusive identifier, while most remaining terminology resides outside source code in documentation, comments, configuration files, and other software artifacts. We further show that repository size, programming language, project functionality, and ecosystem are stronger predictors of term inclusiveness in LF repositories rather than foundation governance. To examine the implications for AI-assisted software development, we conduct a case study evaluating whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct legacy non-inclusive identifiers from surrounding program context. The results show that historical naming decisions remain embedded in model predictions even after identifiers have been renamed. Overall, our study findings provide the first ecosystem-scale assessment of inclusive naming adoption within the Linux Foundation and highlight the importance of addressing terminology residue to support responsible naming and ethically sourced code generation.

AI.tldr: NISCAN, a multilingual static-analysis framework, detects non-inclusive terminology across 461 Linux Foundation repositories. Non-inclusive terms declined ~47% since 2020, but 62.7% of repos still contain at least one Tier-1 non-inclusive identifier, mostly in non-code artifacts. LLMs can reconstruct renamed legacy identifiers from context, highlighting terminology residue risks.
AI.motivation: Despite the Linux Foundation and Inclusive Naming Initiative (INI) recommending replacement of non-inclusive terms (e.g., master/slave, whitelist/blacklist) since 2020, there is limited empirical evidence on long-term adoption across LF projects and the implications for AI-assisted software development.
AI.method: The authors developed NISCAN, a multilingual static-analysis framework that detects non-inclusive terminology using the INI vocabulary. They applied it to conduct an ecosystem-scale study across 461 Linux Foundation repositories, analyzing term prevalence, predictors of inclusiveness, and distribution across artifact types. A case study evaluated whether LLMs can reconstruct legacy non-inclusive identifiers from surrounding program context after renaming.
AI.result: Non-inclusive terminology declined by ~47% since 2020, but adoption is incomplete: 62.7% of repositories still contain at least one Tier-1 non-inclusive identifier. Most remaining terminology exists outside source code (documentation, comments, configuration files). Repository size, programming language, project functionality, and ecosystem are stronger predictors of inclusiveness than foundation governance. LLMs can reconstruct legacy non-inclusive identifiers from program context even after renaming.
AI.conclusion: This is the first ecosystem-scale assessment of inclusive naming adoption within the Linux Foundation. Terminology residue poses risks for responsible naming and ethically sourced code generation, necessitating attention beyond source code to documentation and other artifacts.

title: LLM-Enhanced Hierarchical Heterogeneous Graph Representation Learning for Malicious Python Package Detection
summary: Malicious Python packages have become a major threat to software supply chain ecosystems due to the widespread adoption of open-source repositories such as PyPI. Existing learning-based detection methods struggle to capture the hierarchical organization and heterogeneous interactions among different program entities. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code understanding and semantic reasoning, they are rarely integrated with structural program representations for fine-grained malicious behavior analysis. In this paper, we propose an LLM-enhanced hierarchical heterogeneous graph representation learning framework for malicious Python package detection. The framework constructs a hierarchical heterogeneous code graph that explicitly models heterogeneous code entities and different types of structural dependencies. LLMs are further leveraged to infer function-level semantic roles, introducing an additional layer of semantic heterogeneity. Based on this graph, we develop a hierarchical heterogeneous graph neural network that performs type-aware message passing over different node and edge categories, effectively modeling malicious behavior propagation for accurate package-level classification. The framework also incorporates a function-level attribution mechanism which, combined with LLM reasoning, automatically identifies suspicious functions and localizes fine-grained malicious behaviors without human expert intervention. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that our framework consistently outperforms traditional machine learning methods, graph-based detectors, and state-of-the-art LLMs across packages with varying sizes and dependency complexities, while providing accurate, robust, and interpretable malicious behavior localization.

AI.tldr: Proposes an LLM-enhanced hierarchical heterogeneous graph representation learning framework for detecting malicious Python packages, combining structured code graphs with LLM semantic reasoning to improve detection accuracy and enable fine-grained malicious behavior localization without human intervention.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based detection methods fail to capture hierarchical organization and heterogeneous interactions among program entities. LLMs show strong code understanding but are rarely integrated with structural representations for fine-grained malicious analysis.
AI.method: Constructs a hierarchical heterogeneous code graph modeling diverse code entities and structural dependencies. LLMs infer function-level semantic roles to add semantic heterogeneity. A hierarchical heterogeneous GNN performs type-aware message passing for package-level classification. A function-level attribution mechanism combined with LLM reasoning localizes suspicious functions automatically.
AI.result: The framework consistently outperforms traditional ML methods, graph-based detectors, and state-of-the-art LLMs across packages with varying sizes and dependency complexities, while providing accurate, robust, and interpretable malicious behavior localization.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLM semantic reasoning with hierarchical heterogeneous graph representation learning significantly advances malicious Python package detection, offering both superior classification performance and interpretable fine-grained analysis of malicious behaviors.

title: S-DiverSe: Spanish Diverse Speech
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has advanced remarkably for standard speech, yet speech affected by neurological conditions remains a challenge. We present S-DiverSe (Spanish Diverse Speech), a corpus of 3.2 hours of in-the-wild Spanish speech from 22 speakers with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and stroke. The dataset contains 444 manually transcribed audio segments with metadata on speaker sex, disease type, and intelligibility. S-DiverSe is designed to support ASR evaluation and development for neurologically affected Spanish speech. We describe the dataset, analyze its composition, and report baseline ASR results alongside initial adaptation experiments. Our findings reveal that heuristic text post-processing is more robust than fine-tuning for out-of-domain neurological Spanish speech. This underscores the need for dedicated in-the-wild Spanish benchmarks.

AI.tldr: S-DiverSe is a 3.2-hour corpus of in-the-wild Spanish speech from 22 speakers with ALS, Parkinson's, and stroke, designed to benchmark ASR for neurologically impaired speech. Baseline experiments show heuristic text post-processing outperforms fine-tuning for out-of-domain neurological Spanish speech.
AI.motivation: ASR systems perform poorly on speech affected by neurological conditions such as ALS, Parkinson's disease, and stroke. Moreover, existing dysarthric/neurological speech corpora are predominantly English, leaving Spanish severely underrepresented. There is a pressing need for dedicated, in-the-wild Spanish benchmarks to evaluate and develop ASR for this population.
AI.method: The authors construct S-DiverSe, a corpus of 3.2 hours of in-the-wild Spanish speech collected from 22 speakers across three neurological conditions. The dataset comprises 444 manually transcribed audio segments with rich metadata (speaker sex, disease type, intelligibility). Baseline ASR experiments are conducted using state-of-the-art models, and two adaptation strategies are compared: (1) fine-tuning on neurological speech and (2) heuristic text post-processing applied to ASR outputs.
AI.result: Heuristic text post-processing proves more robust than fine-tuning for improving ASR accuracy on out-of-domain neurological Spanish speech. Fine-tuning, while common, yields limited gains due to domain mismatch and data sparsity.
AI.conclusion: The limited efficacy of fine-tuning underscores the critical need for dedicated in-the-wild Spanish benchmarks like S-DiverSe. The dataset provides a foundational resource for evaluating and advancing ASR for Spanish speakers with neurological conditions, and the findings highlight post-processing as a practical alternative when in-domain training data is scarce.

title: Reward Granularity in RLVR: Comparing Process and Outcome Reward Structures for Mathematical Reasoning in Small Language Models
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving mathematical reasoning in language models. Yet most RLVR work rewards only the final answer (outcome-based rewards), leaving the impact of step-level process supervision (process rewards) underexplored especially for small models that lack the capacity to self-correct under sparse feedback. We systematically compare five reward conditions applied to Qwen2.5-0.5B fine-tuned with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on GSM8K: a no-RL baseline, process-only, outcome-only, and three hybrid weightings ($λ\in \{0.9, 0.5, 0.1\}$ process weight). Process-only supervision achieves 63.73% test accuracy versus 53.75% for outcome-only, a nearly 10-percentage point gap while yielding reasoning traces with higher step validity and lower deviation from ground-truth chain length. Hybrid rewards generally correlate positively with process weight, with one notable anomaly: the low-process / high-outcome configuration ($λ=0.1$) underperforms pure outcome supervision, suggesting conflicting optimization signals. Error analysis using GPT-4o as a judge reveals distinct failure mode distributions: process models generate structurally inconsistent but arithmetically grounded traces, while outcome models produce concise but derivation-error-prone chains. Our results demonstrate that reward granularity is a first-order design decision for RLVR, with process-level supervision substantially improving both accuracy and trace fidelity in small language models.

AI.tldr: Process-level reward supervision substantially outperforms outcome-only rewards for small LMs in mathematical reasoning (63.73% vs 53.75% on GSM8K), with hybrid rewards showing mixed effects and a counterproductive low-process configuration.
AI.motivation: Most RLVR research focuses on outcome-based rewards for final answers, leaving process-level supervision underexplored—particularly for small models that struggle with self-correction under sparse feedback signals.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune Qwen2.5-0.5B using GRPO on GSM8K under five conditions: no-RL baseline, process-only, outcome-only, and three hybrid weightings (λ ∈ {0.9, 0.5, 0.1} process weight). Evaluation uses accuracy, step validity, trace length deviation, and GPT-4o–judged error analysis.
AI.result: Process-only supervision achieves 63.73% vs 53.75% for outcome-only (~10pp gap). Hybrid rewards generally improve with higher process weight, but λ=0.1 underperforms pure outcome supervision. Process models produce structurally inconsistent but arithmetically grounded traces; outcome models yield concise but derivation-error-prone chains.
AI.conclusion: Reward granularity is a first-order design decision in RLVR: process-level supervision significantly boosts both accuracy and reasoning trace fidelity in small LMs, and naively mixing process and outcome rewards can introduce conflicting optimization signals.

title: Embodied Operators and Benchmarking: Toward Reusable and Deployable Embodied Intelligence Systems
summary: Embodied intelligence systems require not only end-to-end policy models, but also reusable functional modules that transform multimodal observations, robot states, human demonstrations, and task contexts into structured representations, decisions, trajectories, control references, and system services. This work defines these modules as embodied operators and studies them as independent yet composable units in embodied intelligence pipelines. We clarify their definition boundary, emphasizing task semantics, standardized input-output contracts, deployability, reusability, and multi-layer optimizability. We further construct a taxonomy covering five categories: detection and segmentation, spatial localization and 3D understanding, hand motion recovery, embodied foundation models and task-decision operators, and planning, control, and system support operators. For each category, we summarize representative functions, technical paradigms, application roles, and practical limitations. Beyond taxonomy, we propose a multi-dimensional benchmark framework that evaluates embodied operators in terms of correctness, end-to-end efficiency, resource usage, temporal stability, portability, interface compatibility, deployment reliability, and downstream task utility. We also discuss workflow-level operator acceleration and open challenges in operator composition, data standardization, world models, VLA safety, edge deployment, and real-world application value. Overall, this work argues that embodied operators should be optimized and evaluated as holistic deployable components, providing a foundation for reusable, scalable, and verifiable embodied intelligence systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "embodied operators" as reusable, composable functional modules in embodied intelligence pipelines, defines their design principles, proposes a five-category taxonomy, and presents a multi-dimensional benchmark framework for holistic evaluation.
AI.motivation: Embodied intelligence systems currently lack standardized, reusable, and independently optimizable functional modules. Beyond end-to-end policy models, there is a need for composable building blocks that transform multimodal inputs into structured representations and control outputs, enabling scalable and verifiable system design.
AI.method: The authors (1) define embodied operators with explicit boundary conditions emphasizing task semantics, standardized I/O contracts, deployability, reusability, and multi-layer optimizability; (2) construct a taxonomy spanning five categories — detection/segmentation, spatial localization/3D understanding, hand motion recovery, embodied foundation models/task-decision operators, and planning/control/system support; (3) propose a multi-dimensional benchmark framework evaluating correctness, end-to-end efficiency, resource usage, temporal stability, portability, interface compatibility, deployment reliability, and downstream task utility.
AI.result: For each of the five operator categories, representative functions, technical paradigms, application roles, and practical limitations are summarized. The benchmark framework captures eight orthogonal evaluation dimensions. Workflow-level acceleration strategies and open challenges in operator composition, data standardization, world models, VLA safety, and edge deployment are identified.
AI.conclusion: Embodied operators should be treated as holistic deployable components — optimized and evaluated as such — to serve as the foundation for reusable, scalable, and verifiable embodied intelligence systems. The paper provides both a conceptual framework and practical evaluation methodology toward this goal.

title: Evaluation and Explainability of Unsupervised Scholarly Collaboration Recommendations
summary: In this paper, we examine unsupervised, content-based collaboration recommendations using publication text in scholarly settings. We compare three families of methods: a TF-IDF baseline, topic-based models (LDA and BERTopic, including clone variants), and embedding-based retrieval using SciBERT with Faiss. To evaluate model behavior beyond simple lexical matching, we introduce a constrained setting where publication overlap between researchers is partially removed while still using historical co-authorship as proxy ground truth for post-hoc evaluation. Results show clear differences across methods. TF-IDF performs best under full information but drops significantly as overlap is reduced. In contrast, topic-based and embedding-based approaches show more stable performance, suggesting they capture broader distributional similarities, rather than relying only on direct lexical overlap. We also examine explainability through two perspectives: intrinsic topic-based explanations and post-hoc, retrieval-based explanations generated using language models. These provide complementary trade-offs between transparency and human readability.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates unsupervised, content-based collaboration recommendations using publication text in academic settings, comparing TF-IDF, topic models (LDA, BERTopic), and SciBERT+Faiss embeddings. A constrained evaluation setting that removes direct publication overlap reveals TF-IDF excels under full information but degrades without lexical overlap, while topic and embedding methods show robust, stable performance. The study also examines intrinsic and post-hoc explainability trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Traditional evaluation of content-based recommendation systems for scholarly collaboration often conflates true semantic matching with simple lexical overlap (e.g., shared publications). The authors aim to disentangle these signals and understand whether topic-based and embedding-based models capture deeper distributional similarities beyond surface-level term matching, while also assessing the explainability of these methods.
AI.method: Three method families are compared: (1) a TF-IDF baseline, (2) topic models including LDA and BERTopic with clone variants, and (3) SciBERT embeddings combined with Faiss for similarity retrieval. A novel constrained evaluation protocol is introduced where publication overlap between researchers is partially removed, while historical co-authorship serves as proxy ground truth for post-hoc evaluation. Explainability is assessed via intrinsic topic-based explanations and post-hoc retrieval-based explanations generated by language models.
AI.result: TF-IDF achieves the best performance under full information but suffers a significant performance drop when publication overlap is reduced. Topic-based (LDA, BERTopic) and embedding-based (SciBERT+Faiss) methods exhibit more stable performance across conditions, indicating they capture broader distributional similarities rather than relying solely on direct lexical overlap. The two explainability approaches offer complementary trade-offs between transparency and human readability.
AI.conclusion: Content-based collaboration recommendation benefits from models that go beyond lexical matching. Topic and embedding methods provide robust, stable recommendations even when direct publication overlap is absent. The choice of explanation method — intrinsic (topic-based) vs. post-hoc (retrieval-based with LMs) — involves a trade-off between transparency and readability, suggesting hybrid approaches may be valuable in practice.

title: Was It Never Collected, or Rewritten Away? A Commit-Provenance Dataset Separating Ingestion Gaps from Upstream History Edits across the World of Code
summary: Any global mirror of open-source version control is incomplete, but the reasons a commit is missing are not interchangeable: a project may have force-pushed it away (so it no longer exists upstream), or the mirror may never have ingested it (a true collection gap). We release a commit-provenance dataset that separates these cases at scale by comparing two views of the same commit graph: the GHArchive event stream, a historical witness of what GitHub advertised at push time, and the World of Code (WoC) V2604 object database, an accumulated union of periodic fetches that never deletes a collected commit. Walking each reference's PushEvent chain reconstructs force-pushes structurally (a before that is not the prior head breaks the fast-forward chain; no recorded flag exists across eras), and joining every advertised commit against WoC membership yields a three-way label. Over 1,118,116,350 advertised commits, 53.35% are present in WoC, 6.47% are rewritten (orphaned by a later force-push, an upstream edit and a correct absence), and 40.18% are never-ingested (the candidate collection gap). About one missing-commit case in fifteen is a rewrite the project erased, not a mirror gap. We release the force-push witness (166,710,831 events over 19,926,250 repositories) and a per-project rollup (78,125,788 repositories; force-pushing observed in 25.47%, a rewritten commit in 12.85%). We treat the 40% never-ingested share as an upper bound on the collection gap and state five reasons it overcounts. The dataset makes mirror-completeness reporting honest, flags rewritten commits as duplicate patch sources for contribution counting, and corrects a 10.82% corpus-wide undercount that history editing imposes on commit-based productivity, with a released per-project correction factor. All artifacts ship as a self-contained, independently hosted replication package keyed to WoC V2604.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a commit-provenance dataset that distinguishes between commits missing from a mirror due to force-pushes (rewritten/erased upstream) versus true collection gaps (never ingested). By cross-referencing the GHArchive event stream with the World of Code database, it labels 1.1B+ advertised commits into three categories: present (53.35%), rewritten (6.47%), and never-ingested (40.18%), and provides correction factors for productivity metrics.
AI.motivation: Open-source version control mirrors are inherently incomplete, but the reasons for missing commits are not equivalent: some are deliberately erased by projects (force-pushes), while others represent genuine collection gaps in the mirror. Without distinguishing these cases, analyses of software evolution, contribution counting, and productivity metrics suffer from systematic errors. The work addresses this by providing a structural method to separate rewritten commits from true gaps at scale.
AI.method: The approach compares two views of the same commit graph: (1) the GHArchive event stream, which records what GitHub advertised at push time as a historical witness, and (2) the World of Code (WoC) V2604 object database, an accumulated union of periodic fetches that never deletes commits. Force-pushes are reconstructed structurally by walking each reference's PushEvent chain — a "before" commit that is not the prior head breaks the fast-forward chain. Every advertised commit is then joined against WoC membership to produce a three-way label: present, rewritten (orphaned by force-push), or never-ingested.
AI.result: Over 1,118,116,350 advertised commits: 53.35% present in WoC, 6.47% rewritten (orphaned by force-push), and 40.18% never-ingested. About 1 in 15 missing commits is a rewrite rather than a mirror gap. Force-pushing was observed in 25.47% of 78,125,788 repositories, with rewritten commits in 12.85%. The 40% never-ingested share is treated as an upper bound on the collection gap, with five reasons given for overcounting. History editing imposes a 10.82% corpus-wide undercount on commit-based productivity metrics.
AI.conclusion: The dataset enables honest mirror-completeness reporting, flags rewritten commits as duplicate patch sources for accurate contribution counting, and corrects a 10.82% undercount in commit-based productivity metrics caused by history editing. All artifacts are released as a self-contained replication package keyed to WoC V2604, including the force-push witness (166.7M events) and per-project rollups.

title: Scalable Differentially Private Data Compression via Diffusion and Stochastic Codes
comment: To appear in ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Probabilistic Inference & Generative Modeling
summary:
The ever-increasing collection of personal data has created mounting pressure to develop technologies that protect sensitive aspects of individual identity. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled framework with strong formal guarantees and has already achieved practical success. However, releasing high-dimensional data, such as images, has remained elusive: releasing uncompressed privatized data requires significant storage. At the same time, no effective data compression scheme exists that can compress high-resolution data with privacy guarantees.
  We address this challenge with DP-DiPP, a compression pipeline that combines stochastic codes with diffusion models. DP-DiPP is highly flexible: the practitioner has direct control over the compression rate-privacy-utility tradeoff. As the theoretical backbone, we extend the Poisson private representation (PPR) to encode the outputs of privacy mechanisms. We then combine it with DiffC, a diffusion-based lossy data compression method, to obtain a differentially private image compressor. Our experiments on privatized image classification on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that DP-DiPP significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving a 10-30 times better compression while retaining comparable privacy guarantees and utility.

AI.tldr: DP-DiPP is a compression pipeline that combines stochastic codes (Poisson private representations) with diffusion models (DiffC) to efficiently compress high-dimensional differentially private data, achieving 10-30x better compression than baselines on CIFAR-10 image classification while maintaining privacy and utility.
AI.motivation: Releasing high-dimensional differentially private data like images is impractical due to massive storage requirements of uncompressed privatized data, and no effective compression scheme exists that can compress such data while preserving formal privacy guarantees.
AI.method: The authors propose DP-DiPP, which extends the Poisson private representation (PPR) framework to encode outputs of privacy mechanisms, and combines it with DiffC, a diffusion-based lossy compression method. This yields a differentially private image compressor where practitioners can directly control the compression rate-privacy-utility tradeoff.
AI.result: On privatized image classification experiments using CIFAR-10, DP-DiPP significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving 10-30 times better compression while retaining comparable privacy guarantees and utility.
AI.conclusion: DP-DiPP provides a practical, flexible solution for compressing high-dimensional differentially private data, making DP-based release of image datasets more storage-efficient and feasible for real-world deployment.

title: TACG: Trajectory-Aware Commit Gating for Diffusion Language Model Decoding
summary: Diffusion language models (DLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked positions, exposing a trajectory of predictive distributions rather than a single instantaneous belief. Most existing decoders ignore this trajectory and commit tokens from the current snapshot alone, conflating confidence with commitment readiness: a transient top-1 peak under incomplete context can be locked in, while candidates with consistent cross-step support are delayed. We propose Trajectory-Aware Commit Gating (TACG), a training-free gate-level decoder that anchors token identities to the base posterior and uses trajectory-aware signals only to decide whether the current proposal is ready to commit. TACG combines Temporal Implicit Logits Guidance (TILG), which keeps an exponential moving average of past logits as a self-reference and contrasts the current logits against this reference in natural-parameter space, with a History Gate (HG) that enforces short-term proposal persistence before commitment. Together with a capped extra-promotion budget, these components yield a stability-constrained commit rule without auxiliary networks or extra forward passes.
