We evaluate TACG on LLaDA, Dream, and LLaDA2-Mini across code (HumanEval, MBPP) and math (GSM8K, MATH500) benchmarks; it typically improves or preserves accuracy while reducing denoising steps and increasing tokens per forward (TPF). The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Clarence-CV/TACG-DLLM.

AI.tldr: TACG is a training-free decoder for diffusion language models that uses trajectory-aware signals (exponential moving average of past logits and short-term proposal persistence) to decide when to commit tokens, improving accuracy while reducing denoising steps and increasing throughput.
AI.motivation: Existing DLLM decoders commit tokens based solely on the current predictive distribution, conflating confidence with commitment readiness. This causes premature locking of transient top-1 peaks under incomplete context while delaying candidates with consistent cross-step support. The authors aim to leverage the full denoising trajectory for better commit decisions without auxiliary networks or extra forward passes.
AI.method: TACG is a training-free gate-level decoder with two components: (1) Temporal Implicit Logits Guidance (TILG), which maintains an exponential moving average of past logits as a self-reference and contrasts current logits against this reference in natural-parameter space; (2) a History Gate (HG) that enforces short-term proposal persistence before allowing commitment. A capped extra-promotion budget constrains the commit rule.
AI.result: Evaluated on LLaDA, Dream, and LLaDA2-Mini across code benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP) and math benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500), TACG typically improves or preserves accuracy while reducing denoising steps and increasing tokens per forward (TPF).
AI.conclusion: TACG demonstrates that trajectory-aware commit gating can yield better efficiency-accuracy trade-offs in diffusion language models without requiring additional training, auxiliary networks, or extra forward passes.

title: Poisson-Gamma Modeling of Inter-Relational Dependencies in Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
comment: Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026). 20 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables
summary: Dynamic knowledge graphs are ubiquitous in today's AI applications, as we represent molecular structures, social relationships, and language information using these graph models. As knowledge graphs evolve over time and are often noisy and incomplete, modeling their temporal and relational dependencies becomes crucial for downstream tasks. To address these challenges, this paper proposes PGRE (Poisson-Gamma Relational Evolution), a probabilistic model for modeling inter-relational dependencies in dynamic knowledge graphs. PGRE represents multi-relational temporal links via a Poisson-Bernoulli formulation. It introduces Gamma-distributed latent variables to capture entity-factor associations and cross-relation dependencies mediated by shared latent communities. A Gamma Markov process further models the temporal evolution of these latent variables, enabling principled characterization of relational dynamics. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that PGRE achieves competitive performance in link prediction, particularly in sparse settings, while revealing meaningful relational evolution patterns in dynamic knowledge graphs.

AI.tldr: PGRE (Poisson-Gamma Relational Evolution) is a probabilistic model for dynamic knowledge graphs that uses a Poisson-Bernoulli formulation with Gamma-distributed latent variables and a Gamma Markov process to capture inter-relational dependencies and temporal evolution, achieving strong link prediction results especially in sparse settings.
AI.motivation: Dynamic knowledge graphs are prevalent in AI applications (molecular structures, social networks, language) but suffer from noise, incompleteness, and temporal evolution. Existing methods inadequately model inter-relational dependencies and temporal dynamics jointly, motivating a principled probabilistic approach.
AI.method: PGRE models multi-relational temporal links via a Poisson-Bernoulli formulation. It introduces Gamma-distributed latent variables to capture entity-factor associations and cross-relation dependencies through shared latent communities. A Gamma Markov process governs the temporal evolution of these latent variables, providing a principled framework for relational dynamics.
AI.result: PGRE achieves competitive link prediction performance on benchmark datasets, with particular strength in sparse data regimes. Beyond predictive accuracy, the model reveals interpretable relational evolution patterns in dynamic knowledge graphs.
AI.conclusion: PGRE offers a principled and interpretable probabilistic framework for dynamic knowledge graph modeling, effectively capturing both cross-relation dependencies and temporal dynamics, with demonstrated practical value in link prediction tasks.

title: Reflective Dialogue or Prompt Refinement? Effects of Tutor Scaffolding on Students' Independent LLM Use for Programming
comment: Best paper award, Published in AIED 2026: The 27th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Education
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) can provide personalized support in learning, several studies have raised concerns regarding their use in education. Importantly, learning depends on how students engage with LLMs. This study examined how two types of LLM-based tutors shape students' prompting practices, learning, and subsequent LLM-use: a Socratic-Guidance (SG) tutor, which structures interaction through dialogic questioning, and a Prompt-Refinement (PR) tutor that guides the formulation of effective prompts. We conducted a two-phase study in a graduate-level mobile robotics course: 66 students used either the SG or PR tutor during a 6-week intervention, followed by 52 students using an unconstrained LLM during a 3-week course project. Results show that while the SG- and PR tutors led to similar task performance and prompting patterns during guided use, they differ in learning outcomes and later LLM-use. SG-students, relative to PR-student, achieved higher learning gains in later sessions, and were more likely to adopt understanding-driven prompting strategies, which are predictive of higher understanding, when using an unconstrained LLM. Although learners perceived the SG tutor as less efficient, the findings suggest that Socratic guidance supports the development of students' capacity to learn with LLMs over time, highlighting its importance for LLM tutor design.

AI.tldr: A study comparing Socratic-Guidance versus Prompt-Refinement LLM tutors found that while both yielded similar immediate task performance, the Socratic approach produced higher learning gains and fostered understanding-driven prompting strategies when students later used unconstrained LLMs.
AI.motivation: Concerns about LLM use in education and the recognition that learning outcomes depend on how students engage with LLMs. There is a need to understand how different LLM-based tutor designs shape not only immediate performance but also students' long-term learning and their capacity to independently learn with LLMs.
AI.method: A two-phase study in a graduate-level mobile robotics course: (1) a 6-week intervention where 66 students used either a Socratic-Guidance (SG) tutor or a Prompt-Refinement (PR) tutor; (2) a subsequent 3-week course project where 52 students used an unconstrained LLM. The study compared task performance, prompting patterns, learning gains, and subsequent LLM-use behaviors between the two groups.
AI.result: Both tutors led to similar task performance and prompting patterns during guided use. However, SG students achieved higher learning gains in later sessions and were more likely to adopt understanding-driven prompting strategies when using the unconstrained LLM. These strategies were predictive of higher understanding. SG students perceived their tutor as less efficient than PR students.
AI.conclusion: Socratic guidance in LLM tutors supports the development of students' capacity to learn with LLMs over time, even if perceived as less efficient. This has important implications for LLM tutor design, suggesting that structuring interaction through dialogic questioning better prepares students for independent LLM use than simply teaching prompt formulation.

title: Rating the Pitch, Not the Product: User Evaluations of LLMs Reflect Expectations More Than Performance
summary: Imagine two users interact with the same LLM. One has been told it is the cutting-edge flagship model; the other, an older, weaker model. They walk away with markedly different ratings of its usefulness and intelligence, yet they used the same model. In a controlled study, 162 participants each used one of six LLMs from two families across three collaborative tasks, after first viewing a landing page that matched, overstated, or understated their model's true capability. This pre-interaction framing shifted user opinions and interaction behavior while task performance did not. Oversold users rated the model more favorably and used more directive prompting, while Undersold users wrote longer, more collaborative prompts. The quality of what users and the model produced together depended only on the model's true capability, not on what users were told. Participants' change in model impressions after use, measured across two impression measures, was not predicted by task performance ($β= -0.01$ and $0.11$, both n.s.), but by whether the model met users' expectations ($β= 0.47$ and $0.50$, both $p < .001$) and how confident they felt working with it ($β= 0.47$ and $0.36$, both $p < .001$). After interaction, users are still rating the pitch, not the product: user-elicited LLM evaluations, including the preference data driving public leaderboards, measure expectation management at least as much as the model itself.

AI.tldr: A controlled study (N=162) shows that pre-interaction framing of LLM capability significantly shapes user ratings and interaction style, even though actual task performance depends solely on the model's true capability. Post-use impressions are predicted by expectation fulfillment and user confidence, not by objective performance—suggesting LLM evaluations measure expectation management as much as model quality.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation paradigms, particularly those relying on user ratings and preference data (e.g., Chatbot Arena), assume users judge models based on their actual capabilities. This paper challenges that assumption by investigating whether pre-interaction expectations—shaped by marketing, branding, or leaderboard positioning—contaminate user evaluations, potentially making them measures of expectation management rather than genuine model quality.
AI.method: 162 participants were randomly assigned to use one of six LLMs (from two model families) across three collaborative tasks. Before interaction, each participant viewed a landing page that either matched, overstated, or undersold the model's true capability (framing manipulation). The study measured: (1) task performance, (2) user interaction behavior (prompt length, directiveness), (3) post-interaction ratings and impression change on two impression measures, and (4) whether impression change was predicted by task performance, expectation fulfillment, or user confidence—using regression analyses.
AI.result: Framing shifted user opinions and behavior: Oversold users rated models more favorably and used more directive prompting; Undersold users wrote longer, more collaborative prompts. However, task output quality depended only on true model capability, not framing. Impression change was not predicted by task performance (β = -0.01 and 0.11, n.s.) but was significantly predicted by expectation fulfillment (β = 0.47 and 0.50, p < .001) and user confidence (β = 0.47 and 0.36, p < .001).
AI.conclusion: User-elicited LLM evaluations are substantially driven by expectation management rather than objective model performance. This has serious implications for the validity of crowdsourced preference data and public leaderboards: they may reflect marketing and framing effects at least as much as the models themselves, undermining their utility as reliable measures of LLM capability.

title: Do All Visual Tokens Matter Equally? Object-Evidence Preserving Token Merging for Vision-Language Retrieval
summary: Multi-vector vision-language retrieval preserves fine-grained visual evidence through maximum-similarity late interaction, but dense image-side tokens make storage and scoring expensive. Existing token compression methods reduce this cost, yet they can remove or collapse object- and region-level evidence that future query tokens may need to select. We propose SaMer, an object-aware token merging framework that compresses image-side post-projector tokens into $K$ representative centroids while preserving the original late-interaction interface. SaMer uses object annotations only during training as a merge prior to discourage cross-instance mixing, requires no ground-truth bounding boxes or detectors at inference time, and adapts only the shared projection layer with frozen vision and language backbones. With $K=64$, SaMer removes more than 93% of image-side tokens and reduces ColPali storage by $16.09\times$, while improving R@1 on Flickr30K and MSCOCO. These gains arise because object-aware merging preserves query-selectable object evidence that pruning or feature-only pooling can remove or collapse. SaMer also outperforms compression baselines and shows stronger phrase-level grounding, suggesting that efficient multi-vector retrieval depends not only on reducing token count, but on preserving the evidence future query tokens need to select.

AI.tldr: SaMer is an object-aware token merging method for multi-vector vision-language retrieval that compresses image tokens into K centroids while preserving query-selectable object evidence. It reduces ColPali storage by 16.09× with K=64 while improving retrieval accuracy, demonstrating that preserving fine-grained evidence matters more than merely reducing token count.
AI.motivation: Existing token compression methods for multi-vector retrieval (e.g., pruning, feature-only pooling) can inadvertently remove or collapse object- and region-level visual evidence that downstream query tokens need to select during late interaction. The authors argue that efficient retrieval depends not just on reducing token count, but on preserving selectable evidence.
AI.method: SaMer (object-aware token merging) compresses post-projector image tokens into K representative centroids via a learned merging process. During training only, it uses object annotations as a merge prior to discourage cross-instance token mixing. At inference, no bounding boxes or detectors are needed. Only the shared projection layer is adapted; vision and language backbones remain frozen.
AI.result: With K=64, SaMer removes >93% of image-side tokens and reduces ColPali storage by 16.09×, while improving R@1 on Flickr30K and MSCOCO. It outperforms compression baselines and shows stronger phrase-level grounding.
AI.conclusion: Efficient multi-vector retrieval depends on preserving the object-level evidence that query tokens need to select, not merely on reducing token count. Object-aware merging achieves both high compression and improved accuracy by maintaining query-selectable visual evidence.

title: A Preliminary Study on Explaining Risk of Code Changes using LLM-Based Prediction Models
summary: Predictions by machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) models are often received skeptically unless they are paired with intelligible explanations. In the context of just-in-time defect prediction, highlighting small portions of a software change (diff) -- beyond rule-based lints -- where risk may be concentrated has not yet been extensively investigated. In this work, we leverage attention weights from an LLM-based Diff Risk Score (DRS) model to highlight parts of a diff that the model focuses on when predicting risk. We aggregate token-level attention into interpretable code units (lines, hunks, and files), and present the top-K units to developers as a lightweight form of guidance during code review. We evaluate our approach using expert-labeled changes that have caused real outages. Results show that the highlighted snippets cover expert-labeled outage-causing change lines 53.85% of the time when highlighting the top-2 hunks, while requiring developers to review 26.28% of the changed lines on average. Because attention is produced during standard model inference, the approach is scalable for large development workflows and can be surfaced in the code review UI with low additional latency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using attention weights from an LLM-based defect prediction model to highlight high-risk code regions in diffs for code review, achieving 53.85% coverage of outage-causing lines while requiring only 26.28% of changed lines to be reviewed.
AI.motivation: ML/AI predictions in defect prediction are often met with skepticism due to lack of explainability. While just-in-time defect prediction exists, there is limited work on fine-grained, attention-based highlighting of risky portions within software diffs beyond rule-based linters.
AI.method: The authors use attention weights from an LLM-based Diff Risk Score (DRS) model, aggregate token-level attention into interpretable code units (lines, hunks, files), and present the top-K units to developers as guidance during code review.
AI.result: Highlighting the top-2 hunks covers expert-labeled outage-causing change lines 53.85% of the time, while requiring developers to review only 26.28% of changed lines on average. The approach adds minimal latency since attention is a byproduct of standard inference.
AI.conclusion: Attention-based highlighting from LLM defect prediction models offers a scalable, low-latency, and interpretable method to guide code reviewers toward high-risk changes, balancing coverage with review effort.

title: Execution Divergence Graphs:Effective Discovery of Control-Flows from Execution Traces as Fuzzing Feedback
summary:
Fuzz testing is a popular approach to the security testing of proprietary software. Efficient testing strategies rely on execution feedback to guide the input generation process, particularly when the basic blocks in the binary can be directly observed and instrumented. Unfortunately, collecting such feedback is impossible in scenarios such as in-situ fuzzing of black-box devices and the fuzzing of obfuscated compiled binaries. In this work, we discuss approaches to guide the fuzzer using feedback derived from a control-flow-graph-like (CFG-like) structure constructed from runtime execution.
  We start by outlining a simple divergence-detection approach that identifies unique execution traces, and then present an improved approach based on an Execution Divergence Graph (EDG). We implement both approaches and demonstrate that they outperform a baseline blind fuzzer. In addition, we discuss particular challenges, such as repeated code execution in loops, and show that the EDG-based approach handles them effectively. We then demonstrate that our approach enables effective fuzzing of a number of obfuscated targets, and compare its performance in scenarios where static instrumentation is impossible. While we focus on a scenario in which full instruction traces are directly observable by the attacker, our scheme can also be applied in scenarios with other feedback channels, such as power consumption.

AI.tldr: This paper presents feedback-driven fuzzing approaches for scenarios where traditional binary instrumentation is impossible (e.g., black-box devices, obfuscated binaries). It proposes a divergence-detection method and an improved Execution Divergence Graph (EDG) approach that constructs CFG-like structures from runtime execution traces, outperforming blind fuzzing and enabling effective fuzzing of obfuscated targets.
AI.motivation: Traditional coverage-guided fuzzing relies on instrumenting basic blocks to collect execution feedback, which is infeasible in two critical scenarios: (1) in-situ fuzzing of black-box devices where the fuzzer cannot modify the target, and (2) fuzzing obfuscated compiled binaries where static instrumentation is blocked. The authors aim to bridge this gap by leveraging externally observable runtime execution traces as an alternative feedback mechanism.
AI.method: The authors propose two approaches: (1) A simple divergence-detection method that identifies unique execution traces by comparing observed instruction sequences. (2) An improved Execution Divergence Graph (EDG) approach that constructs a CFG-like structure from runtime execution traces, capturing control-flow divergences as new paths are discovered. The EDG handles challenges like repeated code in loops. Both methods use the derived structural feedback to guide the fuzzer's input generation. Full instruction traces are assumed observable, though the approach is extensible to side-channel feedback like power consumption.
AI.result: Both the divergence-detection and EDG-based approaches outperform a baseline blind fuzzer. The EDG-based method effectively handles loop-induced repeated code execution and enables successful fuzzing of multiple obfuscated targets. The approach proves viable in scenarios where static instrumentation is impossible.
AI.conclusion: Feedback derived from runtime execution traces — particularly via the EDG approach — provides an effective alternative to traditional instrumentation-based coverage feedback for guiding fuzzers. This enables security testing in previously inaccessible scenarios such as black-box devices and obfuscated binaries, with potential applicability to other side-channel feedback mechanisms.

title: From Gentlemen to Frontiermen: Masculine Formations in English-Language Fiction (1771--1930)
summary: Masculinity in nineteenth-century fiction is not a single ideal but a field of competing scripts. Drawing on 150 British and American canonical novels from the txtLAB Novel450 corpus, published between 1771 and 1930, this paper examines the changing relative prominence of competing models of masculine authority. To focus the analysis on masculine characterisation, the study extracts male-character-centred text windows by using coreference resolution to group names, nominal mentions, and pronouns into character-specific reference chains. It then fits an unsupervised structural topic model with publication year and author gender as topic-prevalence covariates. The model identifies six distinct masculine formations: aristocratic-chivalric, Christian manhood, gentlemanly respectability, country squire, professional-commercial, and imperial/adventure. Across the corpus, formations tied to inherited rank and sacred authority decline, while those organised around paid work and adventure rise. The largest increase occurs not in professional-commercial breadwinning but in imperial/adventure masculinity, particularly the frontier-wilderness register. The trajectory points to a reallocation from inherited and sacred status towards achieved, commercial, and expansionary forms of masculine authority. Adventurous and commercial formations are also more prevalent in novels by authors recorded as male. Because these formations emerge without a seeded vocabulary yet align with categories established in independent scholarship, the article offers a reproducible method for measuring the reorganisation of gendered authority across the long nineteenth century.

AI.tldr: Analyzing 150 British and American canonical novels (1771–1930), this study uses coreference resolution and unsupervised topic modeling to identify six competing models of masculinity. Results show a historical shift from inherited/sacred forms (aristocratic, Christian) toward achieved forms (professional-commercial, imperial/adventure), with the latter increasing most sharply.
AI.motivation: Masculinity in nineteenth-century fiction is not monolithic but comprises multiple competing scripts. The authors aim to quantify how the relative prominence of these masculine formations shifted over time, moving beyond qualitative literary analysis to a reproducible, data-driven measurement of gendered authority across the long nineteenth century.
AI.method: The study uses the txtLAB Novel450 corpus (150 canonical novels, 1771–1930). It applies coreference resolution to group male character mentions (names, nominals, pronouns) into character-specific reference chains, then extracts male-character-centred text windows. An unsupervised structural topic model (STM) is fitted with publication year and author gender as topic-prevalence covariates, identifying six masculine formations without seeded vocabulary.
AI.result: Six masculine formations emerge: (1) aristocratic-chivalric, (2) Christian manhood, (3) gentlemanly respectability, (4) country squire, (5) professional-commercial, and (6) imperial/adventure. Inherited rank and sacred authority decline across the corpus; formations tied to paid work and adventure rise. Imperial/adventure masculinity—especially the frontier-wilderness register—shows the largest increase. Adventurous and commercial formations are also more prevalent in novels by authors recorded as male.
AI.conclusion: The findings point to a historical reallocation of masculine authority from inherited and sacred status toward achieved, commercial, and expansionary forms. The unsupervised method reproduces categories from independent qualitative scholarship, validating a reproducible, computationally grounded approach for tracking the reorganisation of gendered authority in literary corpora.

title: Dynamic Regret for Non-Stationary Linear Bandits via Misspecification Reductions
summary: Many online decision-making problems involve both round-specific feasible actions and drifting reward models: eligible ad impressions, feasible prices, and available treatments can change over time, while user preferences, demand curves, and patient responses may evolve. Motivated by these applications, we study non-stationary linear bandits with round-specific feasible decision sets. Existing methods that obtain the optimal \(\widetilde O(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3})\) dependence, where \(P_T\) is the path length of the reward-parameter sequence, impose an orthogonal-structure assumption on round-specific decision sets, which can be restrictive in contextual applications. We address this gap through a unified misspecification-reduction viewpoint: after partitioning the horizon into blocks, we relate each block's dynamic regret to regret against a fixed-parameter linear bandit benchmark, with the within-block parameter drift entering as bounded misspecification. Restarting algorithms with misspecification-dependent regret guarantees then yields the optimal \(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3}\) dynamic-regret dependence for both linear bandits with general compact decision sets and \(K\)-armed contextual linear bandits.

AI.tldr: This paper studies non-stationary linear bandits with round-specific feasible decision sets. By partitioning the horizon into blocks and framing within-block parameter drift as bounded misspecification, the authors achieve the optimal dynamic-regret rate of \(\widetilde O(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3})\) without requiring restrictive orthogonal-structure assumptions on decision sets, applicable to both general compact linear bandits and K-armed contextual linear bandits.
AI.motivation: Many real-world sequential decision problems (e.g., online advertising, dynamic pricing, clinical trials) feature both time-varying feasible actions and evolving reward models. Existing methods achieving optimal dynamic regret for non-stationary linear bandits impose an orthogonal-structure assumption on round-specific decision sets, which is overly restrictive in contextual applications. The authors aim to remove this assumption while retaining the optimal \(\widetilde O(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3})\) dependence.
AI.method: The authors adopt a misspecification-reduction framework: (1) partition the time horizon into blocks; (2) relate each block's dynamic regret to regret against a fixed-parameter linear bandit benchmark, treating within-block parameter drift as bounded misspecification error; (3) deploy restarting bandit algorithms with misspecification-dependent regret guarantees (e.g., phased elimination or optimistic algorithms robust to misspecification). By carefully tuning block sizes based on the path length \(P_T\), they recover the optimal rate.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves the optimal dynamic-regret bound of \(\widetilde O(T^{2/3}P_T^{1/3})\) for two settings: (a) linear bandits with general compact decision sets, and (b) K-armed contextual linear bandits. This matches existing lower bounds while relaxing the restrictive orthogonal-structure assumption required by prior work.
AI.conclusion: The misspecification-reduction viewpoint provides a unified and flexible framework for non-stationary linear bandits, achieving optimal dynamic regret without structural constraints on feasible sets. The approach bridges non-stationarity and model misspecification, suggesting broader applicability to other non-stationary online learning settings.

title: When Aggregate Alignment Misleads: Auditing Policy Repair Without Per-State Expert Actions
summary: Agentic AI systems are increasingly used to edit, refine, and repair decision policies, but evaluating these edits is difficult when per-state expert action labels are unavailable. We study this problem in a hotel-pricing simulator where an agentic policy editor receives only region-level diagnostic feedback: summaries of how its price distribution differs from a benchmark policy across time, inventory, and market regions. The editor cannot observe benchmark actions, benchmark source code, reward numbers, or held-out outcomes, and may only propose constrained edits to a target-action table. On 5,000 held-out episodes, a multi-restart LLM editor reaches RevPAR 108.47 (95% CI 107.61 - 109.34), close to the benchmark policy's 108.75 (107.81 - 109.68), with paired gap (LLM minus benchmark) -0.276 and 95% CI [-0.692, 0.146]. A cheap diagnostic projection already recovers much of the revenue (107.90), so the LLM editor's distinctive gain is not raw revenue lift alone: it also reduces episode composition distance from 1.153 to 0.609. This is the strongest non-benchmark repair result. This profile is not explained by restart search alone: non-semantic proposers with up to 2,500 evaluations fall 8.77 - 14.57 RevPAR points short. Nor is it explained by plausible prompt format: a shuffled-diagnostic control breaks region-error correspondence and falls to RevPAR 94.30. The match is genuine but partial. A tree editor achieves stronger pooled alignment, 0.214 versus 0.266, and stronger reference-state D1, 0.328 versus 1.197, yet revenue falls to 98.91. These results show that agentic policy repair should be evaluated by whether diagnostic feedback becomes reliable closed-loop outcome, not by a single behavioral distance.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based agentic editor repairs a hotel-pricing decision policy using only region-level diagnostic summaries (no labels, rewards, or benchmark code). It nearly matches benchmark revenue while substantially reducing behavioral distance. Control experiments rule out restart search and prompting artifacts, showing genuine semantic repair. A tree editor achieves better alignment but worse revenue, suggesting repair should be judged by closed-loop outcomes, not distance metrics alone.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems are increasingly used to edit and repair decision policies, but evaluating these edits is challenging when per-state expert action labels are unavailable. The paper addresses the gap between having only coarse, region-level diagnostic feedback and achieving fine-grained policy repair, questioning whether such limited feedback is sufficient for reliable closed-loop behavioral improvement.
AI.method: A multi-restart LLM editor operates in a hotel-pricing simulator, receiving only region-level diagnostic feedback (summaries of price-distribution differences relative to a hidden benchmark, across time, inventory, and market regions). The editor proposes constrained edits to a target-action table without access to benchmark actions, source code, reward values, or held-out outcomes. Controls include: (1) non-semantic proposers with up to 2,500 evaluations to isolate restart-search effects, (2) a shuffled-diagnostic condition that breaks region-error correspondence, and (3) a tree editor for comparison. Evaluation uses 5,000 held-out episodes measuring RevPAR (revenue per available room) and behavioral distance metrics.
AI.result: The LLM editor achieves RevPAR 108.47 (95% CI 107.61–109.34) vs. benchmark 108.75 (107.81–109.68), with paired gap –0.276 (CI [–0.692, 0.146]). A cheap diagnostic projection alone recovers 107.90, so the LLM's distinctive gain is reducing episode composition distance from 1.153 to 0.609. Non-semantic proposers fall 8.77–14.57 RevPAR points short despite 2,500 evaluations. The shuffled-diagnostic control collapses to RevPAR 94.30, confirming semantic dependence. The tree editor achieves stronger pooled alignment (0.214 vs. 0.266) and reference-state D1 (0.328 vs. 1.197) but lower revenue (98.91).
AI.conclusion: Agentic policy repair should be evaluated by whether diagnostic feedback yields reliable closed-loop outcomes, not by a single behavioral distance metric. The LLM editor demonstrates that region-level diagnostics suffice for near-benchmark revenue recovery with meaningful behavioral alignment, but the trade-off between alignment and revenue (as seen with the tree editor) highlights that both dimensions matter and can diverge.

title: A Systematic Methodology for Evaluating Failure Independence in LLM-Generated Code
summary: N-Version Programming (NVP) improves software reliability by executing multiple independent implementations and combining outputs, but its adoption is limited by high cost and the assumption of failure independence, which empirical studies have challenged. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) reduce the cost of generating multiple implementations, shifting focus to whether their failures are independent. We propose the first systematic methodology to assess failure independence in LLM-generated code and apply it to 224 problems across twelve models, five languages, and three prompting strategies. We analyze both structural and behavioral diversity (i.e., whether implementations fail on the same test cases), complemented by N-version reliability analysis under majority voting and manual inspection of the generated code. Structural diversity analysis shows that implementations from the same model are highly similar, while different models produce more distinct solutions. The same trend appears in behavioral diversity, with implementations from different models showing higher diversity yet still failing on the same tests far more often than expected under independence. N-version reliability analysis reinforces this: three- and five-version ensembles realize only 0.43 and 0.44 of the reliability gain achievable under independence, dropping below 0.3 when ensembles are built from the same model. Manual fault analysis shows that even different failure patterns often share root causes. Overall, these results suggest LLM-generated solutions do not satisfy NVP's failure independence assumption, though heterogeneous models help partially. They also validate our methodology as a tool for systematically evaluating failure independence as models evolve.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a systematic methodology to evaluate failure independence in LLM-generated code for N-Version Programming. Testing 224 problems across 12 models, 5 languages, and 3 prompting strategies, it finds that LLM-generated implementations fail the independence assumption: same-model outputs are highly similar structurally and behaviorally, and even cross-model ensembles achieve less than half the theoretical reliability gain. Common root causes underlie many ostensibly different failure patterns.
AI.motivation: N-Version Programming has been limited by high implementation cost and questionable failure independence. LLMs now lower the cost of generating multiple implementations, but it remains unknown whether their failures satisfy the independence assumption critical to NVP's effectiveness.
AI.method: A systematic methodology combining: (1) structural diversity analysis (code similarity metrics), (2) behavioral diversity analysis (overlap in failing test cases), (3) N-version reliability modeling under majority voting to quantify realized vs. theoretical reliability gains, and (4) manual inspection of generated code to identify shared root causes. Applied to 224 problems across twelve LLMs, five programming languages, and three prompting strategies.
AI.result: Same-model implementations exhibit high structural similarity; cross-model implementations are more diverse but still fail together far more often than independence predicts. Three- and five-version ensembles achieve only 0.43 and 0.44 of the theoretical reliability gain, dropping below 0.3 for same-model ensembles. Manual analysis reveals shared root causes even when failure patterns appear distinct.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated code does not satisfy NVP's failure independence assumption. Heterogeneous models provide partial mitigation but insufficient to achieve theoretical reliability gains. The proposed methodology serves as a reusable framework for evaluating failure independence as models evolve.

title: LeanDY: Type-Based and Trace-Based Symbolic Protocol Verification in Lean
summary:
Computer-aided formal verification is a widely used approach for the symbolic analysis of cryptographic protocols. However, many modern protocols rely on features that remain challenging for existing techniques. In particular, reasoning about state, time-dependent behavior, inductively defined data structures, unbounded executions, and conditional secrecy requires a level of expressiveness that is difficult to reconcile with effective automation. As a result, protocol verification has largely followed two disjoint paths: fully automated methods with limited expressiveness, or interactive proofs in general-purpose theorem provers that offer flexibility but only limited, non-specialized automation.
  We present an orthogonal approach that bridges this gap by combining compositional type-based reasoning with trace-based reasoning, enabling modular verification of stateful and unbounded protocols. Guided by the language-and-automation co-design (LAC) principle, our approach delivers protocol-specific automation while retaining high expressiveness. We implement this framework as the LeanDY library for the Lean proof assistant, building on and extending the design of DY*, and combining protocol-specific automation with interactive proofs. Our framework supports, in a unified setting, a broad class of functional and security requirements, including secrecy and authentication for stateful protocols, as well as recursive conditional secrecy for protocols using XOR. We formalize SegWit-style blockchain primitives in LeanDY and demonstrate its expressiveness by carrying out an in-depth formalization of payment channels on top of this blockchain model, verifying punishment mechanisms and properties that depend on chain liveness.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LeanDY, a verification framework combining compositional type-based reasoning with trace-based reasoning to enable modular verification of stateful, unbounded cryptographic protocols with high expressiveness and protocol-specific automation in the Lean proof assistant.
AI.motivation: Existing cryptographic protocol verification suffers from a dichotomy: fully automated methods lack expressiveness for modern protocol features (state, time-dependence, inductive data structures, unbounded executions, conditional secrecy), while interactive theorem provers offer flexibility but limited specialized automation. The authors aim to bridge this gap.
AI.method: The authors apply the language-and-automation co-design (LAC) principle to develop LeanDY, a framework in the Lean proof assistant that extends DY*. It combines compositional type-based reasoning (for modularity) with trace-based reasoning (for stateful and unbounded protocols). The framework supports functional and security requirements including secrecy, authentication, recursive conditional secrecy (e.g., XOR-based protocols), and integrates interactive proofs with protocol-specific automation. A SegWit-style blockchain model is formalized as a case study.
AI.result: LeanDY provides a unified setting for verifying a broad class of properties. The authors demonstrate its expressiveness through an in-depth formalization of payment channels on a SegWit-style blockchain model, successfully verifying punishment mechanisms and properties dependent on chain liveness.
AI.conclusion: The LAC principle enables a practical middle ground between fully automated and fully interactive protocol verification. LeanDY shows that protocol-specific automation combined with interactive proofs can handle challenging features like state, unbounded executions, and conditional secrecy within a unified framework.

title: From Judgments to Issues: Structured Extraction of Legal Reasoning with Citation-Hallucination Control
summary: We present an automated pipeline that decomposes Italian tax-court judgments into individual legal issues and extracts, for each issue, a structured XML representation grounded in the IRAC framework and the legal syllogism. The pipeline targets a corpus of approximately $330{,}000$ first- and second-instance decisions of the Italian tax courts and is built around a capable yet cost-efficient general-purpose model (DeepSeek V3), a choice driven by the need to process several hundred thousand documents at a sustainable cost. To address the well-documented unreliability of large language models on legal citations, we couple the extraction step with an automatic hallucination-detection filter that compares the references produced by the model with those identified in the judgment text by a dedicated parser (Linkoln), normalised to standard identifiers (URN-NIR, ECLI, CELEX). We validate the pipeline on $50$ judgments annotated by two PhDs in tax law, computing inter-annotator agreement and LLM-vs-expert agreement on both issue extraction and legal citations, together with a stand-alone evaluation of the hallucination filter. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first issue-level, expert-validated structured extraction pipeline with hallucination control for Italian tax-court decisions, and it provides a concrete starting point for downstream applications such as issue-level retrieval, citation-network analysis, and the construction of large-scale datasets of legal reasoning.

AI.tldr: An automated pipeline using DeepSeek V3 decomposes Italian tax-court judgments into individual legal issues, producing structured XML representations guided by the IRAC framework and legal syllogism. A hallucination-detection filter cross-references model-generated citations with a dedicated parser (Linkoln) using standard identifiers (URN-NIR, ECLI, CELEX). Validated on 50 expert-annotated judgments, this is the first issue-level structured extraction pipeline with hallucination control for this domain.
AI.motivation: Processing approximately 330,000 Italian tax-court decisions at scale requires automated extraction of structured legal reasoning, but large language models are unreliable on legal citations. The work aims to produce a validated pipeline that balances cost-efficiency with accuracy, enabling downstream applications like issue-level retrieval and citation-network analysis.
AI.method: A pipeline built around DeepSeek V3 (chosen for cost-efficiency at scale) decomposes judgments into individual legal issues and outputs structured XML grounded in the IRAC framework and legal syllogism. An automatic hallucination-detection filter compares model-generated references against those identified by the Linkoln parser, normalized to standard identifiers (URN-NIR, ECLI, CELEX). Validation uses 50 judgments annotated by two tax-law PhDs, measuring inter-annotator agreement and LLM-vs-expert agreement on both issue extraction and citations, plus standalone filter evaluation.
AI.result: The pipeline was validated on 50 expert-annotated judgments, with agreement metrics computed for issue extraction and citation accuracy. The hallucination filter was evaluated independently. The system represents the first issue-level, expert-validated structured extraction pipeline with hallucination control for Italian tax-court decisions.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides a concrete foundation for downstream tasks such as issue-level retrieval, citation-network analysis, and large-scale legal reasoning dataset construction, demonstrating that cost-efficient general-purpose LLMs coupled with targeted hallucination filters can reliably structure legal judgments at scale.

title: Variable Bit-width Quantization: Learning Per-Group Precision for "Bigger-but-Smaller" Language Models
summary: Low-bit quantization shrinks language models but treats precision as a single global hyper-parameter: every weight uses the same bit-width. We introduce Variable Bit-width Quantization (VBQ), a training-time method in which each contiguous group of 64 weights learns its own resolution from {1,2,4,8} bits via a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, trained jointly by an alternating optimization that gives the precision logits a clean, task-aligned signal. VBQ discovers a consistent, strongly heterogeneous allocation within individual projection types, not merely across layers, impossible to express with per-layer methods: 69% of groups collapse to 1 bit, the LM head averages 1.09 bits, while the first MLP block keeps ~2.5 bits. This pattern is stable enough to freeze into a fixed recipe and reuse without further search. The recipe yields a "bigger-but-smaller" regime: a 131M model at 1.82 mean bits reaches perplexity 4.2 on TinyStories, beating a 55M FP16 model (PPL 4.4) at 3.8x less storage, and lets a 1.46B model on FineWeb-Edu match a 593M FP16 control at ~3.7x less storage with 2.5x more parameters. As quality-per-byte, VBQ is 3.9-8.4x more efficient than FP16. The recipe maps directly to packed low-bit storage, so it also accelerates inference: with custom fused dequantize-and-multiply kernels, memory-bandwidth-bound autoregressive decode is faster at equal output, and the speedup grows with scale (parity at 131M, 1.9x at 1.0B, 4.7x at 9B on Apple silicon). A distributional analysis (KL divergence and argmax-flip rate) reveals a striking mechanism: deeper layers progressively self-heal the quantization error injected by early layers. The win is a from-scratch, train-time phenomenon; scaling the search economically beyond 1.5B parameters remains open. VBQ reframes precision as a learnable, non-uniform resource and shows that spending a fixed bit budget unevenly beats spending it uniformly.

AI.tldr: VBQ learns per-group bit-widths (1,2,4,8 bits) during training via Gumbel-Softmax, discovering heterogeneous precision allocation that yields models with lower mean bit-width outperforming larger FP16 models on both perplexity and inference speed.
AI.motivation: Existing quantization methods treat bit-width as a uniform global hyperparameter, ignoring that different weights may benefit from different precision levels. This uniform allocation leaves significant efficiency gains on the table — the authors aim to discover whether non-uniform, learned precision assignment can yield better quality-per-bit tradeoffs.
AI.method: Variable Bit-width Quantization (VBQ): each contiguous group of 64 weights learns its own resolution from {1,2,4,8} bits using a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation over precision logits. Training uses alternating optimization: one step updates the precision logits, the next updates the weights, giving logits a clean task-aligned signal. After training, the discovered allocation pattern can be frozen into a fixed recipe and reused without further search. The recipe maps directly to packed low-bit storage, with custom fused dequantize-and-multiply kernels for accelerated inference.
AI.result: VBQ discovers strongly heterogeneous allocations within projection types: 69% of groups collapse to 1 bit, LM head averages 1.09 bits, while the first MLP block retains ~2.5 bits. A 131M model at 1.82 mean bits achieves PPL 4.2 on TinyStories (vs. 55M FP16 at PPL 4.4) with 3.8× less storage. A 1.46B model on FineWeb-Edu matches a 593M FP16 control at ~3.7× less storage with 2.5× more parameters. Quality-per-byte efficiency is 3.9–8.4× over FP16. Inference speedups: parity at 131M, 1.9× at 1.0B, 4.7× at 9B (Apple silicon). Distributional analysis reveals deeper layers progressively self-heal quantization error from early layers.
AI.conclusion: VBQ reframes precision as a learnable, non-uniform resource, demonstrating that spending a fixed bit budget unevenly beats uniform allocation. The approach produces a "bigger-but-smaller" regime where models with more parameters at lower mean bit-width outperform smaller FP16 counterparts. Scaling the search beyond 1.5B parameters remains an open challenge.

title: From Mobile Data to Business Insights: An End-to-End Analytics Framework for Large-Scale Urban Mobility Analysis and Decision Support
summary: Real time location data derived from mobile applications is a powerful tool for addressing various urban challenges, including tourism planning, parking management, bus route optimization, and resource allocation. Besides, it offers invaluable insights for shaping strategic decisions in commercial domains such as location based services, market share analysis, and behavioral profiling. In this expansive study, we aim to address all of the aforementioned challenges by investigating the behaviors and patterns of smartphone users within urban environments, particularly in the domains of tourism, transportation, and retail. Our approach encompasses the development of a sophisticated data platform from inception to implementation, which includes the formulation of use cases, architectural design, and implementation of modules. We employ state of the art techniques and technologies, including data anonymization, ETL pipelines, and utilizing Google BigQuery and Vertex AI for data processing and machine learning model development. A modular architecture based on reusable analytical building blocks was developed to generate data products that support multiple stakeholder driven use cases. Additionally, we apply interactive data visualization techniques via Power BI to facilitate the effective interpretation of analytical findings by stakeholders. The developed models address a wide range of mobility analytics tasks, including mobility profiling, frequent trajectory mining, area of influence analysis, traffic anomaly detection, and origin destination pattern analysis. The results demonstrate the framework's ability to capture user mobility dynamics at fine spatial and temporal resolutions, providing actionable insights for urban planning and strategic business decision making.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive study developing a modular data platform that processes real-time mobile location data to generate mobility analytics (trajectory mining, anomaly detection, OD patterns) for urban planning and commercial use cases, leveraging Google BigQuery, Vertex AI, and Power BI.
AI.motivation: Real-time mobile location data holds immense potential for solving urban challenges (tourism planning, parking, bus routing, resource allocation) and enabling commercial applications (location-based services, market share analysis, behavioral profiling), yet a unified platform approach addressing multiple stakeholder needs simultaneously is lacking.
AI.method: The authors built an end-to-end data platform from scratch, encompassing use case formulation, architectural design, and module implementation. Key techniques include data anonymization, ETL pipelines, Google BigQuery for data processing, Vertex AI for ML model development, a modular architecture of reusable analytical building blocks, and Power BI for interactive visualization. Analytical tasks include mobility profiling, frequent trajectory mining, area of influence analysis, traffic anomaly detection, and origin-destination pattern analysis.
AI.result: The framework successfully captures user mobility dynamics at fine spatial and temporal resolutions, producing actionable insights for both urban planning and strategic business decision-making across multiple stakeholder-driven use cases.
AI.conclusion: A modular, reusable analytical platform built on modern cloud infrastructure (BigQuery, Vertex AI) and BI tools (Power BI) can effectively transform raw mobile location data into diverse mobility analytics products, serving multiple urban and commercial use cases simultaneously.

title: EvoOtter: Evolutionary Reproduction Test Generator
summary: Before fixing an issue, it is useful to first reproduce it by generating a bug reproduction test (BRT). However, generating a BRT is itself a challenging task, because issue descriptions tend to be informal, making it difficult to determine whether a candidate BRT indeed fails for the reason in the issue. Prior work has attempted to tackle this problem via inference scaling, using large language models to generate many BRTs and patches, then using execution feedback to select and improve them. Unfortunately, this is expensive and the feedback is unreliable. This paper explores evolutionary programming for BRT generation to sharpen the feedback, while enhancing evolutionary programming to keep costs in check. Our new approach, EvoOtter, controls test execution costs via successive halving. Furthermore, it controls LLM costs via batched crossover for an entire generation in a single LLM call, as well as via rule-based code mutations, with a new fitness score tailored for BRTs. As a result, EvoOtter generates state-of-the-art quality BRTs at the fraction of the cost of prior inference-scaling approaches to this problem. More broadly, this paper points at how to efficiently and effectively combine evolutionary programming with large language models for software engineering.

AI.tldr: EvoOtter combines evolutionary programming with LLMs to generate bug reproduction tests (BRTs) efficiently. It uses successive halving to control execution costs, batched crossover to reduce LLM API calls, rule-based mutations, and a specialized fitness score, achieving state-of-the-art BRT quality at a fraction of the cost of prior inference-scaling approaches.
AI.motivation: Generating bug reproduction tests (BRTs) from informal issue descriptions is challenging. Prior inference-scaling approaches using LLMs are expensive and rely on unreliable execution feedback. There is a need for sharper, more cost-effective feedback mechanisms for BRT generation.
AI.method: EvoOtter uses evolutionary programming with three key cost-control mechanisms: (1) successive halving to prune unpromising candidates early and reduce test execution costs; (2) batched crossover, which processes an entire generation in a single LLM call; (3) rule-based code mutations as a cheaper alternative to LLM-based mutation. A novel fitness score tailored specifically for BRT quality guides selection.
AI.result: EvoOtter achieves state-of-the-art quality in BRT generation while operating at a fraction of the cost of prior inference-scaling methods.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary programming can be effectively combined with LLMs for software engineering tasks, yielding both high quality and cost efficiency. EvoOtter demonstrates a principled way to sharpen feedback and control costs in LLM-based code generation pipelines.

title: Securing Multi-Tool AI Agent Chains With Dynamic, Real-Time Compositional Policies
summary: Modern AI agent implementations such as frontier coding agents chain multiple tools at runtime that create a security surface that per-tool guardrails are unable to address, as individually permitted tools can violate organizational policies when composed. We propose the Dynamic Security Control Compositor (DSCC), a two-phase approach to compositional security for multi-tool agent chains. In Phase 1, at session checkout, a Most Restrictive Set (MRS) algorithm composes per-tool security policies into a single effective policy with a formal monotonicity invariant that extending a chain can only tighten the result, blocking incompatible combinations before any tool executes. Outputs of any tool call propagate their classification constraints into a session-level taint state, so subsequent invocations must satisfy the most restrictive constraints seen so far. In Phase 2, at runtime, the system tracks the sensitivity of data the agent touches through a monotonic taint state and revokes the session if the accumulated exposure would make a subsequent tool call a policy violation. Together, these phases provide defense in depth, where static composition prevents unsafe chains from starting, and runtime taint tracking catches violations that emerge from the specific data used. We provide a reference implementation on 32 tools governed by 16 NIST SP 800-53 aligned policies and evaluate it under two composition modes. In the default clearance mode, permitted combinations are partitioned into classification-level clusters, blocking 79.2% of policy pairs and 95.5% of triples. The alternative taint mode admits mixed-classification chains within the exfiltration boundary, blocking 42.5% and 60.5% respectively. We discuss the governance implications for organizations deploying multi-tool agents, including the utility-security tradeoff and the changes needed to operationalize chain-aware policies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Dynamic Security Control Compositor (DSCC), a two-phase framework for compositional security in multi-tool AI agent chains. Phase 1 statically composes per-tool policies using a Most Restrictive Set algorithm to block unsafe chains before execution. Phase 2 dynamically tracks data sensitivity via monotonic taint propagation to revoke sessions that would violate accumulated exposure constraints. Evaluated on 32 tools with 16 NIST SP 800-53 policies, the approach blocks 79.2% of policy pairs and 95.5% of triples in clearance mode.
AI.motivation: Modern AI agents chain multiple tools at runtime, creating a security vulnerability where individually permitted tools can violate organizational policies when composed together. Per-tool guardrails are insufficient because they cannot reason about compositional risks across tool sequences — a well-known limitation analogous to the confused deputy problem in operating system security.
AI.method: The DSCC uses a two-phase approach. Phase 1 (session checkout): a Most Restrictive Set (MRS) algorithm composes per-tool security policies into a single effective policy with a formal monotonicity invariant — extending a chain only tightens the result, blocking incompatible combinations pre-execution. Tool output classification constraints propagate into session-level taint state. Phase 2 (runtime): monotonic taint tracking monitors data sensitivity the agent touches; the session is revoked if accumulated exposure would make a subsequent tool call a policy violation. This provides defense-in-depth: static composition prevents unsafe chains from starting, runtime taint catches data-dependent violations.
AI.result: Evaluated on 32 tools governed by 16 NIST SP 800-53 aligned policies under two modes: (1) Default clearance mode partitions permitted combinations into classification-level clusters, blocking 79.2% of policy pairs and 95.5% of triples. (2) Alternative taint mode admits mixed-classification chains within the exfiltration boundary, blocking 42.5% of pairs and 60.5% of triples.
AI.conclusion: The DSCC provides effective defense-in-depth for multi-tool agent security through complementary static and dynamic enforcement. The authors discuss governance implications including the utility-security tradeoff and operational changes needed for chain-aware policies, highlighting that organizations must balance agent capability against compositional security risk.

title: Efficient Decentralized Multi-task Dataset Valuation via Model Merging
summary: Accurate and efficient dataset valuation is essential for enabling fair and transparent data marketplaces, especially when multiple contributors provide data for training multi-task models. Most existing valuation methods, however, are limited to single-task settings, overlooking scenarios where a buyer aims to optimize performance across multiple downstream tasks. Moreover, traditional valuation approaches, such as Shapley-based or retraining-based methods, are computationally expensive and poorly suited for decentralized environments without a trusted central coordinator and with strict privacy constraints. We propose DMVM (Decentralized Multi-task Valuation via Model Merging), a novel framework that bypasses retraining and data sharing by leveraging task arithmetic to infer dataset contributions directly from model combinations. Instead of retraining or sharing raw data, DMVM quantifies how models trained on different datasets combine in parameter space to infer each dataset's marginal utility across multiple tasks. This formulation yields a valuation process that is scalable, computationally efficient, and explicitly aligned with multi-task generalization behavior. To support decentralized deployment, we introduce a secure aggregation protocol that enables collaborative valuation without revealing individual model parameters or private data. We also provide theoretical error bounds characterizing the approximation quality of DMVM and validate our framework through comprehensive experiments on computer vision and natural language processing tasks.

AI.tldr: DMVM is a decentralized framework for multi-task dataset valuation that uses model merging (task arithmetic) to infer dataset contributions from parameter-space combinations, avoiding costly retraining and data sharing while preserving privacy via secure aggregation.
AI.motivation: Existing dataset valuation methods are limited to single-task settings and rely on computationally expensive Shapley-based or retraining-based approaches. They also require trusted central coordinators and cannot accommodate strict privacy constraints. No existing method addresses multi-task valuation in decentralized environments.
AI.method: DMVM leverages task arithmetic to quantify how models trained on different datasets combine in parameter space, directly inferring each dataset's marginal utility across multiple tasks without retraining or data sharing. A secure aggregation protocol enables decentralized, privacy-preserving collaborative valuation. Theoretical error bounds are derived to characterize approximation quality.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments on computer vision and NLP tasks validate DMVM's effectiveness. The framework achieves scalable, computationally efficient valuation explicitly aligned with multi-task generalization behavior, while the secure aggregation protocol maintains privacy of individual model parameters and data.
AI.conclusion: DMVM offers a practical, scalable solution for fair and transparent multi-task data marketplaces in decentralized settings, overcoming key limitations of single-task, retraining-dependent, and centralized valuation methods.

title: Bootstrap Flow-Map Tree Sampling Enables Online Feedback Driven Search
summary: In many scientific and engineering domains, maximizing discovery within a limited sampling budget demands strategic, observation-guided exploration. While generative models have enabled training-free reward alignment, current methods typically excel in local searches within narrow regions of the underlying distribution. These approaches struggle when preferences are unknown a priori and only revealed through sequential feedback-a scenario demanding broad exploration to uncover high-utility regions. To address this, we introduce Bootstrap Flow-Map-Tree (a.k.a BFMT), a novel computationally efficient sampling framework designed for history-aware global search and alignment under sampling budget constraints. BFMT enables full tree-path construction from any tree depth using a single function evaluation, drastically reducing computational overhead while providing critical foresight for sequential sampling. By enabling dynamic transition time steps scheduling, BFMT efficiently allocates its sampling budget, smoothly transitioning from broad global exploration to fine-grained local refinement of high-utility modes discovered through exploration. Extensive experiments and ablations across diverse search and alignment tasks demonstrate that BFMT substantially outperforms baseline approaches.

AI.tldr: BFMT introduces a tree-structured sampling framework that uses bootstrap flow-map trees for efficient history-aware global exploration and reward alignment under budget constraints, outperforming existing methods by dynamically transitioning from exploration to refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing generative model-based reward alignment methods excel at local search but fail when preferences are unknown a priori and must be discovered through sequential feedback — a setting requiring broad global exploration to identify high-utility regions before refinement.
AI.method: BFMT constructs a flow-map tree that enables full tree-path construction from any depth using single function evaluations, drastically reducing computation. It employs dynamic transition time-step scheduling to allocate the sampling budget efficiently, smoothly shifting from global exploration to local refinement of discovered high-utility modes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and ablations across diverse search and alignment tasks demonstrate that BFMT substantially outperforms baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: BFMT provides an effective, computationally efficient solution for sequential sampling under budget constraints, enabling robust global search and alignment by dynamically balancing exploration and exploitation through its bootstrap flow-map-tree architecture.
